text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Carlos Giménez of Florida has invited Elon Musk to relocate Tesla’s corporate headquarters from Texas to Florida, citing the state’s business environment and the recent Democratic victories in Texas during the November 2026 midterm elections.

In a letter to Musk, Giménez urged the billionaire to consider moving Tesla’s headquarters and expanding its operations to Florida, arguing that the state offers lower taxes, business-friendly regulations and greater economic freedom.

The invitation comes after Democrats secured major victories in Texas, ending decades of Republican dominance in several key statewide contests. Florida Republicans, meanwhile, retained control of all statewide offices, prompting Giménez to present the state as an alternative destination for Musk’s businesses.

Giménez cites Texas political shift

“With the recent election of self-described Democratic Socialists to positions of power in Texas, I share your concerns about excessive government interference, politically motivated investigations, and policies that punish success,” Giménez wrote in his letter.

READ: SpaceX, Tesla to spend $16.8 billion on Terafab plant in Texas (August 6, 2026)

“No company should face political retaliation for creating jobs, investing in American innovation, and contributing to our nation’s prosperity,” he added.

Giménez argued that Florida offers a different regulatory and political environment, with lower taxes and policies designed to attract businesses and investment.

“Florida offers a fundamentally different approach. Our state has championed lower taxes, responsible regulation, and the freedom to innovate without unnecessary government intrusion,” he wrote.

Tesla’s Texas presence remains substantial

Tesla moved its corporate headquarters from California to Austin, Texas, in 2021. The company operates its Gigafactory in Austin, where it manufactures the Model Y and Cybertruck. Musk’s wider Texas business footprint also includes SpaceX facilities, battery operations and other technology projects.

The political shift has raised questions about the future regulatory environment for Musk’s companies. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson have indicated plans for greater scrutiny of certain business arrangements involving Musk’s companies, including state incentives, environmental concerns and public land use.

However, Hinojosa has said she remains open to working with Musk and his companies under conditions that protect Texans’ interests.

Florida renews efforts to attract Musk

Giménez, a former Miami-Dade County mayor, highlighted South Florida’s infrastructure, technology sector and workforce as advantages for Tesla.

READ: Tesla ends Cybertruck production as Musk bets on Robotaxis (November 9, 2026)

The congressman has previously tried to attract Musk’s businesses to Florida. In December 2022, he invited Musk to move X’s headquarters from San Francisco to Miami-Dade County.

title: Editorial: Honda withdraws from withering US market for EVs | Opinion | herald-dispatch.com
description: Former President Joe Biden wanted to lead America into a new age where battery-powered vehicles had replaced those using fossil fuels and internal combustion engines. His problem was that not enough people were willing to follow him and he didn’t get a second term to finish his plan.
text:
Are Americans supposed to be pleased that President Donald Trump is blaming Ukra…

For several months I’ve asked the question: What would happen in November, the f…



A Honda logo is shown at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit on Jan. 14, 2019.

Former President Joe Biden wanted to lead America into a new age where battery-powered vehicles had replaced those using fossil fuels and internal combustion engines. His problem was that not enough people were willing to follow him and he didn’t get a second term to finish his plan.

Auto makers invested heavily in electric vehicle production but eventually learned that consumers were more interested in gasoline-electric hybrids.

On Monday, Nov. 9, American Honda Motor Co. announced it will build a new assembly plant near its existing facility at Marysville, Ohio, northwest of Columbus. The total investment in the plant and in retooling other Honda manufacturing facilities in George and Alabama to support hybrid production in Ohio will be about $3 billion, Honda said. The expansion will create more than 2,000 new American jobs and increase Honda’s auto production capacity to about 1.3 million vehicles a year, Honda said.

“The new Ohio Honda plant will be one of the most advanced in the world when it comes online in 2029 with leading-edge automation, data-driven technologies and flexible production systems to improve efficiency, quality and competitiveness,” Honda said in its official announcement. “While supporting growing demand for hybrid and gasoline-powered vehicles, the plant will provide Honda with the flexibility to adapt production as customer demand, market conditions and electrification trends evolve.”

That’s quite a turnaround from Honda’s former strategy of focusing on EVs. In March, Honda Motor Co. Ltd. said it had canceled the development and market launch of three EV models that had been planned for production in North America. The decision was made as part of the reassessment of the company’s automobile electrification strategy due to various factors including recent changes in the business environment, the company said. American tariff policy and changing consumer tastes in both the United States and China played a role in the decision, Honda said.

Honda had overestimated demand for EVs and suffered an operating loss in the fiscal year that ended March 31.

Last month, the federal Energy Information Administration said 23% of new light-duty vehicles sold in the United States in the third quarter of this year were hybrid electric, battery electric, or plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, down slightly from 24% the third quarter of last year. Sales growth of hybrids has slowed as the average sale price for a new vehicle passed $50,000, according to the EIA. Meanwhile, battery vehicle sales were only 6% of new light-duty vehicle sales, down from 10% in the third quarter of last year.

Honda is not the first major automaker to backtrack on a commitment to build electric vehicles. GM did the same thing about a year ago, and that strategic decision cost the company an estimated $1.6 billion. Ford jumped off the EV train in 2024.

EVs are great for short trips in good weather, but they have their drawbacks. Range can be limited, especially if the vehicle has a heavy load or is towing a trailer. Charging takes more time than filling a gas tank. As EV owners in Chicago discovered in 2024, EVs can be slow or impossible to charge in arctic cold weather. Also, federal tax credits for buying EVs expired in September 2025.

EVs have their place, but with existing technology they are not always the best option for most buyers. Hybrids fill the gap between batteries and internal combustion.

People who supported conversion to electric vehicles often pointed to their environmental benefits in slowing climate change. Since President Donald Trump won his second term, climate change — that formerly existential threat to human existence — has fallen far down on the list of priorities for public discussion. Likewise, companies seldom talk about their ESG — environment, social, governance — efforts now compared to a few years ago.

Why climate change and ESG are almost forgotten now can be debated, but it shows how large companies are just as likely to jump on trends as everyday folks are and how quickly priorities can change before anyone notices.

DENVER, CO – November 11, 2026 – PRESSADVANTAGE –

Climate Alignment is scheduling pre-winter site assessments of rooftop units, furnaces, boilers and split systems for restaurants, breweries, medical facilities and other commercial operators ahead of the heating season, according to the company. Assessments are requested through the company’s website or by phone.

Each assessment follows the scope of the company’s commercial heating repair work, according to its service page. On rooftop units, technicians check heat exchangers, economizers, reversing valves and refrigerant circuits, and on boilers the work includes gas pressure calibration, heat exchanger inspection and a carbon monoxide risk assessment. For food service and cold storage sites, the visit can also cover the heating circuits on walk-in coolers and freezers, including anti-sweat heaters and defrost systems, along with pump and loop diagnostics on glycol chiller systems. The page describes heating failures in medical facilities, breweries and food service as compliance and safety issues, and it frames walk-in heating and defrost failures as a risk to the cold chain.

Elevation is a recurring factor in the work. The company’s service page states that air at 5,280 feet is about 18% less dense than at sea level and that factory settings are engineered for sea level. Repairs include high-altitude orifice kit adjustments and calibration of superheat, subcooling, gas pressure and pressure controls, and the page cites rapid freeze and thaw cycles as a source of stress on condenser coils. The company says it calibrates every repair to high-altitude operating parameters.

“Heating problems often surface on the first cold night of the season. An inspection before winter gives an operator time to plan a repair instead of reacting to a failure,” said Nathan Boeke, owner of Climate Alignment.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that heating systems, water heaters and other gas-, oil- or coal-burning appliances be serviced by a qualified technician every year. The agency reports that more than 400 Americans die each year from unintentional carbon monoxide poisoning not linked to fires and that more than 14,000 are hospitalized.

The company handles commercial systems only and does not service residential split systems, according to its heating page. Scheduled appointments are typically confirmed within one business day, and emergency calls are dispatched 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Office hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Climate Alignment has worked on commercial heating, ventilation, air conditioning and refrigeration systems for more than 12 years, according to the company, which describes itself as a family-owned, licensed and insured contractor. Its technicians hold EPA Section 608 certification, and the company states that its work follows City of Denver mechanical codes and EPA refrigerant handling regulations. Under Section 608 of the Clean Air Act, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency requires technicians who maintain, service, repair or dispose of equipment that could release refrigerants into the atmosphere to be certified.

Beyond heating, the company installs, maintains and repairs walk-in coolers and freezers, reach-in units, display cases, ice machines, remote systems, glycol chillers for breweries and rack systems. Its maintenance programs include calibration, scale prevention and economizer tuning, and the company assists customers with Xcel Energy rebate documentation for qualifying motor and control upgrades, including anti-sweat heater controls, according to its website.

“Many of the same sites run refrigeration and heating side by side. Checking both on one visit lets a kitchen or brewery go into winter with a clear picture of its equipment,” Boeke said.

Operators can request an assessment through the site assessment form on the company’s website. Service details are listed on the Google Business Profile for Climate Alignment.

Information is believed accurate at the time of publication. Contact Climate Alignment directly for current details.

The company installs, maintains and repairs heating systems, rooftop units, walk-in coolers and freezers, ice machines and rack systems for restaurants, breweries, grocery retailers, laboratories and multi-site operators. text:
The California Democrat and current ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee is suspicious of all the “now or never.”

The most important voice in Congress criticizing the Senate’s bipartisan energy permitting deal is Representative Jared Huffman.

A California Democrat who previously worked in environmental legal advocacy, Huffman has long been among the most impassioned lawmakers on climate issues. Under the first Trump administration, his voice was often the loudest calling for oversight and accountability on energy and climate policy. Under the second Trump administration, he has been a spirited defender of offshore wind.

Should Democrats take control of the U.S. House of Representatives in the coming midterm elections, as expected, then Huffman is first in line to become chair of the lower chamber’s Natural Resources Committee. This makes him one of the few people able to armchair quarterback permitting talks in Congress right now.

The proposed legislation currently on the table, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would fundamentally reshape how federal project permitting happens. It would constrain National Environmental Policy Act reviews. It would radically alter transmission approvals. It would let companies sue the government for damages if they can show that an agency was unduly discriminating against them based on fuel type. It would limit state and tribal authority to object against projects under the Clean Water Act. And it would make this whole process more transparent by instituting digital reporting requirements.

Huffman thinks it also gives too much benefit to oil and gas interests, and is an unnecessary capitulation to fossil-friendly Republicans who will likely lose power in this November’s midterm elections, anyway. He wants Democratic lawmakers to wait until after election day to consider what they do with the bill.

I reported on Congress for years and often spoke with Huffman in the Capitol hallways; he knew me on a first-name basis. So last week, when a friend pointed me to a tweet of his criticizing the Senate bill by quoting my writing, I took note. His issue concerned the discrimination provision in the bill, which sets a rolling five-year average for approvals as a baseline for what constitutes normal regulatory behavior. Successful lawsuits under this provision would be paid out of the Judgment Fund, a Justice Department account Trump has used for his offshore wind developer buyouts.

This part of the bill, Huffman wrote, “might pay some clean energy developers money from the judgment fund when they are screwed, but nothing to actually approve their projects. This is potentially a replay of the fake settlements that have bought out offshore wind projects,” he added.

I reached out to Huffman’s team and asked to talk about what he meant by that. What followed was a 20-plus-minute back-and-forth about the future of permitting reform in the U.S. and what may happen after a midterm election defined by public anger over a rush to build another type of large-scale infrastructure: data centers.

The following transcript has been lightly edited for clarity.

So let’s start with your tweet. You quoted a portion of our story about BAAJA that I had written about the “permitting certainty” provisions in the bill, and specifically the fact that developers could be awarded damages under the bill for discriminatory treatment. Could you elaborate on your point?

I don’t want to get too deep into the weeds, but this is the big thing being offered as an end to the war on clean energy, which was always the threshold matter before you get to a bipartisan permitting deal.

It is built on this framework, basically, of cutting checks from the judgment fund. And I believe that requires some close scrutiny and consideration because we have seen this gamed already to the tune of $4 billion to buy out offshore wind developers.

Well I know this can get quite technical, but the underlying point you were making was, this may not be as helpful as people think. I guess I was just wondering if you can you walk me through —

It depends what you want.

If you’re a clean energy developer and you’re worried about your shareholders and your balance sheet, this gives you at least some money when you get screwed. And it may come with some strings attached, like you have to turn around and invest it in [liquified natural gas]. That’s been the playbook from the Trump administration.

If you’re a clean energy CEO — some of them, at least — that helps you mitigate risk. That’s probably better than nothing and will be attractive to some people. But if you care about climate policy [and] whether this is a meaningful assurance of permitting certainty to renewables, I think there’s a lot more to question here.

You also said in your tweet that there’s nothing in the bill to get projects approved. Can you speak to that? Because those who negotiated it clearly say otherwise.

Well, there are shot clocks and all sorts of other things that are designed to speed things up. There’s also broad categories of exemptions — categorical exemptions and other things like that, most of which will benefit fossil fuel projects.

I have no doubt there’s going to be permitting acceleration and certainty for fossil fuel projects. You also have this five-year baseline mechanism being codified here that will further cement a high level of fossil fuel projects for many years to come, and will really operate as a ceiling.

By: Jael Holzman

text:
AURORA, CO – November 11, 2026 – PRESSADVANTAGE –

A+ Hybrid Batteries, a mobile hybrid battery replacement company serving Colorado, Georgia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Virginia, is advising owners of older hybrids to consider replacing a failing battery before replacing the vehicle, one year after the federal electric vehicle tax credit ended. The company said more of its customers are choosing to keep and repair the hybrid they already own rather than trade it in.

NPR reported on September 30, 2026, that the federal tax credit of up to $7,500 for new electric vehicles ended on September 30, 2025, after Congress repealed it as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. According to Edmunds data cited in the report, electric vehicles fell from 11.4 percent of new car sales in September 2025 to 5.8 percent a month later and have held between 5 and 6 percent of sales through 2026. Over the same period, hybrid sales rose almost 27 percent, according to Edmunds.

The NPR report also noted that the average electric vehicle transaction price was over $54,000 in August 2026, compared with an average of just under $50,000 for gas-powered vehicles, according to Cox Automotive. Ivan Drury, director of insights at Edmunds, told NPR that many consumers set aside their electric vehicle plans or bought a hybrid instead, most likely because of the lower price point.

For drivers who already own a hybrid, the question is often what to do when the original battery wears out. Kelley Blue Book estimates that replacing a failed hybrid battery can cost between $2,000 and $8,000 depending on make and model, and says today’s hybrid batteries typically last at least 10 years, or between 100,000 and 150,000 miles. Many early Toyota Prius and Camry Hybrid models may now be past that range while the rest of the vehicle remains in regular use.

A+ Hybrid Batteries said that for owners weighing a new vehicle purchase, a battery replacement on a hybrid that is otherwise in good condition can be a lower-cost way to keep a dependable car on the road. The company services Toyota Prius models from 2001 through 2019, both generations of the Camry Hybrid built from 2007 through 2016, and hybrids from Honda, Ford, Hyundai, Kia, Lexus, Nissan, and Subaru. Technicians travel to a customer’s home, office, or another location, run a module-by-module diagnostic, and replace the battery on-site when it is needed, typically within 30 to 45 minutes.

The company publishes its pricing for Toyota battery replacement on its website. Listed prices start at $950 for a reconditioned battery with a six-month warranty, $1,180 for a reconditioned battery with a three-year warranty, and $2,450 for a new OEM-grade battery with a five-year warranty, with mobile service and installation included. Final cost depends on the model year and the battery selected, and customers pay after the work is complete.

A+ Hybrid Batteries said a diagnostic before any replacement is an important step for owners deciding whether to keep a vehicle. Some drops in fuel economy or power may come from other parts of the hybrid system rather than the battery itself, and the company said it tells customers when the battery is not the cause before any work is done.

“A year ago, a lot of the people who called us assumed a failing hybrid battery meant it was time for a new car. Now we are hearing from more drivers who want to keep the car they already know, especially once they look at what a new vehicle costs. An older Prius or Camry Hybrid with a healthy battery can stay on the road for years, and our job is to give owners an honest diagnosis so they can make that decision with clear numbers in front of them,” said Nahome Yifru, owner of A+ Hybrid Batteries.

A+ Hybrid Batteries was founded on June 24, 2020, and is based in Aurora, Colorado. The company provides mobile hybrid battery diagnostics and replacement for vehicle owners across Colorado, Georgia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Virginia, with locations in Atlanta, Aurora, Baltimore, Dallastown, and Fairfax, and has announced plans to bring its service to even more states soon. Its replacement batteries carry warranties of up to five years depending on the battery selected.

text:
In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition.

The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities.

The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power.

But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them.

Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future.

'Meteoric Growth'

Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles.

At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants.

“The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.”

Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances.

With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand.

Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably.

Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects.

“As we’re dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we’ve already paid for,” Roberts said.

State policies have been a driver of the industry’s growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates.

In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage.

“It’s basically a no-regret path,” Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. “Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there’s battery storage.”

Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they’ve met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit.

Community Concerns

For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke.

Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands.

Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities.

“They’re making us collateral damage,” said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. “We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we’re going to do in our backyard.”

The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials.

Industry leaders say the Moss Landing facility was built using an older design, prior to the issuance of safety standards from the National Fire Protection Association that cover most systems on the grid today. Newer projects use an updated battery chemistry that burns at lower temperatures, and store the batteries in isolated, modular containers so that fires don’t spread to nearby units.

As a result, battery fires have become much more rare and far less devastating. Earlier this month, the Electric Power Research Institute, an independent nonprofit, published an analysis of battery system failures dating back to 2011.

The report found that failures (defined as large thermal events such as arc flashes, fires or explosions) have declined 97% in the U.S. since 2018, when adjusted for the amount of battery power on the grid. The incidents that have happened in new systems have largely remained small and contained, said Lakshmi Srinivasan, who authored the analysis.

“Specific design choices have really reduced not only the likelihood of a failure, but the impact of a failure if it happens,” she told Stateline.

Srinivasan said the risk profile of battery farms is similar to that of electrical transformers, components of the electrical grid that already exist in many communities.

But some communities feel a slim chance of disaster is still too high. Residents in Snoqualmie, Washington, have voiced opposition to a proposed battery project just outside city limits, prompting the city and several neighboring communities to enact moratoriums on such facilities.

“We need to think more carefully about what the worst-case scenario is, not just what’s typical,” said Dan Murphy, a council member in the city of Snoqualmie. “The science says (battery farms) are getting safer, but we’re still early.”

Amid the local backlash, the developer, Jupiter Power, has indicated that it will pursue approval from state-level energy siting regulators, removing the project from King County jurisdiction.

Murphy said his community supports clean energy, but objected to the site location near homes, a playground, a waterway and a critical evacuation route. He said Jupiter Power kept locals in the dark until they thought the project was a done deal.

“We are a very reserved and polite community,” he said. “To see the outcry and the animation and the mobilization, it’s really struck a nerve with our residents.”

In a document responding to community concerns, Jupiter Power noted that battery farms must be built near substations, which are located in close proximity to the communities they serve. That reality, the company said, makes it unrealistic for local officials to demand that battery systems keep their distance from populated areas. In King County, the company found, all 157 substations that are suitable for a battery project are located within a quarter-mile of schools, daycares, hospitals, natural areas or other sensitive sites.

Jupiter Power did not grant an interview request, but referred questions to Clean and Prosperous, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on reducing emissions.

“For any battery storage project there will inherently already be energy infrastructure nearby,” said Kelsey Nyland, communications director with Clean and Prosperous. “It often feels like we expect clean energy projects to be perfect in a way that we don’t expect from fossil fuel projects.”

Nyland noted that Washington state ranks dead last in the nation for clean energy growth, despite its ambitious climate goals. Battery storage, she said, can help population centers in western Washington harness surplus wind and solar power from rural eastern Washington.

She added that Washington has only one operational battery storage facility, making it difficult to alleviate local’s concerns by touring a nearby site.

Similar disputes have played out in dozens of communities across the country, and many have passed temporary measures banning the construction of battery storage facilities.

Earlier this month, a pair of former economic officials from the Biden administration wrote in The Washington Post that battery farms had been caught in a case of “mistaken identity” amid the nationwide backlash to data centers, which have stirred up similar feelings about industrial siting and environmental risks. But while data centers increase pressure on the grid, battery farms reduce it, they wrote, making the “conflation” an expensive mistake.

Some local activists have asked for battery farms to be sited in remote areas, where they would pose fewer risks. But industry leaders say they’re simply following the incentives set forth by utilities, which prioritize projects that can connect to the grid near population centers.

“If you have a source of power right where the power’s being consumed, the more efficient your system’s going to be,” Malaquias Encarnacion, managing director with Carina Energy, a development services firm that works on battery storage projects.

Carina Energy has tracked 175 battery farm moratoriums enacted or proposed by communities across the country. In some cases, Encarnacion said, those actions have been temporary measures enacted by local governments to give themselves time to learn about the issue.

“If I didn’t know anything about it, I would be nervous as well,” he said, encouraging developers to engage with communities early to alleviate those concerns.

text:
The Trump administration is trying to ease regulations around methane emissions from oil wells — and the clock is ticking to make public comments.

Previous 2024 Biden-era rules stated companies needed to get rid of 100% of emissions from wells. Now the Environmental Protection Agency, including Regional Administrator Cyrus Western, is saying methane emissions should be reduced by at least 95%.

“That's a pretty high score … Why should they get dinged?” said Western, the administrator for Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, and other mountain and plains states.

Western said the changes will specifically help operators of low-producing, or “marginal,” wells. He said many of these well operators are small, mom-and-pop businesses that have few employees and produce a few barrels of oil a day.

“ Why would we force them to tie a hand behind their back, and maybe some of them even go out of business entirely, when there's an alternative that sets a very high standard?” Western said.

However, some environmental groups, such as the Environmental Defense Fund, say that standard isn’t high enough. Jon Goldstein is the associate vice president for energy transition at the nonprofit.

“Rolling back these safeguards would mean more wasted energy, more methane pollution and greater health risks for communities living near oil and gas operations,” Goldstein said in a press release.

The EDF also says that the majority of low-producing wells are owned by large companies, not small businesses. Companies with fewer than 10 sites control just 3% of low-producing well sites, while large companies dominate ownership, according to an EDF analysis of information from Enverus, an energy analytics company. It also says these sites account for less than 5% of oil and gas production, but up to half of methane emissions from wells.

It’s not yet clear how much more methane emissions there could be under the Trump proposal, compared to the Biden rules, as the EPA didn’t provide a figure. On its website, though, the agency says that methane traps at least 28 times more heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, accounting for 11% of global emissions.

Juan B. Mancias, tribal chairman of the Carrizo Comecrudo Nation of Texas (Esto’k Gna), also opposes the changes. In public comments to the EPA, he asked the agency to “retain effective methane safeguards.”

“Our ancestral relationship to land is not a commodity to be balanced away solely against industrial operating costs,” Mancias said. “We are the land; its air and waters sustain our people and future generations. EPA must protect those relationships through a defensible, transparent regulatory record.”

Western said that while his agency is easing regulations around emissions, it will still punish wrongdoers.

“This is not a get-out-of-jail-free card for people to just emit pure methane into the atmosphere for days, weeks, or months or years on end,” he said.

The proposal could also eliminate another Biden-era environmental regulation, the Super Emitter Program, which would have required companies to respond to credible reports of major methane leaks.

Those 2024 regulations never went into full effect nationally with the change of administrations, but Colorado became the first state to adopt them in September, according to Colorado Public Radio. The Environmental Defense Fund says Colorado could now cut around 30,000 metric tons of methane from leaking into the atmosphere through 2038.

The public comment period on the proposed changes nationwide goes through Dec. 16.

title: The Unlikely Allies Behind Congress' New Energy Deal - Atmos Magazine
description:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a permitting reform bill that would speed up approvals for energy infrastructure projects on public land.
As you can imagine, environmental and clean energy groups are divided over whether to support the bill and help get it through ASAP, or send it packing.
Whitehouse says BAAJA will be a boon for clean energy.
Clean energy and climate groups echo Whitehouse’s arguments, including Evergreen Action, a group started by former Washington Gov.
A proposal’s congressional approval doesn’t necessarily translate to federal permit approval—and Trump has shown his hand when it comes to clean energy projects.
text:
We rarely hear the word compromise these days, especially in politics. I often feel like bipartisanship died with the last season of The West Wing, or at least the first Trump term.

But a new bill making its way through Congress right now is framed as a solution to a problem industries on both sides of the energy debate have long grappled with: how to get faster approvals to build infrastructure on public lands.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a permitting reform bill that would speed up approvals for energy infrastructure projects on public land. The Senate voted Monday to move BAAJA to a full vote, teeing it up for a fast-track approval.

The bill would more readily greenlight solar arrays, wind farms, and modernize electric grids and power lines. But it would do the same for data centers and gas pipelines.

BAAJA supporters consider it essential to clear infrastructure backlogs, cut the red tape of complex, slow environmental reviews, and get more energy of all kinds online quickly. Opponents argue the bill would negatively impact protected land, weaken species protections, skip tribal and historical reviews, and increase emissions.

As you can imagine, environmental and clean energy groups are divided over whether to support the bill and help get it through ASAP, or send it packing.

It’s important to note that this bill was created with true bipartisan support.

Senate Republicans Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia introduced BAAJA alongside Democrats Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.

And Whitehouse’s support is not something to view lightly. He’s held more than 300 weekly “Time To Wake Up” speeches on the floor since 2012 that press his colleagues to confront the climate crisis, address the financial and environmental impacts of fossil fuels, and reckon with the outsized influence of dark money in politics.

Whitehouse says BAAJA will be a boon for clean energy. “This bill is a BIG step to fight climate change,” he wrote on X this week. “It would lower power sector emissions, accelerate clean energy, and avoid emissions equivalent to those from nearly 35 million gasoline-powered vehicles.”

He also argues that certain provisions in the bill would lower data center costs for ratepayers by forcing companies to pay more for grid expansion. BAAJA could save ratepayers $55 billion over 10 years, according to an independent analysis from Grid Strategies LLC.

Clean energy and climate groups echo Whitehouse’s arguments, including Evergreen Action, a group started by former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee staffers. (Inslee himself has not taken an official stance on the bill).

On the other hand, AI and gas companies also champion the bill for being pro-energy. BAAJA would benefit the gas industry in two ways: by allowing it to build out more of its own energy infrastructure; and by paving the way for more data centers, which are predominantly powered by gas.

The Data Center Coalition, whose members include Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, reportedly spent $480,000 on lobbying between July and September, including on the permitting reform bill. Other groups that divulged their lobbying on the bill include the American Petroleum Institute, the Edison Electric Institute, and the National Mining Association.

API’s aggressive bill advocacy included sending a “BAAJA on the Hill” taco truck around the Capitol building on Tuesday to distribute free tacos.

It read: “Pass permitting reform. Lower energy costs. Brighter Opportunities.”

Many see BAAJA as a rare compromise. But is it worth it?

While considering what compromise might look like in a bill that could pass, I’m reminded of words from political scientist Leah Stokes, whom I spoke with previously about her efforts to pass the largest climate bill in American History: the Inflation Reduction Act.

That bill was trimmed repeatedly: from a $6 trillion reconciliation package, to a $3.5 trillion Build Back Better framework, to a scaled-back $1.75 trillion proposal. In the end, the Inflation Reduction Act passed with nearly $400 billion in climate investments.

It was still a win for the planet, Stokes told me, even in its imperfection.

“I really felt despair sometimes when the bill would shrink,” she said, “but I also felt like, you know, something is better than nothing. And losing out on this huge opportunity to pass a climate bill means that we could wait another decade to make this happen.”

Of course, that doesn’t mean BAAJA is the right compromise. If it passes, it’s important to consider the losers as much as the winners. Gas companies, the AI industry, and solar manufacturers could all make some big gains. But the climate could be left reeling.

The Center for Biological Diversity argues that BAAJA provides “massive long-term structural advantages to the fossil fuel industry and minimal short-term improvements to electricity transmission policy that might marginally benefit renewable energy.” One of its directors likened the bill to a “climate kill shot that condemns our most vulnerable communities to suffer decades more fossil fuel pollution.”

Oil Change International, a nonprofit campaigning for a just transition to clean energy, warns BAAJA would allow for “a massive, unprecedented buildout of gas power plants and pipelines,” arguing that’s why the permitting legislation would “fail to trigger a clean energy revolution.”

But research indicates that long term, the pluses might outweigh the minuses.

Independent research provider Rhodium Group found that yes, the bill will both increase clean energy resources by driving an additional 17-249 GW of clean resources, and increase fossil fuel production by increasing liquefied natural gas exports by 8-15%.

Taken together, though, Rhodium estimates BAAJA could reduce greenhouse gas emissions by between 5 and 148 million metric tons annually by 2040. Allowing clean energy to be deployed more readily—even alongside fossil fuel infrastructure—will arguably allow the industry to grow quickly enough to ultimately eclipse fossil fuels on the market, driving down emissions in the long term.

But that’s if the bill is implemented as promised.

One big concern is federal intervention. A proposal’s congressional approval doesn’t necessarily translate to federal permit approval—and Trump has shown his hand when it comes to clean energy projects.

As climate writer Lissa Harris asked Bill McKibben: “Why do we presume any of these mfers will do anything but wipe their ass with this deal when Boss Baby decides he hates a wind project next year?”

It turns out her concern was well-founded.

Hours after Trump’s Monday BAAJA endorsement, he told reporters at the White House that he wouldn’t approve any wind projects despite the bill. “Wind turbines are a major loser,” he said.

Congressional Democrats, on the brink of power come January, seem keen to slow BAAJA down. Following the midterm election results, analysts at investment banking firm TD Cowen cut their outlook for the bill’s success from roughly 40% to 25%. Timing is on Democrats’ side: A Senate approval would send the bill to the House, and the holidays—when congressional members take time off to go home—are fast approaching.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said last week that the permitting bill falls short, criticizing it for a “failure to adequately protect tribal sovereignty.” Over the weekend, a new amendment was added to BAAJA—77 pages of updates—meant to answer objections from tribes, environmentalists and utilities. Not everyone is convinced.

Even if Democrats take up the bill next year, it’s unclear what it would look like on the heels of such such clear messaging from American voters last week against data centers.

I can’t see Democrats starting their tenure leading the new Congress by trumpeting a bill that benefits the very industry whose opposition helped pave their road to victory.

text:
After a second round of amendments, Oil Change International reaffirms opposition to the Trump-backed Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) and calls on the Senate to reject the bill.

Elizabeth Bast, Executive Director of Oil Change International says:

“The new amendments do nothing to address major concerns about this bill, particularly how it overwhelmingly benefits the fossil fuel industry and Big Tech.

“Even with amendments, BAAJA still fast-tracks fossil fuel projects and makes it virtually impossible for communities to stop them. This bill still limits future administrations’ ability to meaningfully address the climate crisis and enable a just transition away from fossil fuels. It still strips away State and Tribal governments’ power to protect clean water and cultural resources.

“This bill will not address the cost of living crisis that drove so many Americans to the polls last week. The American Petroleum Institute’s (API) own analysis doesn’t show a reduction in energy costs – it simply suggests that prices may not rise as high as they otherwise would. It still leaves energy costs for U.S. households and businesses significantly rising over time.

“This bill will not meaningfully address climate change. We will never make real progress on climate if we continue to prioritize policies, like BAAJA, that help unleash more fossil fuels. Energy sources need to shift from fossil fuels to clean energy – not lock in fossil fuel dominance entrenched in this bill.

“The Senate must not rush to vote on this bill. The amendments are not adequate to address the serious concerns of Tribal Nations, environmental justice communities, and climate and energy experts. Monday’s vote was a clear demonstration that this bill is not ready for final passage, as every Democratic Senator on the Environment and Public Works Committee voted against ranking member Whitehouse’s bill. As senators voted, Trump himself admitted that even with BAAJA in place, his administration would continue to block wind projects.

“Rushing the vote on BAAJA will have grave consequences. Instead, we need policies that will support renewable energy without giving the fossil fuel industry everything it’s been asking for.”

text:
In the wake of Democrats’ sweeping victories across the nation, post-election polling commissioned by organizations focused on clean energy and environmental issues found that energy affordability was at the top of many voters’ minds as they cast their ballots.

On Tuesday, Climate Power, a strategic communications organization focused on building support for climate action, shared polling data examining how energy costs shaped the midterm results. Climate Power, alongside the League of Conservation Voters, EDF Action and the NRDC Action Fund, commissioned Hart Research for an online survey of 1,778 individuals across 62 competitive U.S. House districts who had either voted, or were certain they would be voting.

Breaking down the findings at a press briefing, Jay Campbell, a partner at Hart Research, said while voters were ready to be done with Republicans and President Donald Trump, that rejection did not mean that battleground district voters were enthusiastic about Democrats.

Survey results showed 61% of respondents had negative feelings about Donald Trump, while 57% expressed negative feelings toward congressional Republicans. Even though Democrats won majorities in both the U.S. House and Senate, 46% of voters still held a negative perception of Democrats while 41% said they held positive feelings towards the incoming majority party.

As for the takeaway from these responses, Campbell said the people are giving Democrats a chance in Congress, and that they would need to take on that mantle and prove themselves.

Looking into the issues that were most pressing for voters, the cost of food and groceries “blew everything else out of the water,” Campbell said, with 66% of all voters surveyed listing that as their top issue.

However, two separate energy issues were among the top four concerns for voters. Just below the cost of groceries was the cost of gasoline, which was a deciding factor for 41% of voters. The cost of utilities, such as electricity and heating, was the fourth-most prominent issue for voters, with 32% of survey respondents noting it was a key issue in determining their congressional vote.

“The long and short of it is the cost of food and groceries, the cost of gasoline, the cost of heating, these are what people need to see Democrats working on going forward,” Campbell said. “The affordability crisis is very real, and energy is very much a part of it.”

When asked how the United States produces, delivers and manages energy, 58% of voters said the U.S. should have different policies and approaches from those put forward by Trump, while 28% said that the country should stay the course.

Additionally, respondents were asked who they felt benefited more under the Trump administration’s energy policy, consumers like them, or the oil and gas companies and electrical utilities. Twenty-two percent of voters said they had benefited more from the administration’s energy policy while 78% said the companies had benefited more.

“Even when you look at self-identified Republicans, it’s 61 to 39 saying corporations versus people like me have been benefiting,” Campbell said. “That’s a pretty clear and damning sense of where people stand.”

Moving forward, 62% of respondents said it should be a priority for Congress to bring down electricity prices, while only 7% said it was not what lawmakers should be working on.

Campbell also challenged the notion that clean energy is a liberal-coded idea that only appeals to voters on the far left, noting that a majority of swing district respondents said that clean energy was having a positive impact on energy prices.

“Those who voted for a Republican candidate say that using more clean energy rather than less would make energy more affordable by a margin of 40% to 29%,” Campbell said. “Not overwhelming, but very much on the positive side rather than on the negative side.”

However, there is work left for Democrats to do, Campbell noted, citing polling data that showed only about a third of voters say Democrats are making things better for consumers.

And the voters trust them to do that work, Campbell explained, pointing to a comparison between voters surveyed in January, and the most recent survey, conducted between Oct. 26 and Nov. 6.

In January 30% of voters surveyed said they trust Republicans more than Democrats to lower monthly energy bills compared to 26% who had more faith in the Dems.

However, the more recent survey found 43% of respondents trusted Democrats to lower their energy bills, compared to 24% who had more faith in the Republicans.

In the polling data from October and November, 45% of respondents also said they had more faith that Democrats would prioritize the interests of the consumer over corporate profits compared to 23% who placed their trust on this issue in Republicans. Voters also trusted Democrats more on issues like regulating AI data centers, lowering the cost of gas and diesel and improving the reliability of the electrical grid.

“The narrative around these issues has changed dramatically from what we were hearing in previous elections,” Geoff Garin, the president of Hart Research, told reporters at the top of the press briefing.

“The old Republican mantras of ‘drill, baby, drill’ and American energy dominance were and are wholly irrelevant to the current energy debate,” Garin continued. “Instead, the energy debate now is focused on Trump’s ill-conceived war, on data centers, on price gouging by oil companies, and on Trump’s war on clean energy. Every one of these elements led to a damning indictment of Republicans and gave Democrats the high ground in the energy debate.”

Sustainable Energy & Infrastructure Litigation Updates — November 2026

By Jacob Hupart

Court Decisions. On October 8, 2026, an earlier state court decision dismissing New York City’s lawsuit against major fossil fuel companies under New York’s consumer protection laws for alleged greenwashing (i.e., holding out certain products as more environmentally friendly than advertised) was affirmed on appeal. This decision demonstrates the significant hurdles that governments and private plaintiffs will encounter when trying to impose greenwashing liability on fossil fuel companies, as “the general public . . . is now well aware of the fact that the use of fossil fuels results in greenhouse-gas emissions and is the primary driver of climate change.” In other words, the general level of knowledge concerning climate-related issues has now made it more difficult to impose liability on those involved with fossil fuels because it is hard to prove the fossil fuel companies engaged in deceptive practices when the public is already aware of and has taken into account the nature of their business.

State Regulatory Action. On October 23, 2026, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against First Street Technology, Inc. in connection with allegedly faulty climate risk factors published by First Street for real estate properties. (First Street provides climate risk scores for individual homes and other real estate listed for sale, including through popular homebuying websites.) Specifically, the Florida AG asserts claims under Florida’s consumer protection laws, focusing on alleged flaws in First Street’s methodology, the resultant climate risk scores, and First Street’s failure to publicly disclose all aspects of its methodology. This action effectively seeks to apply the legal playbook developed by state attorneys general in greenwashing litigation targeting ostensibly green consumer products to climate and sustainability data providers.

First Solar and CubicPV entered into a nonexclusive US patent licensing agreement related to perovskite solar technology. The transaction gives First Solar access to CubicPV’s issued and pending US patents as First Solar continues work toward developing perovskite photovoltaic products across multiple US solar market segments. Perovskite solar technology uses a class of semiconductor materials that absorb light and convert it into electricity, offering potential applications in next-generation, high-performance solar cells and modules.

title: LNG at a Legal Crossroads: Export Growth, Regulation and the Gulf Coast
description:
The Gulf Coast LNG (liquid natural gas) industry is entering another period of significant development and evolution.
The Gulf Coast has become central to the U.S. LNG industry, and that position is unlikely to change.
The Gulf Coast LNG Landscape The scale of current LNG development illustrates the stakes and volume of energy development.
The result is a multifaceted Gulf Coast development environment in which a project’s legal exposure can extend well beyond the LNG terminal itself.
What Texas Energy Lawyers Should Be Watching The Gulf Coast LNG industry is entering a period in which growth and legal complexity are advancing simultaneously.
text:
The Gulf Coast LNG (liquid natural gas) industry is entering another period of significant development and evolution. For Texas energy companies and relevant counsel, the future will likely require navigating overlapping federal authorizations, environmental review, pipeline infrastructure, and a changing energy policy landscape.

The Gulf Coast has become central to the U.S. LNG industry, and that position is unlikely to change. Developers are increasingly pursuing new modes of transport (like trains) and expanding existing facilities and related pipeline infrastructure from South Texas to the Texas-Louisiana border. But LNG development is not simply a question of whether a project can be built. The more consequential legal questions arise at the intersections between:

Federal and state jurisdiction

Export authorization and facility permitting

Environmental review and project schedules

Infrastructure and commercial commitments

Regulatory approval and litigation risk

Use of legacy assets in newer projects and successor liability issues

For personal injury attorneys handling energy-related injury and wrongful death claims, these intersections can be critical to understanding the operational circumstances behind an incident. They can be instrumental in identifying potentially responsible parties and evaluating the regulatory framework that may inform litigation.

The Gulf Coast LNG Landscape

The scale of current LNG development illustrates the stakes and volume of energy development. In September 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) issued a draft environmental impact statement for the proposed Corpus Christi Liquefaction Stage 4 and Corpus Christi Pipeline Expansion projects. The proposed expansion would add four liquefaction trains with a maximum capacity of approximately 1,200 billion cubic feet per year, two 220,000-gallon LNG storage tanks, additional marine facilities and related pipeline infrastructure.

At the other end of the Texas Gulf Coast, Rio Grande LNG continues to move through federal regulatory processes in their attempt to secure long-term authorization for exports from a proposed six-train facility in Cameron County. The FERC has separately been conducting environmental review of a proposed Train 6 expansion.

Port Arthur presents another example. Department of Energy (DOE) records reflect ongoing federal authorization activity involving Port Arthur LNG Phase II, including proposed additional liquefaction trains. A September 2026 filing sought authorization for some re-exports from the terminal under that is currently under construction in Jefferson County.

The result is a multifaceted Gulf Coast development environment in which a project’s legal exposure can extend well beyond the LNG terminal itself.

Who Regulates LNG and Why Jurisdiction Matters

One of the first questions counsel should ask is deceptively simple: Which agency has jurisdiction over which part of the project?

For onshore and near-shore LNG export facilities, FERC generally has authority under Section 3 of the Natural Gas Act to authorize siting and construction. FERC also has authority under Section 7 over certain interstate natural gas pipeline facilities. FERC conducts the applicable environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act for projects within its jurisdiction.

The DOE has a separate role concerning the export of the LNG commodity itself. Under Section 3 of the Natural Gas Act, exports to countries with qualifying free-trade agreements are treated differently from exports to non-FTA countries. The DOE conducts a public-interest review for non-FTA exports, considering factors such as domestic supply, energy security, economic impacts, etc.

Other agencies can enter the picture, depending on the issues at hand. The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) establishes and enforces federal safety standards for LNG facilities under 49 C.F.R. Part 193. The U.S. Coast Guard also has responsibilities involving LNG vessels and marine transfer areas.

Closer to home, state agencies, including the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and the Railroad Commission of Texas, may have authority over particular environmental, pipeline or other legal issues.

Pipeline and Infrastructure Dependencies

An LNG terminal cannot operate without the infrastructure that feeds it. Natural gas must be directed to the liquefaction facility. This process requires interstate pipelines, expansions, compression facilities, and interconnections. Additionally, marine infrastructure must be able to accommodate LNG carriers. There are also issues of storage, power, water, roads, and other supporting infrastructure that require separate permits and contractual considerations.

FERC’s current pipeline docket illustrates the scale of that relationship and how the industry is expanding in the Gulf Coast region. One example is the Sabine Crossing Pipeline Project. The project proposal includes a 55.6-mile pipeline spanning Texas and Louisiana with a capacity of 2.7 billion cubic feet per day. There are many other pending projects, but the Sabine Pass project illustrates the extensive reach these projects have.

Litigation and Regulatory Challenges on the Horizon

The next wave of LNG disputes may not resemble traditional environmental litigation. Potential disputes could involve complex and emerging issues:

Permitting and emissions issues

Challenges to federal environmental reviews or project authorizations

Pipeline routing, land-use and property disputes

Ownership and control changes

Marine and navigation concerns

Construction delays

Contractor disputes

Supply and offtake agreements

Force-majeure and change-in-law provisions

Financing and project-development obligations

Safety and operational incidents after projects enter service

Legal exposure in this industry can also evolve over the life of a project, making a lifecycle perspective potentially important. For example, a developer may initially focus on obtaining authorization and financing. But during construction, their attention shifts toward contractor performance, schedule risk and land issues. Then, focus shifts again once operational and regulatory compliance, safety, environmental obligations and commercial performance become more prominent.

That lifecycle perspective may be particularly important for counsel representing companies with multiple projects or long-term infrastructure portfolios.

What Texas Energy Lawyers Should Be Watching

The Gulf Coast LNG industry is entering a period in which growth and legal complexity are advancing simultaneously. For Texas energy lawyers, several issues deserve particular attention.

First – Jurisdictional mapping should occur early. Understanding which agency controls each aspect of a project helps identify where approvals may overlap.

Second – Regulatory assumptions should be stress-tested. Federal energy policy changes. Long-term projects need to account for the possibility that regulatory priorities or agency interpretations will evolve during the project lifecycle.

Third – Infrastructure dependencies deserve the same scrutiny as the LNG facility itself. Pipeline capacity, interconnections, marine facilities and supporting infrastructure can determine whether a project functions as planned and within appropriate safety guidelines.

Finally – Commercial documents should anticipate regulatory uncertainty. Long-term agreements negotiated years before may not apply today when companies encounter circumstances that were difficult to predict. Change-in-law, force-majeure, delay, termination and dispute-resolution provisions can therefore become critical components of project risk allocation.

Major LNG Expansion Means More Awareness of Changing Laws

The Gulf Coast’s LNG expansion presents substantial opportunities for Texas and the broader U.S. energy market. But as the expansion moves forward, important legal questions may arise not from any single regulation or agency, but from the interaction of regulation, infrastructure, contracts and changing energy policy.

For counsel, developers and investors, that is where the legal crossroads begin.

title: Leading small modular nuclear reactor will be late and over budget - Canary Media
description:
North America’s first small modular reactor project is running into two familiar challenges for the nuclear industry: timing and cost.
The Darlington project, located east of Toronto, is the first new nuclear build in Canada in more than three decades.
It’s also the first test of a small modular reactor design that is being pursued by developers in the U.S. and beyond.
The Tennessee Valley Authority received a construction permit for a BWRX-300 from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in September.
Timeline and cost overruns have plagued North American nuclear projects and help explain why reactor construction has been anemic in recent decades.
text:
North America’s first small modular reactor project is running into two familiar challenges for the nuclear industry: timing and cost.

Ontario Power Generation said in a Tuesday earnings release that the first BWRX-300 unit at its Darlington site will not come online by its October 2030 target and will blow past its budget of $7.7 billion Canadian ($5.4 billion U.S.). The utility didn’t share new targets — it’s working on a revised assessment of cost and schedule that it expects ​“to be substantially completed by mid-2027.” It is the project’s second slip: When Ontario Power announced the design in late 2021, it said the reactor could be completed as early as 2028.

The Darlington project, located east of Toronto, is the first new nuclear build in Canada in more than three decades. It’s also the first test of a small modular reactor design that is being pursued by developers in the U.S. and beyond. The Tennessee Valley Authority received a construction permit for a BWRX-300 from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in September. Developer Blue Energy has also started the NRC application process to build a BWRX-300 in Texas.

Unlike other next-gen nuclear designs recently greenlit for construction in the U.S., GE Vernova Hitachi’s BWRX-300 uses the same light-water technology that undergirds most of the world’s existing nuclear fleet today. It’s designed to produce 300 megawatts of carbon-free electricity — a substantial amount, but far less than a conventional large-scale reactor.

Timeline and cost overruns have plagued North American nuclear projects and help explain why reactor construction has been anemic in recent decades. Just look at the latest nuclear power plants to be completed in the U.S.: Georgia Power’s Vogtle units 3 and 4, both large-scale AP-1000 reactors that came online in 2023 and 2024, took an extra seven years and $17 billion to wrap up.

Nevertheless, nuclear energy is seeing resurgent financial and policy support in North America and elsewhere as demand for electricity — especially carbon-free electricity — rises.

The Darlington project is part of that wave. In total, Ontario Power Generation plans to build four units at a cost of $20.9 billion Canadian, and federal and provincial investment funds have since committed up to $3 billion Canadian for minority stakes in the project. In the U.S., the Biden administration backed nuclear power as an anchor for an emissions-free grid, and both Trump administrations have embraced it under the banner of ​“energy dominance.”

Proponents of SMRs argue that smaller, repeatable designs like the BWRX will be cheaper and faster to build than large-scale reactors. The idea is that mass manufacturing and construction of these reactors will create a sort of learning-curve effect, so even if the first unit is expensive to make, the 100th unit will be far cheaper. But right now, this is only a hypothesis. Just two SMR plants are operating commercially worldwide, in Russia and China, and some in the nuclear industry argue that it’s more economical to stick with big reactors.

Given that the Darlington project is the first attempt at building a BWRX-300, some budget and timeline overruns aren’t surprising. Ontario Power Generation itself said that the update ​“reflects GE Vernova Hitachi (GEVH) Nuclear Energy’s ongoing engineering for its first-of-a-kind SMR, which has impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”

“GE Vernova Hitachi is committed to working closely with Ontario Power Generation (OPG) and our partners to deliver the Western world’s first commercial SMR,” a GE Vernova Hitachi spokesperson told Canary Media in an emailed statement. ​“While engineering and design maturity are important considerations, as OPG’s update recognizes, there are multiple interconnected contributions across engineering, procurement and construction, as well as evolving market conditions, including inflation and geopolitical risks.”

While overruns are expected for a first-of-its-kind project, their scale matters. If costs or timelines balloon by too much, it could have a chilling effect on the other efforts to develop BWRX-300 reactors. Vogtle offers a cautionary precedent. Even though its second new reactor was 30% cheaper to build than its first, what’s remembered is the project’s enormous overall price tag.

title: Whose Voices Shape Pollution Policy? | News - McCormick School of Engineering
