text:
Earlier this year, two rPlus Energies plants achieved commercial operation: the Green River Energy Center in Utah and Pleasant Valley Solar 2 in Idaho. By early November, both were helping secure a new loan.

PV Tech's Shreeyashi Ojha reported on November 4 that rPlus has closed a revolving credit facility of up to $450 million. It runs for three years and offers both cash borrowing and letters of credit. The money goes to developing and building the company's near-term solar and storage projects across the American West, and it is backed by cash flows from nearly 1GW of operating assets, with those two plants named first.

Seen from outside, this is one more financing headline in a busy week for solar finance. For a utility procurement lead or a data center energy buyer weighing an independent power producer as a counterparty, it shows something more useful. It shows the order in which a developer turns finished plants into the money for its next ones, and how short that cycle can be.

Construction debt first, then the revolver

Green River combines 400MW of solar with a 400MW/1,600MWh battery system, enough for four hours of storage at full output. In 2024 rPlus raised more than $1 billion in construction debt for the project. Wells Fargo Securities, Truist Securities, MUFG Bank, KeyBanc Capital Markets and Crédit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank led that financing. PacifiCorp buys the plant's power under a power purchase agreement signed in October 2022. Pleasant Valley Solar 2 received a separate $179 million construction loan in December 2024. Groundbreaking and construction mobilisation for each project commenced in April 2025.

Both plants achieved commercial operation and completed term financing earlier this year. Construction loans are tied to one plant and carry its build risk. Once a plant is running and its debt has been moved to long-term terms, it produces cash that lenders can see. The revolver suggests that, for rPlus, that cash was enough to support borrowing at the company level within months of the plants coming online.

The lender list deserves a close look. CIBC's New York Branch served as lead left arranger and administrative agent. It syndicated the facility to six banks: Zions Capital Markets, MUFG, Wells Fargo, KeyBank, Truist Bank and National Bank of Canada. A syndicate this size suggests lenders are comfortable lending against plants that are already producing. Kirkland & Ellis advised rPlus, and Milbank advised the lenders.

Plants that reached full commercial operation on July 21 were, by early November, part of the security behind up to $450 million for rPlus Energies' next round of building. CFO Natalie Jackson called the facility evidence of the team's progress and of lenders' confidence in the company's long-term plans.

Utah, Idaho and a three-party contract

Sandbrook Capital backs rPlus, which operates as an independent power producer: it develops projects and then keeps ownership of them. Utah and Idaho are the focus of its portfolio, which totals more than 12GW of output. In Idaho, its acquisition of the Blacks Creek and Bluebird solar projects from Qcells and Mission Clean Energy took its solar and storage pipeline in the state beyond 1GW. The company is also developing three pumped hydro projects, one each in Wyoming, Nevada and Utah.

Company president Luigi Resta has described the strategy in interviews with PV Tech's sister site Energy-Storage.news. rPlus builds in rural areas that have seen little clean energy development and whose economies have long relied on coal and gas. Speaking about the pumped hydro pipeline in September 2024, he highlighted its ability to provide grid inertia as coal-fired power plants retire. He added that rPlus plans to contract project output through tolling agreements with utilities.

Pleasant Valley is the part large power buyers should study. When PV Tech's Will Norman covered the deal in May 2023, the 200MW Pleasant Valley Solar project had signed a long-term PPA with Idaho Power. Meta had arranged it through an Energy Services Agreement so it could get renewable power from the same grid that serves its new data center in Kuna, Idaho. At the time, rPlus said it was the largest solar project contracted to the Idaho Power system. The structure suggests a large buyer can secure local renewable supply by working through its utility, not only by contracting with a developer directly.

For data center operators that want new local supply in a regulated utility territory, that sequence is a real reference point. A buyer-brokered utility contract led to a plant that is now running and now financeable. And that plant is helping fund the developer's next projects in the same region.

Sizing $450 million against one Utah plant

The figure should not be overread. Green River alone took more than $1 billion in construction debt, more than twice the revolver's ceiling, so this facility will not finance a project of that size by itself. Given its three-year term and letter-of-credit capacity, it most likely covers development spending, credit support and early construction costs on near-term projects. Each large build would probably still get its own project loan. rPlus has not described the split, so that reading stays a conditional one.

A project loan looks very different, and PV Tech's Joseph Loe reported one in October. In Minya, Egypt, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced US$265 million in lending for a new 1.2GW solar PV plant that will sit alongside a 600MWh battery energy storage system. The EBRD itself is putting in US$160 million of that total. Bank of Jordan is providing US$75 million, and the Climate Investment Fund is adding up to US$30 million on concessional terms. The borrower is a single special purpose vehicle, Nefer Menya for Renewable Energy, and the Egyptian Electricity Transmission Company will buy the plant's power under a 25-year PPA. That loan is tied to one plant and one buyer. The rPlus revolver is tied to a group of plants and a pipeline.

What buyers in rPlus territory can ask

For utilities and large buyers in Utah and Idaho, where most of the rPlus pipeline sits, the facility gives a few concrete things to ask any developer, not only this one:

Does the developer have a company-level facility backed by plants already running, or is every project financed alone?

Does that facility include letters of credit, and does its three-year term cover the contract milestones being negotiated?

Which operating assets back it, and how long have they been running?

These are editorial suggestions, not requirements reported in the coverage. Still, they come straight from how this deal is built. A developer that can borrow against operating cash flow is in a different position from one still waiting on its first plant to come online.

The next sign to watch is where the borrowing goes. If Blacks Creek and Bluebird reach construction during the facility's term, or a pumped hydro project signs a utility tolling agreement, that will show which projects the operating plants are funding.

text:
US energy storage manufacturer SolarBridge Technology has introduced the Golden Gate STC-P135, a 135 kW bidirectional power conversion system (PCS) designed for commercial and industrial energy storage applications.

The Delaware-incorporated company, founded in 2025 and headquartered in Dallas, will showcase the modular unit at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas ahead of planned commercial production at its Texas assembly facility in early 2027.

Power conversion systems play a critical role in battery storage by managing electricity flow between battery enclosures, host facilities, and the grid. However, evolving federal trade regulations have elevated equipment sourcing into a primary compliance hurdle for project developers. Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, storage installations that incorporate components from a Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) risk losing eligibility for the 30% federal Investment Tax Credit. Additionally, recent Federal Communications Commission rules restrict the import of foreign-made inverters and power conversion systems lacking pre-existing FCC equipment authorization.

Meeting FEOC and FCC requirements is the reason SolarBridge exists, stated Kemp Qiu, Chief Executive Officer of SolarBridge. Integrators need equipment that keeps their projects eligible for federal incentives, and SolarBridge is building that hardware in Dallas, Qiu said.

Modular architecture

The 135 kW unit aims to address supply constraints in the commercial and industrial sector, where power conversion equipment manufacturers have historically focused on multi-megawatt central architectures. System integrators can scale the modular units up to approximately 1 MW to match site-specific load requirements. SolarBridge also offers an Integrated AC Cabin housing up to four units to deliver 540 kW of aggregated capacity.

The Golden Gate STC-P135 features a rated AC power output of 135 kW, a maximum AC apparent power of 148.5 kVA, and a maximum efficiency of 98.7%. The unit supports a maximum DC voltage of 1500 V and a maximum DC current of 206 A. When the DC bus voltage is between 720 Vdc and 820 Vdc, the power conversion system operates in a three-phase, three-wire grid-connected configuration at 480 Vac.

The system supports both grid-tied and off-grid operations and maintains full power output at ambient temperatures up to 45°C. Its modular design allows individual unit swaps during maintenance without requiring a complete site shutdown.

Customers can pair the hardware with SolarBridge’s proprietary, AI-powered energy management system, which stores customer data on domestic servers to execute demand charge management, time-of-use arbitrage, solar self-consumption, and backup power protocols. The company plans to have its non-FEOC supply chain independently certified by a third-party law firm by early 2027 while completing FCC equipment authorization.

Dallas facility

Manufacturing equipment is scheduled for installation at the company’s Dallas facility in November 2026, with local assembly, functional testing, and software loading commencing in the first quarter of 2027. The facility is expected to employ approximately 50 workers during its initial phase, with a targeted monthly output of 1,000 to 1,500 units, representing up to 2.5 GW of annual production capacity.

Every unit leaving the facility will undergo full-power operational testing prior to shipment to engineering, procurement, and construction firms and system integrators. Select energy storage companies are scheduled to receive sample units for field testing in December 2026.

SolarBridge plans to expand its product lineup in the second quarter of 2027 with the introduction of the STU-P450, a liquid-cooled 450 kW string power conversion system. The higher-capacity model is designed to anchor turnkey utility-scale block stations up to 7.2 MW, which will coincide with a Phase II manufacturing expansion near Dallas.

text:
(Washington, D.C.) – Today, House Science, Space, and Technology Committee Chairman Brian Babin and Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren praised the Senate’s passage of the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026 (S. 3923), introduced by Senator Ted Cruz and a bipartisan group of Senate colleagues.

Chairman Babin and Ranking Member Lofgren issued the following statements:

"Reliable weather forecasts and timely warnings are essential to protecting American lives and property," said Chairman Brian Babin. "Last year's devastating floods in Texas served as a tragic reminder of the need to better predict severe weather and communicate critical information to communities in harm's way. The Weather Act Reauthorization represents an opportunity to modernize our nation's forecasting capabilities and strengthen emergency preparedness. Building on the legislation the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee advanced last September, the Senate-passed bill reflects a bipartisan, bicameral compromise and a shared commitment to protecting American communities. I thank Chairman Cruz, Ranking Member Lofgren, Rep. Lucas, and our colleagues in both chambers for their hard work in reaching this agreement. I look forward to continuing our efforts to get this legislation across the finish line."

"This is a long time coming," said Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren. "The Weather Act Reauthorization will give NOAA the support it needs to carry out its critical mission. I want to thank Chairman Babin, my former Committee partner, Mr. Lucas, and the dedicated staff on both sides of the aisle for getting this to the finish line. The World Meteorological Organization just released its State of the Climate update, emphasizing that the supersized El Niño we are experiencing is expected to bring record heat, flooding, and drought conditions for the next year. Now more than ever, more observations and data are needed to bolster our nation's forecasting capabilities to protect lives, property, the economy, and national security. We have to ensure that NOAA has the tools, staffing, and infrastructure to help support communities prepare for and respond to disasters. This bill will help us do that. I hope the president will see the importance of this legislation and sign it into law soon."

Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee Chairman Ted Cruz and Ranking Member Maria Cantwell also emphasized the importance of the legislation following its passage:

"Today, the Senate took a pivotal step toward ensuring Americans are prepared for severe weather," said Chairman Ted Cruz. "Texans know all too well the devastation storms can bring. The lives lost in the July 4, 2025, Texas floods are a heartbreaking reminder of what is at stake. The Weather Act brings together over a dozen bipartisan bills to modernize radar systems, deliver more accurate and timely forecasts, and improve warnings so families and first responders have more time to act, no matter where they are and no matter the time of day. These improvements will help protect property and, more importantly, save lives in Texas and across the country."

"Americans are facing increasingly dangerous and costly weather disasters, and better forecasts give communities more time to prepare and get out of harm’s way," said Ranking Member Maria Cantwell. "The Weather Act will advance next-generation weather radar, modernize lifesaving warning systems, and improve forecasts for atmospheric rivers and wildfires, like the devastating fires that forced thousands to evacuate in Spokane last month. Today’s Senate passage brings us one step closer to giving forecasters, emergency managers, and communities the tools they need to save lives and protect property."

The Senate-passed legislation builds on the bipartisan Weather Act reauthorization bill advanced by the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee in September 2025. The agreement also incorporates priorities championed by House Republicans, including efforts to modernize NOAA Weather Radio, improve fog forecasting, and address gaps in weather radar coverage.

Gamers as buyers: how the platform SuperPower pooled player subscriptions behind the 110 MW Three W solar farm in Hill County, and Eugster’s hint that other industries will follow next year.

Who carries price risk: why Eugster says a fixed REC price lets corporate buyers back new projects without taking on the price swings of power purchase agreement.

These are turbines. These are rotating kind of, you know, pieces of equipment. And so at some point they are end of life, and we’re gonna see the same thing with solar. And so what do you do? Do you just kind of tear them down and put them in a landfill? Like, that doesn’t feel right. And so with Clearway, we had conversations about how do we extend the life of some of these wind farms? And I think the repower is a nice fit for us because what happens is there’s uncertainty when you repower a wind farm, ‘cause there’s not a lot going on there. It’s getting more so. But it’s hard to put a PPA on that because, you know, a PPA is dependent on performance, right? And so a repowered wind farm, will it last seven years? Will it last 10 years? Will it go— What will the efficiency and the capacity factors be? How will the performance of that wind farm happen? And so what we did is we brought in our REC strip to basically help bring contracted cash flow to that project, and they were going merchant with the power that was generated. So as you can imagine, merchant, it’s hard to kinda operate a resource in a merchant environment ‘cause, you know, prices are all over the place. How do you support O&M and, you know, basic things like that? So our REC contract, which again is coming in at meaningful prices, is making a difference to provide a buffer to continue to operate that wind farm over a long period of time. You know, hopefully 10 years or longer, if we can.

Joshua Rhodes: Yeah. Totally. And like, maybe getting on a little bit of a different similar part of that, a key part of your business model appears to be, you know, demonstrating additionality, right? That the REC revenue generally helps a project financially value, and I think you look for at least a 10 percent improvement in certain project financial metrics. But counterfactuals are hard, so, like, what are y’all doing to prove that that project wouldn’t have gotten built anyways? Like, how do you think about additionality in a world where it’s hard to like, you know, build a counterfactual like that?

Cris Eugster: Yeah. I think it’s kind of a very interesting word, and I think there’s a lot of subjectivity around that. I think when we first started, when Michael and I first started about, and our thinking was, “Let’s aggregate corporate demand,” you know, “Let’s go out to a field and lock up that field, put up solar panels, and that will be the solar system for that, you know, set of corporates.” I think we quickly found, like, the developer world is not easy. There’s a lot of stuff besides kind of an offtake that’s gonna make a project happen. Will that landowner really kind of sign up with you? You know, what kind of mineral rights? Do you have surface rights? You know, it gets very complicated, and projects are not easy to do and not easy to happen. So I think what we learned is there’s not any one single thing that will cause a project to happen. Like, you know, we could have a great PPA or a great REC contract, but if interest rates kinda get too high and that project’s no longer economical, or the landowner has an issue, or there’s some permitting issues, or interconnection agreements kinda get stuck, like, there’s many things that can derail a project. So I think what we look for is that we are a meaningful part of a project, that we’re a material part, and that’s kinda where we got to the 10 percent factor. You know, the SEC 10 percent is an interesting part where you start to disclose kind of ownership, and so we anchored on that 10 percent as a way to say, “Hey, we feel good that we are a meaningful part of this cash flow.” But Josh, Michael and I went we had a lot of back and forth counterfactual. Would this have happened, not happened? Like it’s theoretical and it’s intellectual in some ways, but the real world is much more complicated, and it takes almost a group, you know, mentality to get a clean energy project online. It’s not an individual sport. It’s a team sport, right? You can’t just be a running back and, you know, now you’re winning all the time. You need the whole team in place.

Joshua Rhodes: You build a project, and then we figure out hydraulic fracturing. It... The world changes, like, there’s big, massive changes. You do the best you can with what you got kind of at that time.

Cris Eugster: But it is important that our customers feel like, you know, they are making a difference here. So our developers will go through a scorecard. They’re attesting that this contract is material to them. So we don’t take this thing lightly because it’s not an easy thing to do, so we put a lot of work in it. You know, we put white papers out there. We’ve been very transparent on our methodology. So it is complicated, it is a team sport, but we wanna be a meaningful part of that team with our offtake.

Joshua Rhodes: Yeah, no, and I think that’s a great transition and the, my next question was about, you know, measuring clean energy progress is like Ever.green tries to, you know, measure the actual environmental and community impacts of its projects rather than just counting megawatt hours. Like, how do you think about, you know, putting a megawatt hour of solar onto, say, a relatively coal-heavy region versus, you know, one that, you know, might al-already have a bunch of renewables? Should corporate clean energy county focus more on those regions that avoid more emissions? Is that what some of your clients are also pulling for?

Cris Eugster: We could do a whole podcast on that and probably wouldn’t bring Michael Leggett in here. I mean, it’s really important, Josh, because the standard bodies are trying to raise the bar on RECs, or just procurement in general, and so that is a good thing. I think there’s a huge debate on are we going 24/7 local, or are we going more around sort of additiona— emission, you know, having more of a consequential impact? I think we’re more in that latter bucket because while we think 24/7 and local is ultimately kind of where we wanna be, where you’re matching your energy production to your load, it could be a constraining factor here in the near term here. Because what it does, in our view, is it will emphasize spot market RECs. You know, now you just need to tag a REC with a time stamp and a location. You know, if you procure that to your load, you’re good to go. Well, what about the long-term contract? What about grids that are very dirty? So is this gonna incent a company in California where the grid is pretty clean to basically have to procure local 24/7 spot RECs to match their load versus standing up a project in Wyoming or Georgia where the grid is much less clean. So I think our belief is we wanna tag things, you know, time stamp, location stamp for transparency, but don’t make that a requirement. Because if that’s a requirement, it’s gonna hinder companies to get into long-term contracts in region that are outside of their footprint. And I think you and I know climate change is a global problem. Like, we wanna stand up clean energy in dirty grids, not clean grids.

Joshua Rhodes: Yeah, you get more bang for your buck doing that, as it were, in the clima— the climate doesn’t care, like, you know, where the CO2 is emitted or it doesn’t care about intensity, it cares about tons.

Cris Eugster: Yes.

Joshua Rhodes: Crafting this question was actually kind of interesting ‘cause it reminded me of the ancient days before AI when the things that the big technology companies were fighting over was this 24/7 versus this additionality fight. Like, and I think it was like Google was on one side and Meta was on the other side. There were other folks that were in there. I haven’t heard much of this lately. You know, now it’s just a race to build data centers as fast as possible. I guess it sounds like you’re trying to in— To keep that debate going and kind of inject some discipline into that argument, and is that what I’m reading?

Cris Eugster: We would like to have the debate cl— ‘cause uncertainty is always bad for the market. So if there’s uncertainty, customers are gonna sort of be slow to act. There are standard bodies that are actively trying to kind of set the new standard. Standards haven’t been looked at for the last, you know, dozen plus years. And so the Greenhouse Gas Protocol standard, the SBTi, Science Based Technology Initiative, SBTi standards, so these are voluntary standards, so, you know, but corporates do weigh them in heavily. And so both those standard bodies are kind of having this debate of is this more 24/7 or is it consequential? And so they’ve gotten feedback, but this is being driven by those two standard bodies on where they’re gonna set that standard. And, you know, we thought we’d have clarity here in ‘26. I think it’s getting pushed out to ‘27, but that’s what’s driving it, how these groups are gonna land in terms of what is the next standard for voluntary clean energy procurement.

Joshua Rhodes: I promised we’d talk about data centers ‘cause you can’t have a conversation for more than five minutes about energy without talking about data centers. Energy is AI is energy apparently. So we’re seeing extraordinary growth in electricity demands, you know, particularly from data centers, AI. Many of the companies that are building these have also have ambitious clean energy commitments, but you know, now they’re contributing to like a massive increase in electricity demand. And see, if you were designing a clean energy procurement strategy for a company that’s trying to build a gigawatt of data center in West Texas, what would you actually ask of that company to do to make the grid cleaner?

Cris Eugster: Yeah, I mean, such a great question. I mean, it really is. You know, the big tech, they’ve been the leader in terms of kind of, you know, thinking about sort of the clean energy transition and, you know, these massive PPAs and, you know, what they’ve done. I worry a little bit that now there’s just such a race and the velocity that is needed in the AI data center that it doesn’t matter so much about emissions as much. It’s just they need physical power, and whatever it takes to get physical power, that’s what they’re gonna be looking at. The other thing, Josh, is like, you know, I’ve been a utility guy, and like utilities, the growth has been flat. You know, maybe 2 percent, you got energy efficiency dampening it, and you guys have done great work in this world. Now you’re seeing 2x load, you know, potential load, you know, 5x lo— you know, things that utilities can’t even wrap their minds around. And so where is this power gonna come from? How are rates not gonna go up? How are resources not gonna be used, whether it’s water or environment? I think are super big questions, and you’re trying to solve these questions in a environment where there’s just a race to build more and faster. If you’re slow, you’re gonna lose a seat at the table. And so I would hope that there would be an interest, whether it’s a requirement or just self-interest, to basically build these data centers in a way that minimizes impacts to our environment and our communities. And Michael Webber and I have talked about this. There’s so much money that they should be able to do this the right way. You know? And I’d love to get your take on it. The challenge is the velocity and the competitiveness and the race, that makes it really hard to kind of be thoughtful in how do you do this thing the right way.

Joshua Rhodes: Yeah, no, for sure. I mean, I think that bleeds into like, you know, even community pushback and things on data centers. A lot of it is just this velocity, right? Like I model the electricity grid all the time, and I often make the joke, I’ll model it out as far into the future as you believe the price of natural gas will be. And historically, it’s like 2 percent load growth, and supply chains were built around, you know, supporting 2 percent load growth, at least at ERCOT. Other places a little bit flatter. But yeah, I mean, this is like, you know, 5x the grid in five years. It took us 100 years to get to 91 GW, and you wanna get to 500 GW in five years. Like just ain’t gonna happen, right? You just can’t get that much steel in the ground. Even if we, you know, cloned you a few times, we’re still not gonna get that much steel in the ground. I think it is some of that velocity, right? This whole Batch Zero process is trying to inject some discipline into that. Some of the pauses and the audits and things like that are trying to like, you know, inject sanity into that space, and so hopefully we can know what’s real so that we can actually build the infrastructure around, and the policy around, you know, what is real versus, like, these numbers that nobody believes. But we don’t know what the right number is. And you said earlier, it’s like, you know, business would rather have bad policy than uncertain policy, right? It’s just like at least know where your goalposts are. Even if they’re 200 yards that way, you’ll figure out how to kick the ball through it. But like, you know, if they’re just moving all the time, that’s a tougher one.

Cris Eugster: Yeah. I feel like if we could solve the velocity problem, I think we could figure out the power issue. I think if we don’t solve the velocity issue... And like you said, you know, there are some pretty good movements, and again, led by Texas on some of the Batch Zero and, you know, the slowing things down a bit to get things right. I think if we had more time, the technology’s there to do this thing the right way. And even some of the simple stuff like, “Let’s just do a combined cycle behind the meter.” Like, these data center, they’re gonna value the chips, not the combined cycles. If those chips are saying, “I gotta back off power,” like, you know, in a microsecond, that turbine’s gonna have it— Like, there are fundamental issues on even straightforward designs that I don’t think people have fully thought through, again, because of velocity. They’re just trying to get stuff done.

Joshua Rhodes: I think a lot of like conceptual behind the meter projects have run into the physical limitations of steel and the ability to move, right? It’s just like software’s one thing, steel’s another, right? In terms of being able to move, and it’s like, you know, getting those... If you want five nines of reliability, a single power plant’s not gonna give you that. I don’t care how new it is or how good it is, like, you’re not getting that. That’s why we have a grid, right? It’s like to share that risk around, give you that space. You know, it’s probably a lot easier to do this in a growth environment than like a declining environment, right? Like trying out new structures and projects, it sounds like y’all are doing, like it’s probably easier to try that out in a sector that’s growing versus one that’s stagnating, wouldn’t you say?

Cris Eugster: Yeah, 100 percent. You know, you see some of the, you know, these PPAs from the nuclear side. Like nuclear’s always been a very interesting kind of zero emission resource, but how do you put capital that perceives it as risky? How do you get the regulations to be more efficient? I think because this is a growth environment, I think nuclear’s back in play, which I think is exciting.

Joshua Rhodes: Yeah. No, I mean, I feel like, I think almost anything’s in play right now that is able to make a megawatt hour of electricity, is a really interesting space.

Cris Eugster: I think being in a growth environment is really good, and I think we can be thoughtful and we can do a lot of good things, try a lot of good things. I think the challenge is if we’re running too fast and lose our kind of foresight and strategy and perspective, I think that’s where we get into trouble.

Joshua Rhodes: Yeah. Absolutely. Well, Cris Eugster, thank you for coming on the Energy Capital Podcast.

name: EPA
title: EPA Oil and Gas Enforcement Drops in New Mexico Under Trump - Capital & Main
description:
Capital & Main examined 170 entries tied to oil and gas companies filed on the EPA’s enforcement and compliance webpage for New Mexico.
“EPA enforcement has not declined,” he said.
Recent studies linked oil and gas operations to radioactive airborne plumes and other air pollution in the Permian Basin, the nation’s largest oil field.
While oil and gas enforcement numbers have dropped, the EPA has not been idle in other areas in New Mexico.
Since then, outside watchdogs have called the numbers misleading — primarily because the EPA under Trump is taking credit for work done during the Biden administration.
text:
A review of an Environmental Protection Agency database of enforcement and compliance documents for New Mexico shows a drop in cases dealing with oil and gas operations since the start of the second administration of President Donald Trump.

Capital & Main examined 170 entries tied to oil and gas companies filed on the EPA’s enforcement and compliance webpage for New Mexico. Those entries include inspection reports, information requests and enforcement documents dating back to 2012.

Oil and gas-related enforcement entries bounced around in the single digits before peaking in the first two years of the administration of President Joe Biden: 26 entries for 2021 and 24 for 2022. Ten entries were listed for 2025, most in the opening months of the Trump administration before the agency announced a 23% reduction in its workforce. Eight were recorded in 2026 through Nov. 4.

Cliff Villa, a professor of law at the University of New Mexico School of Law, said he’s noticed a change at the agency.

“EPA has lost a lot of people, including a lot of institutional knowledge,” Villa said. “That’s not easy to replace.” Before joining the university, Villa worked for more than 20 years as an EPA attorney under both Democratic and Republican administrations.

Oil and gas revenues have swelled New Mexico’s coffers to record levels in recent years. At the same time, such operations have directly and indirectly generated record amounts of hard-to-dispose-of oilfield wastewater, raised the specter of $1.6 billion in cleanup costs for abandoned wells and fouled the air in the oilfields. That last issue — cleaning New Mexico’s air — has been the EPA’s main goal in New Mexico in recent years, and the need for help is reflected in how oilfield pollution cases can tie up state resources for years.

Capital & Main sent questions about the declining numbers of enforcement and compliance documents to the EPA’s regional office in Dallas, which oversees New Mexico operations. They were answered by Michael Bastasch, deputy director for regional media and programs in the EPA’s Washington headquarters. He called questions about declining numbers “a baseless narrative.

“EPA enforcement has not declined,” he said.

“EPA has lost a lot of people, including a lot of institutional knowledge.”

~ Cliff Villa, professor of law at University of New Mexico.

Bastasch put the responsibility for policing the oil and gas industry on New Mexico: “New Mexico has delegated authority under the Clean Air Act, which means they take the lead on air quality enforcement within their borders.”

Historically, air quality issues have been the primary cause for EPA oil and gas investigations in New Mexico, and the New Mexico Environment Department does have an agreement — known as a State Implementation Plan — that allows it to take the lead on federal Clean Air Act investigations. Those investigations are generally conducted in partnership with the EPA, not in lieu of the EPA.

James Kenney, the New Mexico Environment Department secretary, worked for years at the EPA before beginning his state job under Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham. In a 2022 interview with Capital & Main, Kenney said the EPA wasn’t allowed in New Mexico under the previous governor, Republican Susana Martinez, and “the first thing we did is invite EPA in.”

The working relationship has changed since then.

“Notably, [the Environment Department] has seen a decrease in joint enforcement actions,” said Drew Goretzka, director of communications at the New Mexico Environment Department. He said that past work took the form of joint inspections, flyovers using optical gas imaging and complicated enforcement actions — areas in which the EPA is able to bring its much larger workforce and money to bear.

For example, in 2019 and 2020, the EPA conducted airborne inspections of New Mexico’s oilfields on behalf of the state. The flights uncovered dozens of leaking facilities, though it resulted in only slow-rolling enforcement actions against a few of the polluting companies.

Asked if flights might return in the future, Bastasch said, “EPA does not comment on whether inspections and compliance monitoring activities will occur.”

Kyle Tisdel, senior attorney and climate and energy program director at the Western Environmental Law Center, said the fallout of decreasing EPA enforcement further burdens state agencies “both in identifying the wells and operators chronically violating emissions standards, and then prosecuting those violations and holding individual operators responsible.”

Goretzka also said that the EPA’s “retreat” adds further compliance and enforcement costs to the state.

“EPA’s lack of enforcement in the Permian Basin makes it more difficult to protect New Mexicans’ air quality.”

~ Drew Goretzka, director of communications at the New Mexico Environment Department.

“EPA’s lack of enforcement in the Permian Basin makes it more difficult to protect New Mexicans’ air quality,” he said.

Recent studies linked oil and gas operations to radioactive airborne plumes and other air pollution in the Permian Basin, the nation’s largest oil field. Asked about the findings, Bastasch dismissed work that was “based on studies performed on data from the Biden Administration that purport to show that air pollution in New Mexico comes from New Mexico.”

Bastasch’s responses exhibited a recurring anti-Biden administration theme, with answers that regularly name-checked the former president.

When asked if the reductions reflect the Trump administration’s plan to “unleash American energy,” he said, “Enforcement will be consistent with the law and the rule of law, unlike during the Biden Administration.”

Bastasch did not respond when asked how or when the Biden administration’s actions were inconsistent with the law.

While oil and gas enforcement numbers have dropped, the EPA has not been idle in other areas in New Mexico. In May, the agency issued around 60 warnings to small water co-ops across the state for failing to file paperwork identifying the kinds of pipes in their systems, a requirement under the Safe Water Drinking Act.

Bastasch said that the EPA concluded more than 2,300 civil enforcement cases between Jan. 20, 2025, and Jan. 19, 2026, “a ten year high — over 400 cases more than in the final year of the Biden Administration.” But those are national figures and not specific to New Mexico.

The EPA began promoting the numbers in March. Since then, outside watchdogs have called the numbers misleading — primarily because the EPA under Trump is taking credit for work done during the Biden administration.

For example, in early September, the EPA issued Compliance Agreements and Final Orders against two of New Mexico’s top-10 oil and gas producers: Chevron USA Inc. for $440,341 and Permian Resources Operating LLC for $691,253. The cases reflect violations found during on-site inspections in 2024 during the Biden administration.

“These fines are not surprising, nor is the fact that the violations were identified by the Biden administration,” said Tisdel, the Western Environmental Law Center lawyer.

He added that state and federal agencies rely on self-reporting by oil and gas companies for day-to-day monitoring. But, “as these fines indicate, there can be substantial gaps between what is reported by industry and the emission violations found here,” he said.

The EPA has worked in New Mexico this year, too. The agency entered into expedited settlement agreements with Occidental Permian Ltd. at its North Hobbs Plant and with Enterprise Products Partners LP at its Dark Horse Treating Facility for not filing required risk management plans on time. Those plans, updated every five years, are used to alert first responders and nearby residents to possible environmental threats.

Settlement agreements are a quick way for companies to resolve violations by paying a fine and promising to fix the underlying problem. According to the agreement documents, Occidental Permian filed its plan a week late in May and paid a $1,600 fine. Enterprise Products Partners filed roughly three weeks late in June and paid a $2,000 fine.

What comes next for the EPA and New Mexico is an open question.

“It will be great again,” predicted Villa, the University of New Mexico professor. “In the meantime, there are many other opportunities for enforcement, including states and tribes and local governments and non-governmental organizations.”

“But my sense is that out of the ruins of this moment, there will be opportunity.”

~ Kyle Tisdel, climate and energy program director at the Western Environmental Law Center.

Villa also highlighted provisions in federal statutes allowing citizen lawsuits where people and organizations can sue companies or the federal government for violating air and water regulations.

In 2022, the conservation group WildEarth Guardians sued OXY USA and OXY USA WTP LP — both subsidiaries of Occidental Petroleum Corp. — over violations of the Clean Air Act. The group said the suit resulted in millions of dollars’ worth of facility upgrades, a $500,000 civil penalty and another $500,000 penalty “to support air quality and public health improvement projects in southeast New Mexico” that eventually resulted in a new mobile air monitoring station for the New Mexico Environment Department.

The dramatic changes at the EPA “won’t simply be reversed by a future administration,” Tisdel cautioned. “But my sense is that out of the ruins of this moment, there will be opportunity … to imagine a future and regulatory and enforcement framework that is commensurate to the mounting crises we face.”

“It does create opportunities, though, for students who are in school today, including my own students,” Villa said. “They will have opportunities to be a part of a rebuilding of the federal government. And I see my job right now as a teacher as helping prepare them for that rebuilding.”

text:
As demand for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) continues to grow and BMW Group transitions towards production of more electric vehicles, the automaker is taking a "local for local" approach to sourcing the sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries used in its Neue Klasse vehicles.

Combining regional supply chains with a globally diversified supplier network, BMW Group has announced new contracts with two additional cell suppliers to localise battery production in both Europe and the US.

Read more: How nearshoring and battery localisation are reshaping Europe’s EV supply chain amid shifting demand, Chinese competition, and policy shifts

With battery investments in flux, Europe’s OEMs push for local supply chains amid geopolitical shifts and Chinese EV competition.

Samsung SDI will be added to the list of manufacturers supplying BMW Group with Gen6 batteries in Europe, as well as existing suppliers CATL and EVE Energy. Meanwhile in the US, a new contract will see these batteries also supplied by LG Energy Solution. According to BMW Group, these additional manufacturers will supply the group from their established plants in the respective regions from the late 2020s onwards.

"Our global partner network with leading cell manufacturers ensures that we have a resilient, flexible and competitive battery cell supply,” commented Hendrik Lang, head of purchasing and quality of high-voltage batteries at BMW.

In addition, Nicolai Martin, member of the board of management of BMW responsible for purchasing and supplier network, noted that diversifying procurement is an integral part of the group's purchasing strategy. He emphasised that being successful in different markets around the world and ensuring the global competitiveness of its products are top priorities from BMW Group.

"To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets," said Martin. "Through our battery cell partnerships, we are actively strengthening value creation in Europe and the US."

Local battery assembly

BMW's "local for local" approach extends beyond battery sourcing to battery assembly too. Currently, production of BMW's Gen6 high-voltage batteries takes place at five recently built production facilities strategically located near its vehicle plants in regions around the world.

By locating these battery assembly facilities in close proximity to existing plants, BMW Group has said it is able to strengthen regional infrastructure and existing facilities, while helping to secure jobs.

The group also noted that this strategy allows it to reduce the distances between its suppliers, its battery facilities and its vehicle plants. In doing so, BMW Group can keep down transport costs, avoid carbon emissions from long-distance shipments and limit the group's exposure to transport-related disruptions.

Upskilling for the whole battery life cycle

Alongside the diversification of suppliers and its investment in building regional battery ecosystems, BMW Group has also focused on building comprehensive in-house expertise in the development, production and recycling of battery cells.

As part of this effort, the group has established a range of competence centres across the Germany state of Bavaria, each exploring different parts of the battery life cycle. For example, at BMW's Battery Cell Competence Center (BCCC) in Munich, experts are exploring new cell technologies for future high-voltage batteries.

And at the group's Cell Manufacturing Competence Center (CMCC) in Parsdorf, research is focused on methods of producing the highest-quality battery cells with the most efficient use of resources.

BMW Group is also working with its partner Encory to build and operate a new Cell Recycling Competence Center (CRCC) in Salching. Here, valuable raw materials will be recovered and reintegrated into the group's production process, using an "innovative direct recycling concept" that BMW Group has developed.

title: Ford tested its Mach-E batteries. How they did after 100000 miles - Detroit Free Press
description:
Ford's data was inspired by a customer who drove over 400,000 miles on the original Mach-E battery.
Ford Motor Co. leaders want the world to know that the automaker's electric vehicle batteries last a really long time.
Ford said as of August this year, across its full 36,000 2021 Mach-E lineup in the U.S. and Canada, its EV batteries maintain an average of 90% health at 100,000 miles.
"Except for early Nissan Leafs that had air-cooled batteries and a lot of early degradation, most EVs have somewhere between 90% and 95% capacity at 100,000 miles.
Bley said Ford's data showed that more than 2,000 of its Mach-Es on the road today have passed 100,000 miles, averaging better than 91% battery health, and more than 30 have passed 200,000 miles while averaging 88%.
text:
Concerns about EV battery longevity and replacement cost remain a significant hurdle for many potential buyers.

Ford's data was inspired by a customer who drove over 400,000 miles on the original Mach-E battery.

Industry experts note that this level of battery durability is impressive but standard across most modern electric vehicles.

Ford Motor Co. leaders want the world to know that the automaker's electric vehicle batteries last a really long time.

But that fact doesn't necessarily make Ford a standout in the car industry where battery technology has advanced across the board where most automakers can assure consumers that, if you buy an EV, you won't need to replace its battery for hundreds of thousands of miles, industry experts said.

"Pretty much all EVs are connected and (automakers) collect telemetry data on things like battery state of health and charging patterns in addition to capturing the data when cars come in for service. So they all have a pretty good idea of how batteries are holding up," Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market research at Telemetry, told the Detroit Free Press. "They typically have 8-10 year/100,000 mile warranties on the battery, so everyone wants to make sure they'll actually last that long."

So on Nov. 9, Ford decided to share its tests publicly to show that its batteries do last that long.

The Dearborn-based automaker issued a media release and published a blog titled: "Five years in, Mustang Mach-E battery data shows what real world electric vehicle durability looks like." The blog points to customer David Blenkle, a Santa Cruz, Californian who runs a small private car service, for inspiring Ford's battery study. Blenkle has driven a whopping 400,000-plus miles in his 2022 Mustang Mach-E on the original battery.

"His battery health has remained strong through unusually high-mileage use," Kevin Vander Laan, Ford's technical leader of high-voltage battery cells and systems, wrote in the blog of Blenke. "His experience gave our team a chance to compare one exceptional ownership case with what we are seeing across the broader fleet. The bigger question was if David’s experience reflected a broader pattern. So, we decided to look back at the Mustang Mach-E owners who started it all: the Class of 2021."

Ford said it found that Blenkle was not an outlier. Other Mach-E owners who clocked high mileage over five years of ownership also retained significant battery strength. Ford said as of August this year, across its full 36,000 2021 Mach-E lineup in the U.S. and Canada, its EV batteries maintain an average of 90% health at 100,000 miles. That means the high-voltage battery pack has lost 10% of its original energy storage capacity, but can still hold and deliver 90% of the range it had when the car was new.

It's impressive, but it is also industry standard, experts said.

"While I haven't seen much third-party data on Mach-E battery durability, other sources have published lots of data on how batteries are holding up, notably recurrentauto.com," Abuelsamid said. "Except for early Nissan Leafs that had air-cooled batteries and a lot of early degradation, most EVs have somewhere between 90% and 95% capacity at 100,000 miles. So Ford's numbers are right in the ballpark."

Expert: Ford's results are likely legit

In fact, Abuelsamid said the Mach-E uses basically the same LG batteries found in a lot of other vehicles. He noted that outside of "some fires triggered by manufacturing flaws," such as the Chevrolet Bolt and Porsche Taycan, "the (batteries) are pretty durable."

While having a manufacturer rate its own products is not the best measure of quality, it's a starting point for reassuring consumers that EVs are durable, Sam Fiorani, vice president of global vehicle forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions, told the Detroit Free Press.

"Among the biggest issues for consumers contemplating an EV purchase is the cost and longevity of the battery," Fiorani said. "The fear that a battery will have a catastrophic problem requiring a fix potentially costing over $10,000 is holding many people back from making the plunge. With so many EVs on the road today, proof of how they are holding up can now be measured and the results used to calm the fears of buyers."

Fiorani said increasingly there are independent companies conducting similar battery testing and comparing the results across brands. Therefore, Ford releasing its data publicly means that "if these outside companies provide results dramatically different than that of the manufacturer, like Ford, it can result in loss of consumer trust. But, in this case, it’s unlikely that Ford is putting its thumb on the scale."

Fiorani added that studies from AVILOO in Europe — an Australian technology company specializing in battery diagnostics — and Standford University in the United States have provided similar industry-wide results, proving that modern EV batteries do not degrade as quickly as the industry initially expected.

"Degradation of about 2% per year falls in line with Ford’s results," Fiorani said.

Mach-E drivers nearly made it to Neptune

Ford spokesman Jake Bley told the Detroit Free Press that the automaker validated its battery health data internally with its high-voltage battery engineering team and then had it "reviewed by peers and confirmed for public release."

Ford said its 36,000 Mach-E's have driven a collective total of about two billion all-electric miles across the United States and Canada in the past five years — that is almost enough miles to reach the planet Neptune.

Bley said Ford's data showed that more than 2,000 of its Mach-Es on the road today have passed 100,000 miles, averaging better than 91% battery health, and more than 30 have passed 200,000 miles while averaging 88%.

Most of the vehicles fall between 87% to 97% battery health, the average being 92%, indicating to Ford engineers that there is a consistent and positive pattern across Ford's real-world fleet.

Ford's Vander Laan said this data matters to Ford primarily because "long-term battery health remains one of the biggest questions for many people considering an electric vehicle, and real-world data like this helps make that conversation more concrete."

In the meantime, Ford uses field data such as this to inform current and future electric vehicle programs. Ford is preparing to launch its new Universal Electric Vehicle platform at its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. The first EV off that new architecture will be the all-electric midsize pickup, Fathom. It will be followed by a family of more EVs, and they will use a different battery than the LG in the Mach-E, Abuelsamid said.

"Mach-E uses LG pouch cells with NMC cathode chemistry," Abuelsamid said. "UEV is using prismatic cells with LFP cathode. LFP should last five to 10 times as long."

Until then, Ford's Vander Laan offered a few habits that help support long-term battery health. First is charging on Level 2 at home for daily driving and saving DC fast charging for the days you need it. Also, help manage temperature extremes when you can such as parking in the shade in the summer. Finally, follow the charge-level recommendations in the Ford App for your specific vehicle. The recommendations are designed for that car's battery system.

title: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's speech at the Clean Energy Transition & Electrification ...
description:
And the question for all countries is: do we learn the lessons of this age, or do we stick our heads in the sand?
And it’s right to say it’s only possible because of the extraordinary transformation we’ve seen over the last two decades in the price of clean energy.
But we also recognise that it’s in our self-interest as a country for all countries to invest in electrification.
And I just want to say one very simple thing: as a Foreign Minister, this is a national security issue.
And it’s time that all Foreign Ministers, Prime Ministers, saw it as a national security issue, because whether it’s food security, infrastructure security, population displacement, these have profound national security implications.
text:
It is right to start with what our populations are seeing, which is more conflict across the world than at any time since World War II, climate breakdown affecting so many countries, and the cost-of-living crisis in food and fuel prices.

And the question for all countries is: do we learn the lessons of this age, or do we stick our heads in the sand?

And we need to learn the lessons.

The first and most profound lesson, and we’ve seen it with the Iran war, with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, is there can’t be security while you are dependent on fossil fuels, because you are subject to the fossil-fuel rollercoaster that you don’t control from geopolitical conflict.

For Britain, half of our recessions since the 1970s have been caused by fossil-fuel crises, and obviously people are being hit very hard.

Even the world’s largest fossil-fuel producer, the United States, is not immune. Vice President Vance has said the Iran war has had real effects on voters.

And what’s true for the US is even more true for fossil-fuel importers, representing 75% of the world’s population.

So, lesson one: don’t believe that fossil-fuel reliance can give us security, because the facts show otherwise.

Second, unlike in the past, there is an alternative to fossil fuels: clean-energy electrification.

I applaud the Turkish Presidency for their vision in putting this idea at the centre of COP31. And it’s right to say it’s only possible because of the extraordinary transformation we’ve seen over the last two decades in the price of clean energy.

And that’s thanks to many people around the room, public and private sectors working together. Costs are plummeting.

The UK is determined to lead by example.

We have a mission for clean power by 2030, new petrol and diesel cars phased out by 2030, and a Warm Homes Plan to electrify heating.

But we also recognise that it’s in our self-interest as a country for all countries to invest in electrification.

So we are announcing an investment of £200 million over the next four years through the Private Infrastructure Development Group, PIDG, which will help to mobilise an estimated $1 billion per year in private capital to support climate-resilient infrastructure in emerging economies across Africa and Asia.

My third and final point is the other part of the perfect storm, which is climate breakdown.

And I just want to say one very simple thing: as a Foreign Minister, this is a national security issue.

And it’s time that all Foreign Ministers, Prime Ministers, saw it as a national security issue, because whether it’s food security, infrastructure security, population displacement, these have profound national security implications.

And resilience will be very much part of our chairmanship of the G20 next year.

The final thing I’ll say: it’s very inspiring to see all of the people in this room and at this COP. Not just because it’s old friends, but because it is a sign of multilateralism: countries working together in their own interests.

And we owe it to the citizens of our countries to do this, to learn the right lessons, and to understand that electrification is the future.

We must make the era of clean-energy electrification come of age.

Thank you so much.

text:
A California company’s plans for a medical radiopharmaceuticals plant in the central Indiana LEAP District is facing questions over whether it could possibly open the door for a nuclear power generation site.

A contract between the Indiana Economic Development Corp. and a subsidiary of Oklo Inc. for land purchases lists several possible uses for the site near Lebanon, including “nuclear power generation, radioisotope production, research and development.”

Democratic legislators challenged an IEDC official during a State Budget Committee meeting Tuesday over the company’s intentions during discussion of the agency’s request for $20 million toward expanding the LEAP District by 185 acres for the project.

Mark Wasky, the IEDC’s senior vice president, told the committee that discussions with Oklo had “focused on radioisotopes,” which are medications that contain a small amount of a radioactive substance.

That did not satisfy Democratic legislators about the future options for the company that describes itself on its website as an “advanced nuclear technology company developing fast fission power plants” along with “building a domestic supply chain for critical isotopes and advanced nuclear fuel recycling capabilities.”

“Can you look us in the eye and say that you’re not going to come back over here and tell us that there will be nuclear generation discussion by that project that could feed into data centers into the LEAP project?” asked Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis.

Wasky replied that nuclear power plants had not been discussed with the IEDC.

“I can’t say today whether or not those conversations may occur in the future, but we have not had any conversations about building power to serve the data center within the LEAP District,” Wasky said.

A few LEAP District opponents protested outside Tuesday’s committee meeting. The district aimed at attracting high-tech businesses now spans some 6,700 acres and has faced persistent public criticism as the state has poured about $1 billion into its development.

Wasky said Oklo’s project would still need to gain approval from Lebanon city and zoning officials before proceeding with construction.

But Rep. Ed DeLaney, D-Indianapolis, criticized what he described as insufficient public disclosure about the development proposal, which was listed on the Budget Committee’s agenda as “Project Phoenix.”

“This is not what people would call a confidence building method and that’s a real problem,” DeLaney told Wasky. “We need confidence in the IEDC.”

Santa Clara, California-based Oklo told the Capital Chronicle that it is considering the LEAP District for a potential “isotope production and processing facility focused initially on producing materials used in targeted cancer treatments.”

“We’re still evaluating the project and engaging with the local community, and no final commitment to build in Indiana has been made,” Oklo spokeswoman Bonita Chester said in an email.

Chester did not address a question about the possibility of electricity generation at the site.

The Budget Committee voted 4-1 to approve the IEDC’s request, with support coming from Sens. Ryan Misher, R-Mishawaka, and David Niezgodski, D-South Bend; Rep. Jeff Thompson, R-Lizton, and State Budget Director Chad Ranney.

Rep. Greg Porter, D-Indianapolis, voted against approval, joining the objections from Qaddoura and DeLaney, who are non-voting members of the committee.

Porter said he saw no harm in waiting until the committee’s next meeting in December to take action for greater transparency.

“I’m asking that we stop this or slow it down,” Porter said. “They can come back and look at it again.”

This story has been updated with comment from Oklo Inc.

text:
The old saying, “Waste not, want not,” rings especially true in America's Battery Belt.

Today, roughly 10% of the material used to make an electric-vehicle battery ends up as manufacturing scrap. But a proposed $110 million project aims to turn that scrap back into material for producing new batteries right here in the U.S. — and do so in as little as seven days.

Behind the effort are two NJIT alumni at Princeton NuEnergy (PNE): co-founder and CEO Chao Yan (M.S. '13, Ph.D. '17) and founding partner and chief operating officer Peng Zhao (M.S. '13).

Since its startup beginnings in 2019, PNE has grown into a pioneer in direct battery recycling — reusing valuable cathode material from scrap instead of breaking it down to recover its metals — just as U.S. battery manufacturing has taken off.

The company has now been selected to negotiate for $50 million in U.S. Department of Energy grant support for a planned facility capable of rejuvenating 3,000 metric tons of cathode material annually.

“No one has moved direct recycling to this scale yet,” Zhao said. “We're bringing this technology to the commercial world with this first-of-its-kind facility. The goal is to build a true domestic closed loop — keeping these critical battery materials in the U.S. and bringing down their cost.”

Cathode material in manufacturing scrap can be essentially brand new, Zhao says, but conventional recycling shreds it into “black mass” to recover metals such as lithium, nickel and cobalt.

Zhao estimates U.S. manufacturing scrap and end-of-life batteries generate roughly 100,000 metric tons of battery waste annually, much of it requiring further processing overseas.

PNE's patented Cathode-to-Cathode® process instead uses low-temperature plasma to clean and restore cathode material for reuse.

“Think about it like you have a dirty spoon,” Zhao explained. “The traditional recycling process is like taking that spoon, melting it down and extracting the metals one by one, then sending them overseas to make a new spoon and importing it back so you can use it. What we do is more like simply putting the spoon in a dishwasher. The cathode material is still good — it just has impurities. We use plasma to clean the surface, remove those impurities, polish it and use it again right away.”

Building the Closed Loop

Above: Engineers oversee battery recycling operations at Princeton NuEnergy's facility in Chester, South Carolina. Credit: Princeton NuEnergy.

PNE plans to save U.S. battery scrap from that globe-spanning journey. Construction of the proposed facility is targeted for early 2027, with the roughly 30-month project expected to begin operating in 2029.

“Battery factories produce manufacturing scrap every day,” Zhao said. “We take that scrap, rejuvenate the cathode material and give it back to our customer to make a new battery. This closed loop is within the United States.”

A DOE-backed study with Argonne National Laboratory found PNE's rejuvenated cathode material could cost about 45% less than comparable virgin material.

“It’s also a national security issue,” Zhao said. “If you fully rely on foreign countries for critical battery materials and something happens geopolitically, how can you build your EV? How can you build your data center? How can you build your defense applications?”

“A lot of direct recycling is still at the lab scale,” Zhao said. “Some approaches use organic solvents that become difficult to handle safely at this scale; others are very expensive. We use low-temperature plasma to remove impurities from cathode active materials, reducing costs and minimizing waste.”

Yan said scaling the technology comes down in part to how PNE builds its facilities. More than 90% of the equipment is commercially available, while the company's proprietary components are designed in modules that can be replicated as production needs grow.

“Depending on the capacity required, we replicate these modules and deploy them in parallel to meet each facility’s production needs,” Yan said. “This modular design allows us to deploy the technology quickly at different scales to meet customers’ varying capacity needs.”

PNE's next Cathode-to-Cathode® facility would also allow other battery manufacturers to validate the company's process before potentially bringing it to their own sites.

For Yan, reaching 3,000 metric tons annually would mark a significant step toward bringing direct recycling into widespread industrial use.

“This facility has the potential to redefine how critical battery materials are recovered and reintroduced into the U.S. supply chain,” Yan said. “More importantly, it establishes a commercially viable model we can replicate across the country.”

PNE plans as many as 10 production lines around the country over the next decade, totaling 30,000 metric tons of annual capacity.

“This is a seed,” Zhao said. “We need to let the seed grow, then go to 10 branches.”

It's a scale far beyond what Zhao envisioned when Yan, whom he knew from their days sharing a dorm at NJIT, began working on his plasma-based purification technology under chemistry professor Lev Krasnoperov nearly a decade ago.

Zhao had taken a different path. An NJIT career fair internship with Panasonic North America became a 10-year career, eventually taking him to a senior manager role in technology commercialization at the Panasonic Innovation Center in Harrison, New Jersey.

When Yan approached him around 2018 about using plasma to recycle batteries, Zhao saw its potential but wasn't convinced the market was ready.

By 2020, the market was catching up. Major automakers were accelerating their electric-vehicle plans and U.S. battery manufacturing was expanding. Zhao left Panasonic the following year to join PNE full time.

Since then, PNE has built toward commercial scale — from early pilot work to its direct recycling line in Texas and a commercial-scale black mass production facility in South Carolina. Zhao said the company has also raised $38 million in equity financing and received or been selected for more than $73 million in federal grant support, including the $50 million DOE funding still under negotiation.

The $110 million facility would be its biggest step yet.

“I always believe we want to do the right thing at the right time with the right people,” Zhao said. “Right now, I feel we have all three.”

title: Prime Minister hails major investment in UK renewables - GOV.UK
description:

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain.
Because for me, a clean energy future is one that brings down bills.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: This is another vote of confidence in British homegrown, clean energy.
Investment in offshore wind and clean power is creating quality jobs and rebuilding industry, while delivering the clean power we need to lower bills and reach net zero.
text:
Thousands of jobs will be supported as two major offshore wind projects mark progress towards delivering clean homegrown energy for millions of homes, ahead of the Prime Minister’s travel to the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Türkiye.

Energy company RWE, together with global investment firm KKR, have announced a total investment of £12 billion, believed to be the biggest of its kind in UK history to date. It will give the green light to its Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind farms, set to be operational by 2030 and delivering clean, secure, homegrown power to homes and businesses that will protect families from global fossil fuel price shocks.

The investment comes as the Prime Minister heads to the COP31 summit, underlining how Britain’s action on climate change and clean energy is bringing good, skilled jobs and new opportunities for local people in industrial and coastal communities across the country.

On top of bolstering the UK’s green energy future, the investment will support more than 2,400 jobs during construction and operation, and once operational, the wind farms will have the capacity to supply the equivalent of around three million UK homes. Alongside making an important contribution to domestic energy security, clean, homegrown power will protect the UK from global energy shocks raising energy prices and bring down bills for good.

The decision marks a major milestone for the project, with the developers now making their final investment commitment to deliver the projects. Onshore works are already well advanced, with construction offshore set to begin in early 2027.

The financing for these projects includes a £1 billion investment from the UK’s National Wealth Fund - the UK’s publicly-owned policy bank that aims to drive more than £100 billion of finance into the UK economy. This investment, the National Wealth Fund’s largest in offshore wind to date, demonstrates how the right use of public money can help unlock private investment and generate a return for the taxpayer, as well as powering homes with clean homegrown power Britain controls.

The government recently announced a new, additional Energy Wealth Fund to take this mission further. The fund will be linked to the Government’s future revenues from the North Sea, investing in renewable and low carbon energy projects and support the net zero transition – starting with a £2 billion injection of funding.

On top of this, Scottish-headquartered SSE has announced that the latest phase of its major offshore wind farm, Berwick Bank B, will back 2,677 skilled jobs in manufacturing, engineering and project delivery across the north of England and Scotland, with the company contracting Siemens Energy for the manufacturing of wind turbines and substation platforms. This includes the creation of 130 new project delivery roles in Glasgow and Montrose.

At its full capacity, Berwick Bank, off the East coast of Scotland, could become the world’s largest offshore wind farm, capable of meeting more than 6% of current UK electricity demand. Its delivery would strengthen long-term energy security and help deliver the homegrown, affordable energy the country needs.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain. And it is great news for billpayers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.

With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain’s future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings.

Our National Wealth Fund means that public investment is working alongside private capital to build homegrown energy and bring a return for the taxpayer. Because for me, a clean energy future is one that brings down bills.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said:

This is another vote of confidence in British homegrown, clean energy.

Investment in offshore wind and clean power is creating quality jobs and rebuilding industry, while delivering the clean power we need to lower bills and reach net zero.

As the world gathers at COP31, Britain is leading from the front as a renewable energy powerhouse, turning the fight against climate change into a brighter future for British companies, industrial communities, and future generations.

CEO of RWE AG Markus Krebber said:

Together with KKR, we are delivering two of the UK’s largest offshore wind projects, strengthening domestic electricity generation and making an important contribution to the country’s long-term energy security.

Co-Head of European Infrastructure at KKR, Vincent Policard, continued:

Our work with RWE demonstrates how private capital can help turn the UK’s energy ambitions into reality, supporting economic growth and delivering critical infrastructure capable of powering around three million UK homes.

SSE Chief Executive Martin Pibworth said:

This is public-private partnership in action. Clear political direction, matched by businesses prepared to invest, is translating into real-world investment in British jobs, skills and manufacturing. From Hull, Newcastle and Manchester to Glasgow and Montrose, you can see what that means for communities across the country.

Berwick Bank B is a huge opportunity for the UK and, working with Siemens Energy, we’re backing those industrial capabilities while building the infrastructure needed for a more affordable and secure energy system.

And it’s a powerful and timely example as world leaders gather at COP31. There is already a clear acknowledgement that clean electrification is the route to decarbonisation, greater energy security and sustainably lower bills. We hope to see the ambition needed to turn that recognition into more investment like this.

The announcement is part of the government’s efforts towards a more affordable, clean energy system, with stronger consumer protections, greater public control and communities sharing in the benefits of renewable and low carbon power.

Last week saw the introduction of the Energy Independence Bill, a down payment on reforms that will put affordability at the heart of the energy system and unlock barriers to delivering clean power.

Measures include bringing rogue operators under greater public oversight, strengthening protections for households and businesses, and giving local people more control over and a greater stake in the clean energy projects built around them.

The government is protecting households from rising costs through removing standing charges and giving households £100 to help them pay their bills this winter, and putting Britain in control of its energy future, through a fair transition to green energy and seizing on the opportunities presented by renewables.

title: MAN electric truck feeds 350 kW back to the grid in SPIRIT-E bidirectional charging project
description:
Led by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), the project tested bidirectional charging at freight forwarder Spedition Schmid’s depot in Regensburg, Germany, from August 2023 to October 2026.
Bidirectional charging functions were developed and tested on the MAN eTGX electric truck and on mobile and stationary charging systems from project partner SBRS.
Using the Equigy platform, the project also demonstrated how electric trucks can help grid operators ease bottlenecks in the electricity network.
The partners say bidirectional charging is particularly attractive for trucks with regular depot dwell times and annual mileage below 100,000 km.
“Through SPIRIT-E, the MAN eTGX has demonstrated that it can serve as a bidirectional energy storage system,” said Georg Grüneißl, Head of Product Strategy at MAN Truck & Bus.
text:
The SPIRIT-E research project, which includes MAN Truck & Bus and Traton R&D, has shown that electric trucks can store energy and feed it back into local and public power grids.

Led by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), the project tested bidirectional charging at freight forwarder Spedition Schmid’s depot in Regensburg, Germany, from August 2023 to October 2026.

Bidirectional charging functions were developed and tested on the MAN eTGX electric truck and on mobile and stationary charging systems from project partner SBRS. The partners coordinated the interfaces between the vehicle, charging station, charging operator control software, site energy management system, electricity trader and grid operator.

The project implemented ISO 15118-20, the standard for communication between vehicles and charging infrastructure during charging and discharging. An eTGX with 480 kWh of usable energy fed electricity through a bidirectional DC charging station at up to 350 kW into the depot’s energy network (vehicle-to-site, or V2S) and the public grid (V2G). The truck also charged other vehicles from its battery (V2V).

In a test environment from software company PowerBot, the partners simulated an electric truck buying electricity when prices are low and selling it when they are high. Using the Equigy platform, the project also demonstrated how electric trucks can help grid operators ease bottlenecks in the electricity network.

Whether bidirectional charging pays off depends on factors including operating profiles, annual mileage, dwell times, battery size, electricity prices, grid charges, on-site power generation and grid connection capacity. The partners say bidirectional charging is particularly attractive for trucks with regular depot dwell times and annual mileage below 100,000 km. According to project calculations, average energy-cost savings are around 10%, and up to 20% under optimal conditions.

“Through SPIRIT-E, the MAN eTGX has demonstrated that it can serve as a bidirectional energy storage system,” said Georg Grüneißl, Head of Product Strategy at MAN Truck & Bus. “We are now working to bring this feature into series production. At the same time, we are developing a consulting concept for our customers that will help them unlock the full potential of this rolling power bank.”
