6 Discussion

The evidence reviewed points to multiple transition pathways rather than a uniform regional trajectory. High-utilization commercial fleets can be attractive candidates for early electrification where operating patterns, vehicle supply, financing and energy infrastructure align. Yet commercial viability cannot be assumed from vehicle utilization alone, and public transport, passenger vehicles and other fuel options remain relevant in different contexts. The principal contribution of the review is a structured comparison of policy questions and implementation constraints, while acknowledging that inconsistent country-level outcome data limit stronger claims about comparative effectiveness.

6.1 Interpretation and policy implications

Cross-border trade and regional value chains may help expand markets for vehicles, batteries and components, but the benefits depend on rules of origin, local productive capacity, customs administration, market size and distribution of gains. AfCFTA-related recommendations should therefore be framed as policy options to evaluate rather than as guaranteed routes to lower prices or rapid industrial upgrading. The available evidence is stronger for identifying coordination needs than for quantifying the effects of specific tariff structures on EV adoption. Accordingly, the policy options discussed below reflect candidate strategies for evaluation under specific country conditions rather than prescriptive or universally proven interventions.

6.1.1 Fiscal restructuring

To catalyze domestic assembly ecosystems, national fiscal frameworks must decisively prioritize completely knocked-down (CKD) kits over completely built-up (CBU) imports. Empirical evidence from India demonstrates that CKD-based localized manufacturing fundamentally builds component supplier capacity ( Athukorala and Veeramani, 2019). When combined with sufficient domestic market scale, this operational shift drives long-term export competitiveness. Furthermore, historical industrial transitions in Australia and South Africa show how strategically phased tariff reductions on CKD inputs attract sustained capital, establishing a solid foundation for technology transfer ( Pursell, 2001). Moving forward, regional policymakers must design fiscal transitions that cushion immediate revenue losses from reduced import duties while rewarding tangible local value addition under AfCFTA guidelines ( Edwards et al., 2024; Fouda Ekobena et al., 2021; Ajibo and Kaime, 2025). Striking this delicate balance is vital to protect nascent domestic industries without fostering monopolistic environments that stifle technological innovation.

6.1.2 Vehicle import duties, industrial incentives, and customs administration

Establishing transparent, predictable tariff structures is essential to support complex e-mobility supply chains. Relevant ASEAN deployment models illustrate how differentiated excise regimes successfully distinguish between CKD, semi-knocked down (SKD), and CBU imports ( Preece, 2015), directly incentivizing industrial upgrading and workforce upskilling ( Preece, 2016). In South Africa, specific policy mechanisms like duty credits and targeted export facilitation instruments historically triggered significant automotive expansion ( Damoense, 2005), offering a valuable blueprint for broader EV integration ( Madani and Mas-Guix, 2011). Nevertheless, restructured tariff classifications must adhere strictly to multilateral World Trade Organization legal frameworks to prevent protracted international trade litigation ( Charnovitz, 2011). Deploying digital, blockchain-backed customs tracking can further reduce administrative friction and combat border corruption, ensuring fiscal incentives effectively reach target industries ( Edwards et al., 2024; Ajibo and Kaime, 2025).

6.1.3 Secondhand vehicle policy

The unmanaged influx of aging, highly polluting ICE vehicles severely compromises local EV manufacturing viability and continental environmental objectives. Historical automotive policy gaps in Nigeria demonstrate how inconsistent secondhand import controls entrench foreign market dominance while stifling indigenous manufacturing capacity ( Ugwueze et al., 2020). Implementing unified Regional Economic Community (REC) frameworks that strictly enforce vehicle age caps is essential for market health ( Saraf, 2016). These restrictions must be combined with stringent baseline emissions standards across all border entry points ( Tai and Ku, 2013). Harmonizing these measures effectively prevents regional carbon dumping, eliminates regulatory arbitrage, and accelerates the transition toward cleaner, locally assembled electric fleets. To mitigate social resistance from low-income consumers dependent on cheap transport, import restrictions must be coupled with accessible vehicle scrappage programs and affordable financing for local EV alternatives ( Knobloch et al., 2020; Faria et al., 2013).

6.1.4 Informal sector participation

Achieving an equitable transition requires actively integrating informal transport operators and independent mechanics into formalized EV value chains. Specialized Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) curricula focused on high-voltage system maintenance are critical to building local technical capacity ( Ariyani et al., 2023), ensuring baseline electrical and operational safety across the evolving sector ( Tangkitvanich and Onodera, 2008). Simultaneously, deploying microfinance facilities and credit guarantees lowers prohibitive financial barriers for independent operators. Utilizing alternative credit scoring models based on mobile money histories can rapidly expand asset financing to previously unbanked carriers. Ultimately, successful industrial upgrading hinges on transparent, inclusive governance and proactive engagement with informal transport unions to navigate political economy dynamics and ensure equitable workforce outcomes ( Black et al., 2020; Nnene et al., 2026).

6.2 Limitations and future research directions

Despite notable progress in alternative vehicle policy design across Sub-Saharan Africa, critical empirical research gaps persist. Future academic scholarship and applied policy research must urgently prioritize four targeted, field-oriented domains. Addressing these specific knowledge deficits is paramount to reducing investment risk and accelerating sustainable fleet deployment ( Harper et al., 2019; Salek et al., 2024; Font et al., 2023).

6.2.1 Battery performance and lifecycle assessment

Lifecycle assessment should compare vehicle production, electricity generation, use-phase energy demand and end-of-life treatment, because the emissions advantage of electric vehicles varies by region and electricity mix ( Knobloch et al., 2020; Hawkins et al., 2013; Faria et al., 2013). Battery performance and service life depend on chemistry, cell design, temperature, state of charge, charging rate, depth of discharge, duty cycle and thermal management strategy. High ambient temperatures can accelerate calendar and cycling degradation, but the magnitude and mechanism depend on chemistry and operating conditions; consequently, effects should not be generalized uniformly across tropical climates ( Harasis et al., 2026; Lehtola and Zahedi, 2021). The evidence base for Sub-Saharan Africa remains limited, so future work should prioritize field measurements that record cell and ambient temperatures, charging behavior, route and load profiles, state of health, capacity retention and failure events. Such data would support locally relevant battery warranties, residual-value estimates, maintenance practices and lifecycle assessments. Lifecycle comparisons should state the battery chemistry, functional unit, electricity mix, replacement assumptions and end-of-life scenario, and should distinguish measured results from modeled estimates.

6.2.2 Battery circularity and second-life use

Second-life battery deployment requires screening for state of health, safety, residual capacity and application-specific performance; reuse should complement, not automatically replace, recycling and material recovery ( Martinez-Laserna et al., 2018; Salek et al., 2024; Font et al., 2023; Harper et al., 2019). Second-life batteries may provide stationary storage after they no longer meet vehicle-performance requirements, but reuse should not be presumed to be economically or environmentally superior to direct recycling in every case. The result depends on state-of-health diagnostics, remaining useful life, testing and repackaging costs, safety controls, system integration, warranty and liability arrangements, and the performance of the alternative storage technology ( Martinez-Laserna et al., 2018; Iqbal et al., 2023). Comparative assessments should evaluate second-life use, new stationary batteries and direct recycling using consistent functional units and system boundaries, while accounting for round-trip efficiency, additional degradation, transport, replacement, recycling yields and the electricity displaced. Research in SSA should also examine collection networks, repair and testing capacity, traceability, standards for repurposed packs, and the allocation of responsibility among importers, vehicle owners, refurbishers and recyclers. Claims of cost savings or emissions benefits should be supported by transparent, locally relevant techno-economic and lifecycle data.

6.2.3 AfCFTA trade integration

AfCFTA implementation can reduce tariff barriers but may also create short-term customs-revenue exposure in some countries; rules of origin and complementary industrial policies are relevant to whether preferential trade supports regional sourcing and value-chain development ( Fouda Ekobena et al., 2021; Edwards et al., 2024; Ajibo and Kaime, 2025). Implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) may create opportunities for regional sourcing, battery-related services and vehicle or component assembly, but this review has not undertaken quantitative trade modeling and therefore cannot estimate the effects on vehicle prices, investment or employment. Future research should examine rules of origin, tariff schedules and pass-through, non-tariff barriers, standards recognition, exchange-rate exposure, market scale, component supply and environmental implications. Analyses should compare plausible scenarios and disclose assumptions about regional demand, local value added and import dependence before making claims about the likely benefits of regional integration.

6.2.4 Managed charging and vehicle-to-grid research

Vehicle-to-grid services may provide flexibility and grid-support value, but their practical benefits depend on market design, charging coordination, battery constraints and the match between vehicle availability and electricity-system needs ( Kempton and Tomić, 2005; Muratori, 2018). Managed charging and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) services may help coordinate vehicle demand with available generation and local network capacity, but their value depends on charging control, grid conditions, tariff design, interoperability, metering, compensation rules and user participation. Time-of-use tariffs should not be assumed to reduce peaks automatically: if many vehicles respond to the same price signal, charging can become synchronized and create a new peak unless tariffs are coordinated with local capacity management ( Lukuyu et al., 2024; Brinkel and van Montfoort, 2026). V2G additionally requires bidirectional vehicles and chargers, appropriate grid codes, battery-warranty provisions and compensation that reflects equipment costs and battery wear. Cycling-related degradation can affect the net benefit of grid services, so pilot projects should measure battery degradation, charging efficiency, revenue, network benefits and distributional effects rather than report gross revenue alone ( Lehtola and Zahedi, 2021). In SSA, pilots should be designed around locally measured feeder constraints, renewable availability, fleet duty cycles and the reliability of communications and control systems; results from other electricity markets should be transferred cautiously.

7 Actionable recommendations

The policy implications of this review are conditional rather than prescriptive for SSA as a whole. Governments should prioritize interventions that respond to documented barriers in their own markets and distinguish policy announcements from funded programs, implementation and measured outcomes. Evidence from the region identifies affordability, electricity-system constraints, charging availability and policy coordination as recurring issues, but their relative importance varies across countries and vehicle segments ( Gicha et al., 2024; Nnene et al., 2026). Recommendations should therefore be implemented through phased, time-bound programs with published baselines, transparent eligibility criteria and independent evaluation.

7.1 Targeted and evaluated fiscal measures

Finance and transport ministries should review the full fiscal treatment of electric and internal-combustion vehicles and assess time-limited incentives against affordability, public revenue, lifecycle emissions and demonstrable local value addition. Incentives should be tied to clearly stated objectives and evaluated for additionality, fiscal cost, distributional effects and the risk of benefiting purchasers who would have adopted the technology without support. Measures intended to encourage local assembly or component production should be assessed against trade obligations, supply-chain capacity and evidence of durable domestic capability; blanket exemptions should not be assumed to generate manufacturing or employment automatically. Governments should publish eligibility rules, expenditure or foregone revenue, uptake by vehicle segment, and periodic evaluation results. Evidence from South Africa illustrates the importance of distinguishing production-side incentives from consumer purchase support ( Mateko et al., 2026).

7.2 Grid-aware charging and tariff design

Utilities and energy regulators should assess anticipated depot and public charging demand before authorizing large fleet deployments. Planning should include feeder and transformer capacity, connection costs and lead times, charging profiles, distribution losses, service reliability and the availability of maintenance support. Priority measures include managed charging, transparent connection procedures and time-of-use tariffs where tariff design reflects system costs and protects vulnerable users. Tariffs should be tested against actual load profiles because a shared price signal can shift or synchronize charging rather than necessarily reduce peak demand. Solar-plus-storage or mini-grid charging should be considered only where site-specific technical and economic assessment supports it, not as a universal substitute for grid reinforcement. Monitoring should report electricity access, reliability, local network capacity, charging-site uptime and renewable-energy share as separate indicators ( Lukuyu et al., 2024; Gicha et al., 2024).

7.3 Secondhand market standards and regional coordination

Transport and environment authorities should review secondhand-vehicle age limits, roadworthiness inspections and emissions standards using evidence on road safety, affordability, air quality, fleet renewal and the practical capacity to enforce the rules. Import restrictions or scrappage schemes should be accompanied by an assessment of effects on lower-income households, informal operators, used-vehicle supply and access to reliable transport. Regional coordination may reduce inconsistent standards and regulatory arbitrage, but should be matched with implementation plans, inspection capacity and affordable mobility alternatives. Because policy adoption alone does not demonstrate effective implementation or EV uptake, proposed measures should be monitored using published indicators and reviewed against observed outcomes ( Nnene et al., 2026; Gicha et al., 2024).

7.4 Inclusive operator finance and workforce development

Transport ministries, municipalities, operator associations, unions, savings and credit cooperative organizations (SACCOs), lenders and technical-training institutions should co-design pilots that reflect daily cash flow, vehicle utilization, route patterns, maintenance access and service requirements. Commercial two- and three-wheelers, minibuses and other high-utilization fleets may offer practical pilot settings where duty cycles and charging or swapping arrangements are suitable, but their suitability should be demonstrated locally rather than assumed across the region ( Pawlak et al., 2023; Abraham et al., 2021). Battery-as-a-Service (BaaS), leasing and pay-as-you-go finance should be compared using total operator payments, contract terms, battery replacement responsibilities, downtime, end-of-contract conditions and ownership risks. Pilot evaluation should track operator income and expenditure, service reliability, vehicle utilization, participation by women and other underrepresented groups where data can be collected ethically, and the distribution of benefits and costs. Training programs should measure competency, certification, employment and repair capacity, not enrolment alone and include safe battery handling and end-of-life procedures.

Implementation should proceed through monitored, reversible pilots and scale only where evidence supports technical, financial, environmental and social viability. For each program, responsible agencies should publish a baseline, target, data source, reporting interval and evaluation method. Common indicators should include vehicles deployed and operational, charging or swapping sites in service, site uptime, connection costs and delays, service interruptions, cost per kilometer, energy source, lifecycle emissions assumptions, operator participation, safety incidents, battery collection and workforce outcomes. Where possible, results should be disaggregated by country, vehicle segment, operator type and gender, while protecting personal and commercially sensitive information. Reporting should distinguish announced policies and installed infrastructure from actual utilization and measured outcomes. Independent review at pre-defined milestones can help determine whether programs should be expanded, redesigned or discontinued, and can improve comparability across countries without implying that their starting conditions are identical ( Transportation Research Board, National Research Council, 2013; Nnene et al., 2026).

8 Conclusion

This Structured Policy and Practice Review finds no basis for assuming a single transport transition pathway across Sub-Saharan Africa. The four country cases illustrate different policy priorities and constraints, while the evidence is not sufficiently comparable to rank their overall effectiveness. High-utilization commercial vehicles may offer an important entry point in settings where duty cycles, charging arrangements and finance align; passenger EVs, public transport electrification and alternative fuels may also be relevant under different conditions.

The review highlights the need to evaluate commercial two- and three-wheelers, buses and minibuses, passenger EVs and other technologies against local operating patterns, affordability, infrastructure and lifecycle emissions. It does not establish that commercial fleets always yield the greatest emissions reductions or fastest payback. Such conclusions require comparable data on vehicle activity, energy use, electricity generation, fuel supply and actual deployment outcomes.

BaaS, leasing and pay-as-you-go finance can change the timing and allocation of upfront costs, but their net benefit depends on fees, contracts, battery replacement responsibility and vehicle utilization. CNG may serve some fleets where gas supply and refueling are reliable and lifecycle emissions are acceptable; it should not be treated as an indispensable bridge fuel. Regional trade and local assembly offer potential opportunities, but their effects on prices and jobs require further evaluation.

Charging infrastructure should be planned around measured demand, network constraints, local renewable resources, reliability and total system cost. Distributed solar and battery storage can be appropriate in some locations, while grid-connected charging may be preferable in others. Future research should prioritize comparable country-level data on vehicle registrations and fleet deployment, charging and swapping availability, operating costs, electricity reliability, battery performance and policy implementation. These limitations constrain the strength of current cross-country conclusions and define a practical agenda for further work.

title: Is Detroit Experiencing a New Manufacturing Boom? - NetNewsLedger
description:
Detroit has spent years shedding the “rust belt” label, and the evidence on the ground suggests something real is happening.
So is Detroit really in the middle of a manufacturing boom?
According to the Detroit Regional Chamber, the Detroit region is home to over 530,000 businesses.
Companies looking to move production closer to customers are finding that Detroit offers both the infrastructure and the people they need.
Detroit benefits from generations of manufacturing know-how, along with community colleges, universities, and apprenticeship programs that train the next wave of machinists, welders, engineers, and technicians.
text:
Detroit has spent years shedding the “rust belt” label, and the evidence on the ground suggests something real is happening. New investment, retooled factories, and a fast-growing network of suppliers and specialty shops are reshaping the region’s industrial landscape. So is Detroit really in the middle of a manufacturing boom? Here’s a closer look at the signs pointing to yes.

A Deep and Diverse Business Base

Manufacturing booms don’t happen in a vacuum. They need a healthy business ecosystem, and Detroit has one. According to the Detroit Regional Chamber, the Detroit region is home to over 530,000 businesses.

That number matters because manufacturers rely on a wide web of partners: engineering firms, logistics providers, material suppliers, software companies, and professional services. When a company expands production, it can find nearly everything it needs within a short drive. Startups benefit as well, since they can plug into established supply chains rather than building from scratch.

A large and varied business community also provides stability. When one industry slows, others can absorb talent and keep the regional economy moving. That resilience is one reason investors continue to view Detroit as a safe place to put capital.

Geography That Supports Growth

Location is another major factor. According to Verified Industrial Properties, the Detroit Region is home to 11 counties along the Great Lakes shoreline, with major metropolitan cities like Ann Arbor, Flint, Dearborn, Novi, and Southfield.

Each of those communities contributes something different. Dearborn carries deep automotive heritage. Ann Arbor offers university research and a steady stream of engineering talent. Novi and Southfield host corporate offices and technical centers, and Flint brings manufacturing history and available industrial space. Together they form a connected region with access to highways, rail, shipping lanes, and the Canadian border.

For manufacturers, that connectivity translates into shorter lead times and lower transportation costs. Companies looking to move production closer to customers are finding that Detroit offers both the infrastructure and the people they need.

Recycling and the Circular Economy

One of the most interesting parts of Detroit’s story is how closely manufacturing is tied to sustainability. According to Big News Network, almost 100% of the cars in the US get recycled, turned into raw materials, and reshaped in the manufacturing process.

That makes the automotive industry one of the most circular in the country. Steel, aluminum, copper, and other metals from retired vehicles flow back into production, reducing the need for virgin materials and cutting energy use. For a region built around automotive manufacturing, this creates additional opportunities in scrap processing, metal recovery, remanufacturing, and materials testing.

As automakers and suppliers face pressure to lower emissions and manage costs, recycled materials become increasingly valuable. Detroit’s long history with metals and vehicles gives it a natural edge in this growing field.

The Shift to Electric and Software-Driven Vehicles

The transition toward electric vehicles is one of the strongest forces driving new investment. Automakers and suppliers are retooling plants, adding battery-related capacity, and developing new components for electrified drivetrains. Software, sensors, and advanced driver-assistance systems are also changing what goes into every vehicle.

These shifts create demand for new skills and new facilities. Even as adoption rates rise and fall, companies are committing long-term dollars to Michigan operations. The ripple effects reach smaller suppliers and machine shops that produce the precision parts these new vehicles require.

Technology Is Changing the Factory Floor

Today’s plants look very different from those of a generation ago. Robotics, automation, additive manufacturing, and real-time data analytics are now commonplace. Sensors monitor equipment health, software predicts maintenance needs, and digital simulations let engineers test changes before touching a production line.

These tools help manufacturers boost quality while controlling costs. They also make smaller shops more competitive, allowing them to take on complex work that once required enormous facilities. As technology advances, factory jobs increasingly involve programming, troubleshooting, and problem-solving, making them more attractive to younger workers.

A Skilled Workforce and Training Pipeline

A boom is only sustainable if there are workers to support it. Detroit benefits from generations of manufacturing know-how, along with community colleges, universities, and apprenticeship programs that train the next wave of machinists, welders, engineers, and technicians.

Still, challenges remain. Many experienced workers are nearing retirement, and employers must work harder to recruit and retain talent. Competitive wages, clear career paths, and modern training are becoming essential. Companies that invest in their people are the ones best positioned to thrive.

Reshoring and Supply Chain Resilience

Disruptions in global shipping and sourcing have convinced many companies to rethink long supply chains. Bringing production closer to home offers more control, faster delivery, and fewer surprises. Detroit’s established supplier networks, industrial properties, and logistics access make it a logical destination for companies reshoring operations.

So, Is It a Boom?

The signs point to a genuine resurgence. A massive business base, strong geography, a circular approach to materials, new vehicle technologies, advanced tools, and a trained workforce are all working together. Challenges such as talent shortages, shifting consumer demand, and economic cycles remain, and no boom is guaranteed to last forever.

But Detroit’s momentum is real, and its advantages are durable. For manufacturers, workers, and investors alike, the Motor City is once again a place where things are being built.

text:
After spending three months developing recommendations on how Fort Worth can best regulate data centers, the Data Center & Infrastructure Commission unveiled its findings to city leaders Tuesday.

The 11-member commission developed 19 recommendations across water and natural resources, land use, economic impact and electricity — all of which are detailed in a 156-page report.

The committee’s findings, some of which build on existing ordinances, were presented to city council members by Michael Slattery, environmental director at Texas Christian University and director of its Institute for Environmental Studies, who was tapped by the city to lead the advisory group. In a meeting following the presentation, council members also held the city’s first public hearing on Fort Worth’s adoption of the 90-day moratorium, as required by state law.

The committee was formed after zoning commissioners in July voted down proposed regulations on zoning requirements for data centers, recommending Fort Worth staffers create stricter ordinances. That vote prompted city officials to make three votes related to data centers on Aug. 11, including the inception of the advisory group and the moratorium process.

Slattery prefaced his presentation to council members by saying data center development is the most contested land-use issue in Fort Worth, adding the commission’s goal was to produce an evaluation of data center development based on fact, not advocacy.

“Skepticism is healthy and it’s exactly why getting the science right in this commission absolutely mattered,” Slattery said.

The report was developed by the advisory group’s 11 members. The formation of the group was approved by the city in early August and consists of representatives with backgrounds in economic development, data centers and related infrastructure, natural resource management and environmental advocacy.

The commission and its findings are intended to guide city staffers on how best to regulate data center development amid a nationwide boom in the tech hubs and opposition from communities.

The recommendations include a potential regulation for the city to require a “zero-water” solution, echoing what Fort Worth officials proposed earlier this year. Under this regulation, data centers would need to equip a nonevaporative, closed-loop technology supplemented with limited adiabatic cooling — the process of cooling ambient air through controlled evaporation.

Commissioners also recommended making water usage publicly available, as well as protecting local water supplies through utility and service reviews.

On proposed electricity regulation, the group’s members recommend Fort Worth require a technical fact sheet from developers and include verifiable commitments that would relieve strain on the electric grid.

The recommendation related to land use that Slattery spoke to most was the committee’s proposal to protect homes with zoning standards that can be measured. That involves requiring a minimum 350-foot setback between homes and a data center and establishing a framework to enforce noise limits.

Setbacks between properties should increase if data centers and their infrastructure’s height increase, Slattery said.

Council member Jeanette Martinez said she would like to see larger setbacks between homes and data centers.

“I foresee that people will probably make that request,” on increased separations between properties, Martinez said.

Asked by council member Chris Nettles how the decision on the proposed setback was made, Slattery explained that the committee analyzed distances between properties in other cities, adding that most residents would like to see data centers located as far away as possible.

“We have to find something that is realistic, that is enforceable. I absolutely hear what you say,” Slattery said.

In a briefing with reporters following the presentation, Slattery said the biggest disagreements among the commission’s members came on the decision to recommend a 350-foot setback.

It was critical for recommendations from the group’s members to be science- and research-backed, Slattery added.

The land-use proposals also call on the city to include thermal impacts and community feedback on data centers in Fort Worth’s 2050 comprehensive plan, the document that details the city’s vision and long-term planning.

The recommendations covering the report’s four sectors were developed to tailor what city officials have authority over. The document details that major power decisions are made by power distributors and state officials.

Council member Elizabeth Beck asked why land-use recommendations did not detail zones in which data centers can be developed.

The committee decided to not make recommendations on how data centers should be zoned so the city could put in place regulations that would be protective of residents without restricting the data center industry, Slattery said.

“I don’t want that to sound like advocacy. … The data center developers that I spoke with wanted certainty and they wanted predictability. And they said, ‘Whatever you folks come up with, we will work with,’” Slattery said.

The commission’s report comes as lawmakers prepare to deliberate various facets of data center operations and development in the upcoming 90th legislative session.

Fort Worth officials went back-and-forth on creating and implementing data center regulations earlier this year, stating local control could be affected by directives from Gov. Greg Abbott — while he serves the remainder of his term — and laws that come out of the Texas Capitol in 2027.

During her campaign run, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa said she would continue a statewide data center moratorium until legislators meet in January, adding she would pass “real protections” for communities, The Texas Tribune reported.

A day after bill filing opened, the Legislature’s agenda was filled with hundreds of bills, including proposals on regulating data centers.

State Rep. Salman Bhojani, D-Euless, who was just reelected to represent House District 92, filed a bill to amend Texas’ water code. It would require data centers to disclose the entity supplying their water and how much resources a development would consume.

Republican Armin Mizani, House District 98 representative-elect and former Keller mayor, filed a bill to give local government officials the authority by a voting process to determine whether a data center can be built in a city or county in which they govern.

Also in their evening meeting, council members held the first hearing on Fort Worth’s adoption of a 90-day moratorium on all new data center projects, as required by state law.

description:

Toyota Motor North America opened its 100-acre, 2.1 million-square-foot Plano campus in 2017 following its relocation from Southern California.

Toyota Motor North America’s new COO Nambu, the incoming COO, is returning to the United States, where he had worked at Toyota Motor Sales USA.
text:
Mark Templin, the current COO of Plano-based Toyota Motor North America, will become president and CEO effective Jan. 1, the automaker said.

Templin will succeed current President and CEO Tetsuo “Ted” Ogawa, who will return to be a senior fellow at parent company Toyota Motor Corp. Hiroshi Nambu, president of Toyota Motor’s business planning and operation division, will take Templin’s place as COO.

To support the transition, Ogawa will serve as senior executive adviser from January through March before becoming a senior fellow in April. In that role, he will manage external affairs at several Toyota-owned businesses.

In a statement, Templin said Ogawa’s “experience and perspective will be invaluable” to the company in his new role at Toyota Motor Corp.

The leadership changes “reflect Toyota’s commitment to developing experienced global leaders and strengthening collaboration across its regions,” the company said.

Overcoming challenges and achieving milestones

Since becoming CEO in 2020, Ogawa has guided Toyota Motor North America through “unprecedented industry challenges,” the company said. Those include the pandemic, supply chain disruptions and regulatory issues.

“His leadership strengthened Toyota’s commitment to building vehicles where it sells them and supporting local communities through investment and job creation,” the company said.

Furthermore, the company said it has reached several North American milestones during Ogawa’s tenure. Among them:

The 2025 opening of a battery factory in North Carolina, the company’s first in-house battery plant outside Japan. The nearly $14 billion plant will create up to 5,100 jobs, Toyota Motor North America said.

Plans to invest up to $10 billion more U.S. operations over the next five years. That would bring the company’s total U.S. investments to almost $60 billion.

Announcement of a $3.6 billion expansion at its San Antonio plant, which makes Tundra pickup trucks and Sequoia SUVs. The expansion will create about 2,000 jobs, the company said.

‘One of the greatest honors of my career’

Also under Ogawa’s leadership, Toyota has bolstered North American manufacturing, R&D, sales, marketing and corporate operations, the company said.

“Leading Toyota in North America has been one of the greatest honors of my career,” Ogawa said in a statement. “I am proud of and deeply grateful to our team members, dealers and partners for strengthening our business and building a foundation for the next generation.”

Ogawa has held leadership roles at Toyota in the U.S., Japan and China since 1984. Before becoming CEO, he was Toyota Motor North America’s executive vice president and COO.

Building on a ‘strong foundation’

When Templin becomes president and CEO in January, he will lead a company with 65,000 employees in North America, including about 4,000 in Plano. Toyota Motor North America opened its 100-acre, 2.1 million-square-foot Plano campus in 2017 following its relocation from Southern California.

“Mark has the experience and vision to build on Toyota’s strong foundation in North America,” Ogawa said. “As the automotive industry continues to evolve, he will strengthen our competitiveness [and] support our team members, dealers and suppliers while delivering products and mobility solutions that meet our customers’ diverse needs.”

Templin took on the COO role in late January 2025.

He previously spent nine years as president and CEO of Plano-based Toyota Motor Credit Corp., which operates as Toyota Financial Services, the automaker’s lending and insurance arm. Templin joined Toyota in 1990 after a six-year stint at Toyota rival General Motors.

Templin praised Ogawa’s leadership, which he said has positioned Toyota Motor North America for “continued success.”

“I’m honored to build on the foundation he established, working alongside our team members, dealers and suppliers to continue earning our customers’ trust and prepare Toyota for the opportunities ahead,” Templin said.

Toyota Motor North America’s new COO

Nambu, the incoming COO, is returning to the United States, where he had worked at Toyota Motor Sales USA.

As the current head of Toyota Motor Corp.’s business planning and operation division, Nambu oversees sales, operations, mobility and value chain initiatives. Earlier, he held roles in Toyota’s sales, manufacturing and technical operations.

“Having worked closely with our North American operations throughout my career, I have tremendous respect for the strength of our team, our dealer and supplier partnerships, and the opportunities ahead,” Nambu said in a statement.

Press Releases

MEDIA ADVISORY: DEEP to host meeting of Governor’s Council on Climate Change, share latest data on greenhouse gases in Connecticut

(HARTFORD) — Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP) will host a virtual meeting of the Governor’s Council on Climate Change (GC3) on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 2:00 p.m., where DEEP officials will share the latest Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Inventory for Connecticut, among other highlights.

On September 3, 2019, Governor Ned Lamont issued Executive Order No. 3, establishing the GC3 to strengthen Connecticut’s commitment to transition to a decarbonized economy and enhanced resiliency to the impacts of climate change. The GC3 is charged with monitoring and reporting on the state’s progress on the implementation of climate mitigation and adaptation strategies annually.

At this meeting, DEEP will share the results of the GHG inventory through the year 2024, the most recent year for which data is available. The inventory serves as an annual public and transparent accounting of our progress towards the state’s statutory emissions reduction targets and informs programs to reduce emissions. The meeting will also provide highlights of the state’s progress on climate adaptation and resilience strategies. Following the presentation, there will be a discussion with GC3 members to share updates and feedback on the state’s progress on climate, and to hear public comments.

Who: Governor Lamont, Acting DEEP Commissioner Emma Cimino, members of the Governor’s Council on Climate Change, DEEP staff

What: Meeting of the Governor’s Council on Climate Change, release of findings from latest Greenhouse Gas Inventory

text:
The public hearing in Millersport on Tuesday evening began with a pre-recorded, monotone narration of a slideshow explaining a proposed data-center power plant and how the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency considers whether to approve air-pollution permits for such facilities.

And the hearing ended with a dramatic piano performance by area resident Thane Evans playing his original composition called “The Compromise” for about 50 people seated in the Millersport Elementary School auditorium.

Evans lives in a Victorian farmstead on Rt. 37 just east of where the hyper-scale data center and power plant site is being stripped of topsoil in preparation for construction. He said after the hearing that he used his five minutes allotted to each speaker to play the piece “because the piano was there and everything is being compromised – the land, our health, the community.”

“We have been completely compromised,” he said. “It’s devastating.”

While Evans and his father, John, who owns the brick farmstead on Rt. 37 that dates to the Civil War era, are directly affected by the industrial complex proposed for 450 acres just east of their back door, Thane Evans said he is concerned about the health effects of air pollution on the community.

“I don’t want to see everyone from children to senior citizens hurt by this,” he said.

Evans was referring to the health effects of anticipated air pollution from the proposed 1,350-megawatt power plant – one of the largest “behind-the-meter” plants to date in Ohio. Behind the meter means that it will serve only one customer – a data center being built by Vantage Data Centers – and will not be connected to the regional electricity grid.

| Read more: Critics say Ohio EPA ‘stretching the rules’ in permitting data-center power plants less efficient and more polluting than ‘best available technology’

Children and senior citizens are most at risk for illnesses associated with the types of pollutants produced by gas-fired power plants, especially fine particulate matter. The “Fairfield Energy Center,” proposed by Advanced Power Services of Boston, would produce the following quantities of pollutants, according to the draft air-pollution permit being discussed at the hearing:

333 tons per year of large particulate matter (PM10)

333 tons per year of fine particulate matter (PM2.5)

86 tons per year of sulfur dioxide (SO2)

486 tons per year of nitrogen oxides (NOX)

686 tons per year of carbon monoxide (CO)

221 tons per year of volatile organic compounds (VOC)

19 tons per year of sulfuric acid mist (H2SO4)

7,232,826 tons of greenhouse gases (not applicable in permit consideration)

| Read more: Public hearing draws some support and plenty of opposition to 500-megawatt power plant for data center

Ohio EPA Director John Logue will decide whether to approve the air-pollution permit, which the EPA staff has recommended that he approve. Anyone who wants to comment on the permit request can do so online through 11:59 p.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12.

Many of those who spoke during the Ohio EPA hearing on the merits of an air-pollution permit for the facility raised concerns about health – and about the equipment that would produce 2,164 tons of air pollutants annually, according to the company’s applications to the Ohio Power Siting Board and the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency.

One after another, such as Robert Slater II, repeated details in the OEPA and OPSB applications for permits that say the company plans to use 40 electricity generating turbines, three diesel-powered back-up generators and a diesel-powered pump for emergency fire suppression that are not the “best available technology” as required by law.

“There is more efficient technology out there,” Slater said.

And Bill Wershing was among several who said the EPA should consider that the micro-climate in the Buckeye Lake region is unique in central Ohio because it is prone to fog and air inversions that can hold whatever is in the air – such as all of those pollutants – close to the ground for long periods of time.

And several speakers, such as Buckeye Lake Village Council member Kellie Green, expressed their concern for the environmental – and economic – impact on the Buckeye Lake region because pollution from the power plant would fall on that area and affect “the environment and our communities.”

Noah Malik, of New Albany, said he came to the hearing in Millersport because he wants the EPA to consider the big picture – the environmental and health effects of multiple “behind-the-meter” power plants on central Ohio.

| Read more: New Albany mayor and council told to ‘do better’ in protecting area residents from gas-fired power plant pollutants

Seven of those plants are proposed, under construction or in operation in New Albany to serve some of the 40 data centers in Licking County, where the New Albany International Business Park is located.

“I’m especially concerned about the cumulative effect of these plants in Ashville, Millersport, New Albany and Hilliard,” Malik said. “Is the Ohio EPA looking at these combined and the effect on the region?”

The EPA was only taking public comments on Tuesday evening – not answering questions – so no one responded.

description:

The six-month pause on approval of any data center development will be used to craft permanent data center regulations for the city.

text:
Two Michigan communities approved measures restricting data center development on Monday, joining a growing list of local governments which have done so.

On Monday night, the Saginaw Township Board of Trustees voted to approve an ordinance regulating the development of data centers in the area.

According to MLive, the 15-page ordinance lays out a number of standards any prospective data center must meet. Noise produced by data centers may not exceed 40 decibels at the property line, buildings and equipment must sit at least 500 feet from residential property, and cooling processes must use a closed-loop or recycled water system, among other regulations.

Developers must notify any residents within half a mile of planned data center sites, and hold a minimum of two community meetings on any proposed developments. Medium and hyperscale data centers, as defined by the ordinance, are restricted to a narrow section of the township.

The ordinance will go into effect on November 16.

Things are moving slightly faster in Romulus, where the city council unanimously approved a 180-day moratorium on data centers, also on Monday night. It took effect immediately.

The six-month pause on approval of any data center development will be used to craft permanent data center regulations for the city.

Several residents present at Monday’s council meeting reportedly asked the city to ban data centers entirely, a sentiment echoed by two council members. Mayor Robert McCraight said any new city ordinances should consider the value smaller data centers may have to local industry.

Neither locality has faced a data center planned for development yet, so both resolutions were passed as a preventive measure. And they are far from the only ones.

A long list of local governments in Michigan have passed restrictions on data center development over the last year. A Michigan Public analysis in July found that as many as 52 local township and city governments across the state had passed data center moratoriums, though more have done so since.

The state’s political environment seems set to grow even more opposed to data centers in the coming months.

While Governor Gretchen Whitmer has generally been supportive of data centers, growing public backlash has led many Michigan politicians to adopt more skeptical stances.

The race to build AI data centers may not require as much new electricity generation as investors fear. Constellation Energy Corp. CEO Joseph Dominguez says the U.S. grid still has years of underused power capacity that could support new data centers — potentially buying the industry time before a much larger wave of new generation is needed.

"We could have probably another six or seven years' worth of stranded capacity," Dominguez said during the company's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 9. The CEO added that the available supply could help data centers come online, depending on how quickly developers build them.

Constellation reported third-quarter adjusted EPS of $5.06, beating the $3.85 estimate, on sales of $9.55 billion, above the $9.37 billion estimate. It also raised its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $12.50 to $12.80 from $11.50 to $12.50, above the $12.15 estimate. The shares jumped 10.5% on Nov. 9.

America's Grid Has More Idle Power Than Investors May Realize

The opportunity is not necessarily about building more power plants. It is about getting more out of the ones already operating.

Dominguez pointed to combined-cycle gas plants in Texas' ERCOT market, saying many are operating well below their potential. While such facilities could reach utilization rates of 80% to 90%, some are running at roughly half those levels, leaving capacity that could support additional electricity demand if operators can move power where it is needed.

Dominguez also noted that many plants remain idle on the grid. The PJM region, which serves parts of the eastern U.S., is tighter, but utilization remains relatively light compared with historical levels.

"There remains a ton of available energy supply out there," Dominguez said. The CEO suggested the current cushion could last until closer to 2035, while acknowledging that it will eventually run out.

Trending: Avoid the #1 Investing Mistake: How Your 'Safe' Holdings Could Be Costing You Big Time

Demand Response Could Stretch the Power Supply Further

The available generation capacity is only part of the equation. Dominguez said Constellation is also exploring how demand response could help accommodate data center growth.

Under these arrangements, electricity customers agree to reduce consumption when the grid comes under pressure. But businesses may need longer-term financial incentives before making physical changes at their facilities to support that flexibility.

Dominguez said Constellation's commercial team is exploring whether payment commitments lasting five, 10 years or longer could encourage customers to participate. That could help free up additional electricity without requiring utilities to build generation solely to meet occasional spikes in demand.

The idea fits the CEO's broader argument that the U.S. faces a peak-capacity challenge rather than an outright shortage of energy. In prepared remarks on the call, Dominguez said storage and demand response could help manage the relatively small number of hours when electricity demand is highest.

What It Means for the AI Power Trade

For investors, the distinction matters. If existing plants can serve more demand, the immediate opportunity may extend beyond companies building new power plants, nuclear reactors or grid infrastructure. Owners of underutilized generation assets could also benefit as data center developers compete for reliable electricity.

That does not eliminate the need for new generation or resolve regional transmission and grid constraints. Available capacity in one market cannot automatically serve a data center in another. But it challenges the assumption that America's AI expansion must run into an immediate nationwide shortage of electricity.

Investors watching Constellation and the broader power trade should pay attention to how quickly data center demand materializes, whether idle capacity can be brought online and whether demand-response agreements become commercially viable.

The next phase of the AI power boom may depend as much on making better use of existing assets as on building new ones.

text:
The company is expected to create 175 new direct jobs while retaining 637 current positions. Louisiana Economic Development estimates the project will result in an additional 185 indirect new jobs, for a total of 360 potential new job opportunities in the Northwest Region.

“Louisiana’s economic momentum is creating new demand across our economy, and we want the companies already invested in our state to be positioned to capture that growth,” LED Secretary Susan B. Bourgeois said.

“GE Vernova’s expansion strengthens that foundation in Shreveport, supporting long-term job growth and creating more opportunities for Louisiana workers.”

The expansion will take place at GE Vernova Transformers’ existing facility at 7000 W. Bert Kouns Industrial Loop in Shreveport and will include new manufacturing equipment, process improvements, and supporting infrastructure across key production areas.

Once complete, the upgrades are expected to increase production of industrial and renewable energy transformers, including those serving digital factories and battery energy storage applications.

General Electric broke ground on the Shreveport facility in 1969, with transformer production beginning the following year. Over more than five decades, the 500,000-square-foot operation has continued to evolve, adding new products and manufacturing capabilities as technology and customer needs have changed.

“Shreveport is proud to support this $34.5 million expansion, which will create 175 new jobs and retain 637 positions,” Mayor Tom Arceneaux said.

“This investment reflects the strength of Shreveport’s skilled workforce, and we appreciate our partnership with Louisiana Economic Development and the assistance provided through the $300,000 performance‑based grant. Together, we’re building sustained economic opportunity for our community.”

Engineering and equipment procurement are underway, with installation expected to continue through the end of 2026 and throughout 2027. Production is expected to reach full capacity in 2028.

To secure the project in Shreveport, the state of Louisiana offered GE Vernova Transformers Shreveport LLC a competitive incentives package that includes a $300,000 performance-based grant for site and infrastructure improvements. The company is also expected to participate in the state’s Quality Jobs and Industrial Tax Exemption programs.
