text:
GE Vernova announced a new $34.5 million investment to expand its transformer manufacturing operations in Shreveport, Louisiana, "strengthening the company’s ability to support growing demand for electrical infrastructure needed to power industry, energy systems and digital technologies," it said on Nov. 10.

The expansion is expected to create 175 direct new jobs, adding to the more than 630 existing positions at the facility. In addition to the 175 new jobs being created, Louisiana Economic Development estimates the project will support an additional 185 indirect jobs, bringing the total potential employment impact to 360 new job opportunities across the Northwest Louisiana region.

To support the expansion, the state of Louisiana offered GE Vernova Transformers Shreveport LLC a competitive incentives package that includes a $300,000 performance-based grant for site and infrastructure improvements. The company is also expected to participate in the state’s Quality Jobs and Industrial Tax Exemption programs.

The expansion will take place at GE Vernova Transformers Shreveport LLC existing facility in Shreveport.

Planned improvements include new manufacturing equipment, process enhancements and supporting infrastructure across key production areas. The upgrades are expected to increase production of industrial and renewable energy transformers. Production is expected to reach full capacity in 2028.

The expansion is part of GE Vernova's broader plan to invest nearly $1.3 billion across its U.S. manufacturing facilities and research centers between 2025 and 2028 to strengthen domestic manufacturing capacity, accelerate innovation, and help meet growing electricity demand.

name: EPA
title: Podcast - How the Midterm Elections Could Reshape Environmental Policy | Insights
authors: Matthew Z. Leopold, Michal I. Freedhoff, Jennifer L. Hernandez
description:
I'm a partner with Holland & Knight here in Washington, D.C., in their environmental practice and formerly with EPA (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency), where I served as the general counsel of the agency.
And before that, I spent about 20 years on Capitol Hill, both the House and the Senate side, committee and personal office, working primarily in the environmental policy space.
Environmental and land use siting and permitting is what we do, and it's very challenging.
As we look at environmental issues, could you talk a little bit about how you see things unfolding in Congress in January?
That will mean that Democrats control the committees of jurisdiction that do work on environmental and energy issues.
text:
Matthew Leopold: Hello, my name is Matt Leopold, and I'm here today to discuss the results of the midterm elections as part of Holland & Knight's midterm post-election podcast series, where we're going to explore the impacts of the election on different industries, companies and policy areas as we head into 2027 and the new Congress. I'm a partner with Holland & Knight here in Washington, D.C., in their environmental practice and formerly with EPA (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency), where I served as the general counsel of the agency. And with me, I have Michal Freedhoff and Jennifer Hernandez, who will introduce themselves.

Michal Freedhoff: Hi there. My name is Michal Freedhoff. I am a senior policy advisor here at Holland & Knight. I came to Holland & Knight pretty much directly from the EPA, where I served as the Senate-confirmed head of the chemicals office for the entirety of the Biden Administration. And before that, I spent about 20 years on Capitol Hill, both the House and the Senate side, committee and personal office, working primarily in the environmental policy space.

Jennifer Hernandez: I'm Jennifer Hernandez. I'm the California representative on this call. I lead the West Coast Environmental and Land Use Group. Environmental and land use siting and permitting is what we do, and it's very challenging. And I'm here to sort of represent both a state perspective, and a blue state at that, in this election debrief.

Matthew Leopold: Thank you both. So, Michal, I would like to start with you, and as you pointed out, you spent time on Capitol Hill before going into EPA and then joining the firm. As we look at environmental issues, could you talk a little bit about how you see things unfolding in Congress in January?

Michal Freedhoff: Sure, Matt. So, first off, I should mention that we're recording this on the afternoon of Wednesday, November 4, before all races have been called, but it's safe to say that there is a commanding majority in both the House and the Senate for the Democrats. That will mean that Democrats control the committees of jurisdiction that do work on environmental and energy issues. On the House side, there will be probably less change than on the Senate side in terms of the specific people involved because Congressman Frank Pallone from New Jersey, was the ranking member on the Energy and Commerce Committee in the last Congress, and he will become the chairman in January.

Similarly, Congressman Jared Huffman was the ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee in the last Congress, and he will become the chairman. On the Senate side, we'll be looking at Senator Heinrich from New Mexico, who will likely take the reins of the Senate Environment and Natural Resources Committee. And he led that committee for the Democrats in the last Congress, but we will see a change in the Environment and Public Works Committee on the Senate side because Senator Whitehouse is expected to become the head of the Senate Judiciary Committee. So we'll expect Senator Jeff Merkley from Oregon to become the new leader and chairman of the Senate Environment Public Works Committee.

Matthew Leopold: Great. So, in light of that and the new leadership, obviously, the priorities are going to be very different. And we know there's going to be a lot of oversight, in particular, of executive agencies. Have you been thinking about what kind of investigations the environmental committees might take up?

Michal Freedhoff: Yeah, you know, if you look at the oversight letters requesting information and documents both from the executive branch in the Trump Administration, as well as from a wide range of private sector companies, you know, you'll see a lot of these letters have already been written. And I think we'll be looking at everything from probing the connections between the past occupations of current administration officials and policy decisions that they may have made. I think we'll see a lot of looking at the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda and how those goals are described by the MAHA-adjacent groups to have not really been realized in the way that they might have hoped. And, you know, some investigating by congressional Democrats as to why particular decisions made by EPA might not have really advanced the MAHA agenda objectives.

I also think some of the various Trump Administration projects related to the golf courses, the arch, the ballroom connections and contributions that companies might have made to those efforts will be an area of focus. And I also think some of the efforts to claw back the funding in the Inflation Reduction Act that were enacted during the Biden Administration and a lot of the grant programs and loan guarantees and contracts and permits that have been rescinded or pulled back by this administration will be another strong area of focus.

Matthew Leopold: That certainly makes sense that a lot of those are coming, and we'll talk in a second about how the administration might react to a lot of those inquiries because I know they've been getting ready for it with the expected change in the House, at a minimum. And now the Senate as well will elevate that, for sure. But before we go on to the executive branch, you know, obviously, everyone's been talking about the permitting bill, also known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Any idea on the chances of passage of that in a lame-duck session? I'm thinking that might be one piece of legislation that could potentially move.

Michal Freedhoff: Yeah, I think it's sort of too soon to tell, given the results from yesterday and the fact that, you know, all the seats haven't been called yet. But I think the pointer to what to expect in the lame duck, which is those last bunch of weeks before the end of this Congress, is a really important one to consider because it's not just the permitting bill, which I agree, before the election, stood a very strong chance of enactment in this Congress. There's also a wide range of other things that touch the energy and environment space. And those include, you know, funding the government and at what levels. It includes the Farm Bill. It includes the reauthorization of the Toxic Substances Control Act fees. It includes the pesticide fees provisions as well.

And I think the question for incoming Democratic chairmen of committees of jurisdiction will be, do I want to clear the decks now and then have two years to work on advancing my own priorities and the priorities of my party, or do I want to carry some of those things over into a new Congress and potentially make some changes to what might have been a good deal before the election, might not look like as good a deal now? So, I think the jury's still out on that, but I think it's going to be a very action-packed and very busy lame-duck session.

Jennifer Hernandez: So, with respect to the view from California and the states more generally, I think it's also going to be noteworthy what isn't on the congressional agenda. There were a number of hearings, for example, around forest management, wildfire response, climate programs of various types, water management, that were fairly pointed in criticizing various California undertakings. And I just don't, obviously, see those kinds of proceedings continuing in the new Congress. And with respect to the permit reform bill, that was a compromise bill. And so, before that compromise was struck, I think the sides were pretty locked down on permit reform for me, but not thee. And the compromise is just that, a compromise. There was widespread opposition in the environmental advocacy community against permit reform, notwithstanding that compromise. And so, for me, one of the telling indications of this election outcome will be the lame-duck session's treatment of permit reform because, more than special interests of any kind, including environmental, I think the electorate spoke around affordability and wanting a more effective form of government. And so, if we devolve and take a pass on this permit reform bill and go to respective corners again, I would view that as an early loss for what the voters are hoping to achieve with a different slate.

Matthew Leopold: I agree that, you know, there seems to be broad agreement we need more infrastructure built in this country, and environmental aspects of permitting, in particular, are a huge impediment to that, whether you're building renewable energy or fossil fuel projects. But kind of turning to the administration's current agenda and focusing, particularly, on EPA and what it's been doing in regulatory reform and deregulation, frankly, my view is, one, as I mentioned, this was anticipated to some degree, and I don't know that the change in Congress is going to dramatically change the trajectory of the agency, particularly with the high-profile deregulatory efforts, like on climate regulation, particularly under the Clean Air Act. The die has been cast, and they've made their major significant proposed rules and completed a number of them already. For example, the endangerment finding has been completed and already in litigation. And the administration did that early so it could focus on defending that and, hopefully, from their perspective, getting it up to the Supreme Court. So, there will certainly be congressional oversight of EPA on climate, the endangerment finding, among other things, but I think the administration is well-prepared to defend that.

And more broadly, you now, I served in the first Trump Administration when the House of Representatives changed hands in the midterm elections and in receiving some of the incoming oversight, the agency can walk and chew gum at the same time, in my view, right? There's a function in which they're going to be responding to congressional oversight, and that does take up a lot of time and effort, but at the same time, the people who are writing the rules at the agency are generally a different group and are somewhat insulated from the back-and-forth between Congress and the agency, with certain exceptions. But I think on the priorities, you know, Administrator Zeldin's list of 50-some-odd deregulatory actions, many of them are well underway or already completed. And I think those will continue forward and, you know, it says to the extent businesses affected are listening. You know, I think you could count on those priorities being completed. As far as beyond those priorities, that's a question because there's certainly limited resources at the agency, but interested to hear what others think.

Michal Freedhoff: I generally agree with what you said, Matt, but I think that it really does absorb a great deal of agency time whenever a principal needs to go and testify before Congress. And it does divert a lot of the energy from the political team away from whatever it is that they're trying to accomplish and towards, you know, whatever defensive measures they feel they have to take based on whatever Congress is doing. But I do fully agree with you. I don't think their agenda is going to change in any way. Jennifer?

Jennifer Hernandez: Yeah, so I think that the longtime sort of catchphrase in California is the last step in the permit process is litigation. And I feel like the rulemaking process has devolved into the last step in that rulemaking is litigation, not just on the EPA side, but also on the DOI side with respect to things like endangered species or some of the habitat-related issues, public lands issues, all heading to litigation. And all of that litigation, I think, is going to consume some time and, depending on its posture, may or may not be ready for review or accepted for review by the Supreme Court. If a huge generalization about this court is permissible, I would say that this court seems disinclined to make big policy decisions that it believes Congress should be making.

And so, however that litigation tsunami continues, I suspect that Congress is going to end up having to make a new law to the extent it wants to advance new legislative priorities that aren't already solidly grounded in existing regs and precedent as it's been shaped, which includes precedent that's new around major questions around climate change and GHG (greenhouse gas). So, I think litigation is going to continue to be a very dominant feature of our rulemaking landscape at the federal level and keep uncertainty alive at the implementation level and at the state level. And that's a syndrome California has already been experiencing now for multiple years with hangover litigation, even from Trump one. So, I think continued uncertainty is an unfortunate byproduct. And frankly, the permit reform bill would help address some of that.

Matthew Leopold: Yeah, I agree totally [with you], Jennifer, on that, and I know the administration's planning to be able to, you know, file the major briefs on defense of their actions in this administration. And so, eyes will be more focused on DOJ over the last couple of years as some of the initiative shifts from the rule makers to the rule defenders. But, I mean, you kind of raised the point about litigation. Much of the litigation is really driven now by state attorneys general. And with the deepening of the Democrat control of state capitals and attorneys general offices, I think we'll see more of that. What's your thinking on how states are going to rise to fill some of the void that they've seen left by the federal government?

Jennifer Hernandez: So, I think that's a very, very interesting question because, while running against Trump and running around the broad theme of affordability were, I think, the dominant themes from yesterday, I don't think the Democratic Party has really grappled with a synthesis between affordability, adequate supply and some of the environmental priorities, especially in the climate arena. And so, I don't think that newly elected governors are simply going to, in what are now blue states, are simply going to sign on to some of the high-cost regulatory priorities that their blue colleagues have undertaken and had to either walk back or qualify or live with to some detriment.

So, I think states have, in many cases, sort of taken some of the lead in how to legislate around climate, especially. And I think that it's going to be a challenge for the newly elected crew to just do what California and New York has done and hope for better affordability outcomes. That seems unlikely. So, I think we're going to see continued uncertainty, Matt, in the litigation arena rather than a straight partisan split.

Matthew Leopold: And I think the one big case, of course, I'm watching, and you're watching, Jennifer, is the Suncor case pending at the Supreme Court, which could have major impacts on the scope of state and local authority with respect to climate regulation or allowance of these so-called climate nuisance suits. So, that's going to be a major decision coming down before June this year.

Thanks, everyone, for tuning in to our podcast series. And stay tuned for more content coming from Holland & Knight on other areas. Thank you.

text:
Renewable energy has a lot of upsides and very few downsides, and that matters when you’re working in local government and are tasked with delivering practical solutions.

Guiding principles for the Pima County Facilities Management team are cost savings, emissions reductions, and stacking every additional benefit possible. Facilities Management takes care of County buildings, keeps track of what's happening across all sites, and looks for priority opportunities that make the most of limited capital funds.

One priority opportunity the County identified is the installation of solar panels above the large parking lot east of the Abrams Public Health Center. Prior to the solar installation, the site was very hot with full sun exposure. Solar radiation breaks down asphalt and plastics, overheats vehicles, and generally accelerates wear. Staff and the public (including those with compromised health and families with newborns) utilizing the facilities didn’t have any covered parking. They and their vehicles were exposed to direct sunlight in a vast hot parking lot, especially during peak summer heat.

With the solar installation, all these conditions improved. Even night lighting to the parking lot improved once the canopy was installed, no longer limited to pole-mounted fixtures and giving the site a noticeably better sense of safety and usefulness. Plus, the County enjoys reduced electric bills and saves taxpayer dollars.

In addition to solar installations run by Facilities Management, the County relies on Solar Service Agreements, specialized public-private partnerships where the County licenses space for a developer to build and maintain a solar installation, and in return we buy the power it delivers. Solar Service Agreements work because developers can offer lower cost energy than traditional utilities while the County saves money and gains on-site infrastructure.

The County also utilizes job order contractors to construct solar installations at County facilities for long-term use and maintenance. This lets us piece out work as needed or blend in-house specialists with contracted support.

Another example of how the County utilizes renewable energy is through community solar installation projects such as the Prairie Fire Solar Farm. This project was made possible through an agreement with Tucson Electric Power, and after more than a decade, the installation still provides low-cost energy to customers on the Go Solar program. New utility programs currently being tested include a bring-your-own-battery model that the County is helping develop.

No matter the method, the outcomes remain consistent: electricity prices are not going down. Rising utility, fuel, and input costs point toward a future built around more solar and batteries. When you reduce grid reliance and add solar — a system with no moving parts — it becomes clear why this approach is a stable investment for the community, for our buildings, and for the taxpayers.

name: North Carolina and Evs
title: The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high - WUNC
description:
The average transaction cost for a new vehicle has reached a record high: $51,109.
The average used car now costs close to $27,000, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive.
In part, vehicles cost more because the cost of making them has gone up for automakers.
"They're just simply holding onto their cars longer," Keating said.
For automakers, a drop in car buyers means they have to compete more with each other for sales.
text:
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

The average transaction cost for a new vehicle has reached a record high: $51,109. That's according to a report out today from the Kelley Blue Book, which is part of the analytics firm Cox Automotive.

That's about $500 above the last record, set in December 2025.

Car prices have been stubbornly high for years, especially since the pandemic, mainly driven by supply chain issues. And they've gotten higher recently, in part thanks to tariffs and to buyers flocking to, and car companies making, larger, fancier vehicles.

Yet there's a little good news: Cars are getting more expensive … more slowly.

While that $51,109 figure is an all-time high, that's only up 2.1% in the past year.

"A 2.1% year-over-year increase is actually below inflation," said Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox Automotive who co-authored the report. Between 2012 and 2021, cars got 3.4% more expensive a year on average, she continued.

The Kelley Blue Book's transaction cost is based on what people wound up paying for a new vehicle — that means whatever's on the sticker price, plus add-ons for fancier features, and minus any incentives, such as dealer discounts.

It also doesn't include one other expense that adds to the cost of owning a car: interest on auto loans. The cost of borrowing has risen over the past several years as the Federal Reserve has kept interest rates high in an effort to drive down inflation. Auto loan rates are now about 11% for used vehicles and over 7% for new ones, according to Edmunds, a car analytics company.

Keating says all of this can add up to some sticker shock for buyers — partly because people don't buy cars all that often and can be surprised by how expensive they've gotten, and partly because of interest rates.

"I mean, we are seeing a true shift in the percentage of your monthly payment that's going towards interest versus towards principal," she said.

Used cars are not a steal

The Kelley Blue Book's average includes all kinds of vehicles — SUVs, pickup trucks, electric vehicles — from all kinds of auto companies, including Toyota, Subaru, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz.

It doesn't, however, include used car sales, which normally make up about two-thirds of total sales. Ivan Drury, director of industry insights at Edmunds, crunched those numbers too and found the same trend. "No matter what you're looking at, the price is up," he said.

The average used car now costs close to $27,000, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive. Vehicles that cost less than that are a "sliver" of the industry, Drury said.

Supply chain challenges, including a semiconductor shortage, during the COVID pandemic meant fewer cars got made. Carmakers had to pick and choose which vehicles to prioritize making — they picked their most profitable models. As a result, fewer used vehicles entered car lots in the early 2020s. So today there's less inventory to choose from.

That's good for people who already own a car, Drury said. It means people can upgrade to a new car without much additional money up front.

But, he continued, "The consumer that I sympathize with the absolute most? The first-time car buyer." Those buyers face a steep down payment, with nothing to trade in.

No matter whether buyers are choosing new or used, data from Edmunds shows that in 2026, they have been financing with lower down payments and longer auto term lengths. "We've just seen those explode," Drury said.

A report from Edmunds found that car buyers financed more than ever, taking out loans worth an average of $44,664 in the past quarter. They also found that more than a quarter of car buyers financed using loans with 84-month-long terms — or longer.

The combination of a small down payment — sometimes in the range of $500 or $1,000 — and a lengthy loan term can get really expensive for buyers in the long term, Drury said, especially with high interest rates.

"So people just say, 'Oh, forget it,' you know. 'I'll just, I'll just choose the longer term length and put less money down. I've got other bills that are pulling at me,'" Drury said.

Why are new cars so expensive?

In part, vehicles cost more because the cost of making them has gone up for automakers. There are now more tariffs on steel and aluminum, as well as on goods imported from Canada. That matters for American automakers who assemble vehicles on both sides of the border. The cost of computer chips (used in sensors and electronics) and copper (used for automotive wiring) has also risen thanks to competing demand from data centers.

But vehicles also cost more because Americans like bigger cars, SUVs and trucks, which tend to come with a higher price tag. The average sticker price for a full-size pickup truck is nearly $72,000, according to the Kelley Blue Book.

American carmakers have largely shifted their gears away from compact sedans. In earnings calls with investors, they've often cited American demand for bigger vehicles.

Plus, as analyst Mike Wall at Mobility Global points out, smaller vehicles offer lower margins for carmakers. "They were sort of that loss leader. It gets the eyeballs in the door," he said.

For the carmakers, they're not making as much money as they would compared to their bigger vehicles with pricier features.

Drury notes, people appreciate those features. They've gotten used to driving with 360-degree cameras, heated seats and parking assist systems. All of these drive up the cost of buying. "No one wants entry-level anymore," he said. "Everybody goes mid-to-upper trim levels."

"People love walking up to their car that already has the air conditioner going when it's 110 degrees outside, and think, 'You know what? I don't have to get in here and potentially burn my hands,'" Drury continued. "So as we get accustomed to more features, more options, we naturally kind of pile on, too. And automakers, they're very aware of that."

A challenging time for automakers

Over the past few years, "automakers have been under incredible stress," Keating said. Yes, there are tariffs and other rising production costs. Many also poured money into developing electric vehicle technology, but EVs still only make up a small slice of the U.S. car market. About 6% of new cars sold are electric, according to Edmunds.

And the market for car buyers is smaller. About 16 million people buy new cars every year — about 1 million fewer since the pandemic.

Notably, fewer people in their late 30s and early 40s are buying cars. "They're just simply holding onto their cars longer," Keating said. Her hypothesis? "That age group and that cohort is simply just dealing with different household pressures for their money and are making the choice to stay in the vehicles that they have."

For the most part, the people buying new cars tend to be older and wealthier. Keating said that might be because older drivers are staying on the road longer. " We have seen this interesting shift towards individuals keeping their licenses longer and therefore more 65 and up, 75 and up individuals are purchasing vehicles than ever before," she said.

For automakers, a drop in car buyers means they have to compete more with each other for sales.

"At the end of the day, each of these competitors are sharing, trying to go after a pie that isn't necessarily growing," Keating said. So instead, " they're stealing share from their competitors as opposed to counting on more consumers entering the picture."

text:
Nuclear startup X-energy announced Monday that it had been given the go-ahead from federal officials to build its first four commercial reactors.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved the construction permit application for four of X-energy’s Xe-100 reactors at a Dow chemical plant in Texas. Each reactor will be capable of generating 80 megawatts of electricity and 200 megawatts of heat. X-energy says the approval is the first for an advanced nuclear reactor at an industrial site in the United States.

The U.S. nuclear industry has pinned its hopes on small modular reactors — or SMRs — like those being developed by X-energy. By shrinking the reactor, proponents say it will speed construction and reduce costs, though those advantages have yet to be proven. No SMR is currently in operation in the U.S., and X-energy says Dow’s reactors won’t be operational until the early 2030s.

X-energy claims that its reactor design, which flows helium gas over uranium-containing fuel pellets, is safer than many existing reactors, but the Union of Concerned Scientists questioned the claim and the speed with which X-energy received the permit.

“The NRC only accomplished this feat by pushing consideration of critical safety questions to a later date—issues the NRC should’ve fully resolved before green lighting construction,” Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety for the organization, said in a statement.

The nuclear industry has benefited from strong interest from hyperscalers and data center developers, who are desperate for any and all sources of electricity. Amazon’s Climate Pledge Fund led X-energy’s $500 million Series C-1, and the big tech company has also committed to buying 5 gigawatts of capacity from the nuclear startup.

X-energy rode that wave of excitement earlier this year when its April initial public offering raised $1 billion. But since then, investors’ optimism has tempered.

The hesitancy isn’t surprising: Nuclear power plants are expensive to build and can take years to complete. Eventually, X-energy hopes to rein in both time and cost, but its first reactors are likely to be pricey.

The new permit approval gave X-energy a small jolt yesterday, though it was only enough to recover last week’s losses. The company’s shares are trading at less than half their initial offering price.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a historic bill that reflects years of bipartisan work to reform our outdated permitting processes while protecting the environment,” said Sen. Schatz (D-Hawaiʻi).

“Permitting delays drive up costs and stall projects, making electricity, housing, and public transportation more expensive. This legislation will help lower costs, build clean energy, modernize America’s grid, cut emissions, and hold data center developers accountable,” he said.

He said this bill is a bipartisan compromise, and called deals like this “tough.”

“We heard from Native leaders and advocates and secured some key changes to improve the historic preservation title and ensure that federal agencies consult with Native Hawaiian organizations, Tribes, and others about historic and cultural resources. I understand these changes won’t be enough for everyone to support the bill, but we’ll continue working to ensure Native Hawaiian organizations and Tribes have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their communities,” said Schatz.

“While BAAJA is not perfect, it represents a rare opportunity to pass strong, bipartisan legislation that will help lower costs and make it easier for American workers to build the things our country needs. I will vote to pass it and will continue working with my colleagues to deliver results for people in Hawaiʻi and across the country,” he said.

Meanwhile, US Sen. Mazie K. Hirono (D-Hawaiʻi), a member of the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, provided the following statement:

“Permitting reform can bring American families cleaner and more affordable energy, but I believe it can be done without weakening environmental protections or our relationships with Indigenous communities. This bill does not stop the Trump regime from stacking the deck for fossil energy at the expense of renewable energy development. While I will evaluate any changes made as discussions continue, I do not support the bill in its current form.”

text:
Memo to the Austin City Council Requesting a New Austin Energy Rate Case

TO: Mayor Kirk Watson, Austin City Council Members

COPY: City Manager T.C. Broadnax, Deputy City Manager Jon Fortune

RE: Time for an Austin Energy Rate Case

Austin Energy’s rates have been increased three times since the utility’s last rate case. These increases of 2% in 2024, 5% in 2025 and 5% in 2026 are just the start. Austin Energy’s projections indicate plans to continue requesting 5% increases every year at least through 2030. Rate increases should only be approved after thoroughly scrutinizing the utility’s spending and what is causing cost increases through a rate case process.

The City of Austin established a robust rate case process for Austin Energy after a large group of Austin Energy customers who live outside Austin city limits successfully challenged Austin Energy rates at the PUC in 2012. That process, which was used in 2016 and 2022, does several things that City Council doesn’t do when approving rate increases during the budget process.

Require a full accounting of expenses in a “cost-of-service study” to justify the need for additional revenue.

Allow all customers the opportunity to formally intervene in a process run by a neutral third party and scrutinize those costs and challenge those costs they think may not be justified. Intervention can be done with or without a lawyer.

Involve a dedicated Consumer Advocate to represent residential and small commercial customers.

Provide for discussion and debate of the methodology used to allocate costs between different customer classes (industrial, commercial, residential). If you want to ensure that costs caused by larger commercial and industrial customers (including data centers) aren’t being paid by residential and small commercial customers, this is an essential step.

Review of proposed rate structures, especially for residential customers. This is the opportunity to ensure that equity and energy conservation priorities are reflected in rate design.

Consider alternate rate proposals from intervenors. Past proposals have included establishing a multifamily rate class and optional time-of-use rates.

Allowing rate increases without proper scrutiny is abdicating your responsibility. It’s your job as utility regulators to give proper scrutiny to proposed rate increases and to ensure that all Austin Energy customers have at least as much opportunity to provide input on rate changes as they would with an investor-owned utility. A city-owned utility should provide for more customer engagement, not less.

When it comes to changing Austin Energy rates, you should look at the Public Utility Commission of Texas for a minimum standard of process. Base rate changes should only be approved after a full rate case. Austin Energy should have to justify any proposed rate increases by pointing to data in its cost-of-service study and defend those proposals to all customers in a rate case.

Austin Energy has already stated that it plans to complete a cost-of-service study early in 2027. In July, the City of Austin Electric Utility Commission passed a resolution in favor of beginning a rate case process in early 2027. City Council should direct the utility to also hire an independent hearing examiner and a qualified consumer advocate. Make it clear that no additional rate increases will be approved until after a full rate case.

description:

text:
South Carolina’s economic development agency wants to turn the state into a powerhouse of energy manufacturing and research.

It’s leaning on a federally-funded research program to make that happen.

For the past three years, a conglomerate of South Carolina colleges, a federal nuclear research laboratory and the state Department of Commerce — collectively known as SC Nexus — earned the right to bill itself as an expert in energy technology.

The effort, which started with the University of South Carolina and Clemson University, was aimed at reeling in more federal research dollars but has also become a tool for luring new employers — and jobs — to the state.

SC Nexus, in October 2023, officially became one of 31 U.S. Commerce Department designated technology hubs across the country, with the goal of creating more high-paying technology jobs and making the nation more competitive in high-tech industries.

A dozen of those hubs, including SC Nexus, went on to receive federal financial backing.

In 2024, the state netted $45 million from the Biden administration’s CHIPS and Science Act, meant to reduce U.S. dependence on China for semiconductors, artificial intelligence, high-powered computing and more.

That initial funding round lined Clemson up for success on a second grant: This year, Clemson partnered with the University of North Carolina at Charlotte on a National Science Foundation grant that could bring in as much as $160 million over the next decade for research related to the power grid.

So far, the two schools have jointly received $15 million. How much they’ll ultimately receive is not yet known.

Energy Research and Training

The $45 million was split four ways. The money paid to expand existing energy test beds at Clemson and at the Savannah River National Laboratory, open a new one at USC, and educate students.

Those three test beds are set to come online through spring and summer, starting in March with Clemson’s Electrical Grid Research Innovation and Development center at the former U.S. Naval Base in North Charleston.

Before the expansion, Clemson researchers had access to a mini-grid that could test technologies up to 15 megawatts. In early spring, that number will increase to 35 megawatts, with the ability to test in remote, rural locations.

“That makes it one of the most advanced grid simulation facilities in the country. It’s a really unique asset,” Cristina Long Paredes, executive director of SC Nexus, told the SC Daily Gazette.

The goal, according to Long Paredes was to get these technologies out of the lab and solving real-world industry issues. As companies come up with new ideas, they can use the Clemson site to test it out, ensuring everything works as planned.

“It’s starting to really elevate the conversation that South Carolina is more than just a manufacturing state,” she said. “We also have the research and development capabilities, specifically in energy.”

This is of particular importance as power companies nationwide are dumping billions into updates to the country’s aging power grid.

In September, the U.S. Department of Energy awarded Duke Energy $50 million to increase the power capacity on its electric grid in the Carolinas. That includes upgrades to power lines and conductors in Greenville and Spartanburg counties.

Come July, South Carolina’s other two test beds are expected to be operational.

At the national nuclear laboratory near Aiken, the testing relates to hackers and cyber attacks on the grid. And at USC, it’s a mini-manufacturing line meant to help build better batteries, essential to the solar industry as well as electric vehicles.

“Again, we want to make sure we help companies and budding entrepreneurs lower their financial risk, getting them to market sooner and thereby enhancing their bottom line and putting more people to work,” Long Paredes said.

For example, Pennsylvania-headquartered EnerSys announced in 2024 it would build a $500 million lithium-ion battery plant in Greenville, employing 500 people when it’s fully operational.

It’s expected to open late next year.

While EnerSys is a $3.75 billion company, the world’s largest industrial battery maker, it plans to use the USC battery test bed for its research and development.

“That’s a great example of recruiting a company into the state and tying them directly to our research and development capabilities,” Long Paredes said.

The hope is that the reverse will be true as well — that companies start out doing research at one of the test sites and ultimately decide to open manufacturing operations here.

Since 2024, more than 25 energy-related companies announced plans to locate in the Palmetto State, pledging more than 4,000 jobs and $3.5 billion in investments.

Educating Students

Part of the federal funding was set aside for scholarships at the state’s technical schools and a hands-on traveling lab meant to get K-12 students interested in energy-related careers.

So far, the state has given out 230 scholarships, each worth between $2,000 and $5,000, to technical college students studying to become linemen for utility companies in the state.

The effort focused on South Carolina’s more rural technical colleges first, Long Paredes said. At Denmark Technical College, for example, three students have already graduated and gone to work at Dominion Energy, energy contractor Gregory Electric and Black River Electric Cooperative.

At the S.C. Governor’s School for Science and Mathematics , the state is offering summer camps and educational workshops once a month just on energy, “to spark conversations and make young people who are just formulating what they’re going to do, see that as a pathway and a career opportunity,” Long Paredes said.

By next school year, South Carolina will have a mobile career exploration bus it can send to K-12 schools, complete with virtual reality glasses that let students practice skills, such as scaling a power pole.

“So when you think of South Carolina, you think of it as an energy state where you can develop, test, and deploy energy technologies,” Long Paredes said. “That includes the research and development capability, that includes the manufacturing side, and it includes the talent pipeline to support each one of those. And all of it is in the name of energy security and national security.”

This story first appeared in South Carolina News Gazette. Read the original here.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy has announced the financial close of a $480 million loan for Arena Energy’s Project Elkhorn in the US Gulf of Mexico.

The multi-year brownfield redevelopment will modernize 22 existing offshore platforms in the Southern Eugene Island area off the coast of Louisiana, a program that is designed to increase Arena Energy’s oil and natural gas production across the continental shelf.

Project Elkhorn will focus on refurbishment, repowering, retooling, replacement, and relocation of platforms; processing and compression upgrades; expansion of production and water-handling capacity; return of idled platforms to service; and development of new subsea natural gas pipeline infrastructure to improve midstream connectivity for future wells.

Financing is structured in up to five tranches through 2030.

Future development drilling, routine operations, plugging and abandonment, and decommissioning remain outside the financed scope, with Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) and Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) retaining full regulatory authority.

At peak production, the project is expected to add up to 38,600 barrels of oil per day and up to 77 million cubic feet of natural gas per day.

Over the life of the project, it is projected to deliver approximately 125 million barrels of oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas, generating an estimated $1.6 billion in additional federal royalties.

Arena Energy currently produces approximately 30,000 barrels of oil per day offshore in the shallow water and shelf regions of the US Gulf.

Arena says that it will execute the work with long-standing partners White Fleet Drilling and Rosefield Pipeline.

“Arena was founded on the belief that the mature fields of the Gulf Shelf still hold vast potential, and Project Elkhorn is a critical part of that strategy,” said Mike Minarovic, CEO and Founder of Arena Energy.

Minarovic added: “The Southern Eugene Island area is one of the most prolific oil-producing regions in American history, and its infrastructure still has decades of productive life ahead. What it needed was long-term capital to match the opportunity. This financing lets us put existing infrastructure back to work, develop proved reserves, and keep producing reliable barrels here at home.”

text:
As the Democratic Party prepares to take control of Congress following the midterm elections, experts at an Indiana University panel Monday discussed how the leadership change could affect federal climate policy.

During an online panel organized by Concerned Scientists at IU in partnership with Advocates for Science at IU titled “Climate Policy After the Midterms: What’s Next?” three experts and a moderator discussed the potential effects of the election on climate legislation, renewable energy and environmental regulations. The experts discussed the potential effects of the election on climate legislation, renewable energy and environmental regulations.

The panel was part of IU’s inaugural Climate Week, which runs Nov. 8-14. The university’s Environmental Resilience Institute organized the week, which is focused on science-informed, community-driven and equity-centered approaches to environmental challenges, with support from the O’Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs and other campus partners.

The panel featured David Watkins, director of government affairs for the climate and energy program at the Union of Concerned Scientists; Marjorie Hershey, professor emeritus of political science at IU; and David Konisky, professor and associate dean for esearch at the O’Neill School. Janet McCabe, former deputy administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency from April 29, 2021, to Oct. 4, 2024, and visiting professor and executive in residence at the O’Neill School, moderated the discussion.

Konisky said the election represented a significant political shift but cautioned that a change in congressional control would not automatically reverse environmental policies enacted during the Trump administration. He said many regulatory changes during the current presidential administration have been made through executive agencies, which means reversing them could require additional administrative action or court proceedings.

Konisky said congressional Democrats could attempt to restore some clean energy incentives affected by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, but that the legislative process and President Donald Trump’s veto power could limit what Congress accomplishes. According to the Internal Revenue Service, the law accelerated the expiration of several energy-related tax credits and deductions.

Watkins said a Democrat-led Congress could increase oversight of the administration through investigations and hearings. He suggested that congressional attention to affordability and potential outside influence on policymaking from fossil fuel lobbying could create opportunities to challenge policies that benefit fossil fuel interests.

For the student organizations behind the event, the discussion was intended to help attendees understand what could change in Washington and how they could participate in shaping policy, ASIU Co-President Bella Matney said.

Matney said ASIU works closely with Concerned Scientists at IU, combining student engagement and perspectives with the experience and connections of faculty members. She also said climate policy had been actively targeted over the past two years and that some of the resulting damage could take years to reverse.

“I hope attendees leave with a better understanding of what's possible over the next two years, as well as what they can do themselves to help push for meaningful change,” Matney said to the Indiana Daily Student.

A recurring theme during the discussion was the importance of connecting climate policy to issues voters prioritize, particularly the cost of living.

Hershey said affordability concerns, including food, gasoline and utility prices, would likely shape how voters judge elected officials. She suggested that climate advocates may have more success when they connect environmental policies to those everyday economic concerns.

Hershey also discussed the election’s implications for Indiana. Democrats broke the Republican supermajority in the Indiana House of Representatives, although Republicans retained control of both the House and the Indiana State Senate. Hershey said the narrower Republican margin in the House could create more opportunities for bipartisan negotiations and give individual legislators greater influence over legislation.

The discussion then turned to data centers and their demand for electricity. Watkins said clean energy could help meet that demand, challenging the argument that new facilities must rely on fossil fuels. Konisky described several energy approaches companies are pursuing, including solar power, battery storage, nuclear energy and natural gas generation.

Konisky also discussed public resistance to data center development, citing concerns about electricity prices, water use and communities having limited influence over decisions that affect their neighborhoods. He described the situation as a “trifecta of distrust,” involving technology companies, utilities and government.

While the panelists expressed uncertainty about major federal climate legislation in the near future, Konisky said states could continue pursuing environmental policies when federal action is limited. He pointed to California as a potential leader in areas such as vehicle emissions standards and environmental regulation.

Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, is supporting this partnership through a broader initiative that provides $2 million in research grants across five U.S. colleges, including the California Institute of Technology, the Ohio State University College of Medicine, Louisiana State University and UTHealth Houston.

Matney emphasized the importance of remaining engaged in politics and holding elected officials accountable, particularly because younger generations will experience the long-term consequences of current decisions.

Michael Hamburger, a member of CSIU, academic adviser to ASIU and a professor emeritus of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at IU, described the election as a possible turning point for science advocacy.

Hamburger said CSIU is an informal, nonpartisan organization that has worked on science policy issues since 2017. He described ASIU as its student-led affiliate and said the organizations hope to engage scientists, students and supporters of science in the legislative process.

“For the past several years, it’s fair to say that the science advocacy community has been ‘playing defense,’ seeking to minimize the negative consequences of administrative action,” Hamburger said. “Now may be an opportunity for our team to move to playing offense and actually make some positive impacts on the trajectory of federal and state support for science in our country.”

description:
It is the first time the NRC has issued a construction permit for a nuclear reactor on an industrial site.
A construction permit alone does not mean that the Long Mott project is moving forward.
Long time coming: The permit was issued to Dow’s wholly owned subsidiary, Long Mott Energy.
The construction permit milestone comes roughly six years after the DOE picked X-energy for the ARDP.
In the spring of 2025, Long Mott Energy submitted a construction permit application and the NRC docketed the application soon after.
text:
Monday’s construction permit issuance for the 320-MWe reactor project at Dow’s UCC Seadrift Operations manufacturing site is historic on multiple fronts:

It is the first construction permit issued for a high-temperature, gas-cooled (HTGR) reactor in nearly 60 years.

It is the first-ever U.S. approval for a pebble-bed HTGR design.

It is the first time the NRC has issued a construction permit for a nuclear reactor on an industrial site.

“This is an important day. Getting the construction permit earlier than expected is reflective of the thorough and efficient work of the NRC, the reforms that have been put in place by Congress over the last six years, and the phenomenal work of the X-energy and Dow teams,” said X-energy CEO Clay Sell.

About the project: Dow has proposed to construct four Xe-100s, an 80-MWe, 200-MWt HTGR that can be deployed in configurations of four to 12 units. As a pebble-bed HTGR, the Xe-100 would be fueled by HALEU TRISO particles encased in graphite pebbles and cooled by helium.

An HTGR produces steam at high temperatures that can be used for electricity production or for industrial purposes. Dow and X-energy have noted this project would do just that, providing both electricity and high-temperature steam. According to the two companies, Long Mott could replace existing energy and steam assets at Seadrift that are nearing their respective ends of life. The four reactors are expected to provide power to the site for 60 years.

Seadrift—Dow’s second-largest site in Texas—produces everyday consumer products like plastics (polyethylene) for wire and cable applications, food and beverage containers, automotive parts, toys, and diapers; glycols for antifreeze, polyester fabrics, and bottles; and oxide derivatives for health and beauty products.

A construction permit alone does not mean that the Long Mott project is moving forward. Both Dow and X-energy have said a final decision hasn't been made yet. “Several important milestones remain before potential construction activities could begin, including continued engineering and design finalization and review by Dow’s Board of Directors,” the Dow announcement said.

A preliminary investment decision is expected in 2027. If approved, construction could begin later this decade, with commercial operation in the early 2030s. The NRC would need to issue an operating license for fuel loading and start-up.

Long time coming: The permit was issued to Dow’s wholly owned subsidiary, Long Mott Energy. The project—a collaboration with X-energy—is part of the Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP). It is one of two full-scale demonstration projects under ARDP, the other being TerraPower’s Natrium power plant project in Wyoming, which received its construction permit earlier this year. The Seadrift project has received roughly $2.15 billion in cost-shared funding from DOE.

The construction permit milestone comes roughly six years after the DOE picked X-energy for the ARDP. While X-energy originally planned to site its ARDP demo near Richland, Wash., and remains engaged with Energy Northwest and Amazon on the planned Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, in 2023 the company entered into an agreement with Dow to build the ARDP demo plant at a Dow site. In the spring of 2025, Long Mott Energy submitted a construction permit application and the NRC docketed the application soon after. The most recent regulatory hurdle the project cleared came this spring, when the NRC completed its environmental assessment of the proposed facility and issued a finding of no significant impact.

Monday’s issuance means a permit decision was reached within 18 months of the review commencing, a target NRC officials set for the process.

“We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction,” said NRC Chairman Ho Nieh.

text:
OTTAWA — The federal government asked Ford Motor to maintain ownership of its assembly plant in Oakville, Ont., and keep up its production there until at least 2038 in exchange for $464.5 million in financing to make gas- and diesel-powered trucks, The Logic has learned.

The Logic reported in May that the federal government awarded the Detroit automaker with the contribution from its flagship Strategic Response Fund to overhaul the facility and scale its production to 100,000 units per year of the F-Series Super Duty line. The award replaced an earlier agreement that would have seen the federal and Ontario governments each contribute $295 million to a $1.8-billion effort to turn Oakville into a hub for electric vehicles.

Newly released government documents shed more light on the conditions that Ottawa sought to attach to the new deal, beyond the public commitment to create some 1,800 jobs.

“Ford Canada shall maintain ownership and ongoing manufacturing operations of its facilities in Oakville, Ont., for the term,” reads a November 2025 term sheet for the agreement that ends in March 2038. The Logic obtained the document through the Access to Information Act.

It remains unclear whether the condition to maintain ownership of the Oakville assembly plant that was proposed in the term sheet, which was valid through March 31, 2026, made it into the final contract between Ottawa and Ford. It has not been released. Ford Canada did not respond to questions about it for this story. The federal innovation department did not provide further details of the contract beyond what is in the public disclosure. “Details of contribution agreements are subject to commercial confidentiality and cannot be disclosed,” said spokesperson Andréa Daigle, including whether the money is repayable.

The terms of such funding agreements have come under greater scrutiny as U.S. President Donald Trump has slapped 25 per cent tariffs on foreign cars and trucks in a bid to reshore manufacturing. Canada imposed counter-tariffs on U.S. autos, with exceptions for companies making vehicles domestically so long as they keep doing it and stick to planned investments.

Last year, Chrysler parent company Stellantis decided to make the Jeep Compass in Illinois, abandoning plans to do so at its assembly plant in Brampton, Ont. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has warned Stellantis that it is in breach of a contract that said it would “create and maintain high-skilled jobs” in Canada in exchange for millions of dollars in federal subsidies. On Monday, Stellantis said it is going ahead with the sale of the idled Brampton plant and related equipment to Ontario-based armoured-vehicle maker Roshel for an undisclosed sum.

After trade talks with the White House collapsed in August, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Canadian negotiators had sought to reduce tariffs on medium- and heavy-duty trucks at the last minute. Janice Charette, Canada’s chief U.S. trade negotiator, said Ottawa had been consistent in asking for relief for the entire auto sector.

The Super Duty F-Series includes the bestselling heavier F-250 and F-350 pickup trucks, as well as utility vehicles such as ambulances. Depending on their weight classification, all are subject to 25 per cent U.S. tariffs on either light-duty vehicles, which have been in effect since April 2025, or medium- and heavy-duty trucks, which the U.S. added last November. There is a partial carve-out for any U.S. content in vehicles that comply with the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement.

Ford CEO Jim Farley has nonetheless been bullish on the role that Oakville will play in its North American supply chain. In an earnings call on Oct. 28, Farley said production volume at Oakville, which reached 3,488 units in October after starting with six in April, is already exceeding expectations. The vehicles made in Oakville started heading to dealerships last month. Highlighting the Oakville plant as an example of how Ford plans to leverage its supply chain to reduce costs, Farley also praised the quality of the trucks made in Ontario as comparable to the Super Duty trucks produced at its main plant in Kentucky.

Oakville will also help Ford keep up the pace when other plants need some downtime next year to get ready to manufacture the next-generation F-150 truck. “The added capacity will give us flexibility for future plant changeovers and support profitable growth in retail, rental and outfitter channels,” Farley said.

In July, Ford announced $1.25 billion in planned spending over three years across its operations in Ontario after securing a new collective agreement with Unifor, the union representing its Canadian employees. That was on top of the $5 billion that Ford is spending in Oakville, which also includes a new stamping plant.

Ford is not alone in betting on the continued integration of the North American auto industry.

On Monday, Honda announced $166 million to restart engine production and retool for new models of hybrid and gas-powered vehicles in Alliston, Ont., as part of $867 million in government-backed planned investments. The Japanese automaker also committed US$3 billion for a new factory in Ohio. Honda said the investments in its “integrated manufacturing network” will boost its North American capacity to 1.9 million vehicles per year.

text:
X-Energy, a developer of advanced nuclear reactors and fuel technology, and Dow through its wholly-owned subsidiary Long Mott Energy, announced that the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has approved the Construction Permit Application (CPA) for the proposed construction of four Xe-100 advanced small modular reactors at Dow’s UCC Seadrift Operations site in Texas.

The CPA approval makes Long Mott Generating Station the first advanced nuclear facility approved for an industrial site in the United States, a historic milestone achieved under the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP). First delivery is expected in the early 2030s, the companies said.

Approval of the construction permit enables X-energy and Dow to continue advancing the proposed project toward construction readiness, finalizing and standardizing the Xe-100 design, maturing the supply chain for long-lead components and materials, and developing an operating license application for submission to the NRC. The companies said this supports Dow’s consideration of the proposed project’s next phases, ensuring the design, equipment, and materials are in place before allocating major capital for full-scale construction.

“Today, the new NRC is issuing America’s first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than half a century,” said NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh. “We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction.”

This marks the first NRC CPA approval of a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in nearly 60 years, the first pebble-bed HTGR approval and the first for a nuclear industrial deployment. The NRC’s review found that the Xe-100 design can be safely sited and constructed within an operating industrial site. The proposed plant is intended to provide both electricity and high-temperature steam to Dow’s site, replacing existing energy and steam assets near their end-of-life. The four Xe-100s deployed at Seadrift are expected to provide industrial power to the site for 60 years.

X-energy’s Xe-100 is an 80 MWe/200 MWt high-temperature gas-cooled reactor meant to ensure safety through the passive physics of its advanced TRISO-X coated particle fuel, as well as traditional defense-in-depth systems. TRISO fuel encompasses, in one component, many barriers to the release of radionuclides, and has been described by the DOE as, “the most robust nuclear fuel on earth.” This safety profile is expected to support a 400-meter emergency planning zone, compared to 10 miles for conventional light-water reactors, which could enable new generation to be safely sited closer to the point of need.

Ben Reinke, X-energy’s Senior Vice President of Global Business Development, previously spoke to Power Engineering about the Xe-100 design, a leading example of what is expected to be nuclear’s next chapter.

Dow is expected to consider a preliminary investment decision in 2027. Full-scale nuclear construction would begin following Dow’s final investment decision, advancing a shared, generational vision for next-generation nuclear technology to commercial scale under ARDP.

text:
China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.

As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.

In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.

Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.

Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”

For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added.

“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”

He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”

China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.

Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way: “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”

China as a ‘doer and go-getter’

The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows.

Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.

The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue.

“Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”

Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed.

Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.

The need for trust

China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.

Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”

If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.

Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.

They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.

For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … so no major drama.”

text:
Boston — Governor Maura Healey today announced the appointment of Aladdine Joroff as Massachusetts Climate Chief, effective Tuesday, November 10. Joroff currently serves as Deputy Climate Chief and Director of Mitigation and Community Resilience in the Governor's Office of Climate Innovation and Resilience. She will succeed Melissa Hoffer, who is departing the administration to serve as President of Vermont Law and Graduate School.

Joroff brings extensive experience in climate policy, environmental law and working with communities to advance climate solutions. As Climate Chief, she will continue to lead the administration's efforts to coordinate climate policy across state government, strengthen the resilience of Massachusetts communities, advance clean energy solutions and support the state's climate goals.

“Aladdine Joroff has been a key member of our climate team, and she knows what it takes to make real progress for Massachusetts residents and businesses,” said Governor Maura Healey. “From helping communities prepare for severe weather to advancing clean energy solutions that lower costs and create jobs, Aladdine brings the experience, expertise and leadership we need to keep moving Massachusetts forward. I'm excited to have her take on this new role, and I'm deeply grateful to Melissa Hoffer for her incredible leadership in establishing this office and helping make Massachusetts a national leader on climate.”

“Cities and towns are on the front lines of climate change, and Aladdine understands how important it is that they have the resources and support they need,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. “She has spent her career working with local leaders to develop practical solutions, and she knows that strong partnerships are essential to building more resilient communities. We look forward to continuing this important work with her as Climate Chief.”

“I'm excited to continue the transformative work Chief Hoffer has led to implement the Healey-Driscoll administration's vision of a government wide approach to climate change,” said Aladdine Joroff. “I look forward to continued collaboration with our partners across the Commonwealth.”

On her first full day in office in January 2023, Governor Healey signed an Executive Order establishing the Office of Climate Innovation and Resilience and creating the nation's first cabinet-level Climate Chief position. The office works across state agencies to advance climate innovation, emissions reduction, adaptation and resilience, ensuring that climate considerations are incorporated into policy and decision-making throughout state government.

Joroff joined the Healey-Driscoll Administration in August 2024 after serving as Director of Climate Policy for the City of Boston. Previously, she spent a decade teaching and practicing at Harvard Law School's Emmett Environmental Law and Policy Clinic, where she worked with Massachusetts municipalities, nonprofit organizations and advocacy groups on environmental and climate issues. She also taught the multidisciplinary Climate Solutions Living Lab, which brought students together to develop innovative approaches to addressing climate change.

Joroff also serves as a Visiting Lecturer on Environmental Science and Public Policy at Harvard University. Earlier in her career, she practiced environmental, energy and land use law at Goodwin and Beveridge & Diamond. She holds a law degree from the University of Pennsylvania and bachelor's and master's degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Hoffer has served as Massachusetts' inaugural Climate Chief since January 2023 until Monday, November 9, helping establish the office and advance the administration's whole-of-government approach to addressing climate change. She will become President of Vermont Law and Graduate School on December 1, 2026.

Its cells and modules power eight High Range electric vehicle models marketed by the Stellantis Group (Peugeot E-3008, E-5008, Jeep Compass, Lancia Gamma, DS N° 7, N° 8, Citroën C5 Aircross, Opel Grandland).

The first block of the Gigafactory is operating on a 5×8 shift pattern, 7 days a week, with scrap rates steadily approaching target levels.

The ramp-up is continuing; industrialisation and scaling up are now well and truly underway.

Module production volume for the month of September alone is close to the total production level achieved by ACC for the whole of 2025.

ACC is successfully supplying Stellantis in line with agreed production plans.

The second production block, with a capacity of 12.9 GWh, is scheduled to commence production in 2027 to power the Mercedes Group’s electric cars.

In a context shaped by geopolitical tensions, rising energy prices, economic uncertainty and climate imperatives, ACC offers a concrete European answer to the challenges of transport electrification. Building and mastering battery technology in Europe is critical to securing strategic supply chains, preserving industrial jobs and know-how, and strengthening the continent’s technological sovereignty.

This is why Europe’s ambition to promote ‘Made in Europe’ must now be swiftly translated into the introduction of an Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), which will provide the necessary support for the demand for batteries manufactured in Europe.

As Allan Swan, CEO of ACC since May 2026, points out, said:

Reaching 5 million cells produced in France is an important milestone for ACC and a clear demonstration of the progress achieved by our teams over the past years.

‘It shows that Europe can develop and industrialise advanced battery technologies at scale.At the same time, the competitiveness challenge remains. Europe must now ensure that its industrial ambitions are supported by a framework that enables battery manufacturing to compete on a level playing field. Only a competitive European offering will be able to meet the demand for ‘Made in the EU’ production.’

ACC will continue to innovate and develop next-generation products offering best-in-class performance and real-world driving range. Combined with faster charging times, these technologies will help accelerate the transition to electric mobility while meeting consumers’ expectations.

title: Carlyle ranks near bottom on climate scorecard amid oil and gas expansion
description:
The 2026 Private Equity Climate Risks Scorecard found that Carlyle again earned a D and ranked as the third-worst firm out of the 20 private equity firms analyzed.
NGP also exited a few upstream oil and gas drilling companies.
