description:
The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has issued a construction permit for a four-reactor nuclear power facility in Texas, marking the first approval for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) in nearly 60 years.
The construction permit marks a significant milestone for advanced nuclear technology in the US.
It is the third advanced reactor construction permit issued by the NRC in 2026 and the agency’s first approval of a multi-module advanced reactor facility.
The agency said its review was completed within an 18-month schedule, demonstrating its ability to assess advanced reactor designs while maintaining its safety requirements.
“Today, the new NRC is issuing America’s first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than half a century,” NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh said.
text:
The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has issued a construction permit for a four-reactor nuclear power facility in Texas, marking the first approval for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) in nearly 60 years.

The Long Mott Generating Station, planned for Calhoun County, Texas, will feature four Xe-100 small modular reactors (SMRs) developed by US-based X-energy. The project is being developed by Long Mott Energy, a wholly owned subsidiary of chemical manufacturer Dow, for its Seadrift Operations site.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

The facility is designed primarily to supply high-temperature steam for industrial processes at Dow’s site. It will also generate electricity, with surplus power exported to the grid.

The construction permit marks a significant milestone for advanced nuclear technology in the US. It is the third advanced reactor construction permit issued by the NRC in 2026 and the agency’s first approval of a multi-module advanced reactor facility.

Four reactors supply industrial steam

The four Xe-100 reactors will have a combined thermal capacity of 800 megawatts (MWth) and an electrical capacity of 320 megawatts (MWe). Each module is designed to generate approximately 80 MWe of electricity while also supplying heat for industrial applications.

Unlike conventional nuclear power plants that primarily generate electricity, the Long Mott facility is designed around the energy requirements of an industrial site. High-temperature steam can support energy-intensive manufacturing operations, potentially replacing conventional fossil-fuel-based heat sources.

More from Energy

See All

The Xe-100 is a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor that uses helium as a coolant and graphite pebbles containing tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) fuel particles. Its pebble-bed core allows fuel to be added during operation, rather than requiring the reactor to shut down for conventional refueling.

The NRC’s approval also marks several regulatory firsts. These include its first construction permit for a pebble-bed reactor, its first approval of a reactor design featuring online refueling, and its first review of an HTGR under its risk-informed, technology-inclusive Licensing Modernization Project framework.

Permit clears construction path

The NRC completed its comprehensive safety evaluation in October, ahead of its scheduled timeline. It had already issued an Environmental Assessment and Finding of No Significant Impact in May.

The agency said its review was completed within an 18-month schedule, demonstrating its ability to assess advanced reactor designs while maintaining its safety requirements.

“Today, the new NRC is issuing America’s first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than half a century,” NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh said.

The permit authorizes Long Mott Energy to construct the facility in accordance with the approved design. However, it does not allow the company to load nuclear fuel or operate the reactors. A separate operating license from the NRC will be required before the plant can begin generating power.

Dow has also clarified that receiving the permit does not constitute a final investment decision to proceed with construction. The company still needs to complete engineering and design work and secure approval from its board. If it proceeds, construction could begin later this decade, with the facility expected to start operating in the early 2030s.

The project is being developed under the US Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, which supports the development and deployment of next-generation nuclear technologies.

name: Congress
title: This Bipartisan Bill Could Make Data Centers Pay | Voice of San Diego
description:
The reforms would accelerate permitting for energy and transmission projects while also limiting environmental review, and put the onus on data center developers to pay for all their own energy costs.
The bill could have big implications for the data center proposed on U.S. Navy land near downtown San Diego.
This 400-plus-page law would force data centers, rather than taxpayers, to pay for all their costs – both the power and the upgrades to the local power grid to keep it running.
While California lawmakers passed similar laws on data centers this last session, they don’t apply to San Diego’s proposed project.
Many backers of the bill say it’s long, arduous permitting processes making it difficult to expand energy grid infrastructure.
text:
Normally this newsletter is dedicated to local San Diego issues. But allow me, for a moment, to fixate on members of Congress.

They’re actually doing something – though how good it will be, on the whole, is up for debate.

A contingent of Democrats and Republicans just wrote the country’s biggest set of permitting reforms in years, and they’re trying to pass it before Democrats take over, following the “blue wave” midterm elections. The reforms would accelerate permitting for energy and transmission projects while also limiting environmental review, and put the onus on data center developers to pay for all their own energy costs.

The Senate got enough votes Monday to limit debate on the so-called BAAJA or Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act and move it forward for a final vote.

The bill could have big implications for the data center proposed on U.S. Navy land near downtown San Diego. This 400-plus-page law would force data centers, rather than taxpayers, to pay for all their costs – both the power and the upgrades to the local power grid to keep it running.

While California lawmakers passed similar laws on data centers this last session, they don’t apply to San Diego’s proposed project. The state doesn’t have jurisdiction over land owned by the U.S. Navy.

For that reason, among others, San Diego Rep. Scott Peters, along with clean energy proponents and developers and labor leaders, urged fellow Democrats to support the bill generated by the currently Republican-controlled Congress.

“Democrats say they want to lower utility costs and combat climate change. Research shows the bipartisan permitting package would do both,” Peters told Politico recently.

If you’d like to go deeper, David Roberts, a clean energy journalist and host of the Volts podcast, spent two hours unpacking its main reforms, chief among them allowing both electric transmission lines (the biggest powerlines carrying energy across state lines) and natural gas pipelines to be built much faster.

Electricity demand by Americans had been stagnant until the recent business of building data centers to fuel artificial intelligence coupled with electrification of cars and buildings exploded. But it takes 10 to 15 years to actually build a new transmission line, the highways of the power grid that can carry power from state to state.

Whole regions of the country are beginning to hit their limit in terms of how much power they can get to customers during heat waves, for example. The culprit? Many backers of the bill say it’s long, arduous permitting processes making it difficult to expand energy grid infrastructure.

Without transmission lines, it’s a lot harder to bring new clean energy projects online, dispatch their power to places that need it and really transition the grid off of fossil fuels.

The kicker is, BAAJA also makes it easier to build things like natural gas pipelines which are not good for the climate. (That’s because natural gas is a fossil fuel burning as almost pure methane, a huge climate heater-upper).

But that’s how lawmakers were able to make this a bipartisan deal. In any good compromise, neither side is happy.

The bet, as Roberts put it, is that both energy sources (Republicans favoring fossil fuels and Democrats favoring clean energy) would be on more equal footing to compete for energy proliferation. To speed up their permitting, both would get to bypass, in large part, the National Environmental Protection Act, which requires an analysis of a project’s environmental impacts. (Projects would still be subject to laws like the Clean Water Act, however.)

Environmental groups like the Center for Biological Diversity have decried this law for that reason.

Daniel Palken, Roberts’ guest who works for the oil-exec-owned Arnold Ventures, says that if this bill passes, it would allow a fair amount more drilling for oil and gas especially on federal land.

The Rhodium Group, an independent research think tank based in New York City, did a bunch of modeling on what the outcome of the bill reforms might be – and the conclusion was to take some bad with the good. The researchers’ paper said that the bill would allow for up to 249 gigawatts of clean resources to be built through 2040 – a 50 percent increase to average U.S. electricity demand now. Liquified natural gas production, mainly to be exported outside the U.S., would increase by up to 15 percent.

They estimate that tradeoff, in the best case scenario for the climate, would reduce economy-wide greenhouse gas emissions by 149 million metric tons by 2040. That’s like taking 32 million cars off the road for one year. But it’s not as astounding as it sounds.

Humanity as a whole needs to reduce greenhouse gas emission by 1,350 billion metric tons to have a 50 percent shot at reducing global warming by 2 degrees Celsius – a level of warming the United Nations predicts will still cause near total destruction of the world’s coral reefs and intensify drought, sea level rise and extreme heat on millions. The U.S. is the biggest emitter, especially if you include our offshoring of much of our manufacturing demand.

But it’s a start, I guess.

In Other News

Rep. Mike Levin says that Congress has taken another step toward getting nuclear waste off of the San Onofre power station site on the coast. (Union Tribune)

If you’re going to the beach in the next few days, make sure you check the tide. The National Weather Service issued a warning beginning Sunday at midnight through Tuesday evening for all San Diego County coastal areas that coastal flooding is expected due to high surf and high tides. (Sac Bee)

A local theater group is putting together an all-indigenous cast for a play about protecting the Tijuana River Valley. (Union-Tribune)

Californians rejected a push by business groups to pass sweeping changes to how California’s landmark environmental law works. (CBS)

Bernie Sanders-backed state insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim declared victory last week with at least 53 percent of the vote. (LA Times)

name: Texas American Energy
title: Senate weighing sweeping energy legislation - WDSU
description:
The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use.
Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity costs helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.
The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.
Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.
Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining.
text:
WASHINGTON —

The Senate on Monday is set to take up bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that face yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity costs helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

Midterm results could complicate bill's passage in lame-duck session

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats' sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act.

The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to share its perspective before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

"Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

Democrats are optimistic the bill will pass both chambers

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” next year.

Whitehouse said Trump's support should help the bill move toward a vote in the House.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.

Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, he said, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers.

Industry leaders are advocating for the bill's passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group.

But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a “terrible mistake” to proceed with the bill in the waning days of the current Congress.

While changes announced Saturday address a few concerns, the bill also comes with a gauntlet of new — and at times conflicting — rules, Campbell said. He said the bill maintains a veneer of federal safeguards while in fact stripping the power of federal agencies, states, tribes and communities to identify and prevent serious harm to health and the environment.

Sara Amundson, president of the Humane World Action Fund, said the bill weakens the scientific foundation of the Endangered Species Act and could create new opportunities to exclude needed wildlife protections.

“This proposed rewrite of the ‘best available science’ standard could give agencies new grounds to unfairly dismiss credible research, including science showing that stronger protections are needed for species at risk," she said, urging lawmakers to drop the provision or oppose the bill.

name: Detroit Environment
title: My veteran journey - State of Michigan
description:
Serving in various staff and command capacities within the Ohio Guard, I retired in October 1999, having attained the rank of captain.
A visit by a U.S. Army recruiter to my high school in the spring of 1977 started my military journey.
This meeting resulted in my joining the Ohio Guard (He related that 100% tuition reimbursement was being offered at the time.)
However, from my experiences as a former U.S. Army soldier and Ohio Army National Guard member, now a seasoned veteran, I have come to agree with fictional character Forrest Gump’s view that “Life is like a box of chocolates.
Less than 1% of the national population actively serve in the military or are serving in a part-time capacity within the National Guard or Reserve.
text:
Following eight-weeks of basic training at Fort Leonard Wood, in Missouri, I attended a six-month U.S. Air Force technical school at Lowry Air Force Base, in Denver, graduating as a Still Photographic Specialist. As a Regular Army soldier within the newly formed all-volunteer army, I became a still photographer assigned to a signal battalion in support of the 4th Infantry Division, Fort Carson, in Colorado.

After three years of active-duty service, being honorably discharged from the Army, I entered The Ohio State University in Columbus, Ohio and joined the 196th Public Affairs Detachment of the Ohio Army National Guard. Following successful completion of The Ohio State University Reserved Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC) training program, I “branch qualified” as an Engineer Officer, obtaining my Bachelor of Science degree in geology. Serving in various staff and command capacities within the Ohio Guard, I retired in October 1999, having attained the rank of captain.

Entering state service in Michigan in 1998 as a geologist, I currently work out of the Warren District Office as a senior environmental quality analyst in the hazardous waste program of the Materials Management Division within the Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE).

Since April 2022, I have been a member of the “EGLE Vets” Employee Resource Group (ERG). As a founding member, I headed up the ERG from its inception through July 2025. Along with a cadre of 10 EGLE veterans who represented military service in each of the U.S. Army, Air Force, Navy, and Marines, I was active in coordinating EGLE Vets’ collaborative multi-departmental training, awareness, and public service efforts, to include the now annually held Earth Day cemetery and grounds cleanup event at the Michigan Veteran Homes at Grand Rapids.

A visit by a U.S. Army recruiter to my high school in the spring of 1977 started my military journey. While attending Ohio State, working part-time as a security guard at a large factory in Columbus, I had a chance meeting with a fellow young security guard, also an Ohio State University student. This meeting resulted in my joining the Ohio Guard (He related that 100% tuition reimbursement was being offered at the time.) and in my changing degree programs from natural resources to geology (He advised me that there was more money to be made as a geologist.). Both pieces of advice certainly affected how my following years would roll out as a newly minted civilian transitioning to become a commissioned officer and citizen soldier of the Ohio Army National Guard.

So many of life’s events aren’t planned; they merely come about by happenstance. However, from my experiences as a former U.S. Army soldier and Ohio Army National Guard member, now a seasoned veteran, I have come to agree with fictional character Forrest Gump’s view that “Life is like a box of chocolates. You never know what you’re gonna get."

Author’s Note: Just over 3,100 veterans are employed by the State of Michigan, approximately 6% of the State of Michigan total workforce. Nationwide, from 5% to 7% of the population are veterans of the United States Armed Forces, extending back to World War II. Less than 1% of the national population actively serve in the military or are serving in a part-time capacity within the National Guard or Reserve.

Fifteen State of Michigan departments have been recognized by the Michigan Veterans Affairs Agency (MVAA) as Veteran-Friendly Employers, with 12 of those departments holding the highest “Gold Level Veteran-Friendly Employer” MVAA designation.

name: Clean Energy
title: Chicago program helps people transition from prison to solar jobs - Canary Media
description:
It’s part of a larger workforce initiative to inject equity into the state’s clean energy transition.
The foundation received a state grant for solar training created by the 2017 Future Energy Jobs Act, a federal grant for solar training in 2021.
Since 2024, it has been among the clean energy workforce hubs created and funded by the state’s 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act.
About three-quarters of Safer’s solar trainees so far have been justice-involved, but others who meet the state criteria are also eligible.
Vincent Jones, who has an IT background, found out about the solar training from a relative who had done it, and he applied while between jobs.
text:
Inside a brick building on Chicago’s West Side — once part of a sprawling Sears Roebuck campus — is an adult transitional center, or halfway house, that’s home to 250 men completing sentences for criminal convictions and preparing to reenter society.

Just down the hallway from their living quarters, a high-ceilinged former gymnasium holds an unexpected sight: a two-story under-construction home, complete with exposed insulation and electric fixtures.

This is where residents of the halfway house, and other men and women who have been involved with the criminal justice system, train for a new chapter in their lives: work in the solar industry.

It’s part of a larger workforce initiative to inject equity into the state’s clean energy transition.

Illinois’ 2017 and 2021 clean energy laws created job training programs that prioritize people from marginalized communities, and include remedial education, interpersonal and professional skills, and wraparound services to help them with childcare, car problems, mental health needs, and other challenges.

The state has a specific focus on including the formerly incarcerated in this effort, and the Safer Foundation, headquartered in this brick building, has been central to achieving that.

Since 1972, the nonprofit has equipped people who were formerly incarcerated with skills and helped them get jobs. Safer President and CEO Mark Yates said that clean energy is a promising sector, offering entry-level jobs, opportunities to advance, and carpentry and electrical experience that also translates to other fields.

Safer says that its relationships with employers like utility-scale developer Millennium Solar Electric and residential installer SunRun help, since companies are often reluctant to hire people with criminal convictions or gaps in work history.

“They’ve been incarcerated beyond technology advances” in many cases, Yates noted, and may have to learn how to use a smartphone, for example, along with mastering solar technology.

In the past three years, more than 100 people have obtained clean energy–related industry certifications through Safer’s training, and 79 of them have gotten jobs, said Katrice Harris, the foundation’s training and employment account executive.

“The types of individuals we serve encounter a little more trouble with barriers, but we have staff fully certified and trained to help push to get these clients employed,” she said. ​“The job development team goes out and makes connections with employers, where they build relationships and create MOUs where employers agree to hire these clients and give them a second chance.”

Holistic approach

Yates said people with criminal convictions are often ​“better workers” than average, ​“because they feel this is their one and only chance to get something right.” But for many, work ethic alone is not enough.

That’s why Safer offers substance abuse recovery, anger management, and other social services in-house, which some trainees need not only for their health but also to comply with court mandates.

“They get workplace and diversity skills training, financial literacy, soft skills,” Harris said. ​“It’s all geared toward getting the guys and women credentially equipped so they can land jobs and become self-sufficient.”

Solar trainees have access to services that Safer offers its clients, including counseling and substance abuse treatment.

There’s an on-site food pantry styled as a grocery store, and Safer personal shoppers help people make their selections. Every detail is aimed at creating a feeling of normalcy and empowerment, Yates said, rather than an ​“institutional” vibe.

Safer also aims to help the significant number of people with criminal convictions who are unhoused, through 148 units of subsidized and affordable housing, as well as services like storing people’s belongings while they’re at work.

A growing pipeline

Safer started its own construction company in 2016, wherein trainees turned employees do renovation and carpentry work for the organization and other clients. Weatherization and solar panel installation were a natural progression of that work.

The foundation received a state grant for solar training created by the 2017 Future Energy Jobs Act, a federal grant for solar training in 2021.

Since 2024, it has been among the clean energy workforce hubs created and funded by the state’s 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act. Trainees receive stipends for participating in the program, which includes a month of basic skills followed by three to six weeks of training in either solar or weatherization. There’s also the possibility of pre-apprenticeships that can lead to labor union jobs.

Yates said Safer’s on-site mock-up house goes beyond what many solar trainings offer, and helps students fully experience what it’s like to work in the industry.

He notes that some trainees are afraid of heights, so the program lets them get comfortable with working on a roof while clipped into safety harnesses. They learn how to wire the home and work with an inverter, gaining experience with the electrical side of solar power.

People who live in areas identified as ​“equity eligible” or meet other criteria — including involvement with the criminal justice or foster care systems — qualify for the trainings under Illinois’ clean energy law. The law also created robust incentives for employers to hire those who meet the equity criteria.

Safer prioritizes people from Chicago’s South Side and West Side, areas with a disproportionate number of low-income communities and a history of disinvestment. About three-quarters of Safer’s solar trainees so far have been justice-involved, but others who meet the state criteria are also eligible.

The organization also has a state grant to launch trainings inside an Illinois prison, for people within three years of their release date. Upon release, they will be sent to Safer for mentorship and connections to employers.

Vincent Jones, who has an IT background, found out about the solar training from a relative who had done it, and he applied while between jobs. Jones utilized the food pantry and received a laptop as part of the program. He was also pleased to realize that Safer could help him expunge his record of a legal problem that did not involve incarceration.

title: Indonesia Just Energy Transition Fund - CPI - Climate Policy Initiative
description:
Indonesia’s net zero goal depends on a major build-out of renewable power.
Reaching 74% renewable electricity by 2060 will require around USD 30.3 billion in investment every year.
Yet clean power investment averaged only USD 1.2 billion a year between 2019 and 2023.
The gap is widest in rural and island communities, where small projects struggle to attract private investors, tariffs must stay affordable for low-income households, and public budgets are limited.
This discussion paper proposes a Just Energy Transition Fund (JETF) to help close that gap.
text:
Indonesia’s net zero goal depends on a major build-out of renewable power. Reaching 74% renewable electricity by 2060 will require around USD 30.3 billion in investment every year. Yet clean power investment averaged only USD 1.2 billion a year between 2019 and 2023.

The gap is widest in rural and island communities, where small projects struggle to attract private investors, tariffs must stay affordable for low-income households, and public budgets are limited. With the national 100-GW Solar PV Acceleration Program under way and off-grid solar expected to add 4.36 GWp of new demand, the opportunity to bring clean energy to these communities is significant, but so is the need for financing that lasts.

This discussion paper proposes a Just Energy Transition Fund (JETF) to help close that gap. Building on the principles of the Just Energy Transition Partnership, the fund would pool public, private, and philanthropic capital to deliver affordable renewable electricity to rural communities and turn it into lasting local benefits, through three focus areas:

Viability gap funding to lower the capital cost of renewable energy projects and keep electricity tariffs affordable

Upskilling and reskilling funding to build the local technical capacity needed to operate and maintain renewable energy systems

Productive use of energy funding to power village enterprises, create green jobs, and raise local incomes

Written as a starting point for dialogue with the Government of Indonesia and stakeholders, the paper offers practical recommendations for establishing a fund that reaches the communities most in need. It examines potential funding sources, governance arrangements, financing instruments, and enabling conditions, while outlining a phased approach to its development, from initial capitalization and pilot deployment to scaling up and institutionalization.

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Countries that want to wean themselves from the fossil fuels that cause climate change will get a road map aimed at guiding them on an economy-transforming journey toward renewable energies at the U.N. climate talks Tuesday.

Brazil, which ran last year's U.N. climate talks, will launch its promised road map to “transition away from fossil fuels” during this year's talks, COP31, taking place in Turkey.

It's an intricate document designed with different “levers” for nations to use to switch from coal, oil and gas to renewable energies, such as wind and solar, which don't release heat-trapping gases that lead to global warming. In a groundbreaking agreement three years ago at climate talks, the world agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels” but didn't provide guidance or details.

That's what Brazil is hoping to provide.

“What we hope to achieve with the road map is making a big problem — that is transitioning away — translating it into smaller actionable solutions,” Brazil's Ana Toni, who was CEO of last year's talks, told The Associated Press. “What we want is to be very pragmatic, helping countries move forward.”

Because all countries are all different, the road map is differentiated so that a nation could look at different tools and make decisions about moving away from fossil fuels, Toni said.

Some people may think this is impossible, but the road map shows that it is possible and a transition to renewable energies is inevitable, she said.

“Actually many countries are doing many things already,” she added.

Toni said it was important for countries to stop building new fossil fuel power plants and infrastructure because those will be come “stranded assets.”

One of the other key “foundational” levers, she said, is getting rid of subsidies that make fossil fuels cheaper and easier.

Brazil, with major oil deposits, is a major fossil fuel exporter while most of its internal energy consumptions comes from hydropower. Toni declined to comment directly on her country's oil exports.

“We'll create a road map that is good not only for Brazil, but for the world,” Toni said.

Environmental group Climate Action Network lauded Brazil and its president Monday “for doing something that feels increasingly revolutionary at a climate summit: working out how to deliver what was agreed.”

Brazil is also presenting other “road maps” during the talks. One deals with deforestation and the other on putting details into promised $1.3 trillion in climate financial aid for poorer nations from rich ones.

“The road maps make clear that, although every country has a different starting point, all countries can start their own path,” said Stela Herschmann, international policy lead for Observatório do Clima, a network of Brazilian environmental organizations. “Brazil has demonstrated the courage and leadership to start this conversation.”

___

Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, and Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India.

text:
Treasury is preparing savings measures as pressure grows to cut the federal battery rebate and EV subsidy in the face of inflation, but clean energy advocates caution that the measures are putting downward pressure on electricity and fuel prices.

Why Are Battery & EV Incentives Under Pressure?

Inflation reached 4.3% in the year to September – prompting the Reserve Bank to hike interest rates for the fifth time this year.

Some economists think the government should reduce federal battery and EV incentives to help curb inflation.

The Opposition wants to go further. In October, it released a plan to axe both programs completely, should it win the next federal election in 2028.

In the meantime, shadow energy minister Dan Tehan is keeping up the pressure.

“If Treasurer Chalmers wants to seriously tackle inflation, he should start by stopping [Energy Minister Chris Bowen]’s batteries blowout – and then continue with Labor’s Net Zero agenda,” Tehan said.

Treasury Looking At Battery Rebate Cuts

The Australian Financial Review reports that Treasury is preparing options to scale back the $7.2 billion Cheaper Home Batteries Program, including further reductions to the upfront subsidy available to households. The move could put Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ cost-cutting drive at odds with Bowen, who has continued to publicly defend the scheme.

More than 600,000 battery systems have been subsidised since the scheme launched in July 2025, a milestone Bowen celebrated on social media on Friday. And demand shows little sign of slowing, with take-up happening far quicker than originally anticipated.

Despite changes introduced in May to reduce subsidies and rein in government spending, around 35,000 home batteries are still being installed every month.

The government first set aside $2.3 billion for the program. In December 2025, it raised that to $7.2 billion.

Treasury’s options reportedly include lowering the subsidy available on the upfront cost of a home battery or requiring participation in a virtual power plant.

With Chalmers now searching for savings ahead of December’s Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook (MYEFO), the battery subsidy has attracted renewed attention.

Ministers Defend The Scheme

Environment Minister Murray Watt confirmed on Saturday that ministers had been asked to identify savings across their portfolios, but praised the battery program as “phenomenally successful”.

Speaking in Brisbane, Watt said potential savings were still being considered through the government’s Expenditure Review Committee.

Meanwhile, Bowen has continued to promote the benefits of the battery program, arguing that widespread household storage is helping reduce electricity costs, including for people who don’t own batteries.

What About The EV Incentive?

There is also growing pressure to slash a tax break for novated leases, which allows the cost of a car lease to be taken directly from an employee’s salary, before taxes are taken out. With a petrol car, a separate tax called Fringe Benefits Tax shrinks the savings, but EVs are exempt.

The EV tax break has cost far more than planned. When the tax break was introduced in 2022, it was expected to cost $205 million over four years. Instead, it cost $2 billion in its first three years, the government’s own review of the scheme found.

Critics say it mostly helps people on high incomes. That’s because the higher your tax rate, the more the tax break is worth. The government’s review cites an industry-commissioned report that found that about 48% of EV buyers earn over $150,000. Only 35% of Australian drivers earn that much.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese over the weekend declined to rule out means-testing subsidies for both home batteries and electric vehicles.

Would Cutting Either Program Backfire?

Supporters of the two schemes argue that both incentives are curbing inflation, not fuelling it.

Petrol is one of the biggest drivers of fuel prices, which jumped almost 15% in August and another 9% in September – the surge of Australians flocking to EVs is reducing pressure on fuel stocks curtailed by conflict overseas.

Gas price rises are also a contributing factor to inflation, while the battery rebate has helped drive wholesale electricity prices down.

Clean energy advocacy group Rewiring Australia is pushing back against the prospect of cuts.

“The inflation spike of the last few years was powered by fossil fuel prices. Every household still running on petrol and gas is exposed to the next price shock, but a home that electrifies is protected from it,” Rewiring Australia founder Saul Griffith said.

Here’s how his main arguments stack up:

Fuel is driving inflation. Petrol prices were a major factor in the latest inflation figure.

Batteries lower power prices. Home batteries help, but so do big grid batteries. And wholesale prices are only one part of your power bill.

Paying off an EV or battery slows spending.

“A household that sacrifices salary for an EV, or takes a loan for a battery, has less money to spend elsewhere in the economy for years. That’s the opposite of a cash handout,” Griffith added.

National Automotive Leasing and Salary Packaging Association CEO Rohan Martin meanwhile says the tax break is helping families in the outer suburbs.

“These aren’t inner-city elites. They’re families in Werribee, Tarneit, Kellyville, and Marsden Park who have a mortgage, a long commute, and are counting every dollar,” he said.

Changes Are Already On The Way

Both the battery and the EV subsidy are already scheduled to be reduced, under changes introduced over the past year.

Battery rebate changes:

In May, new rules for the scheme came in which particularly reduced the incentive for large batteries, which triggered a stampede for batteries – about a fifth of all the battery storage installed under the rebate so far was installed in April 2026, just before the cut;

After the cut, buyers chose smaller batteries. The average size fell from 36 kWh in April to 23 kWh in May and June, the Clean Energy Regulator says.

The next scheduled cut comes on 1 January 2027. This reduction is already locked into the rebate timetable and is separate from any further cuts Treasury may be considering. Use our battery rebate calculator for an exact figure.

EV incentive changes:

The full EV tax break stays until 31 March 2027.

From 1 April 2027, EVs costing more than $75,000 receive a smaller 25% discount instead.

From 1 April 2029, all EVs get the smaller discount.

Existing leases won’t change;

The government says these changes will save $1.7 billion over five years.

For details of the current discounts and eligibility requirements of the federal battery rebate, see our guide to the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. To see if switching from a petrol car to an EV is worth it for you, use our EV Charging Costs Calculator.

SolarQuotes writer Jacob Boyd contributed to this report.

text:
Growth in renewable energy capacity and the adoption of EVs are projected to result in a 0.4 per cent decline in carbon emissions from fossil fuels this year, according to new research by the Global Carbon Project. Major economies such as China, the US, the European Union and Japan are projected to register declines in fossil-fuel emissions. However, India's emissions are projected to increase by 4.4 per cent, higher than the average annual growth rate of 3.5 per cent over the past decade.

Advt

The decline in carbon emissions, while “encouraging”, is being driven partly by geopolitical shocks and is not a sustainable climate solution, said Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter.

The disruption in oil and gas supplies and the resulting energy crisis following the war in the Persian Gulf has been a key factor behind the decline. Carbon emissions from oil are projected to fall 1.9 per cent, while those from gas are expected to decline 0.3 per cent. The decline is partly offset by a 0.6 per cent increase in coal emissions.

While the decline is notable, especially after emissions rose 1.2 per cent in 2025, the report's authors warned that clean-energy growth is not yet fast enough to deliver a sustained reduction in global fossil-fuel emissions.

“A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change,” said Glen Peters, research professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research. China's emissions are projected to decline 0.9 per cent in 2026, following two years of subdued growth. Strong growth in renewable power generation is helping offset a 0.3 per cent rise in coal emissions, the study said. China accounts for 32 per cent of global fossil-fuel emissions and half of the global emissions avoided through renewable energy and EV adoption, while also leading in reforestation and afforestation efforts.

Advt

Emissions in the US are projected to decline 1.3 per cent, mainly due to lower coal use, while emissions in the European Union are expected to fall 1.5 per cent and Japan's by 1 per cent.

text:
Korean Suppliers to Provide Gen6 Cells From European and U.S. Facilities Starting in 2028–2029

Germany’s BMW Group is reshaping its battery supply chain by selecting South Korean suppliers for its next-generation Neue Klasse electric vehicle platform.

BMW announced on Nov. 9 (local time) that it had selected Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution as new suppliers of sixth-generation (Gen6) battery cells. Under the agreements, Samsung SDI will supply cells produced at its European facilities, while LG Energy Solution will provide cells manufactured at its U.S. plants. Deliveries are scheduled to begin between 2028 and 2029. The companies did not disclose the contract values or supply volumes.

The agreements reflect BMW’s “local for local” strategy, which involves sourcing batteries near vehicle production facilities. Samsung SDI plans to use its existing production base in Europe, including facilities in Hungary. The company is already building a 46-millimeter cylindrical battery production line in Hungary, targeting mass production in 2028. However, BMW has not identified the specific plant that will supply cells under the agreement, and it remains unclear whether the Göd facility will be involved.

LG Energy Solution plans to use its North American production facilities, including those in Michigan and Arizona, to supply BMW’s U.S. manufacturing operations. The agreement marks the first time LG Energy Solution will supply batteries for BMW’s fully electric vehicle models, expanding its relationship with the automaker beyond its existing supply of mild-hybrid batteries. The move also aligns with BMW’s strategy to expand local sourcing and production in the United States.

BMW has previously sourced batteries for its European operations from China’s CATL and EVE Energy. Samsung SDI’s addition expands the supplier base to three companies in the region. In North America, LG Energy Solution will become a new supplier, helping BMW diversify its sourcing by country and company. Nicolai Martin, BMW board member responsible for purchasing and supplier network, said procurement diversification was a key element of the group’s purchasing strategy and that BMW was working to strengthen value creation in Europe and the United States.

BMW has also established sixth-generation high-voltage battery pack assembly sites in five locations: Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Germany, Debrecen in Hungary, Shenyang in China, Woodruff in the United States, and San Luis Potosí in Mexico. At these facilities, battery cells will be assembled into packs before being supplied to nearby vehicle production plants.

A key technological change in the sixth-generation system is the shift from the prismatic cells used in the fifth generation to cylindrical cells measuring 46 millimeters in diameter. The new cells are expected to offer more than 20% higher energy density than their predecessors and improve driving range and charging speed by up to 30%. BMW also plans to use Cell-to-Pack technology, which integrates cells directly into battery packs without intermediate modules, to improve efficiency.

The partnership between Samsung SDI and BMW builds on a longstanding relationship. The two companies signed a battery cell supply agreement in 2019 for BMW’s fifth-generation electric vehicles. The contract was valued at 2.9 billion euros and covered deliveries from 2021 through 2031. In October 2025, Samsung SDI also signed a three-party agreement with BMW and U.S.-based solid-state battery developer Solid Power to validate solid-state battery technology.

BMW is pursuing a dual-chemistry strategy to make electric vehicles more accessible. It plans to use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in entry-level models to improve cost competitiveness, while higher-energy-density batteries are intended for its premium models. The specific chemistry of the cells covered by the newly announced agreements has not been disclosed.

As it expands production of Neue Klasse electric vehicles, BMW also plans to bring forward the phaseout of some existing models equipped with fifth-generation batteries. BMW Chief Executive Milan Nedeljković said at a recent third-quarter earnings announcement that the company was accelerating production of electric vehicles equipped with sixth-generation batteries, allowing it to discontinue some existing models earlier than originally planned.

Industry observers say the agreements illustrate how Western automakers are adapting their supply chains amid tighter trade regulations and tariff risks. The European Union’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act is another policy factor encouraging regional production in strategic industries, including batteries and electric vehicles. The proposal aims to strengthen Europe’s manufacturing competitiveness by linking local production requirements to public procurement and industrial support programs.

title: Senate advances sweeping energy legislation in first major action since midterm elections
authors: MATTHEW DALY Associated Press, JENNIFER MCDERMOTT Associated Press, ABC News
description:
The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use.
Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.
Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.
His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development.
When told that wind is part of the bill, Trump replied: “Well, the bill hasn’t been fully negotiated.
text:
WASHINGTON -- The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to power data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now face yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats' sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

"Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

Trump told reporters Monday that he still opposes wind energy. When told that wind is part of the bill, Trump replied: “Well, the bill hasn’t been fully negotiated. I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland voted against moving the legislation forward, in part due to Trump’s opposition to offshore wind. Van Hollen said the bill does not fully address the administration’s efforts to block Maryland’s pending offshore wind project, which he said would lower energy costs for households across the state and create thousands of jobs.

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.

Whitehouse said Trump's support should help the bill move toward a vote in the House.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.

Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, he said.

Capito called the bill “a win for America,'' adding: “We cannot let this moment pass by. The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity ... to come together to show the American people we are listening to you.”

Industry leaders are advocating for the bill's passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group.

But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a “terrible mistake” to proceed with the bill in the waning days of the current Congress.

While changes announced Saturday address a few concerns, the bill also comes with a gauntlet of new — and at times conflicting — rules, Campbell said. He said the bill maintains a veneer of federal safeguards while in fact stripping the power of federal agencies, states, tribes and communities to identify and prevent serious harm to health and the environment.

Sara Amundson, president of the Humane World Action Fund, said the bill weakens the scientific foundation of the Endangered Species Act and could create new opportunities to exclude needed wildlife protections.

“This proposed rewrite of the ‘best available science’ standard could give agencies new grounds to unfairly dismiss credible research, including science showing that stronger protections are needed for species at risk," she said, urging lawmakers to drop the provision or oppose the bill.

___

McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

title: Heinrich's energy permitting reform bill passes Senate procedural vote | - Santa Fe New Mexican
description: The U.S. Senate on Monday approved a procedural vote that speeds up the process of approving controversial legislation aimed at reducing permitting requirements for energy projects across the country.
text:
Oracle is exploring truck delivery of natural gas to fuel Project Jupiter’s data…

The bill seeks to lower energy costs, create jobs and stream…



U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., right, is shown Monday at the U.S. Capitol in Washington where the Senate passed a cloture vote on a controversial bipartisan energy permitting bill Heinrich co-sponsored.

The U.S. Senate on Monday approved a procedural vote that speeds up the process of approving controversial legislation aimed at reducing permitting requirements for energy projects across the country.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act advanced on a 73-25 cloture vote Monday afternoon.

The bill’s sponsors, including Democratic U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, have argued it will decrease electricity rates, implement data center guardrail measures and improve project timelines for renewable energy projects. But the policy has drawn opposition from the rest of New Mexico’s congressional delegation, as well as tribal leaders, other top politicians in New Mexico and environmental advocates, who argue it will reduce avenues for public input on major energy projects.

“BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, so that families can have money in their pockets for more than just keeping the lights on and their homes warm,” Heinrich said during a news conference Monday morning in Washington ahead of the vote. “This bill directly holds data centers accountable, forcing big corporations to pay their full share instead of putting costs on the consumers.”

U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján voted no during the proceeding.

“Making it easier to build clean energy and critical infrastructure projects is important for New Mexico and our nation, and Congress has failed to find a path forward for far too long,” Luján said in a statement. “However, I share the serious concerns raised by New Mexicans across the state, particularly our Pueblo and environmental leaders, and believe they must be addressed. After spending the last month listening to these concerns, I cannot support advancing the bill in its current form.”

The nearly 500-page bill has drawn significant controversy as it attempts to balance streamlined permitting reform with environmental, cultural and historic protections. The policy was amended Saturday in response to pointed concerns from tribal communities and labor unions, Heinrich said.

“I’ve heard directly from tribal leaders about the importance of having a meaningful voice in decisions that affect their communities and affect their ancestral lands,” Heinrich said. “We work to strengthen that dramatically in this manager’s amendment.”

The All Pueblo Council of Governors, which represents the collective voice of 20 pueblo nations in New Mexico and Texas, also rejected the amended version, citing continuous concerns over tribal sovereignty and the lack of meaningful protections.

The council said in a statement Sunday the changes “were negotiated without Pueblo input and still leave all Tribes and all New Mexicans in the same vulnerable position to protect their land, water and cultural resources. Many fatal flaws remain.”

The letter outlined specific concerns over the amendment’s impacts to mining projects included on the federal government’s FAST-41 list — projects already approved to receive streamlined permitting processes.

“[The amendment] also added new complications, including a shorter deadline to file lawsuits against FAST-41 covered projects,” the All Pueblo Council of Governors said in the statement. “This directly impacts proposed uranium mining on Mount Taylor, where the La Jara Mesa project is a FAST-41 covered project.”

In a news conference Friday, U.S. Reps. Melanie Stansbury and Teresa Ledger Fernández said they would oppose the bill in any amended form. Last week, New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez spearheaded a letter from six state attorneys general to Senate leaders, asking them to reject the policy.

New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland, a former Cabinet secretary of the U.S. Department of the Interior, also said she supports tribal communities in their opposition to the bill.

“I opposed the original permitting reform bill and I oppose the amendment. I stand with the Tribal Nations in New Mexico and across the country, who have warned that this legislation denies Tribes meaningful consultation and weakens their ability to protect culturally significant sites,” Haaland said in a statement. “… I know how much faster we need to build to achieve our goals,” she added. “But we will not do it by excluding America’s first land stewards.”

Western Environmental Law Center senior attorney Marlyn Twitchell noted the bill has moved unusually fast for a legislative package of this scope.

“Bills in Congress typically go through what’s called ‘regular order,’ ” Twitchell said. “They’re introduced, they get referred to committees, they have committee hearings, there’s debate among members of each chamber and the public gets to weigh in.”

That has not occurred with this legislation, which seeks to modify environmental protection laws like the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act and the Clean Water Act, Twitchell said.

“This bill was negotiated behind closed doors, introduced the day that the Senate recessed and then voted on the day after they came back,” she said. “There’s been virtually no open airing of the provisions of the bill or discussion about the really consequential nature of it, which is unusual.”

Heinrich and other co-sponsors of the bill — Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va .; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I. — assert the bill would accelerate green energy projects, lower costs for ratepayers and force data center companies to pay for their connections to electric grids.

Bill opponents and over 100 environmental advocacy groups argue this comes at the cost of reduced mechanisms for public input, tribal consultation and possible litigation.

“Places all New Mexicans care about deeply, from Greater Chaco to Mount Taylor to the Upper Pecos Watershed, to the state’s entire network of rivers, streams, and wetlands are all at risk of harm because of this bill. It is an abomination,” Western Environmental Law Center Executive Director Erik Schlenker-Goodrich said.

The bill is expected to be ready for a final vote the week of Nov. 16, he added.

text:
South Korean battery-makers Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution have signed deals to supply battery cells for BMW Group’s sixth-generation high-voltage batteries, the German luxury automaker said Tuesday.

Under the agreement, Samsung SDI will supply cells to BMW’s European facilities, and LG Energy Solution will supply its plants in the US. Both companies will deliver from their production sites in the respective regions, with deliveries expected to begin in the late 2020s.

With the latest addition, BMW’s battery cell suppliers in Europe will include Samsung SDI, China’s CATL and EVE Energy in Europe.

The companies did not disclose the contract value or planned supply volumes.

The agreements are part of BMW’s “local for local” strategy, under which the automaker sources key components close to its high-voltage battery and vehicle production facilities.

“Diversifying procurement is an integral part of the BMW Group’s purchasing strategy,” said Nicolai Martin, member of the Board of Management of BMW AG, which is responsible for purchasing and managing the supplier network.

“To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets. Through our battery cell partnerships, we are actively strengthening value creation in Europe and the US.”

Hendrik Lang, BMW Group’s head of high-voltage battery purchasing and quality, said partnerships with leading battery cell manufacturers worldwide would help the company secure “resilient, flexible and competitive” supply.

BMW is also expanding its localized battery assembly network to support electric vehicle production across major markets.

The automaker has established five new high-voltage battery assembly facilities near its vehicle production plants in Irlbach-Strasskirchen, Germany; Debrecen, Hungary; Shenyang, China; Woodruff, South Carolina; and San Luis Potosi, Mexico.

Battery cells are delivered to these regional facilities, where they are assembled into battery packs for use in BMW's electric vehicles.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

As lawmakers head into the home stretch of the 119th Congress, several bills of interest to manufacturers are expected to pass, like the National Defense Authorization Act and another continuing budget resolution, or have momentum, such as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026.

Below is a summary of many of these bills, including what provisions affect manufacturers and where the bills stand. If there are other manufacturing-related bills you’re following, please let us know what they are.

National Defense Authorization Act

The U.S. Department of Defense is requesting a record $1.5 trillion for fiscal year 2027 to ramp up weapons and military equipment manufacturing. As the U.S.’ war with Iran continues, the country is facing a weapons shortage, which President Donald Trump has repeatedly denied.

The bill aims to stabilize the defense industrial base’s supply chain and manufacturing operations, as well as aid small businesses seeking contracts. The funds would also go toward modernized weapons and munitions systems. Additionally, the agency is requesting funds for initiatives such as $21.4 billion for the F-35 Lightning II.

While Trump announced on Nov. 3 that the United States will no longer provide Israel billions of dollars in military aid in 2027, the NDAA could have a provision to bring the two countries’ militaries and systems closer together.

The provision added over the summer to both the House and Senate versions of the NDAA bill is a proposed clause that could expand U.S.-Israel military ties by consolidating Israeli technology within the U.S. defense supply chain. That could set the stage for the U.S. to share research and development, licensing agreements and co-production and manufacturing with Israel’s defense industry.

The House passed its version of the bill in July, which has been with the Senate since Sept. 14.

Toxic Substances Control Act

It’s been over 10 years since Congress passed the Frank R. Lautenberg Chemical Safety for the 21st Century Act, an amendment under the Toxic Substances Control Act that authorizes the U.S. EPA to test and review new chemicals or novel uses of existing compounds submitted to the agency. The legislation allows the EPA to measure the impact of toxic chemicals, such as perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances or methylene chloride, assessing their impact on public health and natural resources.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Manufacturing Dive free daily newsletter

Chemical trade groups and companies once lauded the safety regulation, but support has dissipated over the years. Chemical manufacturers have experienced delays in the EPA’s new substances review process, which they say has taken longer than the allotted 90 days and impacted their businesses. Moreover, chemical stakeholders say the EPA’s guidelines are inconsistent and that the risks are not science-based.

TSCA’s user fees under the safety amendment were set to expire Sept. 30, which would give Congress an opportunity to propose legislation that could address chemical stakeholders’ concerns. However, lawmakers have been divided on how to fix TSCA, and extended user fees through Dec. 11 as part of a continuing resolution signed in September.

When Congress returns, the clock will be ticking on finding a solution to satisfy chemical makers and ensure chemical safety.

National robotics strategy

Lawmakers introduced a couple of bills over the summer with the goal of establishing a national robotics strategy to spur investment in domestic robotics and make the U.S. more competitive with China, Japan, Germany and other leading countries.

The National Commission on Robotics Act was introduced by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., Jennifer McClellan, D-Va., and Bob Latta, R-Ohio, in February. A Senate version was introduced by Sen. Todd Young and other lawmakers in June. Both have been referred to their respective science and commerce committees.

The bill would establish a commission to examine and provide recommendations on several issues related to the competitiveness of U.S. robotics and the domestic marketplace. These would include foreign actions and policies to advance robotics; supply chain risks; workforce incentives and talent recruitment programs; as well as partnerships with industry, the public and academic institutions.

Under the bill, the commission would deliver an interim report to congress and the president within one year, and a final report with recommendations within two years.

Read More in Labor

Industry advocates have pushed for a national robotics strategy in recent years as manufacturers begin to leverage artificial intelligence and advanced technologies to improve productivity and drive operational efficiencies. They argue that other countries have surpassed them in the robotics race, citing a discrepancy in governmental incentives and lower costs that make U.S. suppliers noncompetitive.

The vast majority of robots are manufactured and deployed overseas. China led robotics adoption around the world and accounted for 59% of global deployments, or 354,200 installations last year, according to the International Federation of Robotics. The U.S., by comparison, had 38,400 installations that year — more than any other country.

Permitting reform

Environmental permitting reform has long been on manufacturers’ and the Trump administration’s wish lists to make projects easier to complete without as much red tape. Those wishes may finally be fulfilled through the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026.

Recently, key manufacturers and their trade groups signed a letter to Senate negotiators urging Congress to pass the legislation this year. However, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has expressed concerns about the bill, as well as what he characterized as a lack of input from House Democrats, Politico reported Nov. 5. This could hurt its chances of passage during the lame-duck session.

Introduced Sept. 30 by Sens. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., Mike Lee, R-Utah, Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.V., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., the legislation addresses many longstanding concerns of manufacturers and other industry representatives.

Read More in Labor

For example, the bill narrows the definition of “major federal actions” subject to National Environmental Policy Act review. In particular, it excludes from NEPA review any projects with no or minimal federal funding or involvement, as well as projects that only receive certain types of federal funding such as loans or loan guarantees.

For activities still subject to NEPA, the bill sets a two-year deadline for an agency to prepare an environmental impact statement and a one-year deadline for an environmental assessment review.

To increase transparency, permitting agencies would be required to develop and maintain a “unified interagency data system” comprising interconnected agency systems and shared services for environmental reviews and authorizations.

Additional bills of interest

Manufacturers and trade groups are also following these bills as they work their way through Congress.

Advanced Manufacturing Jobs in America Act of 2026

The Advanced Manufacturing Jobs in American Act would direct the Department of Labor to initiate pilot projects between local community colleges, state and tribal colleges, local boards, advanced manufacturers and Manufacturing Extension Partnership centers that are focused on education and training programs for advanced manufacturing jobs. The bipartisan legislation was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

MATCH Act

The Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act would tighten and align U.S. export controls on sensitive semiconductor manufacturing equipment with allied nations to prevent China and other adversaries from acquiring critical chipmaking technology and servicing loopholes. Versions of the legislation have been introduced in the House and Senate and are still in committee.

RED Tape Act

The Reducing and Eliminating Duplicative Environmental Regulations Act would remove the requirement under the Clean Air Act that the EPA review and comment on newly authorized federal construction projects and other major federal agency actions that already require National Environmental Policy Act review. The bill passed the House in April and was referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.

FENCES Act

The Foreign Emissions and Nonattainment Clarification for Economic Stability Act would modify the Clean Air Act to exempt states from penalties for ozone and particulate matter emissions that fail to attain national ambient air quality standards but that are outside of a state’s control. The bill passed the House in April and was referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

Robotics Supply Chain Improvement Act

The Robotics Supply Chain Improvement Act would direct the Commerce Department to collect more data and develop standards for new robotics, help keep the U.S. ahead of China and bolster domestic manufacturing globally.

It was introduced on Aug. 6 and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation.

Surface Transportation Reauthorization Bill

Federal surface transportation reauthorization is pending in Congress after the House approved its own five-year package earlier this year in a 62-to-2 vote.

The House bill, titled the Build America 250 Act, proposed an increase of $100 billion over the next decade for Federal Highway Administration programs, including for bridges, transit, rail and motor carriers.

The National Association of Manufacturers has stressed the importance of a healthy transportation infrastructure as companies navigate costly highway congestion, bottlenecked ports and freight delays.

The Biden administration’s Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act was originally set to expire on Sept. 30, but was temporarily extended through Dec. 11. It could be extended again, as the Senate has yet to release its version of the bill.

American Manufacturing Revitalization Exchange Program Act

The American Manufacturing Revitalization Exchange Program Act would help train the next generation of technicians, machinists, engineers and production specialists for the U.S.manufacturing workforce. Specifically, it establishes an international exchange program at the State Department’s Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs. The bill was referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs in June.

Chip EQUIP Act

The Chip EQUIP Act would seek to prevent companies that receive CHIPS Act funding from purchasing specialized manufacturing tools or equipment made by entities owned or controlled by the Chinese government, or other foreign entities of concern. It was reported out of the House Energy and Commerce, and Science, Space and Technology committees in September.

“Just one week after voters resoundingly rejected the Trump agenda, Congress should not be rushing to pass a bill that gives him even more unilateral authority to bypass our laws. This legislation was developed without hearings, meaningful tribal consultation and stakeholder engagement, or the rigorous review that a bill of this magnitude would normally go through. I remain deeply concerned about provisions that would gut protections for clean air and water, undermine tribal sovereignty, and potentially fast-track data center development.

“For Southern Arizona, this bill is not some abstract debate about federal permitting – it is about the water we drink, the air we breathe, the mountains and public lands we cherish, and the future we leave our children. I am especially concerned about a provision that would allow toxic mine tailings to be dumped on public lands in the Coronado National Forest.

“Alarmingly, this legislation could also make it easier for DHS to establish new immigrant detention centers by weakening environmental review requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) — the very law Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes has invoked in challenging the proposed detention facility in Surprise, Arizona. We should not be stripping away critical safeguards to make it easier for this administration to expand its mass detention infrastructure.”

“For these reasons, I am a hard NO on BAAJA.”
