description: (The Center Square) – The U.S. Senate has voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting reform bill that would expedite the buildout of energy-related infrastructure.
text:
High-voltage transmission towers carry power lines at sunset. Photo: Matthew Henry / Burst

(The Center Square) – The U.S. Senate has voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting reform bill that would expedite the buildout of energy-related infrastructure.

The primary purpose of the over 400-page bill is to expedite the permitting approval process for energy-related projects – such as natural gas pipelines, drilling and mining, and data center infrastructure – by scaling back environmental and judicial reviews.

Sponsors of BAAJA say it will increase energy supply, lower electricity costs and create more jobs as the country enters a new era of energy demand. It also requires owners of data centers that draw more than 20 MW of power plugging into the electric grid to pay for the associated grid upgrade costs.

“This is an affordability bill. The American people spoke loud and clear that they wanted results on affordability,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, who helped craft the bill, told reporters prior to the Monday evening vote. “People want to see Congress do good, big things. This is a good, big thing.”

Critics of BAAJA have voiced concerns that it would trample state and local rights, mainly by limiting litigation and local input, overriding environmental rules, and restricting states’ and communities’ ability to deny large projects, including data centers.

The four architects of the bill — U.S. Sens. Martin Heinrich, D-New Mexico; Shelley Moore Capito, R-West Virginia; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Whitehouse — attempted to mitigate concerns from environmental and tribal rights groups with a package of amendments .

Among other measures, the amended bill strengthens impacted tribal governments’ say in transmission permitting planning, allows harms to “human health” and “the environment” to justify agency action against a permit or project, and establishes in the Department of Energy the Data Center Community Assistance Program, which would provide technical assistance on request to communities impacted by data centers.

Those and other changes, Heinrich assured reporters, “don't change what this bill was always about: lowering energy costs, building the infrastructure our country so desperately needs, creating good-paying jobs, protecting our communities, and making sure data centers pay their fair share.”

But several “troubling” provisions in BAAJA remain unaddressed, dozens of critics say, particularly the bill’s amendments to the Clean Water Act regarding pollution control and environmental impact assessments of large-scale projects.

“This permitting legislation is a giveaway to America’s most polluting industries. By loosening bedrock environmental laws, this bill will fast-track toxic industrial agriculture pollution nationwide,” Food and Water Watch’s policy director Rebecca Wolf, joined by dozens of other organizations, stated Monday. “Congress must stop this cynical industry ploy.”

(The Center Square) – Honda on Monday announced plans for a $3 billion manufacturing plant in central Ohio to boost its production of hybrid vehicles, a project that could bring 2,000 jobs to the area between East Liberty and Marysville.

It will be the company’s ninth auto-related production facility in the U.S. with production expected to launch in 2029, the company said in a news release.

The Ohio Tax Credit Authority on Monday approved Honda for an undisclosed amount of tax credit. The exact amount, the authority says, is to be made public after a final agreement is executed. Start of construction is pending government approvals.

“While supporting growing demand for hybrid and gasoline-powered vehicles, the plant will provide Honda with the flexibility to adapt production as customer demand, market conditions and electrification trends evolve,” the company said in a statement made available to The Center Square.

Honda chose Ohio because of its highly skilled workforce and proximity to the company’s American supply base.

“Honda's leadership could have chosen to build this plant anywhere in the world, but they chose Ohio because there are so many advantages to being here,” Gov. Mike DeWine said in a statement. “For almost half a century, Honda and Ohio have grown together, and generations of families have built their careers on Honda's manufacturing lines. Today's announcement isn't just an investment in a new facility - it's an investment in Ohio's people and Ohio's future.”

Ohio was recently voted by the network CNBC as the best state in the U.S. to do business.

“Companies choose Ohio because they can move faster, plan with confidence, and scale without unnecessary roadblocks,” the network said. “With the right sites, reliable infrastructure, abundant energy, storied manufacturing legacy, world-class workforce, and a spirit of innovation, Ohio gives businesses every advantage to compete and win.”

The Ohio plant is part of a growing network of investments the company is making in the U.S. “that will expand and strengthen an integrated U.S. production network to boost production of hybrid-electric vehicles and the engines and hybrid systems that power them,” Honda said Monday.

With investments also in Georgia and Alabama, Honda will eventually make 1.3 million vehicles a year in the United States, according to a release.

“Honda also plans to pursue assistance from JobsOhio, which will be made public after a final agreement is executed,” a release said.

JobsOhio is a private nonprofit corporation funded by profits from liquor franchise rights it purchased from the state of Ohio in 2013, according to its website.

Highlights:

The House Energy and Commerce Committee advanced the Nuclear REFUEL Act (H.R.3978) and the Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act (H.R.5549). The first of these bills, introduced by Reps. Robert Latta (R-Ohio) and Scott Peters (D-Calif.), would streamline nuclear facility safety rules to make it easier to recycle spent fuel, a practice that is not currently legal but would reduce nuclear waste. The second bill, reintroduced by Reps. Morgan Griffith (R-Va.), Kim Schrier (D-Wa.) and Marc Veasey (D-Texas), would simplify federal licensing rules to make it easier to build nuclear power plants.

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) introduced the PURGE Act (H.R.10957) and the Clothing Microplastics Transparency Act of 2026 (H.R.10958) to tackle, mitigate, and regulate microplastics. The first of these bills would direct the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to research strategies and develop a pilot program for mitigating and remediating microplastics in the environment. The second would require clothing companies to clearly label clothes with the quantity of microplastics in them. It would also direct the Federal Trade Commission to promulgate microplastic regulations, such as testing protocols, for these companies.

Rep. Michael Baumgartner (R-Wash.) introduced the Healthy Forests Incentives Act (H.R.10952). The bill would create incentives to thin out high-risk forests and build partnerships between the U.S. Department of Agriculture and businesses to find productive uses for cleared lumber, such as biofuel and laminate. text:
Ohio voters rejected data center projects, raising concerns over farmland protection, electricity demand and the future of rural U.S. communities.

Marcus Ellington is a U.S.-based journalist covering agricultural markets, global trade, and agricultural policy, with an international perspective on their impact across the global agri-food system.

Fuente: AgroLatam.com

Autor: AgroLatam.com

Voters in 18 Ohio communities backed restrictions on data center development across 21 ballot measures on November 3, 2026, reflecting growing opposition to large technology projects in rural areas. According to reporting by Nick Evans in Ohio Capital Journal, the results highlight concerns over farmland preservation, electricity demand, water resources and local control of industrial development. For farmers and agribusinesses, the election underscores growing competition for land and infrastructure in agricultural communities.

The voting margins were decisive. In Wilmington, approximately 80% of voters rejected four rezoning proposals that would have allowed data center development. In Piqua, residents approved a ban by a two-to-one margin and recalled three city commissioners. Meanwhile, more than 87% of voters in Perry supported additional financial safeguards for data centers receiving tax incentives. The results reflect demands for greater oversight of industrial projects and their potential effects on local economies.

Farmland and Rural Infrastructure at the Center of the Debate

The agricultural concerns became particularly visible in Upper Sandusky, northwestern Ohio, where Angela Huffman, a sixth-generation farmer and president of Farm Action, opposed a proposed energy and data center development near her property. Huffman told Ohio Capital Journal that the industry's expansion raised questions about farmland use and the growing pressure on rural infrastructure. The proposed investment, valued at nearly $1 billion, was located approximately 10 miles from her family farm.

Smartland Energy proposed building a 150-megawatt natural gas power plant on 46 acres, intended to supply electricity to a potential data center on an adjacent 100-acre site. The company said it would not own or operate the data center and that any future operator would need local approval. Nevertheless, residents expressed concerns about land use and infrastructure capacity. In November, nearly 77% of Upper Sandusky voters approved a citywide ban on data centers.

The debate comes as the area is already accommodating a Louis Dreyfus Company soybean processing investment, adding demand to local infrastructure. For agricultural producers, electricity reliability, transportation networks and industrial capacity are essential to maintaining competitive operations. Large data centers can introduce additional pressure on those resources, although their actual effects on farm operating costs depend on utility regulations, infrastructure financing and project-specific agreements.

Newsletter Sign Up.

Email:

Industry representatives argue that data centers can generate jobs, tax revenue and investment in local communities. Following the election, Infrastructure for America announced a voluntary commitment focused on transparency, responsible resource use and community engagement. The Data Center Coalition also warned that restricting development could mean losing economic opportunities. Meanwhile, Conserve Ohio is pursuing a statewide ballot initiative for 2027 that would impose additional restrictions on large data centers.

For U.S. agriculture, the Ohio vote highlights a broader land-use challenge. As developers seek rural properties with access to electricity and transportation infrastructure, farmers and local governments must weigh new investment against farmland preservation and existing agricultural needs. The election results show that communities want a greater say in projects that could reshape their local economies, particularly when productive land, public resources and long-term infrastructure costs are at stake.

title: Senate Advances Capito's Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act - Majority News
description:
“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act consists of two parts.
I believe these comprehensive permitting reforms will generate benefits for our country for years to come for three reasons.
“The White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) released a report analyzing the ways that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would benefit families and businesses, and the results are clear.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a win for America, and we cannot let this moment pass us by.
I encourage my colleagues to rise to the importance of this moment, and to vote in favor of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, spoke on the Senate floor to highlight the urgency of passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation to reform our nation’s permitting and environmental review processes and make life more affordable for American families. Following Chairman Capito’s remarks, the Senate advanced BAAJA by a vote of 73-25.

Below are the floor remarks of Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) as prepared for delivery.

“Madam President, for far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty.

“Businesses large and small, looking to invest meaningfully in our country, lack the certainty they need to make decisions. Communities nationwide have waited in regulatory limbo for roads, bridges, energy infrastructure, manufacturing facilities, and other investments that create jobs and strengthen local economies. All this has led to lost jobs, missed economic opportunities, and higher prices across America.

“Data from the National Association of Manufacturers shows that permitting delays are costing America’s manufacturers $12.1 billion every year, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia alone. According to new data from McKinsey, $1.8 trillion of investments are locked up in the federal permitting system right now, including $22.3 billion of sidelined investments in my home state of West Virginia.

“These are projects that could provide good-paying jobs, improve mobility, increase access to clean drinking water, deploy broadband in rural areas, and so much more. The environmental permitting and review processes should be tools for informed decision-making, not reasons that decisions can’t be made. This is not a sustainable way for the United States to compete with the rest of the world, and it is certainly not a sustainable way to address the energy and affordability issues we are facing today.

“It’s no secret that America’s energy demand is growing rapidly to meet the needs of a modern economy. To meet these needs, we must modernize our grid, increase our energy production, and build the infrastructure that will keep America competitive and secure for decades to come.

“It is time for Congress to act. It is, actually, well past time.

“As Chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee, I worked with my Ranking Member, Senator Whitehouse, as well as Chairman Lee of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Ranking Member Heinrich, to introduce a comprehensive permitting reform solution: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA. This bill will unlock economic opportunity, infrastructure development, and energy production across the United States.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act consists of two parts. The first part of the bill is in the EPW Committee’s jurisdiction, and it consists of reforms to the laws that set the framework for our environmental review and permitting processes, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act. The EPW section also provides certainty that permitted projects will retain their permits if they remain in compliance with the law.

“The second part of the bill captures reforms to statutes in the ENR Committee’s jurisdiction, including the National Historic Preservation Act and the Federal Power Act. This section also includes the Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation that will make potential data centers pay their own way instead of American consumers facing increased costs through rising utility bills.

“Together, the package that our committees put together fulfills key policy priorities from members of both sides of the aisle and a diverse set of stakeholders. I believe these comprehensive permitting reforms will generate benefits for our country for years to come for three reasons.

“First, this bill is bipartisan. Senators Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich, and I have worked together throughout this Congress to craft a solution that both Republicans and Democrats can support. That is the only way we can achieve durable and implementable reforms to our environmental review and permitting processes. There is something in this bill for everyone, because it is fair to everyone, and we owe it to the American people to come together as a body and pass this legislation in the weeks ahead.

“Second, this bill will help all types of projects. We cannot adjust the processes for some types of projects, but not others. Projects like coal mines, windmills, gas pipelines, solar farms, and steel mills will all benefit from this legislation.

"Third, the package addresses critical stages of the permitting process. This will create predictability, consistency, and finality in securing a permit. It will allow our laws to balance public health, the environment, and the needs of our economy. Finally, our legislation will prevent unnecessary delays and endless litigation that blocks growth.

“In West Virginia, investments have collapsed under the weight of legal challenges, denying potential benefits to areas that need support the most. When a project sits in the environmental review and permitting processes for years, jobs are not created, critical infrastructure is not built, energy is not brought onto the grid, and ultimately, American families and businesses face higher costs and fewer opportunities.

“The White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) released a report analyzing the ways that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would benefit families and businesses, and the results are clear. According to their analysis, the reforms made under BAAJA would result in $82 billion to $164 billion in additional economic output every year. Families would feel these economic benefits directly, as CEA estimates that for the average American household, real wages will increase, electricity bills will fall, and everyday expenses will be reduced. We cannot continue to let the costs of permitting delays fall onto American families.

“I am no stranger to the challenge of addressing permitting reform in Congress. Throughout my career, I have introduced multiple bills to improve this process. While Congress has passed some very limited reforms through various legislative packages, we have not passed significant reforms to NEPA in several decades.

Republicans and Democrats alike recognize the need for reforms to unlock investment to build projects that are important to our states. On both sides of the aisle, we understand that our constituents need lower costs and good jobs, communities need economic investment, businesses need certainty, and America needs to build. These are not partisan ideals. They are American principles.

“The Trump administration has also rallied behind this deal, supporting our efforts in the Senate to pass durable reforms so we can unleash our nation’s full potential. Additionally, we have made it a priority to have a robust manager’s amendment to this legislation that makes targeted changes based on feedback from our members and stakeholders to further build support.

"I am thankful for my colleagues’ efforts to strengthen BAAJA, and the contributions from members of the House of Representatives as well. This legislation reflects a vast amount of perspectives and priorities, and I’m proud of the product we are voting on today.

“We have received letters of support from over one thousand stakeholder organizations, representing a broad swath of groups across our country, including oil and gas producers and solar energy groups, labor unions, and business associations. They all recognize the urgent need for permitting reform, and the benefits that BAAJA would have on affordability, energy reliability, and economic growth across our country.

“In a statement from the American Petroleum Institute, President and CEO Mike Sommers said, 'Washington has a generational opportunity to fundamentally transform a broken permitting system and help address the affordability challenges facing American consumers. Congress should seize this moment and finish the job.'

“In another statement from the Solar Energy Industries Association, CEO Tim Pawlenty said, 'This is the kind of bipartisan action America needs to meet growing energy demand, put downward pressure on energy prices, and deploy more affordable, exactly reliable solar and storage for American families and businesses.'

“Xan Fishman, Executive Vice President of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said, '[The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act] would fix our permitting processes so that we can review and build efficiently, reducing costs, improving quality of life, growing our economy, and improving economic outcomes.'

“From my home state, the Gas and Oil Association of West Virginia’s President, Rebecca McPhail, said the following, 'GO-WV supports the [Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act]’s stated goals of modernizing federal environmental review, providing certainty for holders of federal permits and authorizations, and supporting an all-of-the-above energy strategy.'

“From the business community, Rodney Davis, Senior Vice President and Head of Government Affairs at the U.S. Chamber, said, 'The Senate's progress toward a comprehensive, bipartisan permitting reform deal brings us one step closer to streamlining the outdated process that is holding up critical projects of all kinds, from energy and water infrastructure to roads, broadband, and manufacturing.’

“Demonstrating the breadth of support this bill has received, the Laborers’ International Union of North America General President, Brent Booker, gave the following statement of support, “'For more than a decade LIUNA has testified before Congress, submitted comments, participated in roundtables, and endorsed numerous iterations of permitting bills… We urge lawmakers in both parties to seize this moment, pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, and finally deliver meaningful permitting reform.'

“And finally, representing a broad coalition of labor groups, in a letter from Sean McGarvey, President of North America’s Building Trades Unions, he said, 'This legislation represents a significant step toward a more efficient permitting system that supports job creation, strengthens America’s energy and infrastructure capabilities, and helps reduce costs for working families.'

“I could not agree more. This is an unprecedented opportunity, and a legislative breakthrough we can accomplish in this unique moment. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a win for America, and we cannot let this moment pass us by.

“The reality is this: over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production and manufacturing capacity to meet increasing demand, and that means making sure our infrastructure projects can be built quickly, efficiently, and responsibly.

“The House has already passed several key pieces of legislation on this matter, including the SPEED Act and the PERMIT Act. Now, it’s our turn in the Senate to act on the opportunity in front of us. I encourage my colleagues to rise to the importance of this moment, and to vote in favor of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

“American growth, competitiveness, and security are at stake. With that, I yield the floor.”

text:
A prominent business group wants Governor Gretchen Whitmer to opt Michigan into a federal education program that's opposed by the state’s largest teachers union.

The Detroit Regional Chamber sent a letter urging Whitmer to join the Federal Education Freedom Tax Credit. The program allows people to make a $1,700 donation to a Scholarship Granting Organization who – in turn – gives out scholarships to students.

More than 30 states have opted into the program so far.

The scholarships can be used for things like books and tutoring. It can also be used for private school tuition – which is driving the hesitancy to adopt the tax credit by some Democrat-led states.

Chamber CEO Sandy Baruah says the political climate isn’t helping either.

“We know that there's some unnecessary controversy around this, just because it is a Trump administration initiative, but we think this is a good one, and I think this supports education,” Baruah said.

The Michigan Constitution bans public money from going toward private schools.

Michigan Education Association spokesman Thomas Morgan said it’s another “voucher scheme.”

“The program was created to weaken public education and divert billions of dollars to private and religious schools and the for-profit companies that service them,” Morgan said.

In 2000, Michigan voters rejected a proposal that would have established a state-funded voucher program.

Last month, Whitmer and four other Democratic governors sent a letter to the U.S. Department of Treasury for more information on the program.

In an op-ed for the Detroit Free Press, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel panned the program.

“I have grave concerns about whether the voucher program violates the Michigan Constitution,” Nessel wrote.

Baruah wasn’t sure about the specifics of this federal program running afoul of state law. He said with Michigan being one of the worst states for childhood literacy something needs to change.

“We should be turning over every stone that improves education for children in the state of Michigan.”

For the MEA, Whitmer allowing the program to start in the state would be a betrayal.

“Opting Michigan into this federal voucher scheme at the end of her term would drown out much of the great work that Governor Whitmer has helped accomplish on behalf of Michigan students and schools and educators,” Morgan said.

text:
During the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration, government policy helped build 2,000 factories, 5,000 ships, and an electrical grid that connected to nearly every home. Last Tuesday’s elections produced a clear mandate for returning to that level of ambition—which Congress may be poised to do with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, being debated this week. To place this in context, a trio of recent books highlights the need for policymakers to make people’s lives better and more affordable by building out core infrastructure like a clean energy grid—and the hurdles to getting there.

Lessons from the Rise and Fall of American Shipbuilding

First up, business journalist Rana Foroohar of the Financial Times is out with Sea Change: America’s New Great Game in the Arctic Circle. It’s part travelogue of her voyage on the US Coast Guard Cutter Healy (America’s lone icebreaker ship), and part policy history of the rise and fall of US shipbuilding. From the icy waters of Alaska to the industrial policies of the Biden and Trump White Houses, Foroohar makes the case that climate change is thawing—and thus making traversable—the Earth’s northernmost reaches.

While this benefits the US by dodging one geoeconomic problem (the volatility of Middle Eastern shipping lanes), it creates another: namely, further dominance of trade by Russia (long a polar power) and China (a newer one). Today, while the US has 185 oceangoing commercial vessels, China has 5,500. China also increasingly dominates ocean research vessels, icebreaking ships, ports, and port cranes around the world.

These physical changes overlap with intellectual ones. As Foroohar argues, the Rooseveltian conception was that control of the seas (which still carry over 80 percent of world trade) amounts to control of commerce, and ultimately what can be profitably produced where. Yet shipbuilding is extremely capital intensive, such that neither government procurement nor the private markets can alone sustain it. It requires both, and this is why governments tend to subsidize their production.

In a 1935 message to Congress, FDR called for subsidies to cover the difference in the cost of building, operating, and subsidizing ships between the US and other countries. “Only by meeting this threefold differential can we expect to maintain a reasonable place in ocean commerce for ships flying the American flag,” he said, “and at the same time maintain American standards” in labor and other respects.

Roosevelt’s policy shot past his initial target of a few hundred vessels many times over. As federal statistics show, over the FDR period, the number of workers employed in shipbuilding went from 63,000 to over 1.7 million. The share of women employed went from 1 to nearly 15 percent. In West Coast ports, the share of Black workers more than doubled from from 3 to 7 percent, as racist institutional barriers broke down. Most of the jobs were good union jobs.

This approach shifted during the neoliberal era of the 1970s to 2010s, which was premised on letting market actors—rather than the public—determine the geography of production, and on seeing production and transportation as separate economic activities that could be disentangled. In the 1980s, the Reagan administration dismantled the Rooseveltian supports for shipbuilding—leaving the playing field open for China (which never fully adopted neoliberal dogma) to increasingly monopolize the sector. As with any monopoly, the temptation to abuse market power abounds, as was on display over the last few years when China restricted the export of raw materials and imposed retaliatory fees on (basically nonexistent) US oceangoing vessels.

Is another US maritime power possible? One major fix Foroohar discusses is an effort led by the United Steelworkers to impose compensatory tariffs to equate the cost of production with China, under the Section 301 trade statute. Another is the SHIPS for America Act, legislation developed by Senators Mark Kelly (D-AZ) and Todd Young (R-IN) and Representatives John Garamendi (D-CA) and Trent Kelly (R-AL). This labor- and business-supported plan would create a Maritime Security Trust Fund that would serve as a durable source of shipbuilding funding outside of the annual congressional appropriations cycle, and create requirements that more ocean-bound trade be carried on US-built ships, as well as other requirements.

But SHIPS faces headwinds in the era of a Congress that passes few laws, and the few that do pass must go through must-pass budget or defense processes. As of this writing, the bill’s sponsors are trying to shoehorn parts of SHIPS into the year-end defense bill.

BAAJA Blast Meets Utility Barons

The challenge of enacting new law is also on display in the current debate in Congress around BAAJA. This legislation would reform electricity transmission permitting to make it easier to connect clean energy to the grid. If state or local governments (or regional transmission organizations) fail to build, this legislation would give federal authorities new tools to unstick progress. This is unquestionably a good thing, and necessary to deliver on the energy and manufacturing goals begun with the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act and CHIPS and Science Act—part of why labor unions are backing it. Moreover, passing BAAJA now means that the next administration can avoid having permitting as a day-one inbox issue, and can move on to more ambitious policies to tackle the climate crisis and bring down energy costs.

Yet, like SHIPS, passage of BAAJA is far from a sure thing. One reason is that utility companies are mobilizing to defeat it. To understand why, there is no better resource than Sandeep Vaheesan’s Democracy in Power: A History of Electrification in the United States. The book gives a granular history of the compromises made over publicly owned and privately owned power in the 1930s.

When it came to energy, FDR had a threefold strategy that was not always internally consistent: expansion of federal power generation and transmission through agencies like the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), federal support for community-controlled rural utilities, and limits on the holding company structure of investor-owned utilities through the Federal Power Act (FPA). The first plank initially antagonized utilities, serving as what FDR alternatively called a “yardstick” that forced private providers, through competition with the public, to offer better service, or a “birch rod” that directly disciplined their excesses. The upside of FDR’s policies was that a quarter of the country now has public or cooperative power.

The downside—described well in Vaheesan’s final chapters—is that, by not fully democratizing the electricity grid, FDR’s policy package made the more public-oriented parts not as public interest–oriented as they could be. The FPA conceded any major federal role in most power generation (outside of emergencies), while the private utilities became invested in maintaining their monopolies at all costs. As a long-term result, neither the public nor private has made as much progress on decarbonization as they should have.

Lawsuits Won’t Save Democracy

But utilities are not the only source of opposition to BAAJA. So too is a network of environmental NGOs that have come to rely on litigation under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and other statutes as their primary business model and theory of change. BAAJA would make recourse to so-called private enforcement laws more difficult. This would surely please Stanford Law School’s Diego Zambrano, whose new book is How Americans Enforce the Law.

Using novel machine learning techniques and old-fashioned lawyering, he identifies an ample landscape of private rights of action, where NGOs or individuals can sue corporations or the government to enforce the law. In other advanced economies, this type of law enforcement is done primarily by the government itself. Not so in America, where there are a whopping 382 federal and over 10,000 state private rights of action—and as much as 98 percent of enforcement is done by private individuals in some areas of the law.

While previous scholarship attributed American lawsuit culture to the so-called “rights revolution” of the 1960s or the Nader’s raiders of the 1970s, Zambrano traces its roots back to the colonial era, and its flourishing to compromises made during the Progressive Era. In what he calls the “choice of 1914,” he argues that the Clayton Act of that year codified the American regulatory approach, allowing private persons to sue over antitrust violations—in part over worries that government might lack the resources, information, will, or independence from oligarchy to enforce the law.

Zambrano sees these latter concerns as potentially good reasons to partially privatize law enforcement. But he also sees risks of this privatization going too far, substituting for actually developing the state capacity that our legal progenitor England has since crafted, or duplicating state capacity where that exists. Zambrano sees labor law litigation as a net positive, because labor departments are underfunded, subject to partisan swings, and can’t adequately police what happens behind a firm’s walls. Private environmental enforcement, in contrast, is organized around policing regulation the state has already conducted, doesn’t compensate for environmental harms, and is increasingly used by fossil interests to block clean energy—the opposite of environmental law’s goals.

What’s the Way Out of This Thicket?

We need a different state—one that is not as hobbled as the post-Roosevelt one has been, but also not as self-dealing as Trump’s. Foroohar calls for the SHIPS Act, Vaheesan calls for a wholesale reimagining of our energy governance (including federal chartering of electric utilities and public options like TVA for the whole country), and Zambrano suggests experimentation with rules that sunset private enforcement after a period of time or tighten standing rules. All valuable, but none are assured of passage. Getting rid of the Senate filibuster is a necessary step to letting majorities govern, as well as multiplying the geometries of bipartisan coalitions.

description:
Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw.
The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.

text:
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.

In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.

For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.

Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.

Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.

Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

Two decisions

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.

Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.

Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.

But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."

"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."

There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.

The case for drilling

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"

Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".

"If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.

Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.

But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.

With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.

The case for electrons

The alternative is to build.

Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.

Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.

All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.

The China question

And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.

And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early.

And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo.

If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.

text:
The Senate on Monday advanced a bipartisan bill that aims to significantly speed up the approval process for critical U.S. infrastructure projects.

The vote, 73-25, allows the Senate to begin debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act bill as it heads toward final passage

The bill, which would reform the permitting process for projects, has emerged as a key priority of Congress’ lame duck session. President Donald Trump, who often opposes bipartisan legislation, has endorsed the package.

The legislation would amend laws like the National Environmental Policy Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act to speed up the review process that hinders the buildout of resources like electricity generation, while also overhauling the process for greenlighting transmission lines.

The bill would also force artificial intelligence companies and data center developers to pay their own way for power and grid enhancements.

Republicans have long argued that environmental laws are too restrictive and hinder the U.S. from building big things like power plants and mines. Democrats, meanwhile, want to speed up the buildout of clean energy projects like solar and wind to lower carbon emissions

Lawmakers have circled a deal to streamline the nation’s complex web of permitting laws for years, but most prior efforts have sputtered. This year, negotiators believe they will catch lightning in a bottle and make BAAJA law before this Congress ends in January.

The lawmakers are touting further tailwinds after last week’s elections, where Democrats wiped out Republicans and seized majorities in both chambers of Congress

“Just one week ago Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the top Democrat and likely incoming Chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, during a Monday morning press conference.

The bill would still require approval by the House of Representatives if it is able to pass the Senate this week. Trump’s endorsement of the effort is likely to help the bill get a vote in the House if it clears the Senate.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Michael Cloud (TX-27) joined X-energy CEO Clay Sell, Dow executives, and Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) leadership at NRC headquarters as the Commission issued a construction permit for the Long Mott Energy project at Dow’s Seadrift Operations in Calhoun County, Texas.

Calhoun County is set to become home to the first commercial nuclear reactor in American history built to power an industrial plant. The permit clears the way for X-energy’s small modular reactors (Xe-100) to supply power and industrial heat to Dow’s Seadrift site. This is the first permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in over 50 years.

What this means for Texas:

Building a nuclear plant takes years of construction work, and running one requires a permanent, highly skilled workforce.

The project brings major new investments and grid power to the area.

Reliable, around-the-clock energy, in any weather, that isn’t tied to fuel prices.

Dow’s Seadrift Operations is a cornerstone of the local economy. Its dependable power and heat help keep the plant competitive.

“Texas’s 27th District is leading the nation into a new era of American energy,” said Congressman Cloud. “This permit will bring jobs, a stronger manufacturing base on the Gulf Coast, and energy built right here at home. Seadrift can power American industry for generations, and this is only the beginning for advanced nuclear energy in Texas,” concluded Congressman Cloud.

Congressman Cloud has been a consistent advocate for the Seadrift project. As a member of the House Appropriations Committee, he helped secure $2.675 billion for the Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP), which supports advanced reactor projects including X-energy’s work at Seadrift. In March, he wrote to urge that nuclear funds be prioritized for the project. X-energy and Dow are now in the construction and long-lead procurement phase of the project. The NRC completed its Environmental Assessment for the site in May.

title: Senate advances sweeping energy legislation in first major action since midterm elections
description:

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.
His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development.

text:
The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now face yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

Midterm results could complicate bill’s passage in lame-duck session

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats’ sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

“Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

Trump told reporters Monday that he still opposes wind energy. When told that wind is part of the bill, Trump replied: “Well, the bill hasn’t been fully negotiated. I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland voted against moving the legislation forward, in part due to Trump’s opposition to offshore wind. Van Hollen said the bill does not fully address the administration’s efforts to block Maryland’s pending offshore wind project, which he said would lower energy costs for households across the state and create thousands of jobs.

Democrats are optimistic the bill will pass both chambers

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” next year.

Whitehouse said Trump’s support should help the bill move toward a vote in the House.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.

Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, he said.

Capito called the bill “a win for America,’’ adding: “We cannot let this moment pass by. The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity ... to come together to show the American people we are listening to you.”

Industry leaders are advocating for the bill’s passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group.

But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a “terrible mistake” to proceed with the bill in the waning days of the current Congress.

While changes announced Saturday address a few concerns, the bill also comes with a gauntlet of new — and at times conflicting — rules, Campbell said. He said the bill maintains a veneer of federal safeguards while in fact stripping the power of federal agencies, states, tribes and communities to identify and prevent serious harm to health and the environment.

Sara Amundson, president of the Humane World Action Fund, said the bill weakens the scientific foundation of the Endangered Species Act and could create new opportunities to exclude needed wildlife protections.

“This proposed rewrite of the ‘best available science’ standard could give agencies new grounds to unfairly dismiss credible research, including science showing that stronger protections are needed for species at risk,” she said, urging lawmakers to drop the provision or oppose the bill.

___

McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

title: The Top Solar Power States In America
description:
The United States has enough installed solar capacity to power more than 50 million homes, according to the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA).
Texas Texas leads the nation in utility-scale solar electricity generation and continues to attract major new projects.
Among its largest developments is the Tehuacana Creek 1 Solar and Battery Energy Storage project, which is expected to add 837 megawatts of solar generation and 418 megawatts of battery storage capacity.
Florida Power & Light and Duke Energy Florida have expanded their solar portfolios, while Jacksonville's municipal utility, JEA, is developing the Miller and Forest Trail Solar Energy Centers.
The Future of Solar Energy in the United States Solar growth extends to states outside the top six.
text:
The United States has enough installed solar capacity to power more than 50 million homes, according to the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA). During the second quarter of 2026, the country added 11.4 gigawatts of solar capacity, a 45% increase over the same period in 2025. Utility-scale projects accounted for most of that growth, while battery storage and transmission upgrades are helping utilities integrate additional solar power into the electricity grid.

California and Texas remain the country's largest solar electricity producers, while Florida, Arizona, and North Carolina are expanding their generating capacity. Nevada is investing in transmission infrastructure to move electricity between the northern and southern parts of the state. These six states are among the country's top solar markets in 2026, with existing capacity, new projects, and infrastructure investments.

Texas

Texas leads the nation in utility-scale solar electricity generation and continues to attract major new projects. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), Texas accounts for approximately 40% of the utility-scale solar capacity scheduled to come online nationwide in 2026. Among its largest developments is the Tehuacana Creek 1 Solar and Battery Energy Storage project, which is expected to add 837 megawatts of solar generation and 418 megawatts of battery storage capacity.

Texas is also expanding its transmission infrastructure to move electricity between generating facilities and population centers. Battery storage development is accelerating, with the EIA projecting nearly 13 gigawatts of new utility-scale battery capacity in the state during 2026. Residential customers can participate in solar buyback programs offered by certain electricity providers, although compensation rates and eligibility vary by utility and electricity plan.

California

California remains the nation's largest producer of total solar electricity when utility-scale and smaller installations are combined. In 2025, the state generated approximately 90,103 gigawatt-hours of solar electricity. California is also testing new approaches to solar development, including Project Nexus, a $20 million pilot that installed solar panels over irrigation canals in the Central Valley. The completed installations generate electricity while researchers evaluate their potential to reduce evaporation and improve water conservation.

Battery storage is another major priority, allowing California to store electricity for use when solar generation declines. The state supports solar and storage projects through programs including the Self-Generation Incentive Program, which provides incentives for qualifying battery installations. Property tax exclusions and assistance for eligible low-income households may also reduce installation costs. However, the federal Residential Clean Energy Credit is no longer available for new residential solar systems placed in service after December 31, 2025.

Florida

Florida ranks third nationally in total solar electricity generation, supported by continued investment in utility-scale installations. Florida Power & Light and Duke Energy Florida have expanded their solar portfolios, while Jacksonville's municipal utility, JEA, is developing the Miller and Forest Trail Solar Energy Centers. Together, the two facilities are expected to provide 125 megawatts of generating capacity, enough electricity to serve more than 22,000 households.

Florida utilities are also investing in battery storage to manage demand and improve electricity availability outside daylight hours. For residential customers, the state provides a sales tax exemption for qualifying solar equipment and a property tax exemption for the added value of eligible renewable energy installations. Net metering is available through participating utilities, although individual program requirements and compensation arrangements vary.

Arizona

Arizona is one of the country's leading solar-producing states, with large installations across its desert regions. The Eleven Mile Solar Center in Pinal County began operating in 2024 with 300 megawatts of solar generation and a battery system capable of storing 1,200 megawatt-hours of electricity. In September 2026, Salt River Project approved the development of the Marigold Energy Center near Stanfield, which is planned to include 600 megawatts of solar generation, 400 megawatts of battery storage capacity, and natural gas generation.

Arizona is also exploring ways to combine solar development with water conservation, including solar panels installed over irrigation canals on Gila River Indian Community land. Homeowners may qualify for a state income tax credit equal to 25% of eligible solar installation costs, capped at $1,000. Qualifying solar equipment also benefits from state tax provisions, while utility compensation programs offer additional options for residents who generate their own electricity.

Nevada

Nevada's extensive desert solar resources have supported some of the country's largest photovoltaic installations. The state is also investing in transmission infrastructure through NV Energy's Greenlink Nevada program. Greenlink West is planned to connect the Las Vegas area with Yerington, while Greenlink North will extend transmission infrastructure toward Ely. These projects are designed to improve electricity transfers between northern and southern Nevada and provide greater access to renewable energy resources.

Residential solar customers served by NV Energy can receive credits for excess electricity exported to the grid. Under the utility's currently open Tier 4 net metering program, qualifying excess generation is credited at 75% of the applicable retail electricity rate, excluding certain charges. Nevada also offers the Nevada BRIGHT program, which helps eligible households access solar installations through leasing arrangements. State tax incentives and financing programs provide additional support for qualifying commercial solar developments.

North Carolina

North Carolina remains one of the Southeast's largest solar electricity producers, with extensive utility-scale installations serving homes, businesses, and industrial customers. Solar development is increasingly accompanied by investments in energy storage and grid resilience. In 2025, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality announced a $5 million Clean Energy Microgrid Initiative to support permanent and mobile solar-powered systems in communities affected by Hurricane Helene.

During 2026, the state advanced plans for up to 24 permanent microgrids across six western counties and two mobile systems that can provide emergency electricity during disasters. North Carolina also made approximately $1.4 million available in November 2026 for qualifying energy-efficient building improvements, including potential solar and battery storage projects. Duke Energy continues to offer solar programs and bill credit arrangements, and commercial and residential installations may qualify for property tax exemptions under state law.

The Future of Solar Energy in the United States

Solar growth extends to states outside the top six. New York reached eight gigawatts of distributed solar capacity in July 2026 and is working toward 10 gigawatts by 2030. In Illinois, a law signed in January 2026 set a cumulative energy storage target of 3,000 megawatts. Georgia Power received approval in September 2026 for 1,137 megawatts of new solar power purchase agreements in Georgia, while Virginia's solar industry is expanding as data center development increases electricity demand.

California and Texas remain the leading producers, while Florida and Arizona are adding substantial generating capacity. Battery storage and transmission upgrades are also influencing how new projects are developed. As electricity demand grows, these investments will determine how effectively solar generation can support the nation's power grid.

The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity ... to come together to show the American people we are listening to you.”

Industry leaders are advocating for the bill's passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group.

But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a “terrible mistake” to proceed with the bill in the waning days of the current Congress.

While changes announced Saturday address a few concerns, the bill also comes with a gauntlet of new — and at times conflicting — rules, Campbell said. He said the bill maintains a veneer of federal safeguards while in fact stripping the power of federal agencies, states, tribes and communities to identify and prevent serious harm to health and the environment.

Sara Amundson, president of the Humane World Action Fund, said the bill weakens the scientific foundation of the Endangered Species Act and could create new opportunities to exclude needed wildlife protections.

“This proposed rewrite of the ‘best available science’ standard could give agencies new grounds to unfairly dismiss credible research, including science showing that stronger protections are needed for species at risk," she said, urging lawmakers to drop the provision or oppose the bill.

McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

text:
(The Center Square) – A coalition of energy and policy organizations sent a letter to President Donald Trump expressing concern over the harm to national security that is posed by publicly traded U.S. companies – such as Amazon, Apple, and Google – being involved in the climate convention, COP31.

Senior Fellow at the Energy & Environment Legal Institute as well as former Trump administration EPA Transition Team Advisor Steve Milloy told The Center Square: “All US companies, public traded or not, that are involved in COP31 represent a threat to the nation.”

COP31 is an annual climate change conference put on by the United Nations.

Milloy told The Center Square that the letter to Trump “targets publicly traded tech companies like Amazon, Apple and Google for two reasons.”

“First, as publicly traded companies that have an affirmative legal duty to be honest when discussing issues related to their business, supporting COP31 is fundamentally dishonest because there is nothing these companies can do to affect climate,” Milloy said.

“So talking about it like they can is inherently dishonest,” Milloy said. “Next, these tech companies have various national security activities and responsibilities.”

Milloy said China pushes climate-related actions at these conferences in effort to hurt U.S. national security.

“Companies involved in our national security should not be teaming up with Communist China against our national security," he said. “The President should bar federal contractors with national security obligations from participating in a process that only works to the benefit of Communist China.”

Signatories of the letter include Milloy’s organization Energy & Environment Legal Institute along with the American Energy Institute, CFACT, Heartland Impact, The Heartland Institute, and Truth in Energy and Climate.

In their letter, the groups expressed support for Trump’s decision to withdraw from the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, while also requesting that the president “take action to ensure that U.S. companies attending the conference do not violate the law and undercut U.S. Policy.”

The letter notes that “both federal law and SEC regulations prohibit [Amazon, Apple and Google] from making false and misleading statements.

“Not only are these companies misleading the public and potentially violating the law by giving the public and investors the impression that they are doing something about supposed ‘climate change,’ but they are also undercutting U.S. foreign policy and national security by participating in COP31,” the letter said.

The Center Square reached out to Amazon, Google, Apple, UN Climate Change, and the White House Press Office for comment. None responded by publishing.

President of The Heartland Institute James Taylor told The Center Square that "publicly traded companies getting in bed with UN global climate governance is a repeat of the societal-wide elimination of our freedoms that took place when government teamed up with big corporations under the guise of fighting COVID and fighting online 'misinformation.'”

“Large corporations should never be allowed to do governments' dirty work that either cannot find the votes to pass through normal legislative processes or is expressly prohibited by our Constitution,” Taylor said

COP31 began on Monday in Turkey.

The climate summit intends to focus on the “implementation of climate solutions and progressing a global energy transition that drives economic growth, more jobs, food security, better health and safety and affordable clean energy.”

description:
If passed, the bill would be a major overhaul of permitting for federal projects, including but not limited to highways, pipelines, and power lines.
It would arguably be the most significant bill, in terms of its economic impact, signed by President Donald Trump during his second term.
The bill would also prevent data centers from passing along their electricity and energy costs to consumers.
Key negotiators in the Senate released an updated version of the bill over the weekend, using a process called a manager’s amendment.
However, just minutes before Monday’s vote on BAAJA, Trump said he would not approve any wind farms, calling the projects “losers.”
text:
Ahead of the vote, advocates of the bill said at least 15 to 20 Democrats are needed to back the bill in order to whip votes in the House.

Better known as BAAJA, the legislation has the support of dozens of clean energy and manufacturing associations, more than 300 solar and storage companies, oil companies, utility firms, some climate change groups, and lawmakers across the aisle.

If passed, the bill would be a major overhaul of permitting for federal projects, including but not limited to highways, pipelines, and power lines. It would arguably be the most significant bill, in terms of its economic impact, signed by President Donald Trump during his second term.

While the test vote indicates the bill is on its way to Trump’s desk, it faces an uphill battle in the House, as many Democrats wish to push permitting discussions to the next Congress, when they hold the majority in both chambers.

However, advocates of the bill say that Democrats won’t be able to strike a better deal that Trump would still be willing to sign.

The current bipartisan deal would streamline the federal permitting process through a number of avenues, including reforming the National Environmental Policy Act, a 55-year-old law that requires federal agencies to evaluate the environmental effects of major actions and decisions relevant to their departments, such as issuing permits and licenses for large projects.

The bill would also reform other bedrock environmental laws, such as the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Endangered Species Act.

Broadly, the legislation would shorten the window for lawsuits challenging environmental reviews for new projects. It also includes measures to accelerate the build-out of transmission infrastructure.

One provision sought by Democrats would make it more difficult for the president to revoke project permits, which is a priority because Trump has halted the construction of renewable energy sources.

The bill would also prevent data centers from passing along their electricity and energy costs to consumers.

Key negotiators in the Senate released an updated version of the bill over the weekend, using a process called a manager’s amendment. The amended legislation includes “clarifying, conforming, and technical edits” meant to address several concerns brought forward by environmental groups, tribal communities, and utilities over the last few weeks.

These changes include extending the window for objections to certain environmental reviews, giving states a pathway to ask the federal regulators to investigate local utility projects, preserving collective bargaining agreements for employees at power marketing administrations, and creating a new data center community assistance program within the Department of Energy.

The manager’s amendment also addresses concerns regarding the permit certainty provisions, as critics claimed the legislation would make it difficult to walk back permits of projects that might have a worse environmental impact than previously thought.

Some of the most prominent changes were made to provisions regarding the National Historic Preservation Act, which were widely criticized by tribal groups. Specifically, the amendment version cuts a measure that would let the secretary of the Interior assume responsibilities of a tribal historic preservation officer in some cases, and strikes a controversial definition of “property of traditional religious or cultural importance.”

It would also require more consultation with tribes and native organizations, and require the Interior Department to provide Tribal Historic Preservation Offices with technical assistance, training, and support.

Heinrich told reporters ahead of the vote on Monday that changes to the legislation would also give tribes an equal seat with states regarding transmission planning and would require federal agencies to consult with tribes early on projects that affect important cultural sites.

The changes to the bill, broadly, did not cause any of the more prominent environmental and climate organizations to drop their opposition. Many, including the Sierra Club, the League of Conservation Voters and The Wilderness Society, redoubled their criticisms and pressed lawmakers not to rush to pass the bill.

National Tribal and Preservation Associations also remain largely opposed to BAAJA. The filmmaker and activist Julian Brave Noisecat, though, described the amendment as a “real effort at compromise.”

He specifically pointed to a change that would exclude records that tribes share with states and the federal government from the Freedom of Information Act “to keep sensitive sacred sites from exposure.”

“That sort of in-the-weeds detail—a nod to tribal data sovereignty—tells me that there’s real effort here to try to honor tribal consultation,” he said.

The amendment also prompted an endorsement from the Edison Electric Institute, which represents utility companies across the U.S. This is a significant show of support as major utilities lobbied against a similar permitting reform proposal led by then-Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.V.) and Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY).

The legislation has the backing of Trump, whose endorsement has been considered crucial in Washington to secure enough Republican votes.

On the eve of the procedural vote, Trump released a statement of support for BAAJA, calling the bill a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE AND DOMINANCE.”

The president said the bill would codify his administration’s “America First” energy agenda and speed up the construction of pipelines, mines, and power plants. He also said it would ensure data centers would build and pay for their own electricity and invest in local communities.

Trump’s comments are the first sign directly from the Oval Office that he would be willing to support legislation that would allow for accelerated deployment of renewable energy resources.

HERE’S WHAT’S IN THE BIPARTISAN MEGABILL MEANT TO ALLOW THE US TO BUILD AGAIN

Democrats have been wary of backing the bipartisan bill for fear that the president would not fairly implement the reforms for wind and solar power.

The Trump administration has attempted to assuage these concerns by advancing wind project reviews under the Department of War. While this could be viewed as a sign of good faith, many wind proponents have been quick to point out that the Pentagon was court-ordered to move forward on the reviews earlier this year, after stalling for months.

However, just minutes before Monday’s vote on BAAJA, Trump said he would not approve any wind farms, calling the projects “losers.”
