text:
A ballot measure that would have changed California environmental review process for construction has been rejected by voters, AP projects.

The measure, Proposition 45, would have made amendments to the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, the landmark 1970 state law requiring agencies to evaluate a project's potential impacts to the environment and to public health.

"This strong rejection of Prop. 45 shows that Californians are willing to fight to keep our air and water clean," said Aruna Prabhala, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, which opposed the measure. "When we can't rely on the federal government to protect our communities and the environment, we need strong state laws to keep us safe. I hope developers heard us loud and clear. We're not interested in giving polluting projects a free pass."

Jennifer Barrera, CEO of the California Chamber of Commerce, released a statement acknowledging the measure's defeat.

"This election has come to an end, but the journey is far from over. There's simply no path forward that doesn't begin with establishing clear and consistent rules for building the essentials of a prosperous future," Barrera said. "We will continue to advocate for reform that's both comprehensive and consequential, and we will hold elected officials accountable for whether they take action that makes a difference."

If approved, the measure would have created new environmental review procedures for projects defined as "essential," according to the state's official voter guide. Essential projects could include housing, clean energy, health facilities such as clinics and medical offices, police and fire stations, and education facilities along with energy and transportation projects.

Prop. 45 would have also tightened time limits for agencies to conduct CEQA review, public comment periods and how courts would review challenges to projects.

"Endless delays, red tape, and frivolous lawsuits make life more expensive and block the projects Californians need—driving up costs for housing, electricity, and water; wasting taxpayer dollars; worsening wildfire risk; increasing traffic; overcrowding schools; and delaying hospital and infrastructure upgrades," supporters said in the voter guide.

Along with the state Chamber of Commerce, supporters of Prop. 45 included the chambers of commerce in dozens of cities, the California Water Association, the state Republican Party and Democratic Assemblymember Buffy Wicks of Oakland.

Meanwhile, opponents of Prop. 45 argued the measure would weaken the state's environmental protections and would limit public input on projects.

"Proposition 45 limits both the environmental review of major new development projects and the public's right to be heard. Prop. 45 lets projects move forward with far less scrutiny of their harms to air, water and public health," opponents said in the voter guide.

Opponents included the state Democratic Party, environmental groups including the Sierra Club and labor groups including the California Federation of Labor Unions and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California.

Prop. 45 caused a split among advocates seeking additional homebuilding to alleviate the state's affordability crisis. While major for-profit and non-profit housing developers backed Prop. 45, pro-housing groups such as California YIMBY and YIMBY Action were neutral.

News

Bipartisan energy permitting bill may advance in lame-duck U.S. Congress session

Reuters – November 4

Several key Democratic architects of proposed bipartisan energy permitting legislation said on Wednesday they would not delay the bill in hopes of securing a better deal next year when Democrats take control of both chambers ‌of Congress. The measure, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, is the culmination of a years-long effort to ⁠pass legislation aimed at speeding construction of transmission lines, mines, and both renewable and fossil fuel energy projects. (Another key Democratic member reportedly wants to hold out for a different deal under the new Congress – see above article.)

California Energy Commission releases $46 million for DERS supporting grid reliability

Energy Storage News – October 29

The California Energy Commission (CEC) has released over $46 million for the state’s Distributed Electricity Backup Assets program. The program provides funding for distributed energy resources (DERS), including BESS, microgrids, and load flexibility technologies that can increase supply or shift load to improve grid reliability and help avoid blackouts during extreme events.

California and Texas are swimming in solar + storage

Renewable Energy World – October 26

California and Texas were able to meet record electricity demand this summer at “vastly reduced” wholesale electricity prices thanks to new solar and storage, per new analysis from the Solar Energy Industries Association. Texans saved $3.55 billion and Californians saved $2.5 billion between June and August 2026, compared to the same period in 2021, SEIA found.

BloombergNEF increases U.S. energy storage deployment forecast by 30%

Utility Dive – October 27

Despite trade barriers and project cost inflation, the U.S. is set to deploy 30% more energy storage capacity over the next 10 years than expected just six months ago, according to BloombergNEF. The group forecasts cumulative U.S. deployments of 213.9 GW by 2030 and 434.4 GW by 2036. In the U.S., near-term drivers include favorable economics for co-located storage and renewables and data centers’ growing appetite for both behind-the-meter and front-of-meter capacity.

Bay Area CCA projects to increase resiliency at critical municipal facilities

Government Technology – November 3

Communities across the San Francisco Bay Area are taking steps to increase energy resiliency and save money through the development of solar generation and BESS projects. Eight project sites in four cities, Berkeley, Fremont, Hayward, and Livermore, are participating in local nonprofit electric service provider Ava Community Energy’s Critical Municipal Facilities program, which will fund the buildout of projects at key municipal facilities including fire stations and community centers.

Revolution Wind offshore wind project enters commercial operation

Power Magazine – November 5

Denmark-headquartered offshore wind developer Orsted said its 704 MW Revolution Wind project off the coast of Rhode Island has reached full commercial operation. Revolution Wind is among the projects impacted by stop-work orders from the Trump administration, which has advanced policies detrimental to renewable energy and offshore wind in particular.

Crux arranges construction-to-term financing for 40 MWh BESS project at UC San Diego

Solar Quarter – October 27

Crux has facilitated construction-to-term loan financing for EnerSmart’s 8 MW/40 MWh battery BESS project at the University of California, San Diego. The BESS project is expected to strengthen the university’s energy resilience and help reduce electricity costs during peak-demand periods.

PowerBank completes 3 MW New York community solar project

Solar Power World – November 3

PowerBank has completed the 3.26 MW Camillus community solar project in Camillus, New York, and has received permission to operate. Solar Advocate Development, LLC, the project’s owner and EPC, built the array on a capped landfill.

Boise plans to tap its geothermal network to heat 300 affordable homes

Canary Media – November 2

Boise, Idaho, operates the country’s largest geothermal heating system, which pipes naturally warmed, 177-degree-Fahrenheit water from underground to about 100 buildings, including the Idaho State Capitol. Last week, Micron Technology gave Boise $2.5 million to build on that expertise. The cash fills a funding gap to extend the geothermal system to a planned affordable housing development with more than 300 units.

text:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today co-led a coalition of 16 attorneys general in sending a second letter to the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works and Energy and Natural Resources Committees regarding the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, commonly known as the permitting reform bill. The draft bill, introduced by a bipartisan group of lawmakers, is a wide-ranging package to reform energy permitting and infrastructure. Previously, Attorney General Bonta and a coalition expressed concerns over the draft legislation. The bill has since been amended, but it is only marginally improved. As currently drafted, the bill still contains problematic provisions that would risk abuse by polluting industries and impinge on state and tribal sovereignty. Today’s letter further highlights concerns with the bill and requests that the Senate postpone voting on the bill until more revisions can be made that ensure the bill achieves its stated goals and contains appropriate environmental and public health protections.

“The next generation of energy demands affordability without sacrificing public health and environmental integrity. We’re not here to let perfect become the enemy of the good, but good at least needs to be within reach,” said Attorney General Bonta. “Currently, this bill would drastically undermine state authority to protect our water quality, historical resources, and tribal resources. Immediate changes are needed to address our concerns and protect our communities. With this letter, we recognize the work in progress but emphasize that there’s still more to do.”

The current draft bill is a varied package that would transform energy permitting and infrastructure. Without further amendment, the bill would harm states’ and tribes’ abilities to protect water, historic, and cultural resources under the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and the Endangered Species Act, and would impinge on state and tribal sovereignty. Additional amendments could ensure the bill achieves its goals of improving clean energy permitting, reducing energy costs, and creating jobs.

The coalition states are home to a wide variety of natural resources, including wind and solar resources, waterways, large landscapes, cultural districts, tribal resources, and parks. In the letter, the states offer a unique and diverse perspective, as they possess significant existing authority under the Clean Water Act and National Historic Preservation Act that the bill would undermine. The states also regularly participate in National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act processes that would be affected by the bill, and the bill’s permitting certainty provisions would impact countless projects in the states.

In sending today’s letter, Attorney General Bonta, Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell, New York Attorney General Letitia James, and Washington Attorney General Nicholas W. Brown co-lead the attorneys general of Colorado, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Oregon, Virginia, Vermont, and the District of Columbia.

text:
Few vehicles have been more widely unloved and often ridiculed than Elon Musk’s attempt to radically redefine the venerable all-American pickup truck. Now it appears that the wedge-shaped stainless-steel monstrosity that is the Tesla Cybertruck is headed for that great scrapyard in the sky.

On Friday, fresh off a shellacking of the candidates he bankrolled in the midterms, Elon Musk posted to X that Cybertruck production would wind down in mid-2027 to free up manufacturing capacity at Tesla’s factory in Austin, Texas, for the new Cybercab, a gold-colored self-driving car that has no pedals or steering wheel. Many will likely say good riddance to the Cybertruck. With a road presence that strives for futuristic but comes off as obnoxious, it came to symbolize Musk’s transformation from a climate-conscious champion of the left—the Cybertruck was, at least, an electric vehicle—to a MAGA-addled, chain saw–wielding, Trump-boosting agent of the right.

Unveiled in 2019, the Cybertruck sought to reimagine the pickup segment with a combination of jaw-dropping technical audacity and arrogance. The brutally angular design was rumored to have sprung directly from the mind of Musk himself, with the mandate to the Tesla design team to make it so. The story I heard was that the ever-childlike Musk drew it with a ruler on a piece of paper, then handed it to head designer Franz von Holzhausen and Tesla’s beleaguered engineers to figure out the details.

True or apocryphal, that scenario captures Musk’s penchant for pursuing self-evidently dumb ideas, which he somehow thinks he can translate into world-changing demands. But this time, the world didn’t want to change.

I covered the reveal of the Cybertruck with a colleague whose spit-take reaction when the Cybertruck rolled out was unforgettable: Is this for real? The vehicle, which does, underneath all those angles, feature a truck bed with a motorized cover, was almost immediately labeled a colossal blunder. The pickup segment is extremely profitable in the U.S. for automakers, and it’s where the country’s perennial top seller, the Ford F-Series, has ruled since the Reagan administration. The goal with the Cybertruck, it seemed, wasn’t to join the pickup-truck segment but to shock it into submission. But as of now, fewer than 75,000 of Musk’s pickups have been sold, a number that is all the more disappointing when you consider that Tesla’s Austin factory was set up to produce 250,000 trucks a year. That might have something to do with the fact that the originally promised price tag was $40,000, also an undershoot of reality: Currently, the base truck is $82,490 (although it appears that Tesla has stopped taking orders for it), the middle level is $92,490, and the top-trim, immaturely named “Cyberbeast” is $102,490.

It was hard to see who the Cybertruck was for. Your average pickup buyer, even if they could afford the Cybertruck, didn’t have much incentive to entertain Musk’s vision. Customers who might have been attracted to an electric truck had the much more functional Rivian R1T to consider. Apart from a polarizing headlight design, the Rivian actually looked like a pickup, while the Cybertruck was auditioning for a part in a Mad Max movie. (Rivian fans could also buy an R1T several years before the Cybertruck eventually arrived; the Tesla didn’t begin being delivered until 2024.) Contractors and farmers in the market for a pickup don’t care about the ability to go from 0 to 60 in under five seconds so much as they need towing capacity and durability. The truck’s windows were supposed to be bulletproof, lending the thing a postapocalyptic vibe, but they embarrassingly cracked during the Cybertruck’s livestreamed launch event at its design studio near Los Angeles. It’s hard to imagine your average farmer being shot at, but it wasn’t a good sign, quality-wise. And potential owners for whom the pickup lifestyle is more aspirational—i.e., they don’t need to haul stuff—could opt for a Ford F-150 King Ranch, a luxurious dream truck with a 14-speaker audio system and real wood interior accents, to make their lives complete.

The death of the Cybertruck isn’t all the Cybertruck’s fault. Tesla is in a massive shift in its business strategy away from electric vehicles and toward self-driving robotaxis, Optimus humanoid robots, and artificial intelligence. The company discontinued both the Model S sedan and Model X SUV earlier this year. The Model 3 four-door and Model Y crossover remain in the lineup—for the moment at least; these are the Teslas that well-to-do liberals are now slapping “I Bought This Before Elon Went Crazy” stickers on, and Tesla hasn’t meaningfully updated either in years. The Semi (an electric semitruck with a massive wraparound windshield) is also sticking around, and of course Tesla just showcased its new Roadster, a supercar that can “fly” (really, it more elevates for very short distances). The sheer impracticality of the car is a signal of where Musk wants to take the company: Human-piloted EVs are in their way out, replaced by Cybercabs summoned on demand. Embracing that transformation, including the production of any army of robots, means that there isn’t room for continued Cybertruck manufacturing at Tesla’s factories.

I like to characterize the Cybertruck as an “exotic” vehicle—a fever-dream hypertruck meant to appeal to crypto bros who had played a lot of Halo and measure success in terms of Lamborghinis in the driveway. To its credit, it was impossible to mistake the Cybertruck for anything else. You were supposed to imagine a fleet of the vehicles rolling off SpaceX Starships that had landed on Mars, possibly driven by androids quoting The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. In the end, the Cybertruck has probably succeeded in delighting its fairly limited core audience—at least the members of that audience who have stuck with it through numerous recalls for stuff like trim pieces that were literally falling off. The Cybertruck certainly provided some sizzle in 2019 when Tesla’s stock price was sliding and Musk appeared to be losing some of his ability to dominate the conversation inside and outside the auto industry. It put stainless steel back into the picture when nobody had given it a second thought since John DeLorean’s cocaine bust or Back to the Future’s flux capacitor. SpaceX reportedly wound up buying thousands of Cybertrucks when sales disappointed and inventory accumulated, providing some valuable insight into how Musk uses his portfolio of companies to prop each other up.

Cybertruck fans—whoever they are out there—can rest assured that it won’t completely disappear from America’s highways anytime soon. It could evolve into something of a collectible: Tesla’s swaggering pre-COVID middle finger to the truck world, an artifact of the company’s do-anything period, an emblem of its triumphant assent to the pinnacle of the EV world. That will reward aficionados who rightly see the Cybertruck as a bold-yet-doomed attempt to break out of the established pickup paradigm and try something wildly different. It’s true: The Cybertruck was a swing for the fences. It was also more than a little stupid.

It is the final hoorah for the 119th Congress. Republicans have just weeks left in control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. The main thing on the agenda: keeping the federal government open. Funding is set to run out on December 11, when a stop-gap measure passed about a month ahead of the midterms expires.

Any funding extension is all but certain to be done through another short-term bill, known as a continuing resolution. The typical government funding process — 12 carefully negotiated appropriations bills — would take time and political will that lawmakers currently lack.

Congress will also need to find a path forward on the National Defense Authorization Act, long considered a must-pass annual military funding package. This year, the bill is quagmired in the unforgiving politics of the Iran war. The conflict is opposed by a majority of Americans — something President Trump has acknowledged was a key force in driving his party out of power.

The House is also likely to vote on an impeachment effort targeting Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Introduced by Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a key figure in forcing the administration's release of the Epstein files, the impeachment measure lists a number of charges, including that the administration failed to properly consult Congress on the military campaign.

Democrats are unlikely to be in a compromising mood on legislation, just weeks away from taking control of both chambers. That means continued work on big-ticket items like the Protect College Sports Act, meant to introduce new regulations around college athlete compensation, and a bipartisan energy permitting overhaul will likely wait until the new term.

With slim majorities in both chambers, they could also have to contend with some attendance problems after a demoralizing performance in last week's midterm elections. That further complicates passing legislation through chambers already governed by the thinnest of majorities.

Mike Ricci, a Republican strategist with the group Seven Letter and aide to former Speakers of the House John Boehner and Paul Ryan, told NPR that a number of forces could help draw reluctant lame duck legislators back to Washington, including winding down their offices, finding new work and attending the White House Christmas party.

Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting the stage for a dramatic vote on whether to remove one of the Trump administration’s most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.

The impeachment resolution was introduced by Massie, a Kentucky Republican, as soon as the House opened for the first day of sessions after the midterms. It largely focuses on the war in Iran but also includes references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.

Massie said the secretary’s actions amount to “high crimes and misdemeanors” and his leadership at the Pentagon “thus warrants impeachment.”

A vote in the House could come by mid-week, putting pressure on Republicans — many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war — but next steps are highly uncertain.

House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent this outcome, and warned lawmakers against impeaching the Defense secretary while the U.S. is engaged in military actions in the Middle East.

“Impeaching a Cabinet secretary right now, especially the Department of War in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that,” Johnson, a Republican, said as he opened the chamber.

“We don’t impeach Cabinet secretaries for political gain or for cheap tricks, and I think that’s what this is and I think everybody knows it.”

Most House Democrats are expected to support impeaching Hegseth, with Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries saying over the weekend it’s time for the Defense secretary to go.

If the House votes to impeach Hegseth, it would next go to the Senate for a potential trial. Republicans remain in the majority in both chambers, until the new Congress convenes in January with Democrats in control.

Hegseth issues his own defense and prepares for a fight

Hegseth maintains he’s eager to litigate the military actions that he and President Donald Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela’s previous leaders.

“If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you’re taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic,” Hegseth told reporters Monday, using the military code names for the Iran war and campaign of strikes to halt the Houthis’ attacks on shipping in the Middle East.

Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday — his first in over 180 days — on the impeachment threat. His last briefing was in May, and he has not held one on the Iran war, strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats or other U.S. military actions since then.

The Pentagon chief is bearing the brunt of anger and calls for his ouster after the Iran war and its economic impact contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections that cost the party control of Congress.

Hegseth waves off impeachment push as ‘noise’

Hegseth, after giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, brushed aside the impeachment push.

“There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success,” he told reporters. He added that “if we want to litigate” the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, “I’m happy to do it all day long.”

“My team, we’re not worried about the noise — it’s what I told the troops, too — ‘don’t worry about the noise,’” he said.

Asked about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive GOP losses in the election, Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and “I agree.”

He largely repeated a line that Secretary of State Marco Rubio said to reporters a day earlier: “It doesn’t have to be necessarily popular, but it can be necessary.”

Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because “someone had to confront the Iranian regime’s pursuit of a nuclear weapon” and said “the choice was don’t act and wish it away or take a bold move.”

Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%.

Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night.

“He’s guilty of two things, basically winning two wars,” Trump said. “I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it’s awfully hard to say let’s impeach somebody who did that.”

Pentagon chief insists ‘Iran is devastated’

Hegseth reiterated that “Iran is devastated,” even though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters’ pocketbooks.

He said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including telling Iran: “Hey, we’re done, and we’re going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it.”

Hegseth’s defense of the war comes after about 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.

With anger in Congress rising, Hegseth has been on a social media blitz, posting a video last week acknowledging the threat of impeachment. He said it would be “all about the politics of personal destruction” and insisted that “won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Since then, scores of political appointees within the Pentagon have posted images of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, “Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic.” The White House also posted a video to social media that featured praise from Trump.

As he campaigned for California governor, Xavier Becerra reflected on the way his Catholic upbringing informs his politics. “The sanctity of life is something that’s really ingrained in you,” the Democrat and former U.S. health and human services secretary said earlier this year.

He then explained his rationale, confounding to some, for supporting abortion rights. Becerra exemplifies how Catholicism’s deep roots often go hand in hand with California’s progressive reputation. That complexity is a snapshot of a larger reality — that American Catholics are in many ways a politically mixed bag.

“There is no Catholic vote,” said David Gibson, the director of Fordham University’s Center on Religion and Culture. White evangelicals for Republicans or Black Protestants for Democrats are more politically reliable religious groups, he said.

With Becerra’s win this week, California has elected five consecutive Catholic governors — a remarkable streak indicative of Catholicism’s enduring influence. “Catholicism is part of the fabric of California culture the way Puritan Protestantism is part of the New England regions,” Gibson said.

Catholic voters — especially Latinos — helped elect Becerra, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters. He became the state’s first elected Latino governor.

Beginning with Gray Davis, who took office in 1999, four of those five governors also have been Democrats. Some have been more vocal about their faith than others — notably Jerry Brown, who was a seminarian in the 1950s.

California is home to more Catholics than any other U.S. state. A Pew Research Center poll in 2024 found that 25% of adults in California identify as Catholic, accounting for almost half of the state’s Christians.

But numbers aside, Catholicism has been woven into the fabric of the state for centuries.

California Catholics are politically diverse

From economically progressive strains of Catholic social teaching and explicit rejections of the death penalty to official teachings against abortion and in vitro fertilization, Catholic theology rarely fits neatly into political categories, which helps explain the unpredictable voting habits.

Take Gov. Gavin Newsom, whose strong support of abortion rights is at odds with Catholic leadership. Yet his announcement this week that he planned to change more than 500 death sentences in the state to life in prison without the possibility of parole was celebrated by the California Catholic Conference, the public policy organization representing the church in California.

“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter.

Some leaders within the church have subverted Trump administration policies, like San Bernardino Bishop Alberto Rojas, who last year formally excused parishioners from their weekly obligation to attend Mass following immigration detentions on parish properties in the diocese.

Others have taken high-profile conservative stances, like San Francisco Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone, who in 2022 barred U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi, a Catholic, from receiving Communion over her support of abortion rights.

About 2 in 10 voters in the California governor’s race were Catholic, and they mostly voted for Becerra, according to The AP Voter Poll. About 6 in 10 Catholic voters supported Becerra, while about 4 in 10 voted for his Republican opponent Steve Hilton.

About 7 in 10 Latino Catholics voted for Becerra, while white Catholics were split between Becerra and Hilton.

Those complex political patterns are also reflected nationally. Catholics were split evenly between Democrats and Republicans.

That’s a modest shift from 2024, when just over half of U.S. Catholics voted for Trump, according to AP VoteCast.

California Catholics are ethnically diverse

Catholics in California are also ethnically diverse. Many are immigrants from Latin America and the Philippines. Resident Tracy Creighton’s ancestry goes back to the missions founded more than two centuries ago by Spanish Franciscan priests.

As the mother of teenagers, Creighton has sought to pass on the importance of serving others and respecting nature — values she believes are both deeply Catholic and Californian.

“I feel in the last several years we have lost our way in terms of being of service to others,” she said, citing Saint Francis of Assisi as a model. “That is why I stay Catholic.”

Catholic faith, history and culture contribute to many Californians’ understanding of themselves, such as their relationship to the 21 missions founded between 1769 and 1823.

“Obviously, the legacy of the missions is a mixed one and has problematic implications,” said Cecilia González-Andrieu, a theology professor at Loyola Marymount University. “For Latina theologians like myself, there’s a need for us to be able to hold that in tension, the fact that within our very selves we have this mix of cultures and bloods.”

Leaders are increasingly reckoning with that tension and how it should be communicated to young people. The history of the missions is included in the statewide public fourth-grade curriculum, which is often accompanied by a field trip to one.

A law signed by Newsom went into effect last year that requires schools to teach in social studies class about how missionaries mistreated Native Americans, and to share Native perspectives.

But mistreatment isn’t the only fraught legacy of the missionaries who arrived in the late 18th century.

“The mission system spread disease and was ill-equipped to deal with the immunological effects of old-world people and their immunities,” said William Deverell, a historian at the University of Southern California. “It’s your major consequential institutional moment which brings with it a horrible demographic decline of the Indigenous population.”

California Catholicism is about more than faith

Despite their complicated legacy, the missions are landmarks. Many still operate as Catholic parishes.

The missions also helped influence the Spanish Colonial Revival style of homes that became signatures of California architecture. “Why I love California so much is the architecture and the beauty of it. And I think Catholicism plays a lot into that,” Creighton said.

Creighton says it’s difficult to overstate the significance of Mission San Luis Rey in Oceanside, near San Diego, where she lives.

“Everyone does their homecoming pictures, their Christmas pictures. It’s just ingrained in us,” she said, adding that even non-Catholics will often take photos there. “It’s a landmark that’s important in who we are here.”

Beyond architecture, Catholic influence is all over many California homes.

Between the crucifixes and votive candles on display, Brian Murillo’s Fresno home is a testament to his Catholic upbringing. The state employee describes himself as a lapsed Catholic who stopped going to Mass because he felt the American church’s leadership was too aligned with Republican politics.

But Murillo, whose father is from Mexico, still says a Hail Mary or an Our Father prayer whenever he leaves the house.

“Sometimes I’ll be cleaning the house and I’ll be doing a prayer or in the car by myself,” he said. “It’s been such a part of my growing up, even to this day.”

In the home-stretch of the L.A. mayor’s race, Mayor Karen Bass and her former ally-turned-challenger Nithya Raman met for the only televised debate of the campaign.

They traded jabs over public safety, homelessness and other core issues for Angelenos. But one dig was particularly eyebrow-raising. It came toward the end of the debate, when Bass chided Raman for her support from bike lane advocates.

“There’s very influential people who are supporting your campaign who are very, very much advocates for bike lanes,” Bass, who conceded the race Thursday, said in the Oct. 13 debate hosted by NBCLA and Telemundo.

“Um, yes,” Mayor-elect Raman can be heard quietly saying as one of the moderators tries to move the conversation along.

While it represented just a moment in the race, the brief exchange encapsulated what was at stake for public transit and bike champions: Maintain the status quo with the current mayor, or take a chance on a candidate who made improving transportation and mobility across L.A. a centerpiece of her campaign.

Since the race was called for Raman by the Associated Press, public transit supporters have been cheering her win.

“I’m just on Cloud 9 right now,” said Jonathan Hale, street safety activist and founder of the grassroots group People’s Vision Zero.

”It is time for a cultural shift towards a city that prioritizes pedestrians and cyclists and people who take public transit,” Hale added. “We finally have a mayor who believes that.”

It’s not just bike lanes. Raman’s successful campaign hinged on a policy platform that viewed broken sidewalks, streetlights in disrepair and pothole-ridden roads not as intractable issues, but urgent crises that can be addressed with better governance.

Raman, who has said she used trains and buses to commute to work in the past, also has her eyes on L.A.’s larger transportation network. On election eve, while riding the L.A. Metro B Line with supporters, Raman said the region can buck its car-centric reputation and be home to a fast, safe and connected transit system.

“That vision is totally achievable, if you have the will. I have the will,” Raman said.

The will of the people meets political will

For years, L.A. voters have signaled their support for better public transit and improved mobility.

More than 70% of L.A. city residents voted in favor of countywide sales tax measures in 2008 and 2016 to fund transportation projects, which have resulted in transit projects like the first section of the D Line extension.

In 2024, two-thirds of voters passed Measure HLA requiring bike, pedestrian and transit improvements throughout L.A.

Streets for All, the influential transportation advocacy group that put up Measure HLA, has supported Raman throughout her political career. Its political action committee buoyed the mayor-elect’s run with nearly $1.7 million in ad spending opposing Bass, according to campaign finance filings.

Its founder and chief executive officer, Michael Schneider, said Raman’s victory further solidifies the sense that Angelenos want to see their built environment improve.

“It's a mainstream moment for safe streets advocacy,” Schneider said.

In her policy platform, Raman promised to “fast track safety improvements by delivering on HLA.” Progress on the voter-approved initiative has been slow and the subject of ongoing legal battles.

Damian Kevitt, the executive director of the street safety nonprofit Streets Are For Everyone, is also optimistic. Kevitt said the nonprofit tried its best to engage Bass and “multiple council members” on the issue of traffic violence, which, in recent years, has killed more Angelenos than homicides.

“Raman's office was one of the few that engaged,” Kevitt said. “Time will tell, but we think that the future looks brighter.”

Raman has said she wants to create a Vision Zero director in the mayor’s office to “make safety the governing lens for every decision made related to our streets.” In 2015, then-Mayor Eric Garcetti adopted a policy framework known as Vision Zero to zero out traffic deaths by 2025.

Now that Raman’s been elected mayor, the future of a contentious road project near Griffith Park could shift. The project emerged as a flashpoint about street safety during the campaign. Raman had pushed for a long-studied lane reduction plan along Forest Lawn Drive. Bass canned that proposal just a few weeks before the project’s groundbreaking and adopted a design to widen the roadway’s lanes instead.

Reinstating her vision for Forest Lawn Drive will require Raman to work with her colleagues on L.A. City Council, nearly all of whom endorsed Bass in the mayoral election. Most have said they’re ready to work with her.

A powerful voice on Metro’s board

The mayor of L.A. has a dedicated seat on the 13-person Metro Board and can appoint three of its members. That accounts for roughly a third of the voting power on the powerful body that makes countywide transportation planning decisions. The rest of the board is made up of all five L.A. County supervisors and non-L.A. city representatives.

Nick Andert, a documentary filmmaker and transit advocate YouTuber, said he wants to see Raman appoint people who use Metro “at least from time to time” and also someone with relevant expertise to transit planning.

Bass' current appointments include the founding member of a faith-based development group in South L.A., Jacquelyn Dupont-Walker, as well as L.A. City Councilmembers Katy Yaroslavsky and Imelda Padilla. When Raman joins the board in December, she’ll have the power to change those appointments.

L.A. County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath said the mayor’s appointees often vote as a bloc. She said disagreements with the L.A. mayor often mean disagreeing with “potentially four votes on the board,” as was the case earlier this year during deliberations over how to extend a Metro rail line into West Hollywood.

Horvath, who endorsed Raman for mayor in October, said she’s looking forward to working with someone who has demonstrated interest in transit. She pointed to Raman’s support of projects like the Sepulveda Transit Corridor and K-Line Northern Extension, and making day-to-day operations of the transit system more reliable.

“Raman has really listened to what people are looking for,” Horvath said. “If we listen to our riders more and make those improvements, those are the things that help bring people into the system.”

The mayor-elect has signaled her support for extending Metro’s operations later into the night, a proposal that Cassy Horton, co-founder of the Downtown L.A. Residents Association, hopes materializes.

“Downtown is a nightlife hub,” Horton said. “It would be a huge game changer, probably reviving nightlife, if trains were running until bars and restaurants close.”

In a statement, Metro congratulated Raman on her victory.

“We look forward to welcoming her to the Board,” Metro said, adding its gratitude to Bass for making Metro a “safer, more welcoming and equitable agency.”

Quick-turn improvements promised in Raman’s first 100 days

As the incoming mayor, Raman will lead city departments that impact transportation and mobility. In her first 100 days in office, Raman has pledged to begin addressing urgent road repairs and potholes. She also said she’ll make public when broken streetlights in the city will be fixed.

“ I love the fact that Nithya Raman has built her agenda on making cities work from the sidewalks up,” said Hilary Norton, executive director of FastLink DTLA.

Norton said cities are successful when residents, including those with disabilities, can travel through local infrastructure with ease.

“ We meet on the sidewalks and we travel together and we interact together, we're bringing our democracy back,” Norton said.

It's been a feature of campaign ads and stump speeches for months: grocery prices are out of control.

Affordability concerns, including high food costs, were top of mind for voters heading into the midterms, as the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran continued to drive up prices. That economic strain helped Democrats win control of both houses of Congress on Tuesday.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the incoming majority would make tackling high prices a priority come January. "It was a tremendous victory for the American people and a strong rebuke of MAGA extremism, which has made life more expensive for everyday Americans despite their promises to lower the high cost of living on day one," he told NPR on Friday.

The question is how Democrats will do that with President Trump still in the Oval Office, willing to wield his veto pen. Senate Democrats won't have a filibuster-proof majority, and Trump may have little appetite to roll back his signature tariffs or reverse course on the Iran war, two of the main causes of high food prices.

Lael Brainard, who leads a public policy group called The Kitchen Table Project, said Americans are nevertheless expecting relief from Washington — and quickly.

"They are feeling like they are getting squeezed by high prices that don't need to be that high," she said.

What Democrats plan to do to lower food prices

Despite the political hurdles, Democrats said they intend to move ahead with plans to cut grocery bills, including by rolling back Trump's tariffs. Those tariffs have not only raised the cost of certain foods and drinks imported to the U.S., but also created other pressures on the food industry by making it more expensive to import things like machine parts and packaging.

The Iran war has led to a surge in energy prices, which has made it more expensive to transport just about everything. Fertilizer costs also grew when the closure of the Strait of Hormuz cut off a significant portion of the global fertilizer trade.

But getting Trump to backtrack on tariffs or the Iran war — or his immigration crackdown, which has led to labor shortages on U.S. farms — could prove tricky for Democrats.

"I think the president would certainly want to find ways to reduce the cost of groceries. Democrats [also] see that in their interest," said Lehigh University political science professor Chris Borick. "The mechanisms, the tools, the levers that would be most readily available to do that — there's quite a bit of distance between the president and Democrats that'll be taking over both the House and the Senate."

Several incoming Democratic senators also floated other proposals during their campaigns that aim to make groceries more affordable.

James Talarico of Texas said he would push back against "attacks" on the federal food assistance programs WIC and SNAP, the latter of which is undergoing a major overhaul by the Trump administration and has seen a precipitous drop in participation since last summer. Kansas' Adam Hamilton announced his support for a national ban on "dynamic pricing" in grocery stores. And multiple candidates, including Roy Cooper of North Carolina, vowed to block food industry mergers they say would raise consumer prices.

Democratic governors take a piece of the affordability pie

Beyond the blue wave in Congress, Democrats also made gains in state capitals across the U.S. on Tuesday. At least 28 states will have Democratic governors beginning next year, and ten state legislative chambers flipped to Democrats, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Incoming state governors have floated their own ideas for how to give residents relief in the grocery aisle.

Keisha Lance Bottoms proposed allowing municipalities in Georgia to suspend or fully eliminate their local sales tax on groceries, baby formula, diapers and more. Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, promised to outlaw "predatory surveillance pricing" and price gouging in grocery stores. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland said the state would explore a policy similar to one in Albuquerque that temporarily waives permitting fees for markets that sell healthy and affordable food in so-called "food deserts," the Albuquerque Journal reported.

However state and federal officials decide to go about lowering prices, Americans say they want to see cheaper groceries soon. According to a poll released by the Kitchen Table Project and Global Strategy Group in September, nearly half of respondents said their most important goal was seeing their grocery bills lowered within six months.

description:
The planned 500,000-square-foot Freedom Separation facility will process mined and recycled rare earth materials into separated oxides used in domestic rare earth metal production.
At full capacity, the facility is expected to process more than 18,000 tons of mixed rare earth feedstock annually and produce more than 4,400 tons of separated rare earth oxides.
Phoenix Tailings said the operation could rank among the world’s largest rare earth separation facilities.
Rare earth materials are essential to manufacturing products and equipment used in defense, health care, electronics, communications and electric vehicles.
Announced in June, the financing is intended to support construction of its rare earth separation system and remains subject to review before finalization.
text:
When Nick Myers was weighing two potential locations for his company’s $375 million rare earth separation facility, he turned to a trusted adviser: his grandfather, a longtime Rochester business owner.

The choice was between Rochester and a site in the Midwest. His grandfather, Nicholas Sfikas, founder of Rochester 100 Inc., didn’t mince words about which location he preferred.

“He told me if I chose the other site, I’d go bankrupt,” Myers said.

Sfikas, 102, believed Rochester has the industrial infrastructure, workforce and quality-of-life amenities needed to make the venture successful. After conducting an in-depth analysis, Myers reached the same conclusion.

Now, the Massachusetts-based Phoenix Tailings is bringing a major piece of its planned $1.2 billion-plus domestic rare earth manufacturing platform to Eastman Business Park, where it plans to build a commercial-scale separation facility.

“I am proud that Phoenix will build the future of American rare earth processing here,” Myers said.

The selection also represents something of a homecoming for Myers, who was raised in Connecticut but spent much of his youth in Rochester. He earned an MBA in marketing from Rochester Institute of Technology in 2015 and played baseball for the Geneva Red Wings, a collegiate baseball team. He later earned an MBA in finance from Northeastern University in 2017 and launched Phoenix Tailings shortly afterward.

His Rochester connections extend beyond his grandfather. Myers has other family in the area, including a cousin who is part of the management team at Rochester 100, which manufactures custom vinyl plastic holders, sleeves and other office and school products.

But family ties weren’t the only factor behind the site selection.

Phoenix Tailings chose Eastman Business Park following a nationwide search, citing its existing industrial buildings, utilities and chemical-processing infrastructure. The company also sees Rochester’s engineering, advanced manufacturing, chemical processing and plant operations workforce as an important advantage.

The planned 500,000-square-foot Freedom Separation facility will process mined and recycled rare earth materials into separated oxides used in domestic rare earth metal production.

At full capacity, the facility is expected to process more than 18,000 tons of mixed rare earth feedstock annually and produce more than 4,400 tons of separated rare earth oxides. Phoenix Tailings said the operation could rank among the world’s largest rare earth separation facilities.

Production is expected to begin ramping up in 2027, with full production targeted for 2028.

Myers said the company is working with Monroe Community College, RIT and the University of Rochester on workforce development efforts. Hiring is expected to begin early next year.

The Rochester operation is projected to support more than 200 direct jobs in New York when fully operational, including about 90 positions at launch.

Across its integrated separation and metallization operations, Phoenix Tailings expects to support more than 500 jobs at facilities in New York, Massachusetts and New Hampshire, as well as a future location.

The company anticipates investing more than $1.2 billion across its U.S. operations.

Building domestic capacity

Phoenix Tailings’ Rochester investment comes as the United States looks to reduce its dependence on China for rare earth processing.

Rare earth materials are essential to manufacturing products and equipment used in defense, health care, electronics, communications and electric vehicles. They are used to produce powerful magnets that help make equipment and technology smaller, faster, stronger and more energy efficient.

Although the materials are critical to a broad range of industries, most rare earth separation currently takes place in China, creating supply-chain vulnerabilities for U.S. manufacturers and defense suppliers, Myers explained.

“America cannot exist if we are waiting for permission from Beijing,” he said.

Phoenix Tailings has developed processes to recover rare earth metals from mining waste and other industrial sources. The company holds more than 100 patents and combines chemistry, industrial equipment and digital infrastructure to expand domestic separation, refining and metal production capabilities.

The company’s name reflects its approach. Tailings is the mining industry’s term for waste material left behind after valuable minerals are extracted. The phoenix, meanwhile, is a mythical bird associated with rebirth.

“Phoenix Tailings represents life being born from the ashes of the waste,” Myers said.

The Rochester facility is part of the company’s broader Freedom Project, an integrated separation-and-metallization platform intended to address a critical gap in U.S. rare earth processing capacity.

The project has attracted both private investment and federal support. Phoenix Tailings has secured a conditional $500 million long-term loan commitment from the U.S. Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital. Announced in June, the financing is intended to support construction of its rare earth separation system and remains subject to review before finalization.

The company also received a $66 million U.S. Department of Energy grant as part of a $147.8 million initiative to demonstrate domestic production of heavy rare earth metals from waste materials.

The Rochester project is on track to receive an estimated $54.2 million in state, local and infrastructure incentives.

The package includes up to $3 million in performance-based tax credits through Empire State Development’s Excelsior Jobs Program, approximately $15.9 million in separate state investment tax credits and another $35.3 million in projected tax savings and anticipated infrastructure funding.

The incentives include tax savings on eligible equipment and construction materials, as well as anticipated funding for power infrastructure improvements. Monroe County programs are also expected to support equipment purchases and workforce training. The benefits remain subject to applicable eligibility requirements, approvals and final award terms.

Gov. Kathy Hochul and U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer have backed the project, which Phoenix Tailings describes as part of a bipartisan effort to strengthen domestic rare earth processing.

The decision to locate the operation in Rochester combines a significant business opportunity with longstanding personal connections to the region, Myers said.

While his grandfather’s advice helped point the company toward Rochester, the region’s industrial assets, workforce and manufacturing heritage ultimately helped make the case.

text:
WASHINGTON, DC — As Congress returns from recess today, 85 organizations signed a letter to Senate negotiators expressing appreciation for their leadership in advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and urging Congress to pass the legislation this year.

The letter, organized by C2ES Action, Ceres, and Third Way, highlights the need for bipartisan action to modernize permitting and reviews and make it easier and faster to build in America at a time of rising electricity demand, increasing pressure on the electric grid, and intensifying global competition for investment.

The signatories span a wide range of sectors and perspectives, including manufacturers, utilities, clean energy companies, start-ups, labor organizations, advocates, technology firms, and policy organizations. Signatories include Alliance for Automotive Innovation, Amrize, Climeworks, Cummins Inc., dsm-firmenich noth America, eBay, Form Energy, GE Vernova, HASI, Heirloom, Hitachi Energy, National Association of Manufacturers, Nucor, Schneider Electric, Siemens USA, Sunrun, Volvo Group North America, Citizens for Responsible Energy Solutions, American Conservation Coalition Action, United Association of Union Plumbers and Pipefitters (UA), and dozens of others.

In the letter, the organizations write:

"We encourage passage of this bipartisan legislation that represents a crucial step toward improving permitting and review processes and modernizing the infrastructure that supports American economic development, energy affordability, emissions reductions, and competitiveness."

The full letter and list of signatories can be found here.

The letter commends the authors of the legislation, Chair Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Ranking Member Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Chair Mike Lee (R-UT), and Ranking Member Martin Heinrich (D-NM), for developing a comprehensive bipartisan approach to addressing permitting and infrastructure challenges while supporting economic growth, reliability, emissions reductions, and energy affordability.

"When critical energy and infrastructure projects get stuck in lengthy permitting processes, Americans pay the price through higher energy costs and missed economic opportunities,” said C2ES Action President Nat Keohane. “This bipartisan legislation recognizes that affordability and competitiveness depend on our ability to build. Congress should move quickly to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act."

“Congress has a clear mandate to bring down energy costs, and the Senate’s bipartisan permitting deal is a concrete way to deliver by accelerating the deployment of affordable clean energy. Passing this bill now would allow lawmakers to focus on implementation next year, bringing immediate affordability benefits and setting the stage for faster clean energy adoption,” said Zach Friedman, senior director, federal policy at Ceres. “Robust support from clean energy advocates, businesses, and labor speaks volumes about the affordability and jobs benefits the bill will bring across the country. It’s time for Congress to get it done.”

“The status quo - an aging grid, sluggish project approvals, growing electricity demand, and skyrocketing prices - is not acceptable and ultimately endangers our economic prosperity” said Third Way Energy Senior Vice President Josh Freed. “This legislation is the product of a huge coalition of negotiators and stakeholders, would be a monumental step towards fixing federal permitting, making energy more affordable, and building a modern and clean American energy system.”

The letter notes that delays and uncertainty in existing permitting and review processes can increase costs, slow infrastructure development, and hinder investment in projects critical to meeting the nation's growing energy needs. The organizations argue that reforms included in the legislation would help accelerate project development while supporting a more reliable, affordable, and modern energy system.

Last week, the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions and Greenline Insights released new analysis highlighting the costs of delayed reform and the expected benefits of the bill’s transmission and interconnection reforms. Compared to a “business as usual” scenario, by 2035 the modeled reforms would enable 170 GW of additional wind, solar, and battery storage capacity, including 83 GW of solar, 67 GW of wind, and 20 GW of battery storage, and expand interregional transmission capacity by 61 GW.

Because new interconnection processes and transmission projects take years to deliver, a delay until 2030 would mean achieving only about 40 percent of the modeled benefits by 2035, while reducing reliability, limiting the expansion of clean technology, and increasing reliance on new, inefficient natural gas “peaking” units. Through 2040, this delay would forgo roughly $55 billion in electricity system savings and 800 million metric tons of emissions reductions.

text:
Transaction monetizes select assets at an attractive valuation, supporting additional share repurchases, debt reduction, and flexibility to redeploy capital at higher returns.

HOUSTON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 9, 2026-- NRG Energy, Inc. (NYSE: NRG) today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to sell six natural gas generation assets to LS Power, for a purchase price of $4 billion in cash, subject to working capital and other closing adjustments. The purchase price represents an implied 2027 valuation multiple of 8.0x EV/Adj. EBITDA.

"We are unlocking substantial value from a select group of assets, while maintaining a robust generation footprint in PJM and ERCOT that provides reliable, affordable power for our customers," said Robert Gaudette, President and Chief Executive Officer of NRG. "This transaction will strengthen our balance sheet, support increased share repurchases and preserve flexibility to invest in growth opportunities with compelling returns. It demonstrates our commitment to disciplined capital allocation and creates long-term value for shareholders."

The sale is targeted to close in the second quarter of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals, including Hart-Scott-Rodino (HSR), Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), and the New York State Public Service Commission (NYSPSC).

The six assets represent 4.9 GW of generation across NYISO (Ravenswood), ISO-NE (Ocean State Power and Wallingford), and ERCOT (Jack County, Johnson County, and R.W. Miller).

NRG remains dedicated to ensuring affordable, reliable power as demand continues to grow. Upon completion, NRG will own and operate 20 GW of generation capacity nationwide. This includes 10 GW of generation in ERCOT, complemented by 10 GW in PJM. By 2028, an additional 1.1 GW is expected to be operational in ERCOT through the Company’s remaining two Texas Energy Fund projects.

Proceeds from the transaction will be used to support NRG's 2027 pro forma capital allocation plan of $3 billion of share repurchases across 2026 and 2027, including an incremental $1 billion expected to begin before the end of the fourth quarter of 2026. Upon closing of the asset sale, NRG plans an additional $2 billion of debt reduction to maintain the Company’s current leverage profile, bringing total planned 2027 debt reduction to $3 billion. The remaining proceeds will be reserved to fund either contracted growth investments or additional debt reduction.

Barclays is serving as lead financial advisor on the transaction and White & Case LLP is serving as legal counsel to NRG.

Conference Call and Webcast

NRG will discuss the transaction during its previously announced earnings conference call on November 9 at 8:00 AM EST / 7:00 AM CST.

Investors, members of the media and the public may access the webcast and presentation materials through NRG's Investor Relations website at www.nrg.com.

The company operates a customer-first platform supported by a diversified supply strategy and the safe, reliable operation of approximately 25 GW of power generation. David Booth

David Booth is Driving’s senior writer as well as the producer of Driving.ca’s Driving into the Future panels and Motor Mouth podcasts. Having written about everything from the exact benefits of Diamond Like Coating (DLC) on motorcycle camshafts to why Range Rovers are the best vehicles for those suffering from opioid-induced constipation, Booth leaves no stone unturned in his quest for automotive veritas. Besides his long tenure with Driving, he was the editor in chief of Autovision magazine for 25 years and his stories have been published in motorcycle magazines around the world including the United States, England, Germany and Australia.

Education

Graduating from Queen Elizabeth High School in 1973, Booth moved from his Northern Quebec hometown of Sept-Iles — also home to Montreal Canadiens great, Guy Carbonneau — to Ottawa to study Mechanical Engineering at Carleton University. There, he wrote a thesis on the then-burgeoning technology of anti-lock brakes for motorcycles and spent time researching the also then-burgeoning use of water tunnels for aerodynamic testing.

Experience

After three years writing for Cycle Canada magazine and another three working for the then oldest magazine in Canada, Canadian Automotive Trade, Booth, along with current Driving writer Brian Harper and then Toronto Star contributor Alex Law, created an automotive editorial services group that supplied road tests, news, and service bulletins to what was then called Southam newspapers.

When Southam became Postmedia with its purchase by Conrad Black and the subsequent introduction of the National Post, Booth was asked to start up the then Driver’s Edge section, which became Driving.ca when Postmedia moved into the digital age. In the past 41 years, Booth has tested well over 500 motorcycles, 1,500 passenger cars, and nearly every significant supercar of the last 30 years. His passion — and proudest achievement — is Motor Mouth, his weekly column that, after some 30 years, remains as incisive and opinionated as ever.

Personal

Booth remains an avid sports enthusiast — read: fitness freak — whose favorite activities include punching boxing bags until his hands bleed and running ski hills with as little respect for the medial meniscus as 65-year-old knees can bear. His true passion, however, remains motorcycles. If he’s not in his garage tinkering with his prized 1983 CB1100RC — or resurrecting another one — he’s riding Italy’s famed Stelvio Pass with his beloved — and much-modified — Suzuki V-Strom 1000.

November 9, 2026

National Taxpayers Union urges all senators to vote “YES” on the Manager’s Amendment to H.R. 2347, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) sponsored by Sens. Capito (R-WV), Lee (R-UT), Whitehouse (D-RI), and Heinrich (D-NM). This legislation would be a meaningful step toward restoring common sense to the federal permitting process, unleashing private investment, creating jobs, and making it easier and more affordable to build the infrastructure America needs.

The need for permitting reform is serious. An increasingly complex web of government red tape suffocates investment and makes it unnecessarily difficult, costly, and time-consuming to build in America. From oil refineries and wind farms to interstate highways and advanced manufacturing facilities, projects that could strengthen our economy, create good-paying jobs, and improve Americans’ quality of life are routinely subjected to years of regulatory delays.

In some cases, securing an energy permit can take more than four and a half years, while approval for a new transmission line can take as long as eight years. These prolonged delays drive up project costs, discourage investment, and ultimately leave consumers and utility ratepayers footing the bill through higher energy prices.

Thankfully, BAAJA fixes these government-caused problems. It includes important provisions to protect approved energy projects from being arbitrarily canceled by future administrations, providing the regulatory certainty businesses need to make billions of dollars in long-term investments across both clean and fossil fuel energy. It also curbs frivolous litigation that has allowed anti-energy activists to tie up major infrastructure projects for years, creating costly uncertainty for developers. It also rightly modernizes the Endangered Species Act and Clean Water Act to ensure projects proceed safely, responsibly, and efficiently.

Permitting reform won’t lead to lower energy prices today, but it will help us meet future energy needs. It means extracting underground oil faster, building more efficient refineries to turn oil into gasoline, and utilizing abundant solar and wind energy to power our homes and businesses. While this bill is imperfect, particularly some of the language pertaining to transmission lining and new mandates on data centers, enacting this legislation would still rank among the most consequential pro-growth achievements of Congress in a generation and should not be delayed.

Roll call votes on the Manager’s Amendment to H.R. 2347 will be included in NTU’s annual rating of Congress and “YES” votes will be considered the pro-taxpayer position.

text:
Congress is back in Washington this week facing a lengthy list of priorities before the end of the year, but toward the top of the agenda should be swiftly passing bipartisan permitting reform. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) represents one of the most consequential pieces of legislation Congress could send to the president’s desk this session. Passing BAAJA would be a meaningful step toward restoring common sense to the federal permitting process, unleashing private investment, creating jobs, and making it easier and more affordable to build the infrastructure America needs.

The need for permitting reform is serious. An increasingly complex web of government red tape suffocates investment and makes it unnecessarily difficult, costly, and time-consuming to build in America. From oil refineries and wind farms to interstate highways and advanced manufacturing facilities, projects that could strengthen our economy, create good-paying jobs, and improve Americans’ quality of life are routinely subjected to years of regulatory delays.

In some cases, securing an energy permit can take more than four and a half years, while approval for a new transmission line can take as long as eight years. These prolonged delays drive up project costs, discourage investment, and ultimately leave consumers and utility ratepayers footing the bill through higher energy prices.

Fortunately, Senate Republicans and Democrats have come together around a bipartisan opportunity to fix this broken system and unleash American economic growth. BAAJA represents a rare, potentially once-in-a-generation opportunity to rein in federal bureaucracy, remove unnecessary barriers to investment, and get the government out of the way of responsible development. The legislation deserves swift consideration and passage so it can reach the president’s desk without delay.

BAAJA includes many important provisions that NTU has advocated for over the years. Specifically, it ensures future administrations cannot simply cancel projects that are approved. That means pipeline companies can build energy infrastructure without fear that a Democratic president will kill their project. Likewise for clean energy projects like wind and solar that could face threats from a Republican president. No one wins from tit-for-tat energy policy. Projects of this scale are capital-intensive, requiring billions of dollars in upfront costs and often take years—or even decades—to recover.

The bill also finally ends “lawfare,” a tactic employed by anti-energy radicals to gum up the permitting process. Currently, lawsuits challenging National Environmental Policy Act reviews can be filed up to six years after a permit approval. This leaves agencies and developers uncertain long after the review has been completed and a permit issued. Consider the Dakota Access Pipeline, which, until recently, was stuck in limbo for almost a decade due to unserious legal challenges. It’s a similar story for SunZia, the largest renewable project in the country.

BAAJA establishes a 150-day statute of limitations for challenging federal agency approvals of energy and mineral projects. That means companies spend less time tied up in courtrooms and more time building the infrastructure America needs.

Additionally, BAAJA includes:

Reforming the Clean Water Act (CWA): Promoting regulatory certainty by refocusing Section 401 certifications on water quality and ending preemptive and retroactive vetoes under the EPA Administrator’s Section 404(c) authority.

Modernizing the Endangered Species Act (ESA): Providing states with greater flexibility to conduct Section 7 consultations and ensuring ESA determinations are grounded in the best available science.

Advancing complementary permitting reforms: Reforming transmission policy to ensure the electric grid can meet growing demand, streamlining the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), unlocking America’s geothermal energy potential, and providing greater certainty in the mining permitting process.

There is growing Beltway speculation that last week’s election results could derail this hard-fought agreement. Even Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next Speaker of the House, has suggested the deal falls short of what his conference wants and that Democrats will seek a “better” agreement in the next Congress.

Let’s hope that doesn’t happen. This agreement represents the best possible outcome for taxpayers, the clean and fossil fuel energy industries, and the countless businesses forced to navigate an increasingly complex federal regulatory system. Delaying action now would risk squandering a rare bipartisan opportunity and could seriously jeopardize the prospects of reaching another agreement anytime soon.

Permitting reform won’t lead to lower energy prices today, but it will help us meet future energy needs. It means extracting underground oil faster, building more efficient refineries to turn oil into gasoline, and utilizing abundant solar and wind energy to power our homes and businesses. The sooner this bill can get to the president’s desk, the sooner energy developers can build again and Americans can enjoy the abundant, cheap energy they deserve.

text:
A Clean Energy Future Built with Rural Communities

BOLD Energy Builders works with rural communities to ensure that the people who live on the land help shape—and share in the benefits of—America’s clean energy future. Through local organizing, education, legal support, and alliances that cross political and cultural divides, BOLD helps residents protect their land and property rights while pursuing energy investments that strengthen their communities.

More About BOLD Energy Builders

Rural America has much of the land needed to expand wind and solar power. Too often, however, outside developers enter communities without first building trust, listening to local concerns, or ensuring that the economic benefits will be widely shared. BOLD advances a different model: treating communities as essential partners in the clean energy transition.

BOLD brings together farmers, ranchers, tribal nations, union workers, climate advocates, and other local leaders around shared priorities—including protecting land and water, strengthening public services, creating good jobs, and keeping rural communities vibrant. Through door-to-door conversations and locally tailored information, its organizers also help residents separate legitimate concerns about energy development from misinformation designed to divide communities.

A central part of BOLD’s approach is helping residents negotiate a legally binding Community Benefit Agreement or CBA. These agreements allow communities to determine how energy projects should be developed and what benefits developers must provide in return. In the New Rockford area of North Dakota, residents secured an agreement connected to a wind project that included new community investments and $350,000 to renovate a historic theater—a gathering place that residents hope will help revitalize their town.

By putting rural residents at the negotiating table, BOLD is demonstrating that communities do not have to choose between clean energy and local control. Its work offers a path toward energy development that respects rural culture, protects property rights, builds community wealth, and gives more people a stake in the transition.

Congress will also need to find a path forward on the National Defense Authorization Act, long considered a must-pass annual military funding package. This year, the bill is quagmired in the unforgiving politics of the Iran war. The conflict is opposed by a majority of Americans — something President Trump has acknowledged was a key force in driving his party out of power.

The House is also likely to vote on an impeachment effort targeting Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Introduced by Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a key figure in forcing the administration's release of the Epstein files, the impeachment measure lists a number of charges, including that the administration failed to properly consult Congress on the military campaign.

Democrats are unlikely to be in a compromising mood on legislation, just weeks away from taking control of both chambers. That means continued work on big-ticket items like the Protect College Sports Act, meant to introduce new regulations around college athlete compensation, and a bipartisan energy permitting overhaul will likely wait until the new term.

With slim majorities in both chambers, they could also have to contend with some attendance problems after a demoralizing performance in last week's midterm elections. That further complicates passing legislation through chambers already governed by the thinnest of majorities.

Mike Ricci, a Republican strategist with the group Seven Letter and aide to former Speakers of the House John Boehner and Paul Ryan, told NPR that a number of forces could help draw reluctant lame duck legislators back to Washington, including winding down their offices, finding new work and attending the White House Christmas party.
