text:
EL CENTRO — Comite Civico del Valle brought the Imperial Valley together on Nov. 4-5 for the 15th annual Environmental Health Leadership Summit at the Old Eucalyptus Schoolhouse in El Centro. Community members, farmworkers, Tribal leaders, scientists, binational partners, local and state officials spent two days on the region’s most pressing health and environmental challenges, and on how to solve them together.

CCV has built the Environmental Health Leadership Summits into a forum where those most affected by pollution sit at the same table as the people who make policy and do the science. This year’s program brought farmworkers and Tribal elders together with state agency leaders, university researchers from San Diego State University, University of California Davis, the Universidad Autónoma de Baja California, California State Polytechnic University (Pomona), UCLA Department of Public Policy and binational partners from Mexicali and Baja California. Community health workers, air monitoring technicians and project leads facilitated and presented workshops throughout both days, sharing the work they do year-round, from community air monitoring to EV infrastructure to farmworker outreach.

Over two days, the summit covered the issues that shape daily life and health in the Imperial Valley:

• The state of environmental health. An opening plenary brought together the California Natural Resources Agency, Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA), the California Department of Public Health and Tracking California to review progress and remaining gaps.

• Lithium Valley and Tribal heritage. CCV and Quechan Tribal leaders, including Elder Preston Arrow-weed and Councilman Farron Owl, discussed lithium, geothermal and solar development alongside water, air quality, sacred sites and the community’s voice in decisions.

• Extreme heat. Researchers, Tracking California and an agricultural worker shared strategies on cooling centers, affordable energy and protections for workers and students.

• Clean air and asthma. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) presented statewide asthma efforts, and OEHHA introduced the new CalEnviroScreen 5.0.

• Community science. CCV air monitoring technicians and researchers from San Diego State University and Tracking California showed how local data on air, toxic metals and the Salton Sea becomes action.

• Clean transportation across the border. A binational plenary with Centro de Energía Renovable y Calidad Ambiental (CERCA), Baja California’s State Energy Commission, California Air Resources Board (CARB), IID and the California Energy Commission explored an EV charging network linking the three Californias.

• Workers’ rights and safety. Plenaries and workshops with the Department of Industrial Relations, California Rural Legal Assistance, UC Davis, the Department of Pesticide Regulation and the Agricultural Labor Relations Board covered heat illness prevention, pesticide safety and protections against retaliation.

• State resources and community benefits. CalEPA, the Strategic Growth Council and DTSC outlined funding and programs, and a closing interactive session with Jobs To Move America and the Climate and Community Institute taught participants how to turn development promises into enforceable Community Benefits Agreements.

Farmworkers Take the Stage

One of the summit’s most powerful moments came when agricultural workers spoke for themselves. The panelists described how dangerous heat, earnings gaps, chemical exposure and limited support systems affect their work and their families. Attendees answered their testimony with sustained applause and words of encouragement, a clear sign of the respect the community holds for the workers who form the foundation of the Imperial Valley economy.

Keynote Leaders

Former Assemblymember Eduardo Garcia delivered the Day 1 keynote, “Imperial Valley: Building on Progress and Shaping the Future.” A longtime champion for the region in Sacramento, Garcia reflected on 15 years of progress that brought greater attention and resources to the Salton Sea, the New River, air quality and climate change. He credited community members and local organizations for driving that progress and outlined what it will take to build a healthier, stronger and more prosperous Imperial Valley for families, workers and future generations.

California Energy Commissioner Noemí Gallardo delivered the Day 2 keynote, “Building California’s Clean Energy Future in the Imperial Valley.” Commissioner Gallardo shared the state’s vision for Lithium Valley and the jobs, businesses and investment that clean energy can bring. She stressed that this growth must protect public health, water and the environment, and that state and local leaders, businesses and residents must guide development together so Imperial Valley families share in the benefits.

California Secretary for Environmental Protection (CalEPA) Yana Garcia delivered a Day 2 keynote, “Building Healthier Communities and a Cleaner Future.” Secretary Garcia spoke on clean air, safe water and building healthier communities, reminding attendees that a healthy environment matters to every Imperial Valley family. She acknowledged that many communities still face air pollution, extreme heat and other environmental concerns. Drawing on her experience leading California’s environmental protection efforts, Secretary Garcia reflected on the progress made and the challenges that remain. She emphasized that protecting public health requires community members, local organizations and government leaders to work together, and she discussed how those partnerships can improve environmental conditions and build a healthier future for Imperial Valley families and generations to come.

California State Senator Steve Padilla, Senate District 18. On behalf of Senator Padilla, Guillermo Hernandez Jr., Deputy District Director for Senator Steve Padilla, delivered a message congratulating CCV on their years of community work and tied the Senator’s legislative work to the summit’s conversations. Responding to the farmworker panel, he highlighted SB 1105, signed in 2024, which lets agricultural workers use paid sick leave during environmental emergencies such as extreme heat, smoke and flooding, and invited workers to contact the office if it is not being honored.

authors: Gary Crusader Editorial Board, Crusader Staff, Toya Smith, Bonnie DeShong
description:

The election results discussed here reflect information available as of the Crusader’s Wednesday, November 4, 2026, press deadline.
The lesson from Indiana and the nation is clear: elections can change leadership, but public confidence must be earned continuously.
text:
The November 3 midterm elections changed the balance of political power in America and delivered a message that cannot be ignored. Democrats won control of both the United States House of Representatives and Senate, creating new checks on President Donald Trump’s administration during the final two years of his term. The outcome extends beyond party labels. Americans used the ballot box to register concerns about the economy, the direction of federal policy and the accountability of those holding public office. Not every voter shared the same grievance or endorsed the same solution. Nevertheless, the results demonstrate that political power is never permanently owned by any party, president or political establishment.

Indiana provided some of the election’s most revealing developments. In a state where Republicans have dominated statewide government for years, Democrat Beau Bayh won the secretary of state race against Republican Max Engling. His victory marked the first Democratic win for statewide office in Indiana since 2012. It also brought renewed attention to election administration, government transparency and the responsibilities of the office Bayh will assume. His family name is familiar in Indiana politics, but his performance must ultimately be judged by his own decisions, his stewardship of public resources and his ability to serve Hoosiers regardless of party affiliation.

Democrats also made significant gains in the Indiana General Assembly, breaking the Republican supermajority in the state House while increasing their representation in the Senate. Republicans still control both chambers. Nevertheless, the changed House balance means the minority party will have greater influence over legislative debates and the decisions that shape public education, health care, taxation and local government. These developments should encourage more serious discussion of policies affecting working families rather than another round of partisan celebration. Indiana residents deserve lawmakers who can disagree without abandoning the work they were elected to perform.

The congressional results were equally consequential. Democratic state Sen. J.D. Ford defeated Republican incumbent Victoria Spartz in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, winning a seat that Republicans had held for decades. In Northwest Indiana, U.S. Rep. Frank J. Mrvan won reelection in the 1st Congressional District, continuing to represent Gary and surrounding communities. U.S. Rep. André Carson also retained his Indianapolis-area seat. Mrvan’s return to Washington is especially important for residents concerned about industrial development, infrastructure, labor protections, environmental conditions and the economic future of the region. His reelection carries an expectation that those concerns will remain visible in the new Congress.

Lake County produced its own historic result with the election of Democrat Jerry Williams as the county’s first Black sheriff. That milestone deserves recognition, but the real measure of his administration will be professional law enforcement, public trust and fair treatment throughout the county. Other Democratic winners included County Council members Darren Washington and Dwight Williams, county commissioner Kyle W. Allen Sr., Treasurer John E. Petalas, Clerk Mike Brown and Auditor Gina Pimentel. Scott Houldieson won the 1st District state Senate race. Together, these outcomes underscored the continued importance of Northwest Indiana in the state’s political life and the responsibility local officeholders carry after election night.

The Gary Crusader believes these victories should sharpen attention to the problems residents face every day. Gary and neighboring communities need investment that produces lasting jobs, stronger schools, safer neighborhoods, dependable infrastructure and housing that working people can afford. Too many residents have heard ambitious promises without seeing sufficient improvement. Historic representation has meaning when it helps deliver opportunity, protects public resources and makes government answerable to the people it serves.

The election results discussed here reflect information available as of the Crusader’s Wednesday, November 4, 2026, press deadline. Some races remained unresolved, and results were subject to final certification. Nationally, Democratic control of Congress will not erase the divisions that shaped this election. Many Republicans still support the president, and their voices remain part of the American electorate. Democrats, meanwhile, must show that oversight and opposition can coexist with responsible governing. The lesson from Indiana and the nation is clear: elections can change leadership, but public confidence must be earned continuously. The voters have made history. Now those entrusted with power must turn that history into public service.

text:
McGuireWoods served as legal adviser to NiSource, one of the nation’s largest fully regulated utilities, and its subsidiaries in connection with a new long-term energy agreement with Microsoft for the tech company’s northwest Indiana data center campus.

Through NiSource Generation Company (GenCo), NiSource is serving new large-load customers under a structure designed to protect existing Northern Indiana Public Service Company (NIPSCO) electric customers from incremental costs and to return value from large-load customers’ use of the existing electric system. McGuireWoods lawyers previously advised NiSource on the development of this innovative model, under which large-load customers fully fund the generation and infrastructure required to serve their needs.

Under the agreement, Microsoft is expected to begin taking electric service under a 20-year term starting in 2028. GenCo will increase its pool portfolio by approximately 1,100 megawatts, and NIPSCO and GenCo will provide the transmission and generation infrastructure needed to serve Microsoft’s data center and NIPSCO’s customers. Microsoft will fully fund all generation and transmission required to serve its load. In connection with the agreement, GenCo has also contracted 600 megawatts of battery storage under a long-term tolling agreement, with the facility to be developed and constructed by an affiliate of AGP Group.

The Microsoft agreement follows McGuireWoods’ work for NiSource in developing GenCo’s model for meeting the data center industry’s energy needs. In 2025, the firm advised NIPSCO and GenCo in structuring an electric service agreement with Amazon to supply up to 3 gigawatts of capacity for Amazon data center sites in NIPSCO’s Northern Indiana service territory.

The McGuireWoods team advising NiSource included Brian Kelly, Jake Spilman, Najwan Nayef, Sam Kettering, Jacob Lubinski, Chris Alderman, Matthew Stuart and Mark Staines. Joanne Katsantonis and Emilie McNally provided overall corporate, board and governance advice.

“This agreement marks another milestone for NiSource’s GenCo model. We are proud to have helped turn an innovative concept into a proven platform for serving the nation’s largest energy users,” said Katsantonis, who co-leads McGuireWoods’ Energy M&A and Finance Practice Group. “Our team has advised on these complex, large-load transactions from the ground up, anticipating and addressing challenges that come with powering data center growth at this scale.”

title: Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund lives again with $550 million in clean energy investments ...
description:
The investments were underwritten by StepStone Group on behalf of the Coalition for Green Capital.
It invested another $275 million across four emerging managers working in clean energy, via a fund of funds strategy anchored by Coalition for Green Capital.
In addition to StepStone, CGC’s strategic partners include Apollo Global Management, Brookfield Asset Management, and Energy Capital Partners.
Energy Capital Partners’ fund makes equity investments in distributed generation projects and other carbon reduction infrastructure.
Brookfield is focusing on private credit for infrastructure projects such as renewable power generation and storage.
text:
The once and future federal fund for green community infrastructure is back.

In a taste of what the Biden-era Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund might yet look like, three sustainable infrastructure providers and four emerging managers have received a combined $550 million in investments from funds that “escaped” the Trump administration’s efforts to claw them back. The investments were underwritten by StepStone Group on behalf of the Coalition for Green Capital.

The administration’s Environmental Protection Agency last March tried to freeze $20 billion in awards under the GGRF, a centerpiece of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. The awards, intended to catalyze decarbonization projects and stand up a network of green lenders that can reach deep into overlooked communities, had been duly approved and distributed to accounts at Citibank. The long litigation to free the funds looks likely to go to the Supreme Court, after the EPA last week challenged an appeals court ruling to unfreeze the funds.

The high court is not expected to make a decision on whether it will take up the case until early next year. If it does not, the funds will be released. If the court accepts the case, it may not be decided until late 2027.

But by moving quickly before the freeze took effect last year, the Coalition for Green Capital, one of the awardees that now goes by CGC, managed to get nearly $2.7 billion out the door and into accounts at four of the coalition’s strategic partners, including some of the largest US private investment firms, as ImpactAlpha first reported last year. The coalition, primarily comprised of state- and local-level green banks, had been awarded a total of $5 billion, the second-largest grant under the GGRF’s National Clean Investment Fund, or NCIF.

Last month, the appeals court confirmed that the already-distributed funds were not subject to the Trump administration’s efforts to claw back the money and shut down the GGRF. The Justice Department had sent CGC a letter earlier this fall saying the $2.7 billion in distributed funds were also subject to the freeze.

Now, the first investments from those “escaped” funds have been made by StepStone Group.

“The idea of having some financial partners was always part of our thinking,” CGC’s Richard Kauffman told ImpactAlpha last year. “$5 billion is a lot of money. It’s not that much money against the scale of the problem we’re trying to tackle. So everything we’re trying to do is transformational.”

New York-based StepStone, which manages some $261 billion in assets, has made three direct investments in clean energy infrastructure providers totalling $275.5 million. It invested another $275 million across four emerging managers working in clean energy, via a fund of funds strategy anchored by Coalition for Green Capital.

The investments, disclosed by CGC in its latest semi-annual report, mark a liberation of sorts for the GGRF program, which has been tied up in a protracted legal battle with the Trump administration since February 2025.

“CGC worked with its partners to close 85 transactions during the first half of 2026, leveraging approximately $560 million NCIF funds to mobilize roughly $5.6 billion in total capital,” the report confirms.

In addition to StepStone, CGC’s strategic partners include Apollo Global Management, Brookfield Asset Management, and Energy Capital Partners. The firms, which together manage more than $2.5 trillion, have kept a low-profile amid the Trump administration’s crackdown and have hesitated to invest the funds, or at least publicize any deals.

Apollo, which got $500 million from CGC, is waiting for things to “resolve,” the firm’s Jonathan Silver said on the sidelines of a Climate Week event in October. But with some $1 trillion in assets under management, that is hardly crimping the firm’s investment, he said.

Go big

The Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund represented the largest direct outlay of the Inflation Reduction Act, the sweeping climate law passed by the Biden administration in 2022. Some $20 billion went to two sub-programs meant to stand up a distributed network of green lenders and to boost the capacity of community development financial institutions and other local lenders to be able to take on the task.

Another $7 billion, for the Solar for All program, was aimed at facilitating solar installations that could lower bills and ease pollution in low-income communities. In September, two separate district court rulings found that the EPA’s cancellation of Solar for All violated procedures and legal requirements; funds have yet to be released.

The incoming Trump administration moved swiftly to freeze the funds, held in accounts set up for the grantees at Citibank. In addition to CGC, the grantees include Climate United, a coalition of nonprofits led by Calvert Impact, and Power Forward Communities. A federal appeals court in August ruled to unfreeze the funds, saying the EPA likely violated the law by attempting to claw back Congressionally mandated funds based on executive policy disagreements.

The grantees agreed to extend the funding freeze to avoid an EPA emergency appeal to the Supreme Court via its so-called “shadow docket,” which fast tracks cases without oral arguments and entails less transparency.

The $2.7 billion channeled by CGC to its four strategic partners represent the biggest operative elements of the ambitious GGRF. CGC initially sought $10 billion to set up a national green bank, but was awarded just half of that. CGC decided it had to go big and move fast to maximize the funds at its disposal.

“Our basic model,” CGC founder and former FCC chairman Reed Hundt told ImpactAlpha in 2024, “is, take our money, have a big multiple with other money and try to have significant impact.” At the time, Hundt declared, “There is no lawful way to get the money back, and any attempt to get the money back would be a violation of the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution as a takings.” Hundt stepped down in November that year and was replaced by Kauffman, an energy and policy veteran.

Apollo, Brookfield, ECP and StepStone were selected from more than three dozen firms that responded to a request for investment proposals issued by CGC in November 2024 and finalized in early 2025. Each partner created a dedicated fund to align with GGRF and CGC program goals to leverage the public funds and mobilize private capital for decarbonization projects. The partners each created their own investment structures and strategy and manage the funds, with CGC taking an active role in sourcing and vetting deals.

In setting up its StepStone CGC Opportunities I fund, the firm sought to invest in advanced clean power and expand access to capital for small and medium-sized fund sponsors as a way to mobilize capital for hard to finance activities such as project development financing.

Its investments include $117.5 million to Galway Sustainable Capital, a specialty financier for renewable energy, energy efficiency, multifamily housing, and other sustainable infrastructure sectors, as part of a $235 million senior secured term loan facility. Washington, DC-based Galways says it deployed $500 million in sustainable infrastructure and resource efficiency investments in 2025.

StepStone also committed $100 million to Eagle Point Credit Management, a Greenwich, Conn.-based investment firm that provides capital to renewable energy, industrial decarbonization and other sustainable infrastructure sectors. The investment is in a low-carbon collateralized loan obligation warehouse facility supporting Eagle Point, which CGC says is one of the first low-carbon infrastructure-focused CLO issuances of its kind.

A third Stepstone deal involved a $40 million investment in CenTrio Energy, a Chicago-based owner and operator of district energy systems, which provide centralized heating, cooling and power generation to nearby businesses, government buildings, and hospitals.The $40 million was part of a broader $485 million senior secured term loan for CenTrio.

All of the deals are expected to mobilize additional private capital, create jobs and cut emissions, in accordance with GGRF requirements.

Energy Capital Partners’ fund makes equity investments in distributed generation projects and other carbon reduction infrastructure. Brookfield is focusing on private credit for infrastructure projects such as renewable power generation and storage.

Apollo’s fund is looking to play a catalytic role in financing projects with hybrid equity and debt solutions.

CGC told ImpactAlpha last year that it had a pipeline of more than 20 transactions that add up to over $3 billion for distributed infrastructure, running the gamut from battery storage and community solar projects to building efficiency, geothermal and zero-emission transportation.

Fund of Funds

CGC also created a fund of funds strategy to help emerging managers developing sustainable projects in underserved areas and sectors attain scale and access to institutional capital. That, it says, addresses its mission “to transform markets by leveraging private sector capital.”

The StepStone fund of funds, anchored by CGC, had backed four emerging managers.

CGC did not disclose names, but the fund has backed four managers including $75 million each to an asset manager targeting large-scale, low-carbon projects across energy, water, and urban infrastructure; an asset manager pursuing mid-sized renewable energy, distributed generation, and dispatchable generation projects; and a manager specializing in energy transition opportunities, such as renewables and storage, renewable fuels, and transmission projects.

It also invested $50 million in a natural infrastructure manager that invests in American farmland transitioning from conventional to organic practices.

The StepStone deals represent the first of CGC’s strategic partnerships to bear fruit. In addition to the $2.7 billion distributed to those partners, CGC in January 2025 made a $200 million equity investment in GreenieRE, an impact-first, decarbonization-focused reinsurer that helps remove obstacles for green projects.

CGC also provided catalytic loans to emerging green banks and other organizations, building their capacity to finance transactions that support the objectives of the NCIF program. In the first half of 2026, these banks and subrecipients closed 21 transactions amounting to $12.4 million, according to the report.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate on Monday is set to take up bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as officials seek to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now faces yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats' sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the landmark National Environmental Policy Act. The 1970 law requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

"Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” next year.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.

Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, he said.

___

McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

text:
U.S. electricity customers averaged 11 hours of power interruptions in 2024, and major events accounted for 80% of that time, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. In recent years, Hurricane Helene left South Carolina residents without power for nearly 53 hours; in August of this year, Gary, Indiana, residents went nearly two weeks without power after severe storms knocked out service. For solar-plus-storage owners, those are someone else’s numbers. The one that counts gets measured at their address, on the day the utility drops.

A system can spend almost all its life running normally on the grid, but functionality when the grid goes down stays unproven until the day it’s needed. A battery capacity figure tells the owner nothing about how it will work off-grid, and neither does a “backup-ready” label.

The Load Promise: What the System Owes the Owner

Power and energy support different parts of backups. Power caps what can run and energy determines run length. A design that confuses the two can look adequate on paper yet fail the owner during an outage.

Good system design (Figure 1) should identify the circuits and equipment that matter. In homes, that means refrigeration, Wi-Fi, lighting, controls, pumps, and heating or cooling. Small commercial sites add point-of-sale equipment or process controls to the same core. Regional differences matter too; a design for a house in the Northeast with no air conditioner differs from one in Arizona, where cooling can be the biggest load. The power from starting current, stepped loads, and equipment controls can create demands an annual energy estimate never show.

The owner’s record should state the supported loads, expected duration, priority order, operator actions, reserve assumptions, and explain what happens as stored energy falls. Written down, it avoids misalignment from the designer, installer, and owner at handoff.

Follow the Complete Change of State

Grid loss changes the role of solar-plus-storage systems, making the building an islanded off-grid system throughout the outage. This takes six steps: detect the loss, safely separate from the utility supply, establish a local voltage and frequency reference, bring solar generation into the island, serve the prioritized loads, and keep protection and monitoring alive.

A battery inverter or another grid-forming source can establish local reference. Most conventional grid-tied photovoltaic (PV) systems without batteries are designed to stop supplying power when the grid is absent. Daylight changes nothing: the sun can blaze on the array all afternoon without pushing a watt into the building.

State of charge, load shedding, and monitoring are additional pieces of this sequence. An owner should know what load the system will shed first, what notification will appear, and whether any action is expected.

Sunrise is Not a Restart

One failure path belongs in every design review: what happens after the battery hits its lower operating limit. In some AC-coupled architectures, the battery inverter establishes the local grid reference that a separate PV inverter follows. If the battery system shuts down after a long outage, that reference can disappear. When sunlight returns, the PV inverter may have no local grid to follow, leaving the site unable to restart from solar alone.

While this issue has historically been common in AC-coupled systems, newer products include controls or reserve strategies intended to address it. The design review should establish whether the equipment on site behaves that way. It should also identify the reserve policy, recovery sequence after a low-state-of-charge shutdown, how non-essential loads are shed, the manufacturer’s documented restart behavior, and any operator action required.

Installed energy doesn’t mean indefinite operation. A backup design must always account for unpredictability in the days ahead.

Commission the Outage Sequence as a System

Everything to this point is intention. A deliberate outage test converts it into evidence. An outage test requires a planned, simulated grid loss performed by qualified personnel under a site-specific procedure. It must reflect the installed architecture, manufacturer instructions, and utility or authority requirements.

The process of an outage test is as follows:

1. An agreed load promise, representative operating conditions, and an allowed starting state of charge.

2. The team confirms supported loads and watches how the system transfers into its off-grid state.

3. The test covers controller status, alarms, load shedding, solar contribution, energy use, and any trip or notification. Voltage and frequency behavior get recorded as needed.

What does a pass look like? From an owner’s perspective, almost nothing if designed properly. Appliances keep running, and the clearest sign anything happened is a system notification.

Finally, the results should record the load promise, test conditions, measured results, settings, alarms, open items, and owner actions. Retest after work on anything that could affect the sequence including controls, firmware, major equipment, or protected loads.

A credible backup claim has two parts: a defined load-and-duration promise and demonstrated end-to-end behavior against it. Put the outage sequence into design review and prove it at acceptance. That test is the one outage anyone gets to schedule. Every outage after commissioning arrives on its own terms, at whatever hour it picks, and by then the results are already fixed.

text:
For the next two weeks, country leaders will be in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual United Nations climate conference, called COP31. This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will loom over the negotiations. Now in its ninth month, the war has sparked a global energy crisis. The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz and spiking oil and natural gas prices have laid bare the fragility of relying on fossil fuels.

But this energy crisis – unlike the energy crisis in the 1970s and the one following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – is different, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

"This is the first time you've really had a global energy shock where you've got really cheap solutions to address it," Bond says.

Those solutions include solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles. In recent months, countries around the world have pivoted sharply towards these technologies. Many of them are produced in China and offer economic security, as well as reduced emissions.

The economic case for climate solution technologies will make it easier for countries to support them at the conference, Bond says. "There's much more opportunity, I think, for people to get behind change at COP."

Here are three things you need to know about this year's COP.

It's all about electrification

Climate technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Bond says that's why some are calling this "the electrification COP."

"The big target that the COP is setting is for the world to increase the electrification rate from around 23% today to around 35% by 2035," Bond says. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra."

These electrification goals assume countries will grow their electricity mix with cleaner renewable energy. Energy experts say that is a reasonable assumption, because that's what has been happening in recent years. Large solar and wind projects provide more cost-competitive energy than natural gas and coal projects, according to financial services firm Lazard.

"Think about solar, wind," says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. "More green energy will help you decarbonize better and faster."

Roadmap off fossil fuels

As the COP process enters its 31st year, many countries have argued that the U.N. process has not done enough to tackle the single biggest driver of climate change: burning fossil fuels.

Fossil fuel producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have consistently opposed having fossil fuel language in the text of final conference agreements.

In April, more than 50 countries came together to discuss ways to phase out oil, gas, and coal at the First International Conference to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels. Conference organizers told NPR the conference was a way to complement the U.N. process.

More than 25 of those nations are developing a legally binding treaty that would advance a phase-out of fossil fuels. Supporters of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative hope more countries will join their cause at COP31.

The U.S. is not in the room

The U.S. State Department told NPR in an email that the U.S. will not be sending a delegation to COP31. They also did not send anyone to last year's COP in Brazil.

The Trump administration has reversed action on climate progress, phasing out subsidies for electric vehicles, solar and wind, reducing regulations for greenhouse gases, and halting renewable energy projects.

Last year, some countries told NPR they were happy that the Trump administration was not at the climate talks. "Generally, it's a good thing they're not here because we have less recalcitrants to deal with," Ralph Regenvanu, minister of climate change of Vanuatu, told NPR then.

But some democratic lawmakers will be at COP31, including Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat representing Rhode Island. Fresh off Democrats' midterm victory sweep, Whitehouse says he and the other lawmakers plan to keep the focus on fossil fuels and a potential carbon pricing mechanism.

text:
Nov. 9, 2026 (PORTLAND, ORE.) — Recognizing the need for local action, and the power of Portland's model, TIME has named Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits Fund (PCEF) leader Sam Baraso to its annual list of climate leaders.

The TIME100 Climate list highlights leaders from around the world who are driving business and policy climate action. Baraso is one of very few local leaders on the list, underscoring PCEF as a blueprint for major local impact and model for other cities. The full list is on TIME.

"I'm honored to be named to this list," Baraso said, "but I share that honor with the Portlanders who've believed in PCEF's potential. I want to especially thank our community leaders who imagined and brought PCEF to life — our community is growing more prosperous and reliant because of you."

Baraso is the program manager for the fund. He brings nearly two decades of experience spanning finance, environmental management, and policy, including serving as the Vice Chair of Oregon's Environmental Quality Commission. He holds a Masters in Environmental Management, Ecosystem Science & Conservation from Duke University, and finance and business degrees from Washington University in St. Louis. View Baraso's headshot.

Over the last six years, PCEF has benefited thousands of Portlanders by:

strengthening local businesses

boosting affordability

improving health

helping people stay housed

restoring and enriching public spaces

producing food

supporting youth

Under Baraso's direction, PCEF has become a significant force in our region's climate work. What began as a community-led ballot initiative is now a nationally recognized model for municipal climate resilience, clean energy deployment, and environmental justice.

"Under Sam's leadership, PCEF has broken ground, increased our community's resilience to climate change, and strengthened our local businesses and job market," said Mayor Keith Wilson. "Now, Portland's work is inspiring communities across the country to see how they too can replicate this program's success. The world knows PCEF, and I'm excited for the world to meet the man behind it."

Created by Portland voters in 2018, PCEF ensures Portland will be ready for and resilient to climate change. It is funded by a small surcharge on the total sales that billion-dollar retail companies earn in Portland. PCEF reinvests that money to reduce carbon, improve efficiency, and boost resilience. Examples include:

Nearly 25,000 portable air conditioning and heat pump units to keep people safe during extreme weather

Community solar projects that will save at least 3,000 low-income Portlanders saving an estimated $12 million over twenty years

Constructing energy efficiencies into over 5,200 multi-family affordable housing units, so low-income Portlanders will have lower or no energy bills

Replacing dozens of diesel commercial vehicles and hundreds of gas fleet cars with electric vehicles

Training, business support, or career coaching for roughly 2,000 people, returning millions of dollars to Portland's economy each year

Planting 3,233 new trees across neighborhoods with low tree density

In partnership with the Portland Bureau of Transportation (PBOT), supporting bike and public transportation by over 6,000 low-income Portlanders, and bike and walk safety education to approximately 13,000 students

Learn more about PCEF's funded projects and past applications

Learn more about PCEF's strategic program funding

About the City of Portland Bureau of Planning and Sustainability

The Portland Bureau of Planning and Sustainability (BPS) oversees a world-renowned waste and recycling system and leads the country in its commitment to digital equity, open data, and protecting communities in the application of technologies. Staff collaborate with partners on neighborhood, economic, historic, and environmental planning and provide research, policy, and technical services to advance energy efficiency and renewable energy, as well as policies and actions to address climate change. The bureau also oversees the innovative Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits Fund (PCEF).

text:
A group of advocacy organizations filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to undo a rule that fast-tracked approval for billions of dollars in electric infrastructure for Meta’s massive data center in north Louisiana, a move that could stymie Entergy’s plans for several new gas-fired power plants.

The suit, filed in Baton Rouge district court, comes amid a wave of anti-AI sentiment across the country. The filings accuse the Louisiana Public Service Commission — which regulates electric utilities — of violating the law when it passed a “lightning directive” in December 2025 to speed up electric infrastructure for large projects, including Meta’s data center. The plaintiffs are three groups who have opposed various aspects of Meta’s data center: Save Our Louisiana, Louisiana Citizens Advocacy Group and the Louisiana Landowners Coalition.

The lightning directive, passed at the behest of PSC member J.P. Coussan, R-Lafayette, allows utilities like Entergy to skip some rules when building infrastructure to power certain high-energy users, including Meta’s “Hyperion” data center.

The suit alleges that the PSC failed to properly notify the public before approving the lighting directive. The state Supreme Court has held that public notice is a requirement for the PSC to change its rules. The directive appeared on a December 2025 LPSC meeting agenda with the notice “Directive on commission’s Lightning Initiative.”

“That short agenda item did not tell the public anything meaningful, because at the time there was no such thing as the commission’s ‘lightning initiative,’” attorneys for the plaintiffs wrote in the lawsuit. Most & Associates, a New Orleans-based firm, is representing the plaintiffs.

Attorney William Most is also representing plaintiffs in another recent lawsuit that alleges open meetings law violations in advancing incentive deals for SpaceX.

Opposition to Meta’s data center has come from the right and the left, with some conservative landowners in north Louisiana railing against plans to expropriate property to build the huge transmission lines needed to power Hyperion.

"Our coalition members are facing forced expropriation, permanent loss of value, and damage to their family farms, private homesteads, and wildlife habitats under a process cooked up behind closed doors,” said Dustin McAnn, head of the Louisiana Landowners Coalition, in a statement. “The Public Service Commission owes Louisiana landowners transparency and constitutional fairness, not secret shortcuts that benefit a multi-billion dollar utility at the expense of everyday Louisianians."

Along with Meta, Applied Digital is also using the fast-track process for another data center in Boyce.

Coussan, the PSC member who authored the rule change, said the commission will likely discuss the lawsuit in private at its next meeting.

“Public engagement with the Public Service Commission is at an all-time high and I believe that is a good thing for the people of Louisiana,” Coussan said.

The suit comes about a week after midterm elections in which voters around the country rebuked data centers; of more than 40 data center restrictions on the ballot across the nation, all but one was approved by voters. Candidates around the country made opposition to data centers a key part of their campaigns.

Gov. Jeff Landry has remained steadfast in his support of data centers, which he has sought to rebrand as “digital factories.” On Sunday, Landry again rejected opposition to data centers, telling Fox News host Peter Doocey that he supports data centers, saying they will bring jobs to Louisiana.

Doocey cited a Fox News poll that found 76% of Americans would oppose having a data center built in their community.

“You didn’t run that poll in Richland Parish and you didn’t poll the teachers in Richland Parish, who went from the lowest paid teachers in Louisiana to the highest paid teachers in Louisiana,” Landry replied. “You look at a parish that had extreme poverty and right now it’s got record amounts of opportunity.”

The lawsuit against the PSC could scramble Entergy and Meta’s plans to get an unprecedented amount of new power plants and transmission lines approved by the end of the year. Entergy and opponents have litigated the plans for the expansion — involving seven new gas-fired power plants — before an administrative law judge. The PSC is expected to vote by December.

The commission has two newly elected members, Republicans Stephanie Hilferty and John Atkins. They will take office in January, moving the PSC from a 3-2 Republican majority to a 4-1 split.

text:
WASHINGTON — Japanese automaker Honda Motor Co. will build a new $3 billion auto plant in central Ohio to make hybrid vehicles, creating 2,000 jobs, it said on Monday, Nov. 9.

The company said the plant will be able to produce 240,000 vehicles annually and begin production in 2029. It will increase its U.S. auto production capacity to 1.3 million vehicles annually, and North American capacity to 1.9 million.

Honda also plans additional new investments in Canada and Ohio, Georgia and Alabama.

The company announced plans in May to add 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models worldwide by 2030. It also announced it would scrap electric vehicle sales goals, and indefinitely suspended an $11 billion Canada EV project as part of a $9 billion EV writedown.

Honda said it will invest in Alabama to build a new V-6 hybrid engine, and retool its Ohio engine plant to build a new four-cylinder engine. It will also retool transmission plants in Ohio and Georgia, and plans to reintroduce engine production in Ontario.

A number of foreign automakers have announced major new investments as they face tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump's administration.

Last month, Volkswagen AG ​luxury unit Audi said it would build a $4 billion assembly plant near Macon, Georgia, to open in the early 2030s that would produce 200,000 SUVs annually and employ 4,500 workers.

Reuters reported last month that Trump's administration had promised tariff relief to Audi to help secure the plant's future. U.S. officials told Audi executives the government plans to offer broad relief from tariffs for automakers making significant investments in US production.

In July, Toyota Motor Corp. said it would spend $3.6 billion to build a 2.5-million-square-foot truck assembly line on its San Antonio, Texas, manufacturing campus and shift some truck production to the U.S. from Mexico.

The Japanese automaker said the expansion would be completed by 2030, creating 2,000 jobs.

Honda Executive Vice President Noriya Kaihara said in September that the automaker ​was close to full production capacity in North America and needed a ​new factory.

This year, Honda indefinitely suspended its Canada EV project, an $11 billion investment plan to produce electric vehicles ​and batteries. It also canceled three planned EVs for ​the U.S. market.

Last year, Honda said it was shifting production of its U.S.-bound five-door Civic hybrid model ​from Japan to Indiana.

In August, Honda said it might not build an eighth assembly plant in ​North America unless the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement on trade was extended. So far, that has not happened amid an escalating trade war between the U.S. and Canada.

title: Environmental Performance Is Now a Leadership Test, Not Just Compliance
description:
Environmental accountability is now a career variable for chief executives in a way it was not five years ago.
Environmental accountability was built as a compliance function because the demands placed on it were primarily regulatory: permits, reporting deadlines, enforcement thresholds.
Organizations that surface environmental risk through standard capital planning processes can act on it before it becomes a constraint.
What Leadership Accountability for Environmental Performance Actually Requires The Conference Board data also contains something useful for executives trying to understand where their peers are moving.

text:
Something worth examining sits inside the Conference Board's C-Suite Outlook 2026. Among large U.S. companies, those with annual revenues above $1 billion, 21.3% of CEOs reported that environmental issues are not central to their growth plans. At the same time, the report shows North American leaders diverging sharply from their European counterparts on environmental priorities, with a significant share of North American executives deprioritizing sustainability entirely. Neither finding is surprising on its own. What makes it notable is the context: it describes one in five large-company U.S. chief executives holding an environmental posture that investors, regulators, and major buyers are actively working to close off.

The gap between what executives believe their environmental exposure requires and what stakeholders are actually demanding from leadership has been widening for several years. In 2026 it has gotten harder to miss. Harvard Law's corporate governance priorities report for 2026 documents a record 39 CEO-targeting activist campaigns in the first ten months of 2025 alone, with ESG-related controversies listed alongside strategic missteps and sustained underperformance as the primary triggers. Between 2018 and 2025, roughly 38% of those campaigns resulted in a leadership change. Environmental accountability is now a career variable for chief executives in a way it was not five years ago.

The Expectations Have Moved. Most Internal Governance Structures Have Not.

The practical problem is organizational. Environmental accountability was built as a compliance function because the demands placed on it were primarily regulatory: permits, reporting deadlines, enforcement thresholds. The governance structures, staffing models, and executive reporting lines designed around that function are not well suited to the current environment, where environmental risk is showing up in earnings forecasts, supply chain continuity, capital access, and strategic positioning.

ESG governance remained fragmented across many organizations heading into the second quarter, with reporting gaps that were visible in January still unresolved in March. The expectation from investors, major buyers, and regulators that companies would have clearer, more integrated sustainability reporting in place by mid-2026 had not been matched by the internal readiness required to produce it. That gap matters not as a reporting problem but as a signal: organizations whose environmental governance is still structured around periodic compliance outputs are not equipped to respond to the real-time, cross-functional demands that environmental accountability now places on executive teams.

Resource, Infrastructure, and Supply Chain Risk Have Made This an Operational Conversation

Part of what has moved environmental performance into executive territory is that its consequences are no longer confined to regulatory exposure. Water availability is affecting site selection decisions. Grid reliability is influencing capital planning for manufacturers and data center operators. Supply chain environmental accountability is reshaping procurement criteria, contract structures, and Scope 3 reporting obligations in ways that procurement and finance teams cannot manage without executive direction on priorities and resource allocation.

Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research found that corporate boards which integrated climate and energy risk into standard capital planning cycles outperformed peers on total shareholder return by a meaningful margin over three-year periods. The mechanism is straightforward: earlier identification of risk creates earlier optionality for response. Organizations that surface environmental risk through standard capital planning processes can act on it before it becomes a constraint. Those that surface it through sustainability reporting cycles, which are quarterly or annual, are working with information that is already behind the decision timeline.

What Leadership Accountability for Environmental Performance Actually Requires

The Conference Board data also contains something useful for executives trying to understand where their peers are moving. Among large companies globally, the share of CEOs reporting that environmental sustainability is not a priority falls to 20%. The divergence with North American figures reflects regulatory environment and litigation risk as much as genuine strategic disagreement: many U.S. executives told the Conference Board that public sustainability commitments carry reputational and litigation risk in the current domestic political environment, particularly where regulatory expectations are less prescriptive than in Europe. That calculation is real, but it does not make environmental exposure go away. It makes it less visible until it surfaces in an earnings call, a capital markets conversation, or an activist campaign.

description:
When the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, Democrats will have the biggest congressional majority in years — but not a filibuster-proof majority or veto-proof majority.
The House majority will be big enough to allow for intra-party divisions and debates rather than require party-line votes.
Given all this, what can and should Democrats do when it comes to climate, energy and the environment?

House Democrats proposed legislation along these lines earlier this year.
text:
“Green Ideas for the New Blue Majority” is a series from UCLA Law faculty exploring legislative opportunities for the 120th Congress.

Democrats achieved a generational landslide victory in the 2026 midterm elections largely by campaigning on affordability, fighting corruption, and acting as a check on unpopular Trump policies.

To date, Democrats have won at least 253 seats in the House and 54 in the Senate. For the first time this century, Democrats won statewide in Texas — including a Senate seat and the governor’s mansion. They won a Senate seat in Kansas, which had not happened in 94 years. Democrats flipped 5 senate seats in states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024 — including in Iowa where Josh Turek, like many, campaigned on the cost of living and a pledge to fight corruption with an additional focus on fighting high cancer rates related to environmental harms.

When the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, Democrats will have the biggest congressional majority in years — but not a filibuster-proof majority or veto-proof majority. The House majority will be big enough to allow for intra-party divisions and debates rather than require party-line votes.

Given all this, what can and should Democrats do when it comes to climate, energy and the environment? Faculty of the UCLA Emmett Institute are thinking about the various ways congressional Democrats could tackle salient voter concerns at the intersection of corruption, pollution, and the cost of living. These include oversight authority, budgetary powers, and working on legislative priorities that might find some cooperation from Republicans and even Trump.

Of particular note is a theme we call toxic corruption. “The phrase ‘polluter pays’ has taken on a new meaning in the Trump Administration,” Ann Carlson says. “It’s bad enough that the Administration has rolled back climate and air pollution regulations on cars, trucks, power plants, and landfills, but they’re also giving polluters a pass for laws that remain on the books. At least 200 industrial facilities are now allowed to spew hazardous air pollutants above legal limits with impunity; and car companies that can’t meet fuel economy standards now pay $0 in penalties for failing to comply. What are these polluters giving the Administration for their get out of jail free cards? The new Congress should use its legislative, budgetary and oversight powers to investigate why EPA isn’t enforcing toxic pollution laws; use reconciliation to reinstate CAFE penalties; and provide extra funding for EPA’s enforcement staff to go after scofflaws.”

Possible course of action include practical goals related to topics in which Democrats have a clear mandate but also more ambitious proposals that might be vetoed but set up a 2029 agenda for a possible Democratic administration. However, there is reason to exercise careful consideration around priorities and messaging. “Democrats should use the next two years to be as productive as possible,” Julia Stein says “They should be looking to make deals to preserve clean energy investment with the group of Republicans that were already opposed to Trump’s push to eliminate that investment on ideological grounds. And when they use oversight and investigatory powers, it should be directly linked to either affordability or public health — ideally both.”

Over the next two months, we’ll be sharing these ideas in greater detail for a new series called “Green Ideas for the New Blue Majority.” Here’s where we see opportunities worth exploring.

Oversight and investigations

Democrats will hold the full investigatory powers of Congress, including the ability to subpoena records for review and compel individuals to testify before lawmakers. They have already indicated that priorities here include corruption and public health. Efforts could center around cleaning up “toxic corruption” — where pollution and corruption meet.

What would this look like? For starters, they could investigate the “pay for play” free passes to polluters: Representatives around the country, including some new House members, could help shine a spotlight on polluting facilities and recent exemptions (202 in 39 states) especially by holding field hearings in local districts.

They could also investigate the corporate influence of the fossil fuel industry as it relates to the coordinated industry-federal campaign to try to preempt state-level climate lawsuits, using subpoenas, hearings and GAO reviews to document such coordination. Alejandro Camacho, who has been closely following the recent Supreme Court case related to state climate lawsuits, says oversight is just one of the ways Democrats can help preserve climate remedies from the fossil fuel industry.

Then there’s health and science: Democrats already released a report documenting how the Trump administration has undermined public health infrastructure and U.S. scientific research into chronic and deadly diseases, they could continue that investigation with a focus on HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Other possible investigations: EPA and DOE decisions to gut climate rules and revoke the Endangerment Finding; the financial deals to kill clean energy projects, offshore wind especially; the lack of environmental review behind the final “harm” rescission from the Endangered Species Act and the risk it creates for more than 1,200 habitat conservation plans.

Budget reconciliation and appropriations

Since 60 votes are required to overcome a filibuster, Democrats can use the budget reconciliation process for passing some provisions with a simple majority. They can and should consider some options for budget reconciliation even if a presidential veto is threatened. Democrats can also add extra requirements of departments through appropriation riders, because appropriations bills are “must-pass” legislation.

Some options here include: Restoration of CAFE standards and penalties, which was previously done through reconciliation; restoration of agency funding for EPA, DOE and for underfunded wildlife agencies to carry out listing and recovery under the Endangered Species Act; fund dedicated NEPA staff, the Permitting Council and digital public tracking of project reviews.

Given all the emphasis on energy affordability and project streamlining here’s another possibility: Restore funding to the Grid Deployment Office, a Department of Energy office tasked with accelerating the regional transmission buildout that is essential to meeting growing energy demand by providing upgrades. Funding for transmission planning & permitting programs fell by roughly 90% between FY2025 and FY 2027 (proposed).

Legislation and resolutions

House Democrats unarguably have a clear mandate to address affordability and Americans’ bipartisan concerns about the development of data centers. They should include in any “New Affordability Agenda” or new federal restrictions on data centers, a broader focus on electricity affordability, utility rates, and renewable energy, among other concerns.

This could take many different forms. One option would be to pass a bill that establishes new incentives for renewable projects and to protect consumers from rising electricity costs due to grid demands from large energy users such as data centers. House Democrats proposed legislation along these lines earlier this year.

On the topic of climate liability, they could pass a bill expressly preserving state and federal statutory and common-law claims for climate-adaptation costs, forcing the President to sign it or veto it on the record. Congress could also adopt a concurrent resolution, and file amicus briefs from members, stating that the Clean Air Act preserves state common-law climate remedies.

title: Windows of Opportunity Open in the States - Legal Planet
description:
These dramatic shifts open up many exciting opportunities for climate and clean energy initiatives.
It is in the state governments where exciting opportunities exist for major policy changes.
The opportunity is biggest in states where Democrats won trifectas: Arizona, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota and Nevada.
That may be especially important in states like Ohio and Texas where polluters have enjoyed a free hand until now.
States are also going to have to start grappling with climate change risks that many preferred to ignore under Republican climate deniers.
text:
The most exciting new prospects for environmental progress are far outside the Beltway

Summary

In the aftermath of the 2026 election, Democrats in Congress can do a lot to hinder Trump's anti-environmental policies but much less to advance their own climate agenda. The real opportunities for progress are in the states. Consider Texas, a state that has long been under iron GOP control and also the country's biggest emitter of carbon. Democrats will now control all statewide offices and one legislative chamber. Or there's Wisconsin, where Democrats will control the governorship and the legislature. These dramatic shifts open up many exciting opportunities for climate and clean energy initiatives. We can’t foresee all the long-term effects, but we do know that in many places the winds are starting to blow in the right direction.

A small event last Thursday captures this moment of change. The Fifth Circuit heard a challenge to Texas’s 2021 anti-ESG law, which gives the Texas Comptroller sweeping powers to blacklist companies that disfavor fossil fuels. The law was vigorously defended by the state’s current Attorney General. But here’s the thing: The new Texas Attorney General will be Nathan Johnson, a Democrat who has no reason to defend the law. And the new Comptroller will be Sarah Eckhardt, another Democrat.

The new Congress will be a significant thorn in the President’s side. But Trump’s veto power will severely limit its ability to enact policies of its own. It is in the state governments where exciting opportunities exist for major policy changes.

The political configuration and policy potential vary state by state. The opportunity is biggest in states where Democrats won trifectas: Arizona, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota and Nevada. The last time this happened in Minnesota, the state’s clean energy policies took major steps forward.

But there have been major changes in other states too. Democrats flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Nevada, Democrats may also end up with the governor’s mansion in Alaska and Kansas. They flipped thirteen legislative chambers. Despite intense gerrymandering, Democrats will have the governor and one legislative chamber in Texas, North Carolina, and Georgia.

Given the focus on affordability right now, we may not see new cap and trade systems or bold new climate targets. But the declining costs of solar, wind, and battery storage mean that removing barriers will directly advance affordability. Support for rooftop and balcony solar is likely to be especially popular. We can also expect to see greater environmental enforcement against polluters as new governors look for ways to improve local quality of life. That may be especially important in states like Ohio and Texas where polluters have enjoyed a free hand until now. States are also going to have to start grappling with climate change risks that many preferred to ignore under Republican climate deniers.

This will be a heady time of change in many states. We can’t foresee the long-term effects, but we do know that in many places the winds are starting to blow in the right direction.

text:
Catawba County News

Catawba County joins NC C-PACE program to support business building improvements

Published: November 09, 2026

Catawba County has joined a program that opens new pathways for businesses to finance investments in energy efficiency, renewable measures, resiliency and water conservation.

The Catawba County Board of Commissioners unanimously voted to participate in North Carolina’s Commercial Property Assessed Capital Expenditure program, which allows private property owners to apply for private financing through a voluntary lien placed on property by local government. The program allows for payback periods over the life of the improvements.

The North Carolina C-PACE program was created by the N.C. General Assembly in 2024.

The program offers another financing tool for property owners to improve commercial, industrial, agricultural and multi-family properties with projects related to key areas identified by the program. This includes properties owned by nonprofit, charitable or religious organizations.

The program can help drive economic development in our community and improve properties.

Qualifying projects include:

Energy efficiency measures: projects that reduce energy use and increase efficiency.

Resiliency measures: projects that increase environmental resiliency, including storm retrofits, flood mitigation and stormwater management.

Renewable energy measures: projects that utilize renewable energy sources.

Water conservation measures: projects that decrease water consumption or demand, and that address safe drinking water.

There are no program costs for Catawba County government. C-PACE is administered by the Economic Development Partnership of North Carolina, which works with private capital providers to help interested property owners apply for C-PACE funding.

This initiative supports the Board of Commissioners’ strategic plan by promoting economic development in Catawba County through private investment and job growth.

Catawba County commissioners adopted a resolution of intent to participate in C-PACE on Oct. 19. On Nov. 2, the board held a public hearing, then adopted a final resolution to join the C-PACE program.

title: What Gets Solar Built After the Tax Credits? A Signed Customer - POWER Magazine
description:
For tax equity, the financing method built on those credits, this is a real ending.
As such, the ones that proceed are the ones with a customer who has signed a long contract at a guaranteed minimum bill.
Lazard’s July 2026 numbers show what the credits were worth: unsubsidized utility-scale solar at $40 to $98 per megawatt-hour, with the production tax credit having pulled the low end down to $16.
Thirty-seven states now have a large-load tariff approved or pending.
What a large-load tariff pays for, on the other hand, is a customer who has committed to a term and a minimum bill.
text:
American utility-scale solar split into two eras on July 4, 2026. Any project that began construction by that date retains its federal tax credits under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s transition rule, while any that missed it must be in service by December 31, 2027, or proceed without them. For tax equity, the financing method built on those credits, this is a real ending.

What replaces it is demand: developers now hold more projects than they can build by 2030. As such, the ones that proceed are the ones with a customer who has signed a long contract at a guaranteed minimum bill.

Lazard’s July 2026 numbers show what the credits were worth: unsubsidized utility-scale solar at $40 to $98 per megawatt-hour, with the production tax credit having pulled the low end down to $16. Because that value was written into statute and the money came from the U.S. Treasury, lenders treated it as the most dependable revenue in a project, which let sponsors get by with fewer signed sales contracts for everything else.

Regulators have created a framework for that at speed: DELTa (Database of Emerging Large-Load Tariffs), the quarterly-updated public tariff database maintained by the Smart Electric Power Alliance and the North Carolina (NC) Clean Energy Technology Center, counted 14 large-load tariff approvals across the entire 2018-2024 period.

The year 2025 on its own produced 29. The first half of 2026 produced 23 in only six months, nearly the 2025 full-year total (Figure 1). Thirty-seven states now have a large-load tariff approved or pending. In addition, eligibility thresholds have moved up, with around two-thirds of the 2025 class between 50 and 150 MW.

Put the approved tariffs side by side and a rate archetype appears (Figure 2). Among the 27 approved filings in DELTa that publish both terms—22 distinct rate designs—minimum bills cluster at 80 to 85 percent of contracted demand, and initial contract terms cluster at 12 to 15 years as written, with the four- or five-year load ramp counted inside the term in some tariffs and added on top of it in others.

AEP Ohio charges 85% across an eight-year firm term on top of a four-year ramp. Dominion’s GS-5 charges 85% for distribution and transmission—60% for generation—across 14 years, its four-year ramp counted inside. Indiana Michigan charges 80% over 12 years with a five-year ramp on top. A Tri-State Generation and Transmission analysis of 11 tariffs found security averaging seven years of minimum bills and exit fees averaging five.

These terms are similar to the contracted revenue line a lender asks for: take-or-pay, an investment-grade counterparty, collateral, with a regulator’s approval behind it. The obvious objection is that these commitments run to the utility, not to any particular solar project—which is quite precisely what the next generation of tariffs changes.

A second generation of tariffs converts that contracted demand directly into new clean supply. Google’s Clean Transition Tariff with NV Energy, for example, funds a 115-MW enhanced geothermal plant and credits Google the plant’s energy and capacity value. A similar Google tariff with Xcel in Minnesota covers wind, solar, and storage, and Georgia Power’s 2025 IRP settlement created a Customer-Identified Resource option inside its CARES program. RMI groups these under bring-your-own (BYO) tariffs: the customer pays the full incremental cost of a specific new resource, the resource gets built, and other ratepayers are insulated from the risk.

For solar developers, supply in this market is already set. Wood Mackenzie counts 216 to 240 GWdc of utility-scale solar safe-harbored—begun in time to keep the credits—most of it before year-end 2025, while its base case holds annual additions flat near 43 GWdc through 2031—about five years of building at that rate, so for the next five years, the question is: which of those projects will get built?

There are three ways large-load demand can support a project: the BYO route referenced above, minimum-bill revenue supporting what the utility buys through its resource plan, or, in ERCOT, which has no tariff of this kind, power purchase agreements (PPA) signed directly with developers. Q1 2026 offtake signings ran 6.3 GWdc, up 15% year over year, led by Texas projects with data and technology buyers.

The tariffs also tend to significantly filter out demand that wasn’t real: AEP Ohio’s data-center interconnection queue fell from 30 GW to 13 GW once its tariff required real financial commitments—Enverus puts the first-year cost to a 100-MW facility near $10 million, and as a result, more than half the queue decided it would rather not. This filtering out is useful, as a load that stays and agrees to those terms is one a utility can plan new generation around.

The ITC paid per megawatt-hour, with a project earning the credit whether it had a twelve-year buyer or a term sheet and a prayer. What a large-load tariff pays for, on the other hand, is a customer who has committed to a term and a minimum bill. Those commitments are approved by state commissions rather than written into federal law, so an election changes what is left of the tax credits and does not touch them. In sum, solar developers now have more safe-harbored projects than they can build by 2030, and what increasingly decides which ones go ahead is whether a buyer has signed.
