title: Jillian Blanchard: The 100 Most Influential Climate Leaders of 2026 - TIME

text:
One of the most exciting aspects of the AI boom is its potential to help the world mitigate and adapt to the climate crisis. Juliet Rothenberg leads the team at Google that’s producing tools to do just that, like the AI weather model WeatherNext, which can now accurately forecast cyclones at least one day earlier than other models, and last year helped the National Hurricane Center predict Hurricane Melissa’s landfall five days in advance. In September, Google rolled out WeatherNext 3, its most advanced and accurate weather model yet. —Jessica Hullinger

What is the single most important action you think the public, or a specific company or government (other than your own), needs to take in the next year to advance the climate agenda?

We need to keep progressing on mitigating climate change, but it’s very clear that we’re headed past the 1.5° Celsius threshold that scientists believe is critical to reducing the most damaging effects of climate change. And especially with the Super El Niño this year, we also need to recognize that climate change is here today. Aligned with the U.N.’s Early Warnings for All initiative, we need to start moving towards a world where no one is surprised by a natural disaster. This means putting in place comprehensive forecasting, monitoring, alerting, and response systems globally, so that we can protect lives and livelihoods from the climate crisis.

What’s one sustainability effort you personally will try to adopt in the next year, and why?

For many of us, air travel is the single largest contributor to our personal carbon footprint; a single long-haul flight can easily eclipse our household, diet, and driving choices combined. We often look at aviation solely through the lens of fuel burn, but short-lived climate forces like contrails actually account for more than a third of aviation's total warming footprint. While my team works on improving the global AI models that have already helped airlines and air traffic control reduce contrails by over half, I want to personally align my consumer habits—making sure my own travel choices support the carriers paving the way for sustainable skies.

That’s why my personal commitment this year is to make my essential travel as contrail-conscious as possible. This means prioritizing airlines that actively participate in contrail avoidance programs, favoring morning or daytime flights when contrails are less warming, or better yet checking out the Google Flights tooltip on the likelihood of contrail warming for a given flight, and also opting for rail over short-haul flights wherever feasible.

What is a climate solution (other than your own) that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?

I’ll share a solution from one of our partners: FireSat, by the Earth Fire Alliance. When fully operational, the FireSat constellation will be able to detect a garage-sized wildfire within 20 minutes, anywhere on Earth. Fire authorities say that this will be a gamechanger for their ability to respond to devastating wildfires, like those in France and Spain this summer, because the greatest gift that we can give firefighters is time.

FireSat has the first 4 satellites in orbit, and a 20-minute revisit will be achieved once the constellation reaches 52 satellites. Google.org, Bezos Earth Fund, and the Moore Foundation have all supported FireSat, and more funding is needed to realize the potential of this vision.

What gives you hope about the future of the planet/climate movement?

I’m tremendously optimistic about the ability of AI to accelerate the rate of scientific progress towards climate-friendly technologies. This is a dramatic change since I started working in the field 22 years ago. As a case in point, our climate teams are now able to build software prototypes for things like satellite detection in less than an hour, which previously would have taken months, and now they can even develop novel hardware solutions in months that would previously have taken years.

Climate change won’t be solved by a single silver bullet. It will take hundreds of practical, durable innovations working in parallel to deliver impact at scale, which is why it’s so exciting that the pace of innovation is accelerating dramatically.

Do you think AI will help or worsen the climate crisis? How?

My job day in and day out is to apply AI to help solve the climate crisis, and I’m a big believer in that potential because we're already seeing it in action. For example, our Contrails project targets an impact equivalent to roughly 4% of the impact that today’s warming will have over the next 20 years (known as global warming potential, or GWP20), or 1-2% of the impact over the next 100 years (GWP100). In live commercial flights across U.S. and international airspace, we’ve proven that AI predictions can help pilots cut contrail formation by more than half, avoiding these warming zones in a way that’s just as simple as avoiding turbulence.

We’re also working with dozens of governments that are using our cutting-edge crisis models for hazards like floods, fires, and cyclones in service of our team’s north star: that no one should ever be surprised by a natural disaster coming their way.

And it’s important to acknowledge that AI will have additional energy demands. My team is hard at work on applying agentic AI for science to accelerate the development of clean, low-cost energy solutions—expect to hear more from us there over time.

The nonprofit Rainforest Alliance, headed by Santiago Gowland, runs one of the world’s largest sustainability certification programs—partnering with farmers and brands around the world to support climate resilient growing practices under its iconic green frog seal. In 2025, the organization’s efforts resulted in some 5.5 million metric tons of emissions being avoided or sequestered.

The group recently announced a new regenerative agriculture standard aimed at transforming the way tropical commodities are grown, certified, and traded. The standard supports farmers looking to better understand and employ regenerative agriculture practices—focusing on areas such as soil health and fertility, biodiversity, and crop resilience. The first crop the framework is focusing on is coffee, but the organization plans to extend the certification to cocoa, citrus, and tea. —Simmone Shah

What is the single most important action you think the public, or a specific company or government (other than your own), needs to take in the next year to advance the climate agenda?

The single most important action we can take to advance the global climate agenda is to accelerate the transition to regenerative agriculture by making it the smart economic choice for producers, supply chains, governments, impact investors, philanthropies, and consumers.

Agriculture, forestry, and other land use account for about 22% of global greenhouse gas emissions. At the same time, nature-based solutions, which protect, restore, and improve ecosystems, could deliver roughly a third of the climate mitigation needed by 2030. Regenerative agriculture connects these two realities by putting nature-based solutions to work on farms. Through practices such as agroforestry, cover cropping, and water conservation, it shifts food production from a process that depletes soil, water, and biodiversity to one that restores them.

No single actor can deliver this transition at scale; it takes an alliance whose individual actions reinforce one another. Food companies provide dependable purchasing agreements that reward regenerative production and share transition costs, making farm investments easier to finance. Governments align agricultural policy and incentives, while philanthropy helps absorb risks that unlock affordable capital.

This investment, combined with practical support on the farm, enables producers to deliver verified results. Brands and retailers make that progress visible through credible, accessible regenerative products. Consumer purchases generate revenue for companies, giving them a commercial reason to expand regenerative sourcing and investment. That growing market attracts more producers and gives participating farmers the income and confidence to reinvest. Verified results and demonstrated demand strengthen the case for further financing, funding the next round of regeneration.

This is how regenerative economies deliver lasting climate benefits: the cycle gives producers and communities the means and incentive to keep protecting and restoring ecosystems. Starting in tropical forest landscapes, where the risks are acute and the immediate gains greatest, we can sustain emissions reductions, carbon storage, and forest protection while safeguarding biodiversity, livelihoods, and food security.

What is a climate solution (other than your own) that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?

We need to put much greater emphasis on local bioeconomies to ensure that forests are worth more standing than cleared. Tropical forests hold vast reserves of living carbon and are estimated to harbor roughly half of the world’s species on just 7% of [all the earth’s] land. Indigenous and community-led forest enterprises connect people’s economic futures to the continued health of their forests.

Take Carmelita, a community in Guatemala’s Maya Biosphere Reserve, as an example. Here, local carpenters turn responsibly harvested timber into furniture. Guides and cooks earn income taking visitors into the forest. The community cooperative invests in fire prevention, forest monitoring, and reforestation. The forest sustains an economy, and that economy helps protect the forest. Across the reserve’s successful community forestry concessions, deforestation has remained near zero for more than 20 years.

This achievement rests on communities having the rights, institutions, and economic opportunities to manage their forests for the long term. Sustaining that success requires investment that strengthens both forest protection and local livelihoods.

I see this as a direct investment in climate mitigation and adaptation. Standing forests retain carbon, protect watersheds, and help regulate local temperatures and water cycles. Those functions help farmers cope with heat and water stress and keep producing food in a changing climate.

Climate investors need to back the institutions and businesses that make forest protection economically durable, helping more communities build on Carmelita’s example. Financing local processing allows communities to retain more value from what they produce, while working capital and dependable buyers give enterprises the stability to grow. Secure community rights, combined with a reliable livelihood from healthy forests, give people both the confidence and the incentive to protect and invest in a forest their children will inherit.

What gives you hope about the future of the planet/climate movement?

That companies are beginning to recognize that their own future depends on investing in people and nature.

Much of the commodity economy was originally built on extractive principles: cheap labor, low returns for farmers, and nature treated as a free resource. Industrial monocultures replaced diverse landscapes with vast fields of a single crop, while externalizing the costs of depleted soils, lost biodiversity, and insecure livelihoods. Climate change has exposed the fragility of that model.

Farms and corporate supply chains have less capacity to withstand shocks when the systems supporting them have been weakened. Regenerative agriculture offers a way to change the status quo. Healthy soils, functioning ecosystems and thriving farming communities create value through more resilient production and greater security of supply. Companies now have a commercial reason to invest in the people and landscapes that deliver those benefits.

Climate action gains staying power when people have a direct stake in its success. Better livelihoods give farmers reasons to continue investing in their land. More resilient production gives businesses reasons to support them. Turning those shared interests into lasting commitments is how we accelerate regeneration. Seeing this work take shape really gives me confidence that we can turn a corner in the climate crisis.

Do you think AI will help or worsen the climate crisis? How?

I believe AI can accelerate climate action, provided we manage its own energy use and emissions.

At the Rainforest Alliance, we already use AI-powered remote sensing and deforestation risk mapping to identify risks in coffee and cocoa supply chains. That work depends on information from farmers and knowledge of conditions on the ground. Human expertise is fundamental to making the technology useful.

Connecting farmers’ knowledge with field, weather, and satellite data can improve advice, identify climate risks, and make verification more accessible. Better evidence must then translate into practical support and financing for farmers restoring soils, integrating trees, and strengthening resilience to climate shocks.

Who controls that information matters. Farmers and Indigenous communities must determine how their knowledge and data are used, and share in the value they create. People must remain responsible for consequential decisions, and farmers must be able to challenge them.

AI’s climate contribution must be judged by measurable results: less forest loss, lower emissions and more farmers equipped to regenerate their land and withstand a changing climate. Those benefits must justify the technology’s environmental cost.

In 2024, Californians threw away some 8.5 million tons of single-use packaging and food ware, according to a study last year; 40 million tons of material was sent to landfill. Under the state’s new Plastic Pollution Prevention and Packaging Producer Responsibility Act, roughly 21% of that waste will be avoided. The new law was spearheaded by State Senator Ben Allen and came into effect this May. It will require 100% of single-use packaging and plastic food-service ware to be recycled or compostable by 2032. Also by that date, there must be a 25% overall reduction in the use of plastic packaging. The plastics and packaging industry will also pay $500 million each year for the next decade—for a total $5 billion—to help mitigate pollution in disadvantaged communities.

What is the single most important action you think the public, or a specific company or government, needs to take in the next year to advance the climate agenda?

The single most important action the United States could take in the next year is to launch a Marshall Plan for electrification — a coordinated, national effort that harnesses the federal government's full power, resources and convening authority to build the infrastructure needed to transition our economy away from fossil fuels.

While we have made tremendous progress developing technologies to decarbonize transportation, buildings and industry, the increasing challenge has become deploying these technologies at scale. Convenient and fast charging remains a substantial barrier to electric vehicle adoption, while inadequate transmission and distribution capacity, and lengthy interconnection timelines, constrain electrification more broadly.

Treating this transition as the nation-building project it is could coordinate federal agencies, states, utilities, labor, manufacturers and the private sector around the common goals of rapidly expanding transmission and distribution capacity, building out a reliable EV charging network, upgrading local grids and removing the permitting, interconnection, financing and supply-chain bottlenecks that slow development. We achieved this level of coordination to build out our rail and highway networks, and we can do it again.

Rather than asking consumers and businesses to make the transition first and hope the infrastructure catches up, we should build the infrastructure that makes the clean-energy choice easy, affordable and practical. Done at the scale the challenge demands, this would not only accelerate emissions reductions, it could strengthen American manufacturing, create jobs, improve energy security and build the modern infrastructure the U.S. economy will need for decades to come.

What’s one sustainability effort you personally will try to adopt in the next year?

I am particularly interested in opportunities to better align climate, housing, fire risk reduction, energy distribution, and insurance policy. As California becomes more difficult and expensive to insure — partly as a result of increasing climate-related risks — we can and should be doing so much more to encourage and incentivize greater climate resiliency and risk reduction efforts in the way we build. I am hoping to spearhead negotiations with insurers, builders, local governments, consumer advocates, environmentalists, utilities and fire experts to help regions of California better plan for and deploy technologies and assets, while also changing codes in ways that will significantly reduce risk, make our communities safer and lower the massive human and environmental costs of catastrophic wildfires.

What is a climate solution that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?

Smart land-use planning has failed to receive the attention and investment it deserves. We spend enormous amounts of time and resources to make our transportation, buildings and energy systems cleaner, but comparatively little addressing a fundamental driver of emissions: where and what we build.

Land use and transportation are inseparable. When housing is located far from jobs, schools, shopping and services, we lock families into longer commutes and a greater dependence on cars. Building more housing in existing communities, creating walkable mixed-use neighborhoods and investing in biking infrastructure, transit and other alternatives to driving would substantially reduce vehicle miles traveled (VMT) and thus emissions.

This matters even in a future dominated by EVs. California's climate agency has concluded that vehicle electrification alone will not be enough to achieve carbon neutrality, and that changes in transportation, housing and land use are also necessary. Smart growth can reduce VMT and the various resources needed for our transportation system.

Beyond transportation benefits, building within existing communities can reduce pressure to develop into open space and natural lands, make better use of existing public infrastructure, support more efficient housing and help communities preserve landscapes that store carbon and provide resilience to wildfire, flooding and extreme heat. And land use also matters in terms of climate disasters, costs, liabilities and crises. When we build in high-risk areas without building to the highest safety standards, we not only make insurance more expensive and less available, we increase the chances of catastrophic financial, public health and environmental disasters, such as those we saw with the recent fires we have experienced in California.

Land use remains something of an orphan in climate policy but deserves to be treated as a priority in its own right. While clean energy, EVs, batteries, firefighting, home and energy-infrastructure hardening and other technologies have identifiable projects and funding streams, land use decisions are dispersed across thousands of local and siloed decisions between zoning, housing, transit, parking, energy, infrastructure, public safety and development. Stronger coordination and planning with all of the key parties would help us solve this jigsaw puzzle and make it easier for people to operate within a community, insure their homes and keep their communities safe.

The climate fight isn't only about changing the fuel that powers our economy; it's also about designing communities that are safer and require less energy and fewer resources. Smart land use is one of the few strategies that can deliver these benefits simultaneously.

The single most important action we can take to advance the global climate agenda is to accelerate the transition to regenerative agriculture by making it the smart economic choice for producers, supply chains, governments, impact investors, philanthropies, and consumers.

Agriculture, forestry, and other land use account for about 22% of global greenhouse gas emissions. At the same time, nature-based solutions, which protect, restore, and improve ecosystems, could deliver roughly a third of the climate mitigation needed by 2030. Regenerative agriculture connects these two realities by putting nature-based solutions to work on farms. Through practices such as agroforestry, cover cropping, and water conservation, it shifts food production from a process that depletes soil, water, and biodiversity to one that restores them.

No single actor can deliver this transition at scale; it takes an alliance whose individual actions reinforce one another. Food companies provide dependable purchasing agreements that reward regenerative production and share transition costs, making farm investments easier to finance. Governments align agricultural policy and incentives, while philanthropy helps absorb risks that unlock affordable capital.

This investment, combined with practical support on the farm, enables producers to deliver verified results. Brands and retailers make that progress visible through credible, accessible regenerative products. Consumer purchases generate revenue for companies, giving them a commercial reason to expand regenerative sourcing and investment. That growing market attracts more producers and gives participating farmers the income and confidence to reinvest. Verified results and demonstrated demand strengthen the case for further financing, funding the next round of regeneration.

This is how regenerative economies deliver lasting climate benefits: the cycle gives producers and communities the means and incentive to keep protecting and restoring ecosystems. Starting in tropical forest landscapes, where the risks are acute and the immediate gains greatest, we can sustain emissions reductions, carbon storage, and forest protection while safeguarding biodiversity, livelihoods, and food security.

What is a climate solution (other than your own) that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?

We need to put much greater emphasis on local bioeconomies to ensure that forests are worth more standing than cleared. Tropical forests hold vast reserves of living carbon and are estimated to harbor roughly half of the world’s species on just 7% of [all the earth’s] land. Indigenous and community-led forest enterprises connect people’s economic futures to the continued health of their forests.

Take Carmelita, a community in Guatemala’s Maya Biosphere Reserve, as an example. Here, local carpenters turn responsibly harvested timber into furniture. Guides and cooks earn income taking visitors into the forest. The community cooperative invests in fire prevention, forest monitoring, and reforestation. The forest sustains an economy, and that economy helps protect the forest. Across the reserve’s successful community forestry concessions, deforestation has remained near zero for more than 20 years.

This achievement rests on communities having the rights, institutions, and economic opportunities to manage their forests for the long term. Sustaining that success requires investment that strengthens both forest protection and local livelihoods.

I see this as a direct investment in climate mitigation and adaptation. Standing forests retain carbon, protect watersheds, and help regulate local temperatures and water cycles. Those functions help farmers cope with heat and water stress and keep producing food in a changing climate.

Climate investors need to back the institutions and businesses that make forest protection economically durable, helping more communities build on Carmelita’s example. Financing local processing allows communities to retain more value from what they produce, while working capital and dependable buyers give enterprises the stability to grow. Secure community rights, combined with a reliable livelihood from healthy forests, give people both the confidence and the incentive to protect and invest in a forest their children will inherit.

What gives you hope about the future of the planet/climate movement?

That companies are beginning to recognize that their own future depends on investing in people and nature.

Much of the commodity economy was originally built on extractive principles: cheap labor, low returns for farmers, and nature treated as a free resource. Industrial monocultures replaced diverse landscapes with vast fields of a single crop, while externalizing the costs of depleted soils, lost biodiversity, and insecure livelihoods. Climate change has exposed the fragility of that model.

Farms and corporate supply chains have less capacity to withstand shocks when the systems supporting them have been weakened. Regenerative agriculture offers a way to change the status quo. Healthy soils, functioning ecosystems and thriving farming communities create value through more resilient production and greater security of supply. Companies now have a commercial reason to invest in the people and landscapes that deliver those benefits.

Climate action gains staying power when people have a direct stake in its success. Better livelihoods give farmers reasons to continue investing in their land. More resilient production gives businesses reasons to support them. Turning those shared interests into lasting commitments is how we accelerate regeneration. Seeing this work take shape really gives me confidence that we can turn a corner in the climate crisis.

Do you think AI will help or worsen the climate crisis? How?

I believe AI can accelerate climate action, provided we manage its own energy use and emissions.

At the Rainforest Alliance, we already use AI-powered remote sensing and deforestation risk mapping to identify risks in coffee and cocoa supply chains. That work depends on information from farmers and knowledge of conditions on the ground. Human expertise is fundamental to making the technology useful.

text:
Construction on the first phase of the 1.2 GW Big Rooter Power solar project got underway in July at Panamint Capital’s Twin Oaks power station in Robertson County, Texas. The project will be the largest solar project constructed at an existing coal mining site and the largest brownfield renewable energy project in North America, according to Panamint.

The energy infrastructure investor recently closed on the first phase of a $1.8 billion green loan to finance construction. Proceeds from the $769 million first phase will fund ongoing construction of the 491 MW Big Rooter West portion of the project. The over $1 billion second phase of the Green Loan will finance construction of Big Rooter East, the project’s 658 MW second stage.

Located halfway between Dallas and Houston, Big Rooter Power is being built on 1,804 hectares of reclaimed coal mine land and operating interconnection infrastructure at Panamint’s 349 MW coal-fired Twin Oaks Complex. The campus combines power generation, surface mining, energy storage, data center capacity, and high voltage transmission.

“When Big Rooter is complete, the Twin Oaks complex will have 1.5 GW of operating thermal and renewable power, in addition to over 20 miles of new 345 kV transmission, 1.6 GWh of battery energy storage and 790 MW of Batch Zero data center capacity under development across our 10,000-acre site,” said Apolka Totth, Panamint’s chief executive officer.

Panamint reports it signed a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) with an unnamed corporation. “Our long-term power purchase agreement with one of country’s largest companies will ensure the electricity we generate at Big Rooter will power job creation in the American economy into the 2050s,” said Bill Stanton, managing director of development at Panamint.

Construction of both Big Rooter West and Big Rooter East is expected to create over 800 jobs, Panamint reports.

Big Rooter East is the 658 MW second phase of the project and is slated to begin construction in December 2026 and enter commercial operation in August 2029. Financing on that phase is expected to close in Q1 2027.

Panamint reports it is committed to selecting domestic renewable energy companies. Solv Energy will provide EPC services for the project, including solar, substation and transmission infrastructure. First Solar will provide approximately 2 million solar panels manufactured in Ohio, Louisiana and Alabama. California-based Nextpower will deploy its NX Horizon solar tracker systems with Hail Pro-75 and NX Navigator software. In addition, the projects reportedly will use over 34,000 tons of domestically manufactured steel.

Nevada-based Panamint Capital is a woman-led energy investment company founded in 2019 thathad 718 MW of energy generating capacity in operation in 2025.

The company’s sustainability report points to the Twin Oaks station as an example of its redevelopment efforts that focus on preparing existing sites for utility-scale solar, storage and thermal projects. These projects, the report says, “extend the productive use of existing infrastructure through clean energy investments that support local employment and drive long-term economic value in the communities where we operate.”

title: Michael Sheldrick: The 100 Most Influential Climate Leaders of 2026 - TIME
description:
The most important thing governments can do is stop asking people to choose between climate action and the cost of living.
I want to spend more time sharing stories about climate action that is actually working.
We already know many of the things we need to build to address climate change, including transitioning to clean energy.
We need to keep progressing on mitigating climate change, but it’s very clear that we’re headed past the 1.5° Celsius threshold that scientists believe is critical to reducing the most damaging effects of climate change.
And especially with the Super El Niño this year, we also need to recognize that climate change is here today.
text:
Michael Sheldrick helps turn public pressure into financial commitments. The Global Citizen co-founder’s work connects the fight against poverty with climate action. At the end of 2025, Global Citizen’s “Protect the Amazon" campaign secured more than $1 billion in pledges from international banks, governments, corporations, and philanthropies. The money is expected to safeguard about 75 million acres of Amazon rainforest by funding conservation, sustainable innovation, and Indigenous protections, as well as helping some 5 million people upskill for employment in the clean energy workforce. —Jessica Hullinger

What is the single most important action you think the public, or a specific company or government, needs to take in the next year to advance the climate agenda?

The most important thing governments can do is stop asking people to choose between climate action and the cost of living. For most people, climate change is not an abstract debate about targets or gigawatts. They are thinking about the cost of electricity and fuel, whether they can find a good job and whether the lights stay on. Climate policy needs to meet people there. The goal should be to make cleaner energy cheaper and more reliable, while ensuring workers and communities benefit from the new industries and investment that come with it.

This matters because people are more likely to support change when they can see and feel it improving their own lives. I've seen that firsthand in the coal town of Collie in Western Australia. Workers were far more willing to embrace a future beyond coal when they could see what it meant for them: investment in their community, new industries and good jobs.

But communities like Collie cannot make that shift on their own. New industries require significant private investment, and governments have a critical role in helping de-risk that investment through targeted public funding, guarantees and incentives. Done well, relatively limited public support can unlock much larger flows of private capital and ensure communities are not left behind.

Australia now has an opportunity to demonstrate this approach through its leadership of the COP31 negotiations. It already has some of the building blocks, from support for household solar and batteries that can lower power bills to programs supporting workers and coal communities. It can build on these measures at home and use COP31 to champion the model internationally, including across the Pacific.

Climate action will move faster when people experience it not as another sacrifice, but as a practical answer to the things they already care about: lower costs, reliable energy, good jobs and stronger communities.

What’s one sustainability effort you personally will try to adopt in the next year?

I want to spend more time sharing stories about climate action that is actually working.

I recently coauthored a Stanford-led study of more than 30,000 people that examined what motivates people to take collective action on climate change. The strongest approach was simple: show people that collective action has worked before and delivered real change. Doing so increased participants’ willingness to act, from sharing climate information and joining climate organizations to signing petitions and contacting elected representatives.

The finding reinforced something I had long argued in my book, From Ideas to Impact: When people see progress, they are more likely to believe their own actions matter.

I see this even around my parents’ dinner table in Australia. With the help of government incentives, my dad recently installed solar and a home battery. He now proudly pulls out an app showing friends how much power he is generating, what he is saving and how much electricity he is sending back into the grid. Inevitably, people want to know how they can do it too.

That is how change can become contagious. So my personal commitment this year is to find and share more stories of climate action working, and connect them to practical ways people can act themselves. In an age of climate anxiety, we need to show people not only what is going wrong, but what they can do about it. Visible progress creates agency, and agency creates action.

What is a climate solution that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?

One climate solution that deserves far more attention is policy that helps lower income households overcome the upfront costs of clean energy. Solar panels, batteries, insulation and heat pumps can lower household energy bills for years. But they often require significant investment upfront. That creates a paradox: Households that could benefit most from lower energy costs are often the least able to afford the technologies that deliver them. Renters face an additional barrier because they do not control those investment decisions.

Governments can change that equation through targeted incentives, affordable finance and minimum energy standards for rental properties when they are sold, renovated or major equipment is replaced. The principle should be simple: Those who have the least should not be the last to benefit from cheaper, cleaner energy.

My friend Thom Woodroofe makes a broader version of this argument in his recent book Power, Prosperity & Planet: We need to design the energy transition from the household up. We spend a lot of time talking about how many gigawatts of renewable energy we need to build. We spend much less time asking who gets the savings.

Getting that right matters beyond household bills. When people can see that the transition is making their lives better, they have a stake in its success. That builds the social licence needed to move faster, and makes climate progress harder to reverse. The transition should not ask those with the least to shoulder the greatest burden. It should give them the greatest reason to want it to succeed.

What gives you hope about the future of the planet?

What gives me hope is meeting people who can already see themselves in a cleaner future.

Last year, while working with partners during South Africa’s G20 presidency to help scale renewable energy and the jobs that can come with it, I met two young trainee solar technicians, Luke and Keanu. They were learning their trade at a solar academy, but their ambitions went far beyond installing panels. They talked about starting with rooftop solar, then one day building and supplying solar for Africa’s growing data centers and, eventually, helping power humanity into space.

That stayed with me. We hear a lot about young people being apathetic or pessimistic about the future. Luke and Keanu were neither. They saw clean energy not as a burden or sacrifice, but as an opportunity to learn skills, build a business and participate in industries that will shape their generation.

I heard something similar from coal workers I met in South Africa. There was understandable sadness about an industry that had supported families and communities for generations, but also recognition that change was coming. What mattered was whether they and their communities would receive the investment and support needed to build a future on the other side of it.

That gives me hope. Sometimes we assume people don't understand the scale of the climate challenge or are unwilling to change. I think many understand it perfectly well. They simply want to know there is a place for them in what comes next. Our job is to help make sure there is.

Do you think AI will help or worsen the climate crisis?

AI can accelerate the drive toward cheaper energy, but it won't happen by itself. The crucial question is: What type of energy AI makes cheaper?

It can make clean energy, grids and industrial processes more efficient and affordable. But it can also make oil extraction cheaper and drive greater energy consumption. Greater efficiency alone does not guarantee lower emissions.

The biggest opportunity I see is turning AI’s enormous electricity demand into a financing engine for new clean power, storage and grids. Long-term commitments from companies buying that power could help get infrastructure built, including in places where projects currently struggle to attract capital. Meeting the same demand with decades of new fossil fuel infrastructure could leave us worse off.

So I’m hopeful, but the benefit has to be earned. We already know many of the things we need to build to address climate change, including transitioning to clean energy. AI’s greatest contribution may be helping make it affordable and deployable at scale. We should judge its impact by whether it accelerates that progress and whether countries and communities that currently struggle to finance it can share in the benefits.

One of the most exciting aspects of the AI boom is its potential to help the world mitigate and adapt to the climate crisis. Juliet Rothenberg leads the team at Google that’s producing tools to do just that, like the AI weather model WeatherNext, which can now accurately forecast cyclones at least one day earlier than other models, and last year helped the National Hurricane Center predict Hurricane Melissa’s landfall five days in advance. In September, Google rolled out WeatherNext 3, its most advanced and accurate weather model yet. —Jessica Hullinger

What is the single most important action you think the public, or a specific company or government (other than your own), needs to take in the next year to advance the climate agenda?

We need to keep progressing on mitigating climate change, but it’s very clear that we’re headed past the 1.5° Celsius threshold that scientists believe is critical to reducing the most damaging effects of climate change. And especially with the Super El Niño this year, we also need to recognize that climate change is here today. Aligned with the U.N.’s Early Warnings for All initiative, we need to start moving towards a world where no one is surprised by a natural disaster. This means putting in place comprehensive forecasting, monitoring, alerting, and response systems globally, so that we can protect lives and livelihoods from the climate crisis.

What’s one sustainability effort you personally will try to adopt in the next year, and why?

For many of us, air travel is the single largest contributor to our personal carbon footprint; a single long-haul flight can easily eclipse our household, diet, and driving choices combined. We often look at aviation solely through the lens of fuel burn, but short-lived climate forces like contrails actually account for more than a third of aviation's total warming footprint. While my team works on improving the global AI models that have already helped airlines and air traffic control reduce contrails by over half, I want to personally align my consumer habits—making sure my own travel choices support the carriers paving the way for sustainable skies.

That’s why my personal commitment this year is to make my essential travel as contrail-conscious as possible. This means prioritizing airlines that actively participate in contrail avoidance programs, favoring morning or daytime flights when contrails are less warming, or better yet checking out the Google Flights tooltip on the likelihood of contrail warming for a given flight, and also opting for rail over short-haul flights wherever feasible.

What is a climate solution (other than your own) that isn't getting the attention or funding it deserves?

I’ll share a solution from one of our partners: FireSat, by the Earth Fire Alliance. When fully operational, the FireSat constellation will be able to detect a garage-sized wildfire within 20 minutes, anywhere on Earth. Fire authorities say that this will be a gamechanger for their ability to respond to devastating wildfires, like those in France and Spain this summer, because the greatest gift that we can give firefighters is time.

FireSat has the first 4 satellites in orbit, and a 20-minute revisit will be achieved once the constellation reaches 52 satellites. Google.org, Bezos Earth Fund, and the Moore Foundation have all supported FireSat, and more funding is needed to realize the potential of this vision.

What gives you hope about the future of the planet/climate movement?

I’m tremendously optimistic about the ability of AI to accelerate the rate of scientific progress towards climate-friendly technologies. This is a dramatic change since I started working in the field 22 years ago. As a case in point, our climate teams are now able to build software prototypes for things like satellite detection in less than an hour, which previously would have taken months, and now they can even develop novel hardware solutions in months that would previously have taken years.

Climate change won’t be solved by a single silver bullet. It will take hundreds of practical, durable innovations working in parallel to deliver impact at scale, which is why it’s so exciting that the pace of innovation is accelerating dramatically.

Do you think AI will help or worsen the climate crisis? How?

My job day in and day out is to apply AI to help solve the climate crisis, and I’m a big believer in that potential because we're already seeing it in action. For example, our Contrails project targets an impact equivalent to roughly 4% of the impact that today’s warming will have over the next 20 years (known as global warming potential, or GWP20), or 1-2% of the impact over the next 100 years (GWP100). In live commercial flights across U.S. and international airspace, we’ve proven that AI predictions can help pilots cut contrail formation by more than half, avoiding these warming zones in a way that’s just as simple as avoiding turbulence.

We’re also working with dozens of governments that are using our cutting-edge crisis models for hazards like floods, fires, and cyclones in service of our team’s north star: that no one should ever be surprised by a natural disaster coming their way.

title: This Bipartisan Energy Deal Could Clear the Way for Trump's Arch - Mother Jones
authors: Rachel Santarsiero, Stephanie Mencimer, Alex Nguyen, Marianne Lavelle, Dan Gearino, Anna Merlan, Kate Yoder, Sophie Hurwitz, Gabriella Gladney, Jake Bittle

One camp, mainly renewable energy companies and think tanks, have praised a future boom in renewable energy projects such as offshore wind or solar farms, which often get bogged down by lengthy review processes.

text:
Now that the most historic midterm election in memory is almost over, some of the more mundane, and yet potentially significant, issues in the new political landscape are emerging. One of them—far less dramatic than a Blue Texas, the first Black woman Governor, and the “epic fail” of Republican gerrymandering—is a controversial permitting reform deal that has the potential to shape the trajectory of the US energy infrastructure buildout for decades to come. Should this measure pass, it could also expedite President Donald Trump’s construction makeover of Washington, DC.

On Monday, the lame-duck Senate will vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a measure aimed to ease the regulatory barriers of a permitting system that is unanimously considered antiquated. Introduced by a bi-partisan group of Senators in September—Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Heinrich Martin (D-NM), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV)—the bill would overhaul federal environmental regulations and review standards to speed up the development of transmission lines, power grids, power plants, and gas pipelines. But questions over whether streamlining of infrastructure development is worth rolling back foundational environmental protections has erupted in a “civil war” between different factions of the climate movement. And now, because of the impending Democratic majority in Congress, the calculus has changed on whether some Democrats think a better deal can be struck in the new year.

Perhaps the biggest debates over the bill have centered on its proposed acceleration of critical energy infrastructure projects. One camp, mainly renewable energy companies and think tanks, have praised a future boom in renewable energy projects such as offshore wind or solar farms, which often get bogged down by lengthy review processes. The other camp—activists, environmentalists, and lawyers—have warned the bill is a Trojan Horse: it may appear to be environmentally friendly, but contains within it a “drill-baby-drill” pass for the fossil fuel industry. Aside from the energy impact of this legislation, a growing chorus of critics argue that the bill also would give the government permission to gut an array of existing critical historical and cultural regulations, threatening tribal sovereignty and federal public lands, including those in Washington, DC.

Since taking office for a second time, Trump has been seemingly obsessed with an assortment of so-called “beautification” efforts—from a gilded White House Ballroom born from the ashes of the East Wing, to the towering (and fascistic) Triumphal Arch near Arlington National Cemetery, to the “golf course of his dreams” at Haines Point, a public park beloved by DC residents and tourists—all while ignoring mandated congressional approval.

Mounting legal changes, most recently when a federal judge blocked construction of his arch, have delayed much of the construction. But some of his initiatives, such as the East Wing of the White House and the Reflecting Pool, have proceeded despite legal challenges. Historic preservation groups argue that BAAJA would remove a key barrier to Trump’s construction frenzy by recasting National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) that’s been on the books for six decades and is a provision of BAAJA.

Signed by President Johnson in 1966, and championed by Lady Bird Johnson through her beautification campaign, this act has protected both cherished and virtually unknown historical and archeological sites across the country. Christopher Cody, senior associate general counsel for the National Trust for Historic Preservation, a privately funded, nonprofit that works alongside government to save America’s historic sites—helped explain why the law was enacted in the first place. “The federal government was doing things in our communities and in our states that destroyed our historic resources,” he told me, “and the American people wanted a bigger say.” When a wave of urban renewal projects in the 1950s and 60s gutted local landmarks and reorientated regional priorities around the automobile to favor major roadway and highway construction, local and state government leaders “wanted to have a voice before the federal government came into [their] communities and destroyed [their] historic resources.”

According to Cody, BAAJA would gut Section 106 of the NHPA, which is part of the act that requires federal agencies both to consider the effects of their actions on historic properties and places, and consult with local historic preservation, archeological, and landscape experts. “BAAJA would eliminate all Section 106 consultation for all the administration’s projects in DC,” Cody said. “There is a poison pill in this bill that says, at the outset of any undertaking, a federal agency head can simply declare that other considerations outweigh historic preservation.”

Cody acknowledges that these concerns “only a small part of this bill.” But even though small, it is one that would bring sweeping changes in the approval process for construction projects—including where the government is allowed to build. Another fundamental change is how federal agencies consider the “adverse effects” of their projects. In other words, if the proposed construction would significantly diminish the historic integrity of a site, through its location, design, setting, materials, or even the feelings associated with a place. While some of these considerations might be more subjective than others, a watered-down NHPA would give the government full autonomy to determine what is or is not considered to be detrimental. Under this new system, Cody noted, “None of the projects in DC would even qualify as having adverse effects.”

Consider the Triumphal Arch, which the National Park Service identified would have adversely visually affect more than 40 nearby properties, including such significant historical sites such as Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. BAAJA “would move the goalpost,” Cody said, regarding what physical, visual, and character-defining impacts are considered worthwhile to preserve—and which can be bulldozed. “It’s just an incredibly problematic bill,” he concluded, “that is going to lead to more problems than it’s going to solve.”

Recently, John Podesta—former Clinton, Obama, and Biden advisor on climate change and energy policy—said that the proposed permitting bill would hand President Trump “not just a loaded gun” but a “loaded Howitzer” to go after public lands. Moreover, it would “permit stuff that even if it’s illegal can’t be reversed by the courts.” As reported by Heatmap, Podesta said, “They’re going to have a permit gorge like you’ve never seen, not really caring about whether they’re going through the legal steps to do it.”

Of course, the devastation would extend well beyond the historic integrity of buildings and spaces in the Nation’s Capital. Other staunch opponents of the bill, such as the Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF), which is a plaintiff and co-plaintiff on ongoing D.C. construction project lawsuits, argue that the effects will be felt on tribal lands by severing “cultural lifeways” of Native people across the country. “This is really a kind of worst-case scenario for tribal lands and tribal preservation,” said Charles Birnbaum, Founding President and CEO of TCLF. “This country has been known for its erasure of stories, whether it’s tribal lands, or African American communities that were redlined. I don’t really see how we as a culture could allow [the government] to purposely destroy [this] heritage.”

text:
Potential U.S. Policy Shifts Could Benefit ESS, Hydrogen and Solar Businesses, Though Legislative Hurdles Remain

Democratic gains in both chambers of the U.S. Congress following the midterm elections could bring greater scrutiny of President Donald Trump's fossil fuel-focused energy policies. The results have also raised the possibility that Democrats will seek to restore clean energy tax credits and other industry support measures, drawing attention to the North American business prospects of South Korean companies in energy storage systems (ESS), hydrogen and solar power.

Financial and industry sources expect the election results to prompt a reassessment of policy uncertainty across the clean energy sector. South Korea's battery industry, in particular, is looking to North American ESS operations as a potential growth driver. According to market research firm SNE Research, LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI together held approximately 20.9% of the North American ESS market in the first three quarters of 2026, up from 13.4% in the same period last year. The increase reflects a growing market presence for the two companies, rather than the combined share of all three major Korean battery makers.

The Democrats' support for strengthening battery supply chains outside China could create opportunities for South Korean suppliers. The country's major battery makers, including LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On, are working with domestic materials companies such as POSCO Future M and L&F, which produce lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials, as they seek to diversify their raw material supply chains. Lee An-na, an analyst at Yuanta Securities Korea, projected in a research report that North American-made battery cells could gain a cost advantage of more than 40% over Chinese-made products when tariffs and subsidies are taken into account, potentially helping local suppliers expand their market share.

In the solar sector, Hanwha Qcells and OCI Holdings are seen as potential beneficiaries because of their production facilities and supply chains outside China. Hanwha Qcells began producing solar cells at its facility in Cartersville, Georgia, in July 2026, while OCI Holdings has established a non-Chinese polysilicon supply chain through its Malaysian subsidiary. Equipment manufacturers such as GnBS Eco could also benefit if investment in U.S. solar manufacturing facilities picks up.

However, a change in congressional control is unlikely to lead to sweeping policy shifts immediately. Although Democrats won majorities in both chambers, they do not hold the two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate needed to override a presidential veto. An industry official said major changes to laws and policies could therefore be limited, while negotiations with the administration could still lead to gradual adjustments.

Potentially tighter oversight of data centers is another factor for the industry. If lawmakers introduce stricter requirements for AI-related infrastructure and data center electricity use, some new projects could face additional constraints. On the other hand, requiring large power consumers to bear more of the costs of grid upgrades could increase demand for alternative power solutions and related equipment. The extent to which companies such as Enchem, Doosan Fuel Cell and mPLUS benefit will depend on their ability to secure specific projects and convert orders into revenue.

Ultimately, South Korean companies' prospects will depend not only on policy developments but also on their ability to win orders and establish competitive local production bases. While the election results have changed the policy outlook, the timing and scale of any impact on individual companies will vary according to customers' investment schedules and facility ramp-up plans.

title: China goes Detroit with full-size family SUV EVs that roads can't bear - Notebookcheck
authors: Daniel Zlatev, Daniel went, from the infinite scroll, move of our existence
description:
The reasons that the Chinese automakers in the world's largest car market are doing it are the same that Detroit does it for: demand and profit.
In other words, the typical new Chinese EV is now the kind of vehicle one would expect to see in a Texas parking lot.
The US is also noticing the impact of the heavier electric vehicles on road surfaces.
According to some studies, electric cars are damaging road infrastructure much more than ICE vehicles, as they are heavier.
That is why states are increasingly mulling or implementing an EV road tax that is often higher than the one for gas vehicles.
text:
Chinese carmakers used to be known for compact, city-friendly EVs. That reputation is fading fast. According to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), SUVs measuring 5 to 5.5 meters (16.4 to 18 feet) made up 56% of all new SUV launches in the first ten months of 2026. In 2024, that figure sat at just 17%, as the market share of full-size damily SUVs more than tripled in size in the span of just two years.

The reasons that the Chinese automakers in the world's largest car market are doing it are the same that Detroit does it for: demand and profit. CPCA chief Cui Dongshu blames fierce price competition, with large SUVs and MPVs serving as a showcase for technology and a way to protect margins. The end of subsidies and rising costs have also hurt small car development.

It's not just SUVs, as the newly announced BYD Altior limo can attest. Among new energy vehicle launches, the share of models longer than 5 meters has climbed from 34% to 58% in two years, while the 4.5 to 5 meter class has shrunk from 55% to 40%. In other words, the typical new Chinese EV is now the kind of vehicle one would expect to see in a Texas parking lot.

Bigger bodies mean bigger batteries, and that’s where the trouble starts. Nio CEO William Li recently pointed out that some models carry packs of up to 120 kWh weighing 700 to 800 kg (1,543 to 1,764 lbs). By his math, a car that is 1.2 times heavier does roughly 2.07 times the damage to the road. That comes from the "fourth-power law" of pavement engineering, in which damage scales with axle load raised to the fourth power.

Nio is practicing what Li preaches, as its packs typically weigh 400 to 500 kg (882 to 1,102 lbs), which means accepting smaller capacity and making up for the lost range with more efficient drivetrains. He admits he doesn’t know whether the market will reward that. Each extra kilogram (2.2 lbs) also needs his personal sign-off in terms of added value.

Local regulators are starting to react, too. A new mandatory energy-consumption standard that took effect in January ties limits to curb weight, and authorities are reportedly studying a weight-based tax. Cui has also suggested standards for economy cars and support for micro EVs. In the meantime, China's EV industry is making the same bet Detroit once did with upsizing.

The US is also noticing the impact of the heavier electric vehicles on road surfaces. According to some studies, electric cars are damaging road infrastructure much more than ICE vehicles, as they are heavier. The Highway Trust Fund that is responsible for their maintenance, however, faces a funding shortfall just as EV adoption increases. That is why states are increasingly mulling or implementing an EV road tax that is often higher than the one for gas vehicles.

text:
THE British government is expected to cut its electric vehicle sales target for 2030 by about a quarter to around 60%, the Guardian said on Sunday, citing government sources.

The 2024 mandate requires carmakers to ensure zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) contribute a rising share of annual sales, with the 2026 target of 33%, rising to 80% in 2030 and 100% by 2035.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, is expected to finalise the plan after a meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday, the newspaper said.

Haigh will probably approve a 2030 target of about 60% and extend flexibility until 2034, it added.

"The government is united in its commitment to the ZEV mandate, and no decisions have been taken," a government spokesperson told Reuters, reaffirming commitment to the 2030 phase-out of all new cars with only petrol and diesel engines.

The mandate consultation would not alter the zero-emissions target for all new car and van sales by 2035, the spokesperson added.

Options set out in August by Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government could ease pressure on carmakers to switch new sales to zero-emission vehicles, with existing targets under review.

Carmakers say supply chain disruptions and poor consumer demand make it tough to comply with the mandate.

Battery-electric vehicles made up 26.6% of new car sales year to date, off the 33% target for 2026, the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders said last week, urging "substantive" target changes to pull them closer to demand. - Reuters

name: North Carolina Environment
title: Lessons from Apex: How Community Perspectives Can Shape Better Data Center Policy
description:
Apex and Public Opinion about Data Centers Taking a step back, the concerns raised by Apex residents are largely emblematic of public opinion on local data center development generally.
Data centers are currently facing considerable pushback across the country, with high-profile community mobilizations happening in Tucson, Northern Virginia (the “Data Center Alley”), and Memphis.
A Roadmap for Local Governments As demonstrated in Apex, local governments, residents, and community organizers often don’t see eye to eye on what a new data center means to the community.
Instead, existing framework incentivizes data center development through aggressive tax exemptions, including sales-and-use tax breaks on construction, equipment, and electricity.
[8] Our findings underscore the need for the North Carolina state government to critically assess its data center development policies.
text:
The rise of AI and cloud services over the past decade has brought a rapid buildout of data centers to meet surging compute demands. As a global leader in AI, the United States hosts approximately 5,400 of the world’s 12,000 global data centers—a number that is projected to grow 10 percent annually through 2030.[1]

North Carolina has emerged as a key destination in this national expansion. The state currently hosts at least 97 data centers.[2] That number is expected to roughly double over the next decade as firms like Amazon and Apple continue to invest in large-scale data center infrastructure in the state. Companies are drawn to North Carolina by its affordable land, robust energy grid, strategic East Coast location, and favorable tax incentives.

However, this rapid development raises critical questions about localized impacts on the communities in which data centers are built. Residents increasingly worry about surging utility rates, water and energy consumption, and environmental and health risks like air and noise pollution. These concerns have sparked community pushback against proposed developments across the state and country. Examining local perspectives is critical to ensuring residents do not bear the costs of technological development.

Study Background

A team of graduate student researchers from Duke University collaborated with the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society to study community perspectives on new data center development in North Carolina. The Benton Institute was interested in this research for several reasons, including its work with the Blue Ridge Broadband Alliance in Western North Carolina, and the emerging national conversation around AI adoption, data centers, and their relationships with broadband. The research team’s goal was to understand the benefits and challenges identified by communities when data centers come to town, and how these perspectives can help shape policies that mitigate harms and expand local benefits.

A real-world case of community engagement with a data center project emerged during project design, so the study specifically focused on Apex, North Carolina, where the New Hill Digital Campus was proposed in September 2025. If built, the Digital Campus would have spanned 190 acres and consumed 300 megawatts at peak capacity.[3]

When plans for the Digital Campus became public, tensions quickly emerged between Apex residents, local policymakers, and the developer, Natelli Investments. Concerned residents organized to voice their concerns and urge the town to reject the proposal. Natelli tried to address questions and frame the Digital Campus as a critical source of tax revenue for the town. Town officials, caught in the middle, attempted to weigh the potential economic benefits of the Digital Campus with the environmental and social harms to make a decision on whether or not to allow the development. These tensions made Apex a great case study to understand how community voices can shape smarter, more proactive infrastructure policies.

Research Findings

The research team interviewed eight Apex community members and five subject matter experts to identify what issues were most salient and pressing in the community. Five core themes emerged from these conversations: transparency of the plan, pollution, financial investment, governance and regulation, and resource use and extraction.

1. Transparency of the Plan

Community members overwhelmingly felt that Natelli Investments was not transparent about its plan for Digital Campus’s operations. They raised numerous transparency concerns including the misrepresentation of megawatt usage, failure to address questions about utility prices, and lack of disclosure around the project’s evaporative water-cooling process. Participants were also frustrated that negotiations between Natelli and local policymakers were held behind closed doors and with minimal community input. Notably, community members didn’t know which technology company would be occupying the Digital Campus.

2. Pollution

Community members and experts were afraid that the New Hill Digital Campus would pollute the town’s air, water, and soundscape, putting residents at risk of environmental health hazards. Participants were primarily concerned about water and noise pollution. They feared that polishing and aerosolization during the evaporative cooling process would leave contaminants in local water sources and deposit corrosive minerals on nearby homes and cars, resulting in damaged property and negative health outcomes for the community. Many also voiced worries about the persistent, low-frequency hum associated with data centers, which could disrupt the lives and sleep of residents, particularly children and neurodivergent individuals.

3. Financial Investment

Community members were skeptical that the Digital Campus would create the financial benefit promised by Natelli Investments—namely job creation, tax revenue, and economic development. Some participants also worried that benefits would not be distributed to the local community, but would instead be received by landowners, developers, out-of-town workers, and consumers of digital services. While some participants acknowledged short-term economic benefits like temporary construction jobs, they anticipated limited meaningful impacts in the long run.

4. Governance and Regulation

Community members felt that local policies and governments failed to protect the community from the potential adverse impacts of data centers. Notably, some participants worked in the technology sector and were deeply familiar with AI and data center infrastructure, with multiple sharing that they were not against AI. However, they were frustrated with the lack of adequate regulation to curb the pace of development and mitigate specific harms to health, the environment, and the local community. Some participants pointed to specific legislation that they supported—such as North Carolina House Bill 1002, which would protect residents from utility rate increases caused by data centers. Notably, multiple community members shared appreciation for Apex officials that they felt were taking the Digital Campus seriously and listening to the community’s concerns.

5. Resource Use and Extraction

Community members were concerned that the Digital Campus would lead to the overuse and overextraction of finite local resources—such as water, land, electricity, and fuel—resulting in a lower quality of life for Apex residents. These concerns were closely tied with the scale and intensity of the project.

Concerns about electricity were especially prominent. Many North Carolina residents experienced blackouts amid the back-to-back winter storms and prolonged freezing temperatures that hit the South in recent winters. As a result, they did not trust the local power grid to deliver consistent service once the new data center went online. In addition, community members worried that the data center would result in surging utility prices.

Apex and Public Opinion about Data Centers

Taking a step back, the concerns raised by Apex residents are largely emblematic of public opinion on local data center development generally. Data centers are currently facing considerable pushback across the country, with high-profile community mobilizations happening in Tucson, Northern Virginia (the “Data Center Alley”), and Memphis.[4] According to a Gallup poll conducted in March, 2026, 7 in 10 Americans oppose local construction of AI data centers.[5]

As in Apex, Americans are also mixed on data center impacts in different areas. A Pew Research poll conducted in January found that Americans generally view data centers as being negative in terms of environmental impacts, home energy costs, and local quality of life, but are more likely to anticipate positive economic impacts.[6] This reflects the mood in Apex: while environmental harms and utility costs sparked widespread alarm, residents viewed the project’s economic promises with mild skepticism rather than major concern.

A Roadmap for Local Governments

As demonstrated in Apex, local governments, residents, and community organizers often don’t see eye to eye on what a new data center means to the community. While government officials may view these projects as an economic boon, many community members and activists fear that they’ll strain local infrastructure, put residents’ health at risk, deteriorate the beauty and of the community, and fall short on promises to grow the local economy.

To confront these tensions, local governments should establish mechanisms or procedures for accountability with or for the community. The research team’s analysis of the case study and review of guidance for host communities suggests that local governments incorporate both independent expertise and systematic community input when considering data center projects. We propose the following five-step roadmap that local governments can adopt to align infrastructure decisions with local priorities and context.

Step 1: Engage Independent Expertise at the Start of Negotiations

At the beginning stages of negotiations for a large digital infrastructure project, local governments should consult with independent, unbiased experts who can assess the technical, environmental, and economic impacts. This may require maintaining pre-approved consultant lists or establishing accountability mechanisms for developers. In the Apex case, this step may have reduced concern that the developer was misrepresenting the energy use associated with the facility by providing a trusted evaluation for all stakeholders to review.

Step 2: Inform the Community and Gather Their Priorities Early

Local governments should establish formal processes for gathering community input on the proposed data center infrastructure, such as through public forums. Community engagement should begin as early as possible—ideally before plans are officially filed—and continue consistently and transparently throughout all stages of zoning and approval. We also recommend that local leaders proactively seek input on the areas of resource use, pollution, financial investments, transparency, and governance. Current practices that shroud data center negotiations in secrecy produce distrust in the community; opening the process to the community offers greater opportunity for residents’ participation and to gain buy-in.

Step 3: Consider the Full Range of Policy Tools

Local governments should evaluate multiple policy mechanisms, drawing from existing toolkits and best practices like MediaJustice’s Site Fight Guide.[7] Policy interventions include but are not limited to community benefits agreements (CBAs), moratoriums, conditional use permits, zoning ordinances, and strict water and energy use regulations. There is not necessarily one solution for all communities when it comes to data centers: consider those protections that assuage community concerns. While the Apex case ended in a withdrawn proposal, a set of policy interventions may have created conditions that residents could live with.

Step 4: Tailor Policy Tools to Local Context

Once a policy choice is identified, the choice should then be carefully tailored to reflect the specific priorities identified through community engagement. Any regulatory framework should directly incorporate local preferences into concrete demands and requirements. This step was not part of the Apex case, where it would have allowed local officials to bridge the gap between abstract community feedback and enforceable zoning regulations.

Step 5: Use Community Priorities to Evaluate and Choose From Policy Options

Local governments should make their ultimate decision by evaluating all policy options in the context of the community’s biggest priorities. This can be done by referring back to each of the top priorities identified in Step 2 and deciding—such as through explicit criteria—whether they are reflected by the policy. Where feasible, governments can conduct a full cost-benefit analysis that reflects the local harms and benefits to the community. In the Apex Case, this approach would have provided a structured mechanism to weigh the project’s projected economic benefits against the community’s concerns.

Lessons for North Carolina State Government and Advocates

Listening to residents leads to better infrastructure decisions

The study identified key takeaways for state governments and advocates. Specifically, participants noted that North Carolina lacks statewide policies to protect residents. Instead, existing framework incentivizes data center development through aggressive tax exemptions, including sales-and-use tax breaks on construction, equipment, and electricity.[8]

Our findings underscore the need for the North Carolina state government to critically assess its data center development policies. Specifically, the resident perspectives gathered in this study justify a formal review of existing tax incentives to ensure these corporate benefits do not overshadow community priorities. While the state recently repealed the electricity tax exemption in its July budget, incentives for support equipment, software, and business property remain active.[9] These localized insights signal that expanding statewide policies is a necessary step to safeguard the long-term interests of residents. The state can also look to expand policies to protect the priorities and interests of their residents. North Carolina can also direct its AI Leadership Council—which is tasked with driving innovation and advancing trustworthy AI—to integrate community engagement into its research into the impacts of new data centers on residents.[10]

For advocacy groups, the findings highlight a clear path forward: mobilize early to force community perspectives into local infrastructure decisions. When a community faces risks from a proposed data center, proactive intervention is critical. Initiating dialogue with local governments and developers during the earliest planning phases ensures that resident concerns are factored into the project before agreements are finalized. Additionally, advocates can take steps to assist local governments in following the proposed roadmap. For example, advocacy groups can curate lists of independent experts that the government can consult with, and direct governments to existing resources.

As data centers continue to expand across North Carolina and the country, Apex highlights an important lesson: listening to residents leads to better infrastructure decisions. After Natelli Investments pulled its application due to community pushback, the town heard its residents and took an encouraging first step—placing a 12-month moratorium on new data center projects in order to research local impacts. By continuing down this road and centering community perspectives, Apex can set a bold example for how to design infrastructure policy that works for the people—not against them.

To learn more about the findings and takeaways from this research, read the full report.

Muniba Khan is a Master of Public Policy candidate at Duke University's Sanford School of Public Policy, concentrating in technology policy. Her work examines the community impacts of emerging technologies, technology governance, and digital equity.

title: This Midwest farm once raised thousands of hogs. Why is it growing mushrooms instead?
description:
