text:
For the next two weeks, country leaders will be in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual United Nations climate conference, called COP31. This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will loom over the negotiations. Now in its ninth month, the war has sparked a global energy crisis. The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz and spiking oil and natural gas prices have laid bare the fragility of relying on fossil fuels.

But this energy crisis – unlike the energy crisis in the 1970s and the one following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – is different, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

"This is the first time you've really had a global energy shock where you've got really cheap solutions to address it," Bond says.

Those solutions include solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles. In recent months, countries around the world have pivoted sharply towards these technologies. Many of them are produced in China and offer economic security, as well as reduced emissions.

The economic case for climate solution technologies will make it easier for countries to support them at the conference, Bond says. "There's much more opportunity, I think, for people to get behind change at COP."

Here are three things you need to know about this year's COP.

It's all about electrification

Climate technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Bond says that's why some are calling this "the electrification COP."

"The big target that the COP is setting is for the world to increase the electrification rate from around 23% today to around 35% by 2035," Bond says. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra."

These electrification goals assume countries will grow their electricity mix with cleaner renewable energy. Energy experts say that is a reasonable assumption, because that's what has been happening in recent years. Large solar and wind projects provide more cost-competitive energy than natural gas and coal projects, according to financial services firm Lazard.

"Think about solar, wind," says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. "More green energy will help you decarbonize better and faster."

Roadmap off fossil fuels

As the COP process enters its 31st year, many countries have argued that the U.N. process has not done enough to tackle the single biggest driver of climate change: burning fossil fuels.

Fossil fuel producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have consistently opposed having fossil fuel language in the text of final conference agreements.

In April, more than 50 countries came together to discuss ways to phase out oil, gas, and coal at the First International Conference to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels. Conference organizers told NPR the conference was a way to complement the U.N. process.

More than 25 of those nations are developing a legally binding treaty that would advance a phase-out of fossil fuels. Supporters of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative hope more countries will join their cause at COP31.

The U.S. is not in the room

The U.S. State Department told NPR in an email that the U.S. will not be sending a delegation to COP31. They also did not send anyone to last year's COP in Brazil.

WASHINGTON D.C. — More than 300 solar and storage companies are urging Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), S. 5653, warning that outdated federal permitting processes and grid infrastructure bottlenecks are delaying critical energy projects and driving up electricity costs.

In a letter to congressional leaders, the companies call on lawmakers to quickly send the bipartisan legislation to the President’s desk. The signatories note that solar and storage account for 70% of new electricity capacity added to the grid thus far in 2026, while $120 billion in clean energy investment remains caught in permitting delays.

“You can’t lower energy costs if you can’t build the energy projects, and these companies know that this bipartisan legislation will help get America building again,” said Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA).

BAAJA would modernize the federal permitting system by ensuring fair treatment for all technologies, protecting lawfully issued permits from politically motivated delays, establishing predictable timelines for federal reviews and judicial proceedings, modernizing transmission planning, and expanding distributed energy resources’ access to wholesale electricity markets.

New SEIA analysis shows that BAAJA could unlock 167 gigawatts of additional solar capacity between 2028 and 2035, bringing solar to over 18% of U.S. electricity generation by 2035. The analysis finds that the bill’s reforms could reduce cumulative power sector CO2 emissions by approximately 20% and avoid $54 billion in public health damages.

The message from more than 300 companies comes as voters made clear in the midterm elections that lowering energy costs is a top concern. Permitting reform is urgently needed to meet rising demand and get more reliable, affordable solar and storage projects built.

TAIPEI, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Delta marks its 19th consecutive year of participation in the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (UNFCCC COP31), which opens today in Antalya, Türkiye. Delta will support the host country's "35×35" initiative, targeting a 35% electrification goal by 2035, by sharing how smart microgrids accelerate electrification at an official side event. Earlier, at the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) in late October, Delta partnered with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) to showcase the world's first application of the Species Threat Abatement and Restoration (STAR) metric for coral restoration and conservation assessment. Through international collaboration, Delta addresses climate mitigation and adaptation challenges with technological innovation and ecosystem restoration.

Shan-Shan Guo, Vice Chairperson of the Delta Electronics Foundation, said, "As global electrification accelerates and AI drives growing electricity demand, Delta leverages its core technologies to improve energy efficiency and resilience through microgrids and smart energy management, support electrification, and help AI data centers increase their use of clean energy. As Delta celebrates its 55th anniversary, we are participating in international climate conferences under the theme 'Smarter is Greener.' At COP31, our EMEA leadership and Foundation colleagues will engage with international thought leaders at official side events and the France Pavilion. We also shared our coral restoration experience and achievements at CBD COP17. Through innovative technology, we hope to collaborate with climate partners and move forward toward a more sustainable future."

During COP31, Delta will host its 9th official side event in the Blue Zone, joining the Association for Renewable Energy and Clean Technology (REA) and the German Federal Environmental Foundation (DBU) to exchange insights on microgrid applications. Delta will also share its experience deploying microgrids in Indigenous communities to strengthen disaster resilience. In 2025, renewable electricity accounted for 91% of Delta's global electricity consumption, and Delta achieved its RE100 target in 32 countries.

Delta Presents World-Leading Coral Restoration Experience at CBD COP17

Wim Chang, CEO of the Delta Electronics Foundation, said, "Delta combines technology with coral restoration and conservation, aiming to preserve more than half of the coral species in the Pacific Ocean by 2030. This year, in partnership with IUCN, we became the first globally to apply the STAR metric to coral reef areas where Delta conducts restoration. By scientifically quantifying threats to species survival, we aim to make conservation outcomes more measurable and credible."

Nicholas Macfarlane, Head of Conservation Science and Technology at IUCN, said, "We are delighted to have partnered with Delta on the world's first application of the marine STAR metric. This collaboration demonstrates the potential of corporate and scientific partnerships, and we look forward to advancing marine biodiversity through innovative, measurable conservation strategies."

At CBD COP17 in late October, Delta presented its research at the Nature Pavilion, a flagship venue hosted by IUCN. This year, Delta applied the STAR methodology to coral reef areas in Kenting, Taiwan, and calibrated the results against IUCN's global database, aligning its restoration methodology with international standards.

Delta also invited Professor David Obura, lead author of the coral chapter of the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, to a side event at the Ocean Pavilion. Together with international organizations including the UK's Plymouth Marine Laboratory (PML) and the International Coral Reef Society (ICRS), participants discussed ways to strengthen coral reef resilience.

From biodiversity conservation to electrification goals, leveraging scientific research and technological innovation to address global environmental challenges remains a core focus for the United Nations. To help the international community combat climate change and biodiversity loss, Delta has participated in two COP summits 22 times, and hosted or been invited to 43 side events to date.

Delta, founded in 1971, and listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (code:2308), is a global leader in switching power supplies and thermal management products with a thriving portfolio of IoT-based smart energy-saving systems and solutions in the fields of industrial automation, building automation, telecom power, data center infrastructure, EV charging, renewable energy, energy storage and display, to nurture the development of smart manufacturing and sustainable cities. As a world-class corporate citizen guided by its mission statement, "To provide innovative, clean and energy-efficient solutions for a better tomorrow," Delta leverages its core competence in high-efficiency power electronics and its ESG-embedded business model to address key environmental issues, such as climate change. Delta serves customers through its sales offices, R&D centers and manufacturing facilities spread over close to 200 locations across 5 continents.

Throughout its history, Delta has received various global awards and recognition for its business achievements, innovative technologies and dedication to ESG. Since 2011, Delta has been listed on the Dow Jones Best-in-Class World Index (formerly the DJSI World Index of Dow Jones Sustainability™ Indices) for 15 consecutive years. Delta has also won CDP with double A List for 4 times for its substantial contribution to climate change and water security issues and has been named Supplier Engagement Leader for its continuous development of a sustainable value chain for 8 consecutive years.

text:
Input

2026-11-09 18:13:55

Updated

2026-11-09 18:13:55

[Financial News] Academics and the government agreed that the benchmark for assessing greenhouse gas emissions from cars should shift from tailpipe emissions to life-cycle assessment (LCA), which covers everything from production to disposal. But they differed over the carbon-reduction benefits of EVs as measured by LCA: some said EVs emit no less carbon than internal-combustion vehicles, while others said the gap is growing. The government plans to sharply increase next year its support for small and midsize parts suppliers, which face a heavy burden in calculating LCA figures.

Min Kyung-deok, a professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Seoul National University, and Park Jun-hong, head of the Mobility and Environment Research Center at the National Institute of Environmental Research, each gave a presentation at the 2026 KAIDA Automotive Policy Seminar at FKI Tower in Yeongdeungpo District, Seoul, on the 9th. Their topics were “Proposals for Automotive Environmental Policy in an Era of Major Transformation in the Automotive Industry” and “The Current State of Environmental Regulations for Motor Vehicles Manufactured in Korea and Future Directions,” respectively.

■ “EVs also emit as much carbon as internal-combustion vehicles”

Current regulations on greenhouse gas emissions from cars count only the carbon dioxide (CO2) emitted from the tailpipe while a vehicle is being driven. EVs, which have no tailpipe, are calculated as having “zero” emissions. LCA, by contrast, adds up all the carbon emitted over a vehicle’s lifetime, from extracting raw materials and manufacturing parts and the vehicle to driving, scrapping and recycling it.

Professor Min pointed out, “All of our country’s current policies, regulations and incentives are determined by whether CO2 or exhaust gases come out of the tailpipe.”

He said, “Nitrogen oxides (NOx) and fine particulate matter (PM) have an immediate impact on city residents, but CO2 is a global problem,” adding, “It is somewhat more appropriate to view CO2 from an LCA perspective.” Air pollutants harm the areas where they are emitted, whereas CO2 contributes to global warming no matter where it is released.

As supporting evidence, he cited LCA data released by Hyundai Motor. Total carbon emissions across the life cycle, from production to disposal, were 39.9 tCO2eq (tonnes of CO2 equivalent) for the internal-combustion version of the Hyundai Kona and 33.2 tCO2eq for the Hyundai Kona Electric. The electric commercial vehicle Hyundai ST1 recorded 42.3 tCO2eq, while the second-generation Hyundai Nexo recorded 39.2 tCO2eq, including 3.6 tonnes from parts manufacturing. EVs emit less while being driven, but produce substantial carbon emissions during battery manufacturing.

Professor Min explained, “People think EV emissions are zero, but from an LCA perspective, EVs emit no less carbon than internal-combustion vehicles,” adding, “Much more CO2 is emitted when batteries are made.”

LCA is already being factored into subsidies overseas. France converts the carbon footprint of production and transport into an environmental score and provides subsidies only for EVs scoring 60 or higher. The United Kingdom sets subsidy levels according to the electricity carbon-emissions factors of the countries where vehicles are assembled and battery cells are produced. The system means that cars made in countries with a higher share of coal-fired power receive smaller subsidies.

In Korea, a draft notice on “Regulations on Methods for Life-Cycle Assessment of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Motor Vehicles” was announced for public comment on the 7th of last month. However, manufacturers submit the information voluntarily if they choose, so it is not yet linked to regulations or subsidies. Professor Min proposed that subsidies and other systems should also shift to an LCA basis over the long term.

On hybrids, he said, “They can certainly play a role for the next 20 to 30 years,” adding, “To do that, their efficiency must also improve.” He also called for increased investment, noting that although the government’s overall R&D budget rose 19.5% this year, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy’s automotive R&D budget fell 6.9%, from 499 billion won to 464.5 billion won.

■ “LCA is still an estimate ... support for small and midsize parts suppliers to increase”

Center Director Park urged caution in interpreting LCA results. “LCA is based on modeling and, in a sense, is closer to an estimate,” he said. “Most of the research results currently available are at Level 1 or 2, with a high degree of uncertainty.”

LCA is divided into Levels 1 through 4 according to precision. Levels 1 and 2 estimate a vehicle’s carbon emissions using average values from commercial databases. Starting at Level 3, measured data—including the energy used in the actual manufacturing process and the proportion of recycled materials—is incorporated for key components that account for a large share of carbon emissions. Greater precision increases reliability, but also places a heavier burden on parts suppliers, who must calculate the data themselves.

The United Nations World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations (WP29) considers Level 3 the minimum required to use LCA for regulations or government reporting. The idea is that calculations need to be more precise when used for policymaking. France and the United Kingdom, however, set EV subsidies using less detailed calculations. Under the two countries’ systems, vehicles produced outside Europe are excluded from subsidy eligibility.

Center Director Park said, “They use simple Level 1 or 2 calculations for subsidies,” adding, “You can probably guess why.” He was pointing out that LCA is being used to favor vehicles produced domestically or within the region, rather than to assess carbon emissions precisely.

His view differed from Professor Min’s on EV assessments. LCA assumes a vehicle is used for 15 to 20 years and calculates emissions over that period as well. Center Director Park said, “If the expansion of renewable energy over that time is also factored in, the figure for EVs could be lower than the values currently known.” In other words, as electricity generation becomes cleaner, the carbon emissions associated with the electricity used to charge EVs also fall.

He said, “A few years ago, some results showed hybrids and EVs were comparable, but recent results seem to show that the gap is growing.”

On institutionalizing LCA, he said, “There is a very long way to go,” and stated that the government would take a phased approach. First it will establish a calculation method, then proceed to voluntary reporting by manufacturers, and then introduce standards. Incentives will also be considered as part of the process.

He also outlined plans to expand support for small and midsize parts suppliers. Center Director Park said that large manufacturers such as Hyundai Motor are building up their capabilities, while smaller suppliers further down the supply chain are facing considerable difficulties.

He said, “Under a 2025–2026 pilot program, we are spending around 1.2 billion won a year to support small businesses with their calculations,” adding, “We plan to sharply increase the level of support next year.” The plan is to broaden assistance beyond calculation and verification to include consulting on emissions-reduction technologies. He said the specific amount could be disclosed after the National Assembly’s budget review.

■ “Cars as a main source of fine-dust pollution is an outdated notion” ... Greenhouse gas standards pressure automakers to “switch power sources”

He assessed that efforts to control emissions from internal-combustion vehicles had delivered results. Compared with their peak levels in the 2000s, the share of total air pollutant emissions attributable to road vehicles (mobile sources on roads) had fallen by 2023 from 46% to 2% for PM10, from 42% to 28% for NOx, and from 17% to 3% for volatile organic compounds (VOCs).

Center Director Park stressed, “Vehicle exhaust emissions have fallen so much that I can say the claim that cars are a major source of fine-dust pollution is no longer valid.”

On greenhouse gas standards, he explained, “They may appear to regulate tailpipe CO2, but in practice they are a system that requires a shift in power sources.” As the standards become stricter, improving the efficiency of internal-combustion vehicles alone will no longer be enough to meet them, making a successive shift to hybrids, plug-in hybrids and EVs unavoidable.

According to Center Director Park, hybrids, too, have difficulty reducing CO2 emissions below 90 grams per kilometer because of the characteristics of their systems. Meeting the 2030 standard of 70 g/km with room to spare would require plug-in-hybrid-level performance. In July, the government announced for public comment a proposal to tighten the standard to 54 g/km. By August this year, the share of zero-emission vehicles (EVs and hydrogen vehicles) among new passenger cars had exceeded 24% for the first time.

Regulations are also being prepared for pollutants produced beyond the tailpipe. These are fine particles generated as brakes and tires wear down, and are considered a source of fine dust and microplastics. The European Union (EU) began applying standards for wear particles to newly introduced brake systems this month, and Korea is also considering adopting them.

For tires, discussions on international testing methods are being delayed because results from tests conducted on actual roads do not match those from indoor drum testing equipment. The government is pursuing domestic legislation, in consultation with industry and importers, for the Euro 7 heavy-duty vehicle standards that take effect in 2028.

text:
Samsung will supply cells to BMW facilities in Europe while LG will provide them to plants in the US starting in the late 2020s, BMW said Monday. In Europe, BMW also uses cells from China’s CATL and EVE Energy Co.

The new partnerships come as BMW is scaling up production globally of its sixth-generation high-voltage batteries. The parts are central to its new generation of electric models such as the iX3 sport utility vehicle. The company is accelerating the phase-out of its older battery models, it said last week.

Along with a facility in China, the manufacturer has built up assembly plants for its latest batteries in Germany, Hungary, Mexico and South Carolina. It’s pushing to reduce distances between its suppliers that feed cells into those sites, and where it makes cars, it said.

The decision underscores how European and US carmakers are pushing to curtail their reliance on key components out of China. The country dominates global battery production and the processing of key materials, leaving carmakers exposed on capacity closer to their plants in Europe and North America.

Separately, the European Union is working on new regulation to encourage more local manufacturing. The rules as part of the Industrial Accelerator Act target certain thresholds where a majority of a vehicle must be made in the bloc to qualify for a range of subsidies.

text:
CHRISTIANA, Tenn. — As sunlight fell between the gaps in flinty November clouds, I found myself impressed by the quietness of the lawn mowers in a Middle Tennessee solar field. Instead of the obnoxious roar of diesel engines, they just produced an occasional moo.

Six months ago, Tennessee’s largest solar developer, Silicon Ranch, channeled its nomenclature and brought cattle to this 3.25-megawatt solar project. The 15-member herd rotates among 15 paddocks marked out by simple electrical wire, munching Bermuda grass that grows in the shade of the panels, which sit on higher-than-usual steel piles. The cows seem amenable to the situation, judging by how plump they’ve become in that short time.

This is the first commercially viable utility-scale project combining solar and cattle farming in the U.S., according to Silicon Ranch (an earlier 2-MW project from AES sought to prove the concept in Massachusetts’ community solar market). If the model takes off, it could boost revenues for farmers while producing more clean, cheap electricity in regions that don’t have a lot of wide-open, unused spaces to develop. And it might remedy a major obstacle to ongoing solar growth.

The U.S. builds more solar installations than any other form of power plant these days. But the industry’s upstart success story is colliding with a bulwark of local opposition from communities that don’t like the idea of this relatively new technology taking over their landscapes. One way around that conflict is to use the same land for solar power and agriculture.

The solar industry already has adopted sheep grazing as a mainstream approach to cutting grass at project sites, while supporting a secondary market for domestic meat. Researchers have also found that grasses and some crops grow better in the shade of photovoltaic panels than in an open field. But the burgeoning ​“agrivoltaics” sector has almost entirely excluded one of the major pillars of American agriculture — cattle ranching — for the simple reason that rambunctious bovines could easily wreck the carefully calibrated solar panels.

“If you’re designing a solar facility that is suitable for cattle grazing, it generally requires more specific and unique design,” said Terry Jennings, principal team leader for renewable energy at the Electric Power Research Institute, a nonprofit that studies the electricity sector. That ​“adds cost to the overall project, which is challenging for utilities or electric power companies.” But he noted that research on this topic is still pretty new, and a lot of uncertainty remains around ​“how cows really interact with the solar panels.”

To go mainstream, and help meet America’s soaring demand for electricity with more carbon-free generation, cattle-friendly solar needs to appeal to large-scale developers who rigorously maximize megawatt-hours generated per acre while minimizing cost.

In the countryside about 45 minutes southeast of its Nashville headquarters, Silicon Ranch has found that the commonly understood challenges for cattle grazing alongside solar were a little overblown.

“I thought it would work — I just didn’t think it would work this well,” said Loran Shallenberger, a longtime farmer who now runs Silicon Ranch’s Regenerative Energy and Agrivoltaics division.

Shallenberger’s team designed a system to withstand the presence of cows at a minimal cost premium. Even for this first utility-scale installation, they held the cost of fortifying the arrays to just 3% over the standard design, Shallenberger said, and nonetheless sold the power to local utility Middle Tennessee Electric for cheaper than the wholesale rates it was paying to the Tennessee Valley Authority.

As far as climate solutions go, this doesn’t deal with the immense greenhouse gas emissions that arise from cow burps and farts; many climate activists want to phase out commercial cattle entirely for that reason, or for animal welfare motivations. But as long as cattle production is widespread in the U.S., doubling-booking pastureland for solar production could produce more clean energy in a space-constrained world.

Taller piles, strategic tilts, docile cattle

Clever innovations in solar rarely go anywhere. Entrepreneurs might drive a news cycle with ​“solar freakin’ roadways” or solar roof tiles, but to succeed in this market requires ruthless efficiency and streamlined repeatability. Throwing a herd of cattle into the mix does not, at first glance, conform to that industrial mantra.

Shallenberger had ready answers for my journalistic skepticism.

On the hardware side, after studying the matter with a grant from the Department of Energy, Silicon Ranch resisted the urge to build towering solar supports, which would require even more steel underground to ensure stability. Instead, the company developed and patented a system dubbed CattleTracker: mildly elevated steel piles with customized controls for the tracker, supplied by NextPower.

Trackers typically rotate throughout the day to eke every last bit of electricity out of the sun’s arc. At the Christiana solar farm, the trackers in that active paddock go into ​“graze mode,” which limits their rotation from a maximum tilt of 60 degrees from the ground to 20 or 30 degrees — so the lower edges of the panels remain above the animals’ heads. At a regular solar farm, the low end of a fully tilted solar panel is 24 inches off the ground, but I could walk beneath the CattleTracker system with just a little ducking.

The cattle do their part to make this work.

Shallenberger bought a herd of Murray Greys, an Australian breed that ​“are widely regarded as having uniformly calm dispositions” — the kind of cattle you could grab a beer with. That docility makes them less inclined to damage solar equipment or charge at a technician who’s checking out the site. They helpfully don’t grow very tall, and they have ​“consistently good carcasses,” industry lingo for qualities like high meat-to-bone ratio and well-marbled steaks. Plus, Murray Greys can fatten up on grass alone, so they could be ready for market in 18 to 24 months without a stop at a feedlot.

I saw one specimen scratch its head against a steel pile, but none of the herd could reach the sensitive equipment. The concern is that if the cows hit the solar panels hard enough, they could cause microfractures that over time diminish electricity production. Shallenberger said that if he were building the site now, he’d drop the pile height by 6 or 12 inches, because it turned out to be a little overbuilt.

Benefits for cattle and solar alike

The nationwide cattle inventory has fallen to its lowest point in 75 years, as prolonged drought hits the vast arid ranchland of the Western states. Rising beef prices have incentivized ranchers in wetter parts of the country to get into the game. Tennessee, Shallenberger told me, is already one of the biggest cattle states east of the Mississippi.

Abundant local water sources aside, this was a particularly harsh summer in Tennessee.

“If you’ve ever been out in a cattle ranch and there’s a single tree out in the middle of the pasture, they’re going to congregate around it for shade,” Silicon Ranch Chief Commercial Officer Matt Beasley said from his office in Nashville. Consequently, the cattle perform better under the shelter of solar arrays than in the open range, he noted.

The solar canopy also protects the grasses, keeping them green and dewy, even as nearby fields blanch and crisp in the sunlight. Shallanberger rotates the herd every few days, a key tenet of regenerative farming philosophy, so they munch on fresh grass while the rest of the field grows back. They move through all 15 paddocks in about 45 days; if the site relied on mechanical mowers, they’d trim every 45 days, too.

That cycle also keeps the grasses from shading the panels or messing with the machinery.

Vegetation management is one of the most significant costs for solar plant maintenance in the Southeast, Shallenberger said. In the first six months, the cattle took care of about 75% of the mowing — he had to bring in conventional equipment for some woody weeds that the cattle don’t care for. Once the pasture is more established, the herd could handle up to 95% of the site’s mowing needs.

“The team had this anthem: It’s got to be good for the land, good for the animal, and good for the solar,” Beasley said. ​“If it’s not good for all three, we’re not doing it.”

CattleTracker does reduce solar production slightly, given the limited tilt on the small subset of panels in the active paddock. Silicon Ranch is happy to trade that loss for the drastic reduction in major operational costs. The herd doesn’t need the hands-on attention that sheep require; a camera watches to ensure they have enough water, and an attendant visits twice a week to move paddocks and perform a wellness check.

Prospects for growth

Cattle-friendly solar’s bucolic charm is undeniable, but its impact hinges on widespread adoption.

“The hope is that it can be mainstream,” Shallenberger said. He pointed out that it doesn’t take more labor to open a paddock gate for 100 animals as opposed to 10, so the operational cost savings should scale favorably for larger solar projects.

Silicon Ranch expanded its use of sheep for pruning solar fields after its executives got to know Will Harris, a leader in the regenerative farming movement whose land neighbors a Silicon Ranch project in southwest Georgia. The developer acquired 400 ewes in 2022 and has grown the herd to 5,000 through selective breeding. Silicon Ranch also partners with 14 sheep-farming families across six states for managed grazing.

“In the back of our minds has always been, Can we replicate this with cattle?” said Beasley. Now, the team is scouring its development portfolio for sites to deploy CattleTracker. Silicon Ranch builds projects up to 300 MW, and hasn’t found any reason that cattle couldn’t graze at that scale.

“It’s not too long down the road that you’ll be able to try a beef burger or a steak raised on Silicon Ranch land,” Beasley said.

text:
The Democrats’ victory in both chambers of Congress in the 2026 US midterm elections could reshape Washington’s energy policy priorities, with implications for energy investment and US–Gulf economic relations, although experts expect bilateral ties to remain resilient, supported by longstanding investments in conventional energy infrastructure and growing clean energy cooperation.

Oil markets respond to post-election expectations

Inflation and elevated fuel prices emerged as key concerns for voters ahead of the midterms, increasing pressure on Washington to address energy costs amid regional instability. Expectations of renewed US–Iran diplomatic engagement have also weighed on oil prices, as markets assess the prospects of easing tensions and reduced risks to energy supplies.

Brent crude fell below $100 a barrel on November 4 for the first time in nearly a month, following the Democratic sweep in the midterms. Brent dropped to $96.82 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude dropped to $90 per barrel on Monday, at 11:20 am AST Arabia.

“Given the Democrats’ control Congress, there will likely be more scrutiny over the war, while funding it could become more difficult,” ING analysts Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey said in a note Thursday.

Shivkumar Rohira, CEO EMEA at Klay Group, expects the election outcome to increase pressure for diplomatic engagement, although the impact on oil markets will depend on developments in the region.

“We expect the Democratic victory to increase political pressure for de-escalation in the Middle East, particularly in relation to Iran,” Rohira said. “This could gradually reduce the geopolitical risk premium embedded in oil prices, although sustained improvement would depend on tangible progress in regional security and the normalization of shipping routes.”

However, Karen E. Young, senior fellow of the Economics and Energy Initiative at the Middle East Institute, said the election outcome could reinforce perceptions that US security commitments in the Middle East are becoming less of a priority, potentially increasing costs for Gulf energy producers.

“For the GCC producers, this raises the cost of CapEx and OpEx, such that export route redundancies, new storage arrangements with customers, and new defensive outlays all make their fiscal obligations tighter,” Young said.

Beyond diplomatic expectations, changes in congressional oversight could also influence US sanctions policy, with implications for global oil supply and Gulf producers.

Young noted that Congress could pressure executive agencies to enforce oil sanctions against Russia more strictly. While “this could be beneficial to Gulf producers,” it would not necessarily ease pressures in refined product markets, she added.

Hamza Dweik, head of trading (MENA) at Saxo Bank, said tougher enforcement of sanctions on Iranian oil could create commercial opportunities for Gulf producers.

“If Iranian barrels become harder or more expensive to move, legitimate producers such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE could capture some of the displaced demand, particularly from Asian refiners,” Dweik said.

Similarly, Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer of Century Financial Services, said stricter enforcement of sanctions on Iranian and Russian crude could tighten global oil supply and strengthen OPEC+ pricing leverage.

“However, the group’s response would depend on available spare capacity, demand conditions, inventory levels and the extent of actual supply disruptions,” Valecha added. Despite these potential policy shifts, analysts caution against overstating Congress's ability to shape international energy markets, given the executive branch's authority over foreign policy and sanctions implementation.

“Congress has considerable influence, but Democratic control of Congress does not mean Democrats now control US trade or foreign policy,” said Rickinder Chima, global economist at BMI, a Fitch Solutions company.

Impact on energy investments

Despite potential shifts in US energy policy following the midterms, analysts expect investment ties between the US and Gulf economies to remain resilient, supported by longstanding commercial relationships and substantial commitments across conventional energy, LNG infrastructure, and clean energy technologies.

Gulf sovereign wealth funds have expanded their exposure to US energy assets and technology companies, while US firms continue to invest in major energy projects across the GCC, supporting the region's economic diversification and energy transition strategies.

In October, US-based Activate Capital, a growth equity investment firm focused on energy technology and smart infrastructure, joined the Qatar Investment Authority's (QIA) $3 billion Fund of Funds program.

QIA also participated in a consortium to acquire US energy company AES Corporation in March 2026 for $15 per share in cash, valuing the company's equity at approximately $10.7 billion.

Meanwhile, the UAE's Mubadala Energy entered the US energy market in August 2025 by acquiring a 24.1% stake in Caturus, an integrated natural gas and LNG platform focused on supplying lower-emission fuel to domestic and international markets.

Investment flows also extend in the opposite direction. In May 2023, US-based Air Products & Chemicals partnered with Saudi Arabia's NEOM Company, backed by the Public Investment Fund (PIF), and ACWA Power to develop an $8.4 billion green hydrogen facility in NEOM.

Daniel Brett, Head of Research and Data at Global SWF, said Gulf sovereign wealth funds may adopt a more cautious approach to new US investments requiring regulatory approvals or access to restricted technologies. However, he expects established investment relationships to remain intact.

“Gulf funds have spent years building relationships with US managers and companies and are not going to abandon those because Congress has changed hands,” Brett told Forbes Middle East.

Beyond sovereign wealth fund investments, broader energy partnerships note the scale of economic ties between the US and Gulf states.

The UAE plans to increase its existing $70 billion investment in the US energy sector to $440 billion by 2035, according to statements made by ADNOC CEO Sultan Al Jaber in 2025. The planned investments are expected to generate $29 billion in annual economic impact and support 470,000 American jobs, according to the UAE Embassy in Washington.

In January 2026, ADNOC's international investment arm, XRG, announced plans to increase its stake in Rio Grande LNG by 7.6 percentage points, expanding its investment in the LNG export facility at the Port of Brownsville, Texas.

Saudi Arabia has also strengthened its energy investment ties with the US. In November 2025, Saudi Aramco signed 17 memoranda of understanding (MoUs) and agreements with major US companies, with a combined potential value exceeding $30 billion. These followed $90 billion worth of agreements announced in May 2025, including upstream and downstream projects in Louisiana and South Texas.

Such investments create economic incentives for both political parties to maintain strong commercial ties, according to Valecha. “Those investments mean jobs and tax revenue in districts held by both Democrats and Republicans, so few lawmakers have an interest in seeing the relationship damaged,” he noted.

Chima similarly emphasized the economic benefits Washington derives from its relationships with Gulf investors and businesses. “The US benefits directly from Gulf investment, trade and sales, giving Washington substantial economic interests that should limit the scope for a major deterioration in bilateral trade and investment relations,” Chima explained.

text:
Outdated power grids are a major hurdle in the transition to renewable energy, since older systems often can't absorb all the electricity from new, cleaner sources.

This threatens global efforts to curb climate change by reducing fossil fuels and switching to renewable energy such as solar and wind. At U.N. climate talks kicking off this week, co-hosts Turkey and Australia want more ambitious goals to slash fossil fuels, install renewables and upgrade grids.

Grid concerns are gaining urgency this year as nations race to improve their energy security following the Iran war. The U.N. recently launched a new initiative to rally funding for grid upgrades in Africa and Southeast Asia.

“There needs to be a massive, massive, massive scaling up of investments into grids if we are going to get close to meeting our climate, energy and development goals,” Selwin Hart, special adviser to the U.N. secretary-general on climate action, said.

Climate talks address grid bottleneck

At the U.N. climate talks, hosted in the Turkish resort city of Antalya, organizers describe modern and reliable electric grids as “the backbone of the clean energy system.”

But billions of dollars are needed to upgrade out-of-date grids. These steep costs could hinder further renewable energy installations.

During the U.N. General Assembly in September, the global body launched a Global Grids Accelerator to speed up international funding for electricity infrastructure in Africa and Southeast Asia.

“We’re very confident that the long-term trend is an acceleration of the pace of the energy transition, but we need the infrastructure, grids and storage, to really keep pace,” Hart said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Annual investment in electricity generation, such as building new power plants, has risen by almost 70% since 2015, reaching $1 trillion a year, according to the International Energy Agency. Yet the agency noted annual grid spending has risen at less than half that pace.

To meet electricity demand through 2030, the IEA calculates annual grid investment must increase by about 50% from today’s $400 billion per year. Any delays will substantially increase global emissions by prolonging reliance on fossil fuels, the IEA warns.

“Power grids have not been readied enough for the scaleup of renewable electricity generation,” said Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University. “We have been complacent in the past and now the grid has become a real bottleneck.”

Old grids slow energy transition

Power grids deliver electricity from power plants to homes through a network of transmission and distribution lines, substations and transformers.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Originally designed around large, centralized power plants, many of today's power grids were built like one-way roads, with producers sending electricity to consumers. These older one-directional grids are being overwhelmed by demand surges and a boom in renewables.

Grids have a maximum capacity of electricity that they can safely store, transport and distribute. If a grid is already at capacity, solar and wind farms can be instructed to limit their electricity output, a process known as curtailment.

China and India, which have installed impressive amounts of renewables, can't take full advantage of the massive buildout for this reason.

China curtailed 360 terawatt-hours — close to the equivalent of the United Kingdom's annual electricity demand — of wind and solar electricity in the first half of 2026, according to Global Energy Monitor and the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

India curtailed 11 terawatt-hours of solar generation — enough electricity to power about 10 million homes — over the course of 15 months spanning 2025 and 2026 because of insufficient transmission and storage capacity, according to the energy think tank Ember.

Curtailing solar and wind generation while fossil fuels continue to supply electricity is a blow to climate efforts, especially since China and India are among the world's largest emitters, said James Abraham, with the New Delhi-based Council on Energy, Environment and Water.

To transition away from fossil fuels, he said, "you need a grid changeover. You need a grid transformation.”

Solutions exist, despite funding concerns

Upgrading existing grids to be more flexible could increase efficiency by allowing electricity flows to adjust to supply and demand. It could help areas with excess solar and wind energy send it to places with higher electricity demand and fewer energy resources.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Newer, more flexible grids could also make it easier for utility companies to exchange electricity with households that have solar panels or battery storage.

But many countries can't afford to take these steps, or at least not quickly enough, according to Abraham, who said “the need is now. It’s a time tension rather than anything else.”

Global energy security concerns deepen

The Iran war's energy shock built up momentum for the energy transition, especially in hard-hit regions like Southeast Asia, but investment in renewables is outpacing grid development, said Gahee Han, with the Seoul-based nonprofit Solutions for Our Climate.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Unless we upgrade our power grid in Asia, Asia will have no choice but to rely on the conventional power plants, like gas or coal,” she said. “It’s nonsense to rely on those power plants, especially considering the energy crisis.”

One of the solutions being promoted by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is an interconnected power grid that would allow countries to trade power more easily, adding a safeguard against future shocks.

Interest in the ambitious plan, which is still in its infancy, is growing, according to Abdul Razib Dawood, executive director of the ASEAN Center for Energy.

“We have this crisis that will unify the region. You need your neighbors," he said. “This is an opportunity for us to really strengthen the cooperation.”

title: EU Electrification Action Plan: Powering Europe's Grid | World Economic Forum
authors: Laurent Bataille, Europe Operations, Schneider Electric
description:
Having been constrained by fragmented policies, aging infrastructure and an economic model that favours fossil fuels, the EU announced its Electrification Action Plan in July 2026 as a welcome step.
Moving towards a binding and predictable European electrification target would give businesses the confidence needed to make long-term investment decisions to decarbonize.
Royal Avebe, a Netherlands-based starch and plant‑protein cooperative, just electrified one of its production facilities without requiring reinforcement of the electricity grid.
Addressing the last mile Electrification policy will only succeed if Europe can connect electrification projects to the grid.
The Electrification Action Plan and EU Grids Package must therefore operate as one system plan, rather than two separate policy tracks.
text:
The EU knows it needs to electrify further – but for many in the bloc, that progress is not moving fast enough. Europe can change that though.

Europe’s energy system is stuck in a costly holding pattern. The global energy crises of recent years have reinforced the risks of imported fossil fuels: notably in the form of volatile energy prices, supply insecurity and added exposure to geopolitical events beyond its control.

As emphasized in European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech at the EU Parliament on 16 September 2026, the electrification of Europe’s buildings, infrastructure and industries has been heralded as the solution to Europe’s energy sovereignty, enabling its energy system to run on local, clean power sources. Yet, the bloc’s electrification rate has remained largely stagnant at around 23% over the past decade.

Having been constrained by fragmented policies, aging infrastructure and an economic model that favours fossil fuels, the EU announced its Electrification Action Plan in July 2026 as a welcome step. Its proposed target (albeit non-binding) to reach a 46% electrification rate by 2040 could provide a clearer direction of travel. The European Commission estimates that reaching this level could save the EU up to €260 billion annually on its fossil fuel import bill by 2040.

But Europe cannot afford another decade of slow progress. The real test will be moving from ambition to delivery.

EU electrification's decisive phase

Businesses need certainty that clean electricity will have long-term price competitiveness in comparison to fossil fuels, and that national measures will follow the direction set in Brussels. A factory looking to electrify an industrial process does not need another long-term aspiration. It needs a viable business case, predictable policy, access to funding and confidence that the necessary grid connection will arrive on time.

This requires clearer sector signals and incentives, particularly for the parts of the economy that can move fastest. It also means using EU and national funding to de-risk projects and attract private investment.

The 2040 target is an important start, but a non-binding ambition will only go so far. Moving towards a binding and predictable European electrification target would give businesses the confidence needed to make long-term investment decisions to decarbonize. Collaboration will be equally important. Through the World Economic Forum’s Future of Power Systems initiative, public and private-sector leaders are working to identify how power systems can become more resilient, flexible and investment-ready.

Royal Avebe, a Netherlands-based starch and plant‑protein cooperative, just electrified one of its production facilities without requiring reinforcement of the electricity grid. By focusing on digital energy management, the business provides greater visibility of energy use across its manufacturing environment, supporting more informed operational decisions and helping to decarbonize.

Its upgrades, which included significant hardware changes, show that deeper electrification is possible without waiting on grid expansions. It is a reminder that electrification is not simply about replacing one energy source with another; it is about making industrial energy use more intelligent and more efficient.

These portable power banks deliver fast EV charging where the grid falls short

02:10

Unlocking European energy's low-hanging fruit

Europe can move the dial fastest by prioritizing applications where the technology is already available and the economics can work today.

Take transport. Targeted support for corporate fleet electrification could accelerate demand for electric vehicles while expanding the second-hand EV market, making electric mobility accessible to more people.

Buildings offer another major opportunity, particularly because reducing their energy consumption does not necessarily require people to change their everyday habits.

Existing measures such as the Energy Efficiency Directive and Energy Performance of Buildings Directive can support near-term action. Scaling building automation and control systems could save up to 450 TWh of energy annually, avoid 64 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions and reduce energy bills by €36 billion.

Addressing the last mile

Electrification policy will only succeed if Europe can connect electrification projects to the grid.

Around half of the continent’s grid infrastructure is more than 40 years old. At the distribution level, grid constraints, connection delays and limited visibility are already preventing viable projects from moving into deployment. More than €100 billion of renewable energy and storage projects, representing approximately 830 GW of connection capacity, are waiting for distribution-level grid connections. The Electrification Action Plan and EU Grids Package must therefore operate as one system plan, rather than two separate policy tracks.

Investment in grids is essential, but Europe can also make better use of the infrastructure it already has. Digital grid-enhancing technologies could increase network capacity by between 20% and 40% by 2040 while cutting costs by around 35% compared with traditional expansion.

This is how Europe turns millions of individual technologies into an intelligent, responsive energy system.

Making the economics of electrification work

Ultimately, people and businesses will only electrify at scale if electricity becomes the most attractive economic option.

The Electrification Action Plan correctly recognizes that electricity should not be taxed more heavily than gas. But taxation remains a national competence, so progress will depend on Member States acting with sufficient speed and consistency.

Europe must address the pricing structures, taxes, levies and network charges that distort the comparison between electricity and gas. It must also rebalance incentives away from fossil fuels, and do so with innovative solutions due to fiscally constrained national budgets.

Time to break the deadlock

Electrification will not scale on ambition alone. It must be treated as core European infrastructure, essential to the continent’s security, competitiveness and sustainability.

The Electrification Action Plan is Europe’s opportunity to break free from a decade of stagnation. That means setting a stronger direction, prioritizing sectors ready to move, modernizing the grid and making electricity economically preferable to fossil fuels.

Every euro invested in electrification is a euro invested in Europe’s industrial future, energy resilience and long-term sovereignty. European industry stands ready to accelerate. The opportunity is there. Now, Europe must create the conditions to seize it.

title: Trump Says He Backs Energy Permitting Bill on Eve of Senate Vote
description:

text:
A bipartisan plan to speed the federal approval process for major energy and infrastructure projects received the endorsement of President Donald Trump on the eve of a key Senate vote on the bill.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump said in a social media post Sunday that urged senators to vote in favor the bill.

The Senate is slated Monday to take a procedural vote on the measure, seen as a once-in-a-generation chance to overhaul the byzantine system for approving projects needed to modernize power grids, build artificial-intelligence data centers and revitalize clean energy development.

The legislation is supported from groups including oil companies and renewable energy developers, but faces hurdles to passage in the two remaining months Congress is in session. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is opposing the bill in its current form, arguing it hasn’t received enough input from House Democrats. Other progressive Democrats say they should use their newfound control of Congress next year to negotiate for a better deal.

Democratic Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, as well as Republican Senators Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah, unveiled a new version of the bill Saturday, but several environmental groups said they still opposed it.

“After closely evaluating the full bill and the newly released substitute amendment alongside our state and territorial affiliates, Tribal partners, environmental justice partners, hunting, fishing, and outdoor recreation partners, water coalition partners, and other conservation partners, we have concluded we cannot support the legislation in its current form,” Collin O’Mara, president of the National Wildlife Federation said in a statement Sunday.

title: TELF AG on India's Plans to Strengthen Lithium and Nickel Refining Capacity - Vocal Media
description:
India is expanding its industrial ambitions in the battery materials sector through a new government program designed to support domestic lithium and nickel processing.
Why Is India Expanding Its Lithium and Nickel Processing Capacity?
India's government has recently approved a program worth approximately $297 million to develop new industrial facilities dedicated to lithium and nickel processing.
According to Reuters, the program will finance four facilities: two dedicated to lithium processing and two focused on nickel.
Does India Need Domestic Mineral Deposits to Develop Refining Capacity?
text:
India is expanding its industrial ambitions in the battery materials sector through a new government program designed to support domestic lithium and nickel processing. With approximately $297 million allocated to the initiative, the country aims to develop high-purity mineral products for battery manufacturing and other advanced industrial applications. The strategy reflects a broader transformation in global raw materials policies, where refining capacity and industrial integration are becoming increasingly important components of supply chain competitiveness.

Key takeaway: India's latest initiative highlights the growing importance of mineral processing in national industrial strategies, demonstrating how countries can strengthen their battery supply chains without necessarily relying exclusively on domestically extracted resources.

Why Is India Expanding Its Lithium and Nickel Processing Capacity?

India's government has recently approved a program worth approximately $297 million to develop new industrial facilities dedicated to lithium and nickel processing. According to information reported by Reuters, the initiative will support the establishment of four processing plants, including two for lithium and two for nickel.

The program represents another step in India's efforts to strengthen its position in the global battery industry. Over the past several years, the country has introduced various measures intended to secure access to critical minerals, diversify international partnerships, and encourage domestic manufacturing.

The latest initiative, however, focuses on a different stage of the supply chain. Rather than concentrating exclusively on mineral extraction or imports, it aims to develop the industrial infrastructure required to transform raw materials into products suitable for manufacturing.

"Countries are increasingly recognizing that the availability of mineral resources represents only one part of a much broader industrial equation. Processing technologies, specialized facilities, and technical expertise can determine how effectively those resources contribute to domestic manufacturing," says Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG.

Four Facilities Dedicated to High-Purity Mineral Products

The planned facilities will concentrate on producing materials that meet the technical requirements of advanced industries, particularly battery manufacturing.

For lithium, the processing operations could produce refined compounds such as lithium carbonate and lithium hydroxide. These substances are widely used in the production of cathode materials for several lithium-ion battery chemistries.

Nickel processing will follow a comparable industrial approach. The facilities could produce high-purity Class 1 nickel or battery-grade nickel sulfate, which is commonly used in the manufacturing of cathode precursors for nickel-containing batteries.

The program also establishes implementation deadlines. Beneficiaries are expected to complete their projects within three years of receiving support, although a maximum period of five years is permitted.

These requirements indicate an intention to translate public financial support into operational industrial capacity within a defined timeframe.

How Could Mineral Refining Strengthen India's Battery Supply Chain?

One of the main characteristics of modern battery supply chains is the number of industrial transformations required between mineral extraction and finished battery production.

Lithium-bearing minerals, for example, generally undergo several processing and chemical conversion stages before becoming compounds suitable for battery manufacturing. Nickel follows its own sequence of refining and chemical transformation, depending on the original feedstock and the intended final application.

Consequently, the presence of mineral deposits does not automatically guarantee access to battery-grade materials.

"Battery production depends on a sequence of interconnected industrial activities. Refining is particularly interesting because it creates a connection between the extraction of mineral resources and the manufacturing of advanced components, including cathode materials," explains Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG.

Developing these capabilities domestically could help India reduce its exposure to certain international processing bottlenecks while encouraging greater cooperation between chemical producers, battery manufacturers, and other industrial operators.

Refining Capacity Without Complete Mining Self-Sufficiency

Another interesting feature of the initiative concerns the potential origin of the raw materials.

India's future processing facilities could handle minerals extracted domestically as well as imported feedstocks. This distinction is important because it separates two objectives that are sometimes treated as interchangeable: securing mineral resources and establishing national refining capabilities.

A country may remain dependent on foreign mining operations while developing a competitive domestic industry for processing and transforming those materials.

For India, this approach could support a more diversified supply chain structure, combining international sourcing relationships with domestic industrial production.

It could also encourage investment in specialized technologies, workforce training, and the chemical processes required to manufacture high-purity mineral products.

What Could India's Strategy Mean for the Electric Vehicle Industry?

India's processing initiative is closely connected to its broader ambitions in electric mobility and battery manufacturing.

The development of domestic refining capabilities could create opportunities for producers of cathode materials, battery cells, and other components. It may also contribute to the emergence of industrial clusters where different stages of battery manufacturing operate in closer geographical proximity.

However, the program's effectiveness will depend on several factors, including access to suitable feedstocks, processing costs, technical performance, and the ability of new facilities to meet demanding product specifications.

"Establishing processing capacity can provide a foundation for further industrial development, but its long-term contribution will also depend on the ability to connect these facilities with downstream manufacturers and maintain consistent production standards," concludes Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG.

India's initiative also illustrates a broader international trend. As demand for advanced materials continues to evolve, governments are paying increasing attention to the intermediate stages of mineral supply chains.

The strategic question is no longer limited to where minerals are extracted. It increasingly concerns where they are refined, how they are transformed, and which industries can use the resulting products.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is the Objective of India's New Lithium and Nickel Program?

The initiative aims to establish domestic processing capacity for lithium and nickel, supporting the production of high-purity materials used in batteries and other advanced industrial applications.

How Many Processing Plants Will the Program Support?

According to Reuters, the program will finance four facilities: two dedicated to lithium processing and two focused on nickel.

Why Are Lithium and Nickel Important for Battery Manufacturing?

Lithium compounds are used in several lithium-ion battery chemistries, while nickel sulfate is an important input for producing cathode materials in nickel-containing batteries.

Does India Need Domestic Mineral Deposits to Develop Refining Capacity?

Not necessarily. Processing facilities can use imported mineral feedstocks, allowing a country to expand its domestic refining industry without achieving complete self-sufficiency in mineral extraction.

title: Into the weeds: UT San Antonio engineers turn excess seaweed into a circular solution
description:
Every summer, massive mats of golden-brown Sargassum seaweed wash ashore along the Gulf Coast.
From seaweed to sea cleaner: The fabrication process The process begins with Sargassum collected along the Texas coast.
Kavadiya and co-principal investigator Vikram Kapoor, PhD, Klesse Endowed Professor, Civil and Environmental Engineering, and Construction Management, transform the decaying seaweed into water treatment technology.
The UT San Antonio team is developing a renewable and reusable alternative.
This analysis will ultimately help coastal communities and government agencies evaluate the modules as a potential solution at scale.
text:
Every summer, massive mats of golden-brown Sargassum seaweed wash ashore along the Gulf Coast. In small doses, the seaweed drifts in the open ocean and provides shelter for marine life, but recent overgrowth of the species has wreaked havoc.

Millions of tons pile up on beaches and rot, suffocating ecosystems, driving away tourists and releasing toxic gases like hydrogen sulfide. The trigger lies upstream, where agricultural and urban runoff dumps excess nitrogen and phosphorus into coastal waterways, feeding algal blooms and leading to massive marine “dead zones.”

Researchers in the UT San Antonio Margie and Bill Klesse College of Engineering and Integrated Design are tackling both issues — nutrient pollution and Sargassum inundation — in one circular solution.

Shalinee Kavadiya, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Biomedical and Chemical Engineering, is leading a team that is transforming harvested Sargassum into 3D-printed, reusable filtration modules designed to catch runoff nutrients before they reach the ocean.

“The problems of Sargassum inundation and overgrowth, nutrient pollution, and waste management tend to be treated independently,” said Kavadiya, who is also a part of the Institute of Water, Research, Sustainability and Policy. “Our research connects them and addresses them all together with a sustainable manufacturing solution.”

Beginning September 2026, the project is supported by a three-year grant of $735,532 from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency through the Gulf of America Program.

From seaweed to sea cleaner: The fabrication process

The process begins with Sargassum collected along the Texas coast.

Kavadiya and co-principal investigator Vikram Kapoor, PhD, Klesse Endowed Professor, Civil and Environmental Engineering, and Construction Management, transform the decaying seaweed into water treatment technology.

The team dries and powders the seaweed, then converts it into organic, inorganic and composite materials. These materials are then used to fabricate porous filtration units, which include a 3D-printed backbone and a coating of functional material that can bind with nutrients like phosphorus and nitrogen.

The modules are stacked with varying pore sizes, so the system traps physical sediment at the front, where water enters, and collects dissolved chemicals deeper inside.

“3D printing makes it easy and reproducible to fabricate filtration units while offering control over their physical form,” Kavadiya said, adding that the structures are easy to separate and recover from water after nutrient capture.

The design also supports one of the project’s goals: creating a filtration system that can be reused rather than discarded after one use.

A sustainable, circular design for long-term use

Traditional commercial stormwater filters rely heavily on single-use minerals that end up in landfills once saturated. The UT San Antonio team is developing a renewable and reusable alternative.

“As we keep using the filter, the coating may start to degrade,” Kavadiya said. “But the underlying lattice backbone is recyclable and reusable, so we can re-coat it and use it again for nutrient capture.”

The researchers will test the filtration system in the field to assess its efficiency and durability. This analysis will ultimately help coastal communities and government agencies evaluate the modules as a potential solution at scale.

By the end of the project, Kavadiya expects the team will “be able to tell how frequently you would need to replace the filter based on the water flow and what size filter works best for a given area,” among other logistical details.

“We are going to do an economic analysis to understand how this technology compares to the existing technology right now,” she added.

In the long term, Kavadiya hopes to explore ways to recycle the nutrients collected in her filters, which could potentially be reused as fertilizer in agriculture.

“We want to shift the focus from waste management to resource recovery. We are not just managing the waste, but recovering a resource that still has value,” she said.
